10590-lady-mary-wortley-montague-her-lif:
Lewis Melville's biography follows Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, who lived from 1689 to 1762 and left one of the liveliest letter collections of her age. Born Mary Pierrepont, she learned Latin and Italian as a girl, shone as a young "toast" of London society, and married Edward Wortley Montagu after a bold courtship. Her letters mix wit, gossip, and sharp views of the world.

Melville traces her childhood, marriage, travels, and later years, quoting freely from her letters to friends and family. Readers meet a clever, outspoken woman writing about courts, cities, and society across Europe. The book works both as a life story and as a door into the letters that made Lady Mary famous.
14583-the-continental-monthly-vol-1-no-3:
The Continental Monthly for March 1862, devoted to literature and national policy, addressed a Union readership in the Civil War's first year. Its opening essay asks what the North should do with revolted provinces after victory.

Other pieces discuss Southern aids to the North, cotton's power, the Trinity River valley of Texas, and a traveler's robe of honor abroad, mixing politics with literature. The magazine's voice is earnest and pro-Union, impatient with British sympathy for the South. The issue is a valuable window on Northern opinion as the war hardened.
16272-the-continental-monthly-vol-2-no-1:
Volume two, number one of The Continental Monthly, printed by John F. Trow in New York for July through December 1862, calls itself devoted to literature and national policy. Number seven inside lists What Shall Be the End?, Bone Ornaments, the fifth Molly O'Molly Papers, glances from the Senate gallery, the fifth Maccaroni and Canvas, For the Hour of Triumph, In Transitu, Among the Pines, Was He Successful?, and Newbern as it was.

Essays, stories, poems, and war reporting mingle in a magazine trying to steady a nation at war with letters and argument. The Continental's blend of culture and policy marks it as a serious Northern monthly. Readers of Civil War print culture will find a varied, thoughtful number.
28926-diary-from-march-4-1861-to-novembe:
Adam Gurowski kept this diary from March 4, 1861, to November 12, 1862, published in Boston in 1862. Gurowski, a Polish exile living in Washington, recorded what he heard and saw himself, and what he heard from others whose truthfulness he trusted. He wrote impressions at once, believing first impressions the purest and best.

The diary is dedicated to the widowed wives, bereaved mothers, sisters, sweethearts, and orphans of the loyal states. Its pages hold the talk, warnings, and forebodings of Washington during the Civil War's first twenty months. Readers get a passionate, opinionated eyewitness record, valuable precisely because Gurowski wrote hot, not cool, about a nation tearing itself apart.
29583-shoulder-straps-a-novel-of-new-yor:
Henry Morford's novel of New York and the army in 1862, entered for copyright in 1863 by T. B. Peterson and Brothers of Philadelphia, follows two friends: Walter Lane Harding, merchant, and Tom Leslie, journalist. A torn dress and a stalwart champion open their story, with Tom's tale of Dexter Ralston woven in. Morford aimed, as he says, to present a faithful picture of relations in life and society grown from the war as side issues.

The novel moves between New York drawing rooms and army camps, showing how the Civil War reshaped private lives. Its interest lies less in battles than in manners, money, and marriage under strain. Readers of Civil War fiction will find a vivid, home-front novel from the war's own years.
4132-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-14-jan:
January 1661 to 1662 opens with an invitation sent before Pepys and his wife are up, from Lady Sandwich, to come and dine. Office work fills the morning, and at noon they go to a good and great dinner, with Mr. William Montagu and his lady among the company.

Pepys judges the lady's looks with his usual bluntness, and notes the talk and dishes in full. The volume pairs great dinners with daily office duty, as Pepys climbs the social ladder one invitation at a time. Readers will enjoy the diary's food, fashion, and frank opinion.
4133-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-15-mar:
March 1661 to 1662 opens with Pepys paying Sir William Batten forty pounds he has owed for half a year, borrowed money now repaid. He spends the morning at the office, dines at home, and then faces his uncle Thomas in high words of difference.

The quarrel ends quietly, though Pepys fears it will not stay so. Family money, office routine, and sharp talk fill these spring entries, with the diary's usual care for sums and slights. Readers get a close view of how kin and credit tangled in a Navy clerk's rising life.
4134-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-16-may:
May 1662 sets Pepys out very early from Portsmouth with Sir George Carteret and Sir William Pen, their clerks beside them. By noon they reach Petersfield, several yard officers accompanying them so far, and dine there merrily.

At dinner comes Lord Carlingford from London, bound for Portsmouth, and the road becomes a meeting place of Navy business. The volume follows a working trip across southern towns, with ships, yards, and dinners along the way. Readers will enjoy Pepys on the road, where travel and office blur into one long day. Pepys turns the journey itself into office work, counting the trip among the month's Navy business.
4135-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-17-jul:
July 1662 sends Pepys to the office till past noon, then by water to Deptford with Captain Cuttance. There the Royal James, the ship his lord sailed in on the last voyage, is paying off under Sir William Batten and Sir William Pen.

Dinner follows with Mr. Shepley and other Navy men, in the working rhythm of the summer dockyards. The volume shows the Navy Office at its daily task: paying ships, settling men, and keeping accounts. Readers who like the machinery of history will enjoy Pepys among ships, yards, and pay tables.
4136-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-18-sep:
September 1662 sends Pepys betimes to his office and among his workmen, then by coach with Batten and Pen to St. James's. It is the first day of meeting there by the Duke's order, but the Duke is going out with his Duchess and sends them on their way.

The volume follows the Navy Board's move to new quarters and new routines, with workmen, coaches, and ducal audiences. Pepys notes each change of place as a change in his working life. Readers get a precise picture of how a government board found its rooms and its rhythm.
4137-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-19-nov:
November 1662 begins with workmen in the house and a morning sitting at the office, then a great dinner at Trinity House. Pepys goes with Mr. Creede, found at his house at noon, to a feast of much company, where talk turns to a Captain Evans and his elder brother.

Winter entries mix building work, office sittings, and company dinners, with Pepys noting each guest and dish. The volume closes the year in the diary's familiar key: business by day, good cheer by night. Readers get late autumn London through one man's full, frank days.
4807-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
In this seventh volume, dated 1855, Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1561 to 1562. Chapter three argues that the inquisition was the great cause of the revolt, and describes its three varieties. The Spanish inquisition, the episcopal inquisition in the Netherlands, and the papal inquisition established in the provinces by Charles V are set out in turn.

Charles's instructions to inquisitors, renewed by Philip, lead to Inquisitor Titelmann and instances of his manner of proceeding. Spanish and Netherland inquisitions are compared, showing how a machinery of persecution, pressed harder under Philip, turned religious grievance into political revolt. Motley makes the inquisition, not taxation or pride alone, the engine of rebellion in this volume. Readers get a stark account of persecution as policy, and of the Netherlands' answer to it.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Abraham Lincoln's war presidency fills this sixth volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. The volume spans 1861 to 1869, covering Lincoln and then Johnson in two distinct epochs. Lincoln's administration pursued the great civil war, while Johnson's sought peace and restoration. Richardson prints their papers as the record of the nation's gravest trial.
arxiv-2509-00062:
Justin Jung, working alone, presents Scaffold Diffusion in 2025, a model that generates sparse 3D voxel builds with many block types. Voxels are cube units that fill a 3D grid. Memory grows as the cube of grid size, and most cubes sit empty, which skews training. Past generators tend to yield dull or broken forms under such sparsity.

By treating voxels as tokens, like words in text, the model uses discrete diffusion, a method that corrupts and then restores set choices step by step. Tests use Minecraft house builds from the 3D-Craft set, where data are more than ninety-eight percent empty. The model still yields realistic, coherent houses where prior tools and a step-by-step variant fail. An interactive viewer shows samples and the build process.
arxiv-2509-00462:
Jiannan Xu, with two co-authors, Gujie Li and Jane Yi Jiang, asks whether large language models favor writing that looks like their own. They study hiring, where job seekers use such models to polish resumes and firms use the same tools to screen them.

Xu and his co-authors run a large controlled resume test and find models prefer their own resumes over human or rival model ones, even when quality is held equal. Tests across many jobs show users of the screening model gain a clear edge in shortlisting. Simple steps that cut self-recognition reduce the bias by more than half, which matters for fair hiring.
arxiv-2509-00662:
Vamsi Shankar Simhadri, with three co-authors, Yichang Xiong, Habiba Farrukh, and Xiaokuan Zhang, presents the first broad security analysis of virtual reality firmware. Headsets such as Meta Quest 3 gather rich sensor data for immersion, and most run customized Android systems, which brings both Android flaws and new risks from tracking services.

Simhadri and his co-authors collected over three hundred firmware versions from Quest and Pico and studied them across kernel, system binary and library, and application layers over time. They found missing kernel security features, weak binary hardening, uneven permission enforcement, and inadequate SELinux policy enforcement. Their recommendations aim to help vendors, developers, and users build a safer virtual reality ecosystem.
arxiv-2509-00762:
R Luque leads a team of ninety authors on the TOI-2141 planetary system. The system holds a transiting sub-Neptune around a Sun-like star. A sub-Neptune is a planet smaller than Neptune. This one crosses its star on a long orbit. The team adds new photometry from TESS and CHEOPS. They also add radial velocity data from HARPS-N.

Joint Bayesian analyses refine the planet's radius and mass. Both values are far more precise than before. Radial velocity data track the star's wobble from unseen planets. They reveal two more companions that do not transit. One has a short period and one a long period. The transiting planet seems to hold a volatile envelope over an Earth-like core. Its hydrogen-rich air may have suffered mild loss to space.
arxiv-2509-01062:
Takahiro Uemura, Kenta Takata, and Masaya Notomi study paired light cavities with a symmetry known as anti-PT symmetry, where gain and loss are balanced in a flipped way. Such systems have exceptional points, special settings where two states merge into one. The link between those points and real laser behavior had been unclear.

Using two coupled cavities with gain that saturates, the team shows an exceptional point lines up with a split point in the steady states. That split sits right at the threshold where lasing starts, and it stays visible above that threshold. It also marks a shift between two forms of motion, limit cycles and synced states, tying linear theory to observed nonlinear behavior.
arxiv-2509-01462:
Event-B is a formal method for building correct software and hardware, state by state. Liveness is a key part of its checks. It is the guarantee that good things will happen in time. Klaus-Dieter Schewe, with five co-authors, extends the logic of Event-B. Whole traces, full runs of a machine, can now be described. Yet the formulas still speak about single states.

A state fixes all traces that start from it. The authors isolate a fragment of the logic, called TREBL. It can express all liveness conditions of interest. They give sound rules for deriving claims in that fragment. They also prove relative completeness. Any valid claim can be derived once the machine is refined enough. Such refinements always exist. Security examples illustrate the theory in this first part.
arxiv-2509-01762:
Alokit Mishra and Ryyan Akhtar compare classic and deep methods for sorting songs by genre. Genre sorting powers music search, playlists, and discovery tools. The classic side uses support vector machines and grouped methods fed with hand built sound traits. The deep side uses a neural network that reads pitch charts of the audio directly. Both are tested on the widely used GTZAN song set.

The classic support vector machine wins on accuracy in this head to head test. The authors credit the small size of the data set, where built in traits curb overfitting by the larger network. Deep models can memorize small sets instead of learning broad rules. The result is a case for keeping craft based traits in real audio tools.
arxiv-2509-02062:
Yuvraj Muralichandran, Noam I Libeskind, and Elmo Tempel measure how galaxy spins align with cosmic filaments. Filaments are the thread like strands of the cosmic web where galaxies gather. Theory says halos gain spin early, so spin should track nearby web structure. Data come from the Siena Galaxy Atlas, the largest public catalog used here, cross matched with filaments traced from a major sky survey.

Tens of thousands of disk and elliptical galaxies near filament spines form the sample. Elliptical spin normals lean strongly perpendicular to their filaments, far beyond chance. Spiral spins show a much weaker but real alignment signal. Both signals peak at set distances from the spine. Careful selection by distance and brightness can strengthen the signal further.
arxiv-2509-02162:
Gabriele Bianchi, Richard J Gardner, Paolo Gronchi, and Markus Kiderlen study how well polarizations can near general rearrangements of functions. A rearrangement sorts the values of a function into a symmetric fall, the base of the famed Polya-Szego bound. Polarizations are the most plain such sorts, a flip of one half space at a time. That bound holds with full force for polarizations, so near forms gain an easy proof path.

The theory of such sorts and their set maps grows here with a stress on near forms. Brock sorts, a smooth class, prove out of reach of that near path. Each set map in mild terms gives a linked shrink map as a fresh tool for proofs. Broad near form results flow from that tool in the work. The text sorts which bounds gain proofs by this route.
arxiv-2509-02462:
Mohamed El Louadi wrote a 2025 essay questioning why Wikipedia is widely used yet routinely barred as a citable source in academic work. Students and professors consult it daily, but citing it still draws objections.

El Louadi does not simply argue that Wikipedia deserves source status. Instead, the essay claims its reliability is often understated, while traditional academic sources enjoy inflated trust despite growing problems in scientific publishing. The rejection, on this view, rests on an outdated bias about where knowledge may come from. The essay points to Wikipedia's verification practices as a counterweight. It invites educators to judge sources by their checking mechanisms rather than by habit or prestige alone.
arxiv-2509-02562:
Guillaume Blanc and Alice Contat wrote a 2025 probability paper on graph burning, a process where fire spreads along edges at unit speed while new fires are lit step by step. They move the game onto a discrete torus, a grid whose edges wrap around.

Two random versions are studied, where each new ignition point is chosen by chance. The main result covers ignitions drawn uniformly from the vertices not yet burned. As the torus grows, the random burning time settles near a constant times a power of the side length, with high probability. That constant comes from a generalised Blasius equation, a known differential equation from fluid theory, through its explosion time. The link joins a combinatorial game to classical analysis.
arxiv-2509-02662:
Yilun Ma and sixteen co-authors wrote a 2025 astronomy paper. It hunts the brightest little red dots. These are a puzzling class of compact red objects. The James Webb Space Telescope found them in the early universe. Their numbers dwarf quasar counts at faint levels.

Whether such objects also rule at quasar-like brightness needed a wide search. Webb's fields are too small for that. The team scanned over fifteen square degrees of sky. Imaging ran from near-ultraviolet to infrared. Only one candidate appeared. Its density sits far below quasar density at the same brightness. With Webb samples added, the brightness distribution cuts off sharply. The authors conclude these objects run on low-mass black holes. Their feeding rates span a narrow range.
arxiv-2509-02962:
Shuai Jiang and 5 co-authors tackled a 2025 factory inspection problem: finding surface defects when some sensors may be missing. Their setting joins color images with 3D scans of industrial products. In real plants, uncertain sensor availability means one stream can vanish at any time.

The authors use prompt learning, where small learned cues steer a large model, across the two visual streams. Separate cue types keep the streams consistent, adapt each one to its own pattern, and fill gaps left by a missing sensor. Text descriptions act as a bridge, with paired prompts giving the system normal and defective wordings to contrast. Tests under heavy missing rates beat prior methods on defect scoring at image and pixel level.
arxiv-2509-03062:
S M Rafiuddin presented a 2025 method for reading highly cursive handwritten characters. Flowing, joined handwriting is far harder for computers to classify than neat, separated letters. Letters blur into each other, and standard neural networks lose accuracy as the shapes grow more tangled.

The proposed system, ADA-GAN, pairs a generative adversarial network with an outside classifier. In such a network, one part invents fake character images while another judges whether they look real. Passing fakes, lightly perturbed versions that clear a confidence bar, join the real training data. That extra data made the classifier more robust than plain convolutional networks as character complexity rose. The approach targets scripts and styles where cursive forms dominate.
arxiv-2509-03762:
Sathwik Chadaga and one co-author set out to learn to route and schedule traffic in queueing networks when transmission costs are unknown in a 2025 research paper. Each time slot, a controller observes noisy costs only for the edges it uses. It must keep the network stable, serving queues without letting them grow forever, while also minimising total expected cost. That creates an exploration-exploitation tension that ordinary bandit methods cannot handle.

Their policy joins Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty optimisation, a classic queue control technique, with an optimistic penalty borrowed from multi-armed bandit learning. Optimism means treating uncertain edges as if they were promising, which encourages useful exploration. A static optimisation problem first lower-bounds the best achievable cost, giving a benchmark. The policy's regret, its extra cost versus an informed controller, grows sub-linearly with time, at a rate they prove. Simulations confirm the pattern in practice.
arxiv-2509-03862:
A 2025 research paper by Ankit Kumar and one co-author tests the stability of neutron stars built from two fluids: nuclear matter plus dark matter that interacts only through gravity. Such mixtures allow outcomes, including twin stars, two stable configurations sharing one mass, differing in radius and make-up.

Stability is probed with radial oscillations. Working in full relativity, the authors solve the eigenvalue problem for small radial perturbations and trace the critical line separating stable from unstable stars. A turning-point criterion, built from extrema of mass and particle numbers, reproduces nearly identical boundaries. Two dark matter candidates are studied: mirror matter, and self-interacting fermions. Varying the microphysics, from nuclear equation of state to dark matter mass and coupling, reshapes the boundaries and contours. Some configurations reach nuclear central densities more than twice the single-fluid instability threshold. The results guide readings of neutron star data.
arxiv-2509-04062:
Xintai Chen and four co-authors design a wireless system whose antennas can move, in a 2025 engineering paper. Shifting an antenna's position can catch a stronger signal, much like moving around a room for better reception. Their setup serves many users at once with many antennas at both ends. The goal is the highest total data rate averaged over changing conditions, planned on two time scales.

Fast decisions at the receiver use fresh channel readings, meaning live signal measurements. Slower choices at the transmitter rely on long-run statistics instead. The team's step-by-step methods beat fixed-antenna benchmarks in simulations. A flat, sliding movement option also worked well with simpler math.
arxiv-2509-04262:
Rahul Basu and two co-authors sort a rhythmic brightness pattern seen in pulsars in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose radio pulses arrive like clockwork. Some show periodic amplitude modulation, a regular swelling and fading of pulse strength that can be mistaken for drifting subpulses. The team analyzed single pulses from seventeen such pulsars, six of them new detections, and built a statistical scheme to mark each intensity state.

Three broad families emerged. In phase-stationary cases, most of the pulse window brightens and fades together. Other pulsars shift the active spot within the window, and some modulate only in bursts. Clear categories should sharpen future emission studies.
arxiv-2509-04562:
Mathias Schultheis and two co-authors review nuclear stellar discs, the flattened rotating star systems at galaxy centers, in a 2025 review paper. Such discs appear in galaxies of both early and late types. The review gathers their demographics, motions, stellar ages and chemistry, metal-content gradients, and star formation histories. Scaling relations connect disc properties to their host galaxies, and comparisons with nuclear star clusters sharpen the contrasts.

Links with nuclear rings, bars, and clusters are explored, and the discs serve as tracers of slow, bar-driven galaxy evolution, even dating the bars themselves. The Milky Way's own disc gets a dedicated case study with resolved stars. Most discs likely formed stars in place from bar-funneled gas, the authors argue.
arxiv-2509-05062:
Photons can condense into a single quantum state inside a semiconductor microcavity, even at room temperature. The effect turns light itself into a shared quantum state. José L. Figueiredo, lead author with six co-authors, build a quantum kinetic theory of that process in a 2025 paper. Strong but incoherent light-matter interaction drives the system, and pumping can be continuous or electrical.

Their microscopic model shows carrier-carrier Coulomb scattering dominates thermalisation at high carrier densities. That contrasts with dye-based condensates, where molecular vibrations govern relaxation. The theory predicts thermal, condensed, multimode, and lasing phases matching recent experiments. Cavity detuning emerges as a control knob for designing coherent light sources.
arxiv-2509-05162:
In federated learning, the central aggregator itself might cheat by biasing the combined model. Simone Bottoni, lead author with three co-authors, design a protocol letting clients verify the aggregator's work in a 2025 security paper. The aggregator is the server that merges all updates. Clients must check the aggregated result without exposing their private model updates.

Secure aggregation protects individual updates. A linearly homomorphic authenticator scheme then supports efficient verification of the combined result. Context-hiding multi-key techniques keep the verification privacy-preserving. No client update is exposed by the check itself. The authors show the approach scales to networks with millions of parameters at low overhead. Clients can therefore detect tampering by a malicious aggregator.
arxiv-2509-05462:
Program control flow, loops and branches together with data operations, is given a category-based model by Grigory Kondyrev and David I. Spivak in a 2025 mathematics and computer science paper. Earlier work modelled control flow alone using traced categories, abstract settings where a feedback loop operation is available.

The authors define a wiring diagram syntax covering copying, deleting, reordering, and applying fixed functions to variables. They show the relevant category of polynomial functors is traced, and that a standard construction then extends to a compact double category. An operational structure tracks how values travel through a diagram, and they prove it agrees with the direct meaning, where a filled diagram evaluates to a partial function.
arxiv-2509-05762:
Machines with one counter, a single number they can raise and lower, are learned from examples by Shibashis Guha, Anirban Majumdar, and Prince Mathew in a 2025 computer science paper. One-counter automata are a classic model between simple finite automata and full computers, used in verification.

Their passive algorithm, adapted from a state-merging method for regular languages, builds a deterministic real-time one-counter automaton consistent with any valid sample set. A method for mixing this passive learning with active querying is also given, with an implementation. Experiments show the approach scales better than the leading existing algorithms. A visibly one-counter variant, where the input dictates counter moves, is evaluated too.
arxiv-2509-05962:
Short educational videos generated by language models are tested in a 2025 paper led by Lazaros Stavrinou with five co-authors. Brief reels suit microlearning, but most are hand-made, and the effects of automated ones on learning and trust were unclear. The team's system, ReelsEd, turns long lecture videos into structured short reels while keeping the instructor's own material.

In a between-subject study with sixty-two university students, ReelsEd beat traditional long-form video on engagement, quiz performance, and task efficiency, without raising cognitive load. Students reported high trust and praised clarity, usefulness, and easy navigation. The authors draw design lessons for generative tools that respect usability, learner agency, and teaching goals.
arxiv-2509-06062:
Two species whose relationship flips with crowding are modeled in a 2025 paper by Chloë Mian and three co-authors. Partners can help each other when rare and harm each other when dense, sliding between mutualism and parasitism. The authors build a general model with fixed rules and density-dependent costs and benefits within and between species, covering competition and predation as special cases.

Through differential equations and phase portraits, they derive basic rules for how the equilibria are arranged. Equilibrium indices alternate along isoclines under broad geometric conditions, and lasting cycles can appear when a relationship mixes mutualistic and parasitic phases. Strictly mutualistic regions, by contrast, cannot generate cycles locally. The framework gives ecologists a common language for systems whose interactions refuse to stay one thing.
arxiv-2509-06162:
Smaller arithmetic circuits for neural networks, bought with a sliver of accuracy, are the goal of an improved approximate computing method in a 2025 paper led by Morteza Rezaalipour with five co-authors. Edge devices must balance inference energy against classification accuracy, and approximate computing trades a little of the second for a lot of the first. The team improves a Boolean rewriting technique called XPAT.

Their change is a new tunable template based on product sharing, designed so template parameters track the area of the built circuit closely. Experiments show the method converges better toward low-area solutions and finds stronger approximations than the original XPAT and two other leading approaches, at the same accuracy loss. The target operators are the small adders and multipliers neural networks use everywhere.
arxiv-2509-06462:
Charge spreading across a molecule is the focus of a 2025 theoretical chemistry paper by Sarai Dery Folkestad and one co-author. The authors build a configuration interaction framework, a method that mixes many electron arrangements to describe a molecule. Their aim is both numerical accuracy and a clearer picture of how electrons move.

Inside, the energy operator is written with determinants that keep charge in one place. Separate diagonal steps then give smooth adiabatic states and charge-localized states, meaning states tied to one site. The first kind reads as blended hybrids of electron patterns. The second gives a clean start and end point for electron transfer, plus a firm value for their coupling. Applied to the water dimer, the model shows small overall spreading, yet certain ionic parts prove essential for a correct account.
arxiv-2509-06562:
An idea first defined for groups is widened to looser algebraic structures by I. Buchinskiy and three co-authors in a 2025 algebra paper. Marginal sets were introduced in 2019 for groups, where they helped improve some key exchange schemes, the protocols that let two parties agree on a secret. Semigroups and semirings drop some of the rules groups obey.

The authors define marginal sets for semigroups and semirings and show how to build some of them for tropical matrix versions, where arithmetic uses minimum-plus rules borrowed from optimization. They then apply the new sets to strengthen key exchange schemes built over semigroups. Extending the concept matters because many real protocols use these weaker structures, and tools proven only for groups leave them out. The work carries a group-theoretic security idea into that wider setting.
arxiv-2509-06762:
Accelerating mirrors whose motion is adjusted can manufacture a special quantum vacuum state, according to Arash Azizi in a solo 2025 theoretical physics paper. The state, called the kappa-gamma vacuum, is a thermal, single-mode squeezed state with a tunable angle. Mirrors that accelerate are a classic laboratory analog for such effects.

One standard trajectory sets the thermal weights, fixed by the parameter kappa. A weak boundary drive, equivalent to a time-dependent surface impedance, rotates the squeeze angle set by gamma without changing those weights at leading order. Detector responses split cleanly: inertial detectors see an exact thermal law, while accelerated ones reveal gamma through interference, with selective suppression when frequencies match. Wave-packet simulations confirm the phase imprint. The split between trajectory and boundary control turns abstract squeeze parameters into knobs experimenters can turn.
arxiv-2509-06962:
Fixed point theorems are extended to spaces where distances are chances spread over values by Elvin Rada in a solo 2025 math paper. The setting is probabilistic cone metric spaces, which combine spread-out distance functions with cone-valued order. Two classic families of mappings are covered: Kannan-type and Chatterjea-type contractions.

Using the spread properties of probabilistic metrics and the order of cones, Rada develops contraction conditions that guarantee fixed points exist and are unique. The results extend classic fixed point theory into settings with built-in uncertainty. Uses named include stochastic processes, random operators, and modeling uncertainty in functional equations. Fixed points in random settings underpin step-by-step methods that must converge despite randomness. Widening the class of spaces and mappings covered thus has practical as well as theoretical value.
arxiv-2509-07062:
Shi Feng, Penghao Zhu, Johannes Knolle, and Michael Knap explain a puzzle in quantum magnets in a 2025 paper. Some gapless spin liquid candidates, exotic states of matter, show almost no heat flow, though theory says they should carry heat well. The team show that the block can arise from the state itself, with no flaws or dirt in the material.

They study a ladder-shaped model in a magnetic field. In it, each spin splits into two kinds of new particle: heavy visons and light spinons. At mid-range fields, the heavy visons barely move, so they act like frozen disorder that traps the light spinons for a time. That trap chokes heat flow at most test scales. Flow comes back only at ultra-low scales, too low for most lab gear to reach.
arxiv-2509-07162:
Martin Matak and 3 co-authors describe a better way for robots to pick which grasp to try in a 2025 paper. A common pipeline first generates candidate grasps, ranks them, then plans a path to the best one. If no path exists, planners restart on lower-ranked grasps, which wastes time and lowers the chance of success.

The new approach plans paths to a whole set of grasp targets first. Only then does the evaluator judge success odds at the end point of each planned path. The robot carries out the path judged most likely to succeed. Tests across different objects, grasp generators, and planners beat the older pipeline. The method also worked in the real world, in new rooms with different shelves and table heights, which shows it is not tied to one lab setup.
arxiv-2509-07262:
Jeremy B. Hume, in a solo 2025 paper, characterizes when the singular ideal in a class of operator algebras is zero. The algebras come from étale groupoids, structured sets that encode symmetry and dynamics, and feed into C*-algebra theory, a branch of functional analysis. A nonzero singular ideal signals hidden singular behavior that can distort the algebra's representation theory.

Hume shows the ideal vanishes exactly when every unit sits, in a group-theoretic sense, inside limit sets built from the well-behaved Hausdorff part of the unit space. The proof studies how restriction maps to closed invariant subsets compress to homomorphisms on the algebras. A simpler algebraic test is also proved when the isotropy group algebras have a certain ideal intersection property. That property is verified for direct limits of virtually torsion-free solvable groups, widening the test's reach.
arxiv-2509-07362:
A self-driving system that knows exactly where it is can navigate safely, but city streets challenge camera-based positioning methods. Yandi Yang leads a team of 8 in a 2025 research paper on visual localization. Textureless walls, sharp viewpoint changes, and slow drift all hurt image-based methods. The authors turn to airborne laser scanning, which maps cities from the air in three dimensions, as a prior map.

The team built a large dataset pairing ground-level images from mobile mapping vehicles with airborne point clouds. The data covers Wuhan, Hong Kong, and San Francisco. They also describe how they generated reliable ground truth at city scale. Existing image-to-point-cloud algorithms are then benchmarked under these cross-platform conditions. The dataset and benchmark give researchers a shared testbed for making visual localization steadier in dense urban areas.
arxiv-2509-07562:
Daniel Holmes and 1 co-author pair theory with software for equivariant Gromov-Witten invariants in a 2025 paper. These invariants count curves on spaces with symmetry, and GKM theory computes them from a graph that encodes the symmetry's fixed points. A localization formula does the heavy lifting, but it depended on an auxiliary choice called a compatible connection.

The authors prove the formula's output does not depend on that choice and give an equivalent version with no auxiliary choices at all. They then release a software package, GKMtools.jl, that computes the invariants and quantum products straight from the GKM graph. Applications range from Calabi-Yau bundles over the projective line to twisted flag manifolds, realizability questions for abstract graphs, classical curve counting, and quantum Schubert calculus. The package aims to make these computations routine for geometers.
arxiv-2509-08362:
Black hole mergers in Gauss-Bonnet gravity must obey entropy bounds, and Neeraj Kumar with 2 co-authors work out what Rényi statistics allow in a 2025 gravitation paper. The setting is five-dimensional anti-de Sitter spacetime with static black holes. Two equal-mass black holes merge, and the question is which final masses the generalised entropy permits.

A general Rényi entropy expression is calculated, then used to bound the post-merger mass as the Rényi parameter varies. Results are compared with ordinary general relativity, and the Gauss-Bonnet correction term significantly changes the bounds. Entropy laws act as consistency police for modified gravity: any merger outcome they forbid is a prediction experiments and simulations can check.
arxiv-2509-08762:
Alex Divoux and 3 co-authors prove a coarse version of Menger's theorem for graphs with bounded path-width in a 2025 paper. Menger's theorem links disjoint paths between two sets with small separating sets. The coarse version asks for paths that stay far apart.

Earlier work showed the claim is false in general, using graphs with large tree-like parts. Here, if a certain planar graph is excluded as a minor, the coarse claim holds for all graphs. That includes graphs of bounded path-width and series-parallel graphs. The path-width case is surprising, since the claim fails for bounded tree-width. The paper is part five of a series.
arxiv-2509-09062:
Pedro Bittar and 2 co-authors interpret rare four-jet events at the Large Hadron Collider in a 2025 paper. The CMS experiment saw two events with very high total mass, each splitting into two jet pairs of equal mass. Such structure suggests a heavy particle decaying into lighter ones.

Supersymmetry with a single R-parity violating term offers an explanation, where R-parity is a symmetry that is usually assumed exact. Light resonances are identified with first generation squarks, and the heavy one with a later generation down squark. Constraints shaping that reading are discussed, and a defined scenario is outlined. Forthcoming collider data can test the predictions.
arxiv-2509-09162:
James Chok and 3 co-authors present a two-system paradigm unifying Monte Carlo samplers in a 2025 paper. Mean field, ensemble chain, and adaptive samplers were historically seen as distinct. Their framework brings all three under one roof.

A set of particles is split in two halves, and each half proposes updates for the other in turn. Finite ensemble versions approximate an ideal mean field sampler, while time averaged statistics recover adaptive methods. New overdamped and underdamped Langevin samplers are derived in this form. Benchmarks show higher effective sample sizes per gradient and faster wall clock throughput than No-U-Turn Sampler baselines, especially in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2509-09462:
Alexander Ryzhov and 6 co-authors measured how swapping hydrogen isotopes changes dielectric relaxation in ice and water in a 2025 physics paper. They covered four isotopic forms and filled a frequency band where earlier readings were sparse and disagreed with each other. Careful cross-checking was used so the new numbers could be trusted across solid and liquid samples alike.

In ice, relaxation sped up or slowed with temperature in an activated pattern whose energy did not depend on isotope. The heavy-to-light rate ratio stayed near two across the tested range. That scaling fits a picture of a proton hopping over an energy barrier under strong friction, rather than whole molecules turning.
arxiv-2509-09562:
Maria Tsedrik and 2 co-authors offer a cleaner way to measure evolving dark energy in a 2025 cosmology paper. Full-shape studies of galaxy clustering can suffer prior-volume effects, where the sheer size of a parameter region drags reported values away from the true peak. Their fix redefines the nuisance parameters inside the effective theory used to model large-scale structure, so amplitude effects are absorbed directly.

After the change, peak values sit inside the reported intervals, and the large shifts seen before disappear. Checks on synthetic BOSS and DESI style data support the method. Fitted to real survey data with other probes, the evolving dark energy values lean toward the region favoured by combined DESI, microwave background, and supernova results.
arxiv-2509-09762:
Alexandre Emsenhuber and 10 co-authors grade a planet formation model against a real survey in 2025, the seventh instalment of a population synthesis series. Synthetic planet families from the Generation 3 Bern model, built around sun-like stars through core accretion, are set beside the HARPS and Coralie radial velocity sample. The fake population is first filtered the same way real observations are limited, so the contest stays fair.

Many headline patterns match: close sub-Neptunes beside distant giants, a two-peaked mass spread with a sparse desert, and average multiplicity near the observed value. Faults remain plain too. The model makes too many planets overall, too many giants, a desert too empty, orbits too round, and a metal effect too weak for the authors' liking.
arxiv-2509-09862:
Milind Upadhyay and 1 co-author benchmark annealing machines against ordinary solvers in 2025 on two industrial optimisation jobs. Many hard problems grow too fast for classical hardware, and quantum or digital annealers promise near-best answers once a job is cast as a quadratic binary puzzle. Whether that promise pays is an empirical question, so the pair measure mapping effort, wiring density, and penalty design alongside cost and solving time.

Contenders ranged from a Fujitsu digital annealer and D-Wave hybrid quantum systems to leading classical mixed-integer and constraint solvers. The test jobs chose pathways through reaction networks and picked codons for messenger RNA design. Comparing every solver on shared metrics shows where the annealing route earns its keep and where classical tools still lead.
arxiv-2509-10162:
Planning under a flawed model is the problem Tamir Shazman and three co-authors address in this 2025 paper on decision-making for automated agents. Agents often plan by simulating futures from a learned model, but a model trained on little data can mislead them or push them toward unsafe choices.

The authors present Robust Sparse Sampling, an online planner that guards against model error while it acts. It computes a cautious value for each option using sample average methods, and it comes with finite-sample performance guarantees. The method works even for endless or continuous state spaces, and its costs do not grow with the size of that space. In tests it beats ordinary sparse sampling when conditions are uncertain.
arxiv-2509-10362:
Zimu Wang and 2 co-authors build a risk mapping tool for extreme rainfall in this 2025 paper. Heavy rain over wide areas can trigger flooding, landslides, and failures that compound each other. Their framework joins graph neural networks with r-Pareto processes, a tool from extreme value theory, to learn how extremes at different places depend on each other.

Trained on two decades of NASA satellite rainfall records and checked against high-emission climate projections, the model draws coherent high-risk zones and tracks how long they last. Tropical monsoon and convective belts stood out as persistent danger areas. The method beat baseline tools at flagging risky grid cells and is offered for planning, preparedness, and climate policy work.
arxiv-2509-10762:
Arlen Kumar and Leanid Palkhouski audit how AI answer engines choose their citations in this 2025 paper. Engines such as Perplexity and Google AI Overviews now answer questions directly and cite web pages as evidence. The authors built GEO-16, a sixteen-part scoring framework that grades pages on quality signals and rolls them into one normalized score.

They ran dozens of product-related prompts through three engines and collected well over a thousand citations for audit. Pages the engines cited differed in quality by engine, and signals tied to metadata, freshness, and structured data tracked citation most strongly. Overall page quality predicted citation well. The authors turn the results into a practical playbook for publishers who want to be cited.
arxiv-2509-11262:
Eyal Buks and Boris A. Malomed study a fiber laser with a chilled section in this 2025 paper. The device is a loop of optical fiber containing an erbium-doped stretch cooled to cryogenic temperatures. Such a laser was recently found to produce an optical comb with an unusual structure, and this work asks what role polarization plays in how it runs.

Experiments show the laser works across many modes at once, and those modes keep a relatively high degree of mutual coherence, which is not guaranteed in multimode operation. Understanding that behavior matters because the setup is proposed for practical jobs: spectroscopy, communications, and storing quantum data. The paper maps how polarization shapes the comb's operation.
arxiv-2509-11462:
Hyeonseok Yang, Shoki Koyanagi, and Yoshitaka Tanimura extend a strong simulation method for open quantum systems. This 2025 physics paper treats a subsystem in three dimensions. A U(1) gauge field that varies in time acts on it. Its surroundings cannot be treated with the usual shortcuts. Quantum noise ties its own memory time to the size of energy swings.

The authors start from hierarchical equations of motion with the gauge field in them. A move to the Wigner picture yields quantum hierarchical Fokker-Planck equations. Gauge invariance and rotational symmetry both survive. A test case is an Aharonov-Bohm ring in a heat bath. The team computes equilibrium forms, absorption spectra, and ring currents. A persistent current is predicted in a lossy setting. It needs a long-memory bath and low temperature.
arxiv-2509-11662:
Feilong Chen and seven co-authors train a multimodal language model on hardware the field mostly ignores. This 2025 artificial intelligence paper notes a block to open research. Top models train on a narrow set of accelerator platforms. Their data recipes stay secret.

The team built MindSpeed-MLLM, a training framework for Ascend NPUs. Dense and mixture-of-experts models train stably and fast on it. Data production and mixing recipes are published for each stage. Their model, MindVL, trained end to end on that hardware. Data efficiency stood out. The eight-billion size matched a leading rival on a tenth of its data. The giant experts version matched a big-data rival on a thirtieth. Checkpoint weight averaging added further gains.
arxiv-2509-11862:
Haodi Ma, Vyom Pathak, and Daisy Zhe Wang bolt symbolic scaffolding onto video question answering. This 2025 artificial intelligence paper treats questions about videos. Spatial, temporal, and causal reasoning are all demanded. Today's vision-language models often lean on shallow correlations. Their temporal grounding stays weak. Their reasoning is hard to inspect.

The authors study symbolic scene graphs as a middle signal. Such graphs record objects and their relations in structured form. Their framework, SG-VLM, joins frozen vision-language models with scene graph grounding. Prompting and visual localization do the joining. No retraining is required. Three benchmarks and two model families were tested. Causal and temporal reasoning improved. Gains over the strongest models were modest. The work maps what symbolic grounding can and cannot yet add.
arxiv-2509-11962:
Mixed signals arrive tangled over space and time. The sources are unknown in advance. Mika Sipilä and two co-authors tackle that unmixing task in 2025. Their tool is a variational autoencoder with autoregressive parts. It is built to be identifiable, and it suits data that is nonlinear and nonstationary.

Unmixing helps only if the parts found are the true parts. A lucky mix that fits the data is not enough. Recent theory shows how to promise true recovery. This model bakes that promise in. Each hidden part follows its own autoregressive process, with dynamics that change over time. In simulations, the method matches top rivals at unmixing. On real air pollution and weather data, it forecasts future fields over space and time. It holds its own against several known methods.
arxiv-2509-12162:
Aymen Balti and 6 co-authors explore measuring mental states at work in a 2025 paper that joins virtual reality, brain recordings, and mathematics. Participants entered a stressful work scenario in virtual reality, first built as training for bank employees facing high-stakes situations. The controlled setup let the researchers pair self-reports with neural data.

Electroencephalography, which records electrical activity from the scalp, given the objective signal. An method inferred emotional states from those recordings combined with participants' own assessments. The authors then propose mathematical models for how mental states change over time. Their aim is a quantitative approach, one based on numbers, to emotional handling. Such models could inform training that adapts to the learner in demanding workplaces.
arxiv-2509-12362:
A small asteroid was spotted in space, tracked to a predicted fall over Normandy, and recovered as meteorites, giving science a rare start-to-finish impact record. Auriane Egal and ninety-six co-authors report the full case of asteroid 2023 CX1 in 2025, from telescope sightings to laboratory study of the L chondrite fragments.

Instead of shredding gradually, the roughly seventy-centimeter rock burst apart at about twenty-eight kilometers up, dumping nearly all its energy in one concentrated blast. A spherical shock of that kind threatens more ground damage than the usual drawn-out breakup. The authors urge planetary defense plans to prepare evacuations under such bursts.
arxiv-2509-12462:
Encrypted traffic still leaks which website a person visited, and classifiers trained on scripted browsing fail badly on real people. Chuxu Song and three co-authors argue in 2025 that human browsing is far more varied than lab data admits, and they rebuild the data pipeline for website fingerprinting around that fact.

Their agents, teams of language models role-playing personas, browse the live web and generate realistic traffic at a fraction of the cost of human collection. Models trained on scripted data score under a tenth correct on human traces. Training on the agent-made traffic lifts accuracy into the eighty percent range.
arxiv-2509-12662:
Finding a person in a camera archive from a written description sounds simple until the description is vague and labeling training photos by hand costs a fortune. Zequn Xie and five co-authors remove the hand labeling in 2025 with chat-driven text generation and interaction for person retrieval.

One module holds simulated dialogues with a multimodal model to mint rich pseudo-descriptions of person images, with no manual supervision. The other refines a user's query at search time through dialogue, resolving vagueness and gaps that plague real requests. Together the annotation-free pair matches or beats supervised systems on standard evaluations.
arxiv-2509-13062:
Daria Khemelevskaia, Nikolai Solodovchenko and six co-authors build the smallest blue nanolaser yet in 2025. Bright tiny pixels for sharp screens and augmented sight need full color at nano scale. Blue single-grain lasers had stayed above the wave size.

Crystals grown in wet chemistry sit on silver. Sizes span a few hundred nanometers. The smallest grain is far below a cubic wave in bulk. It lases near the blue edge at cold heat levels. Light and matter waves couple strongly with grain modes boosted by silver. No stored charge build is needed. That mix beats prior blue designs.
arxiv-2509-13362:
Xian-Hui Ge links in 2025 quantum Tsallis statistics to strange metal transport in one frame. The quantum Tsallis spread returns to Fermi-Dirac at the unit parameter. Small deviations add a correction tied to a deformed Schwarzian action for soft modes.

Soft modes scatter electrons via the golden rule. Rates give Fermi-liquid acts at low heat and linear resistivity at high heat. Memory matrix work yields linear magnetoresistance and a Hall angle matching the two-lifetime picture. Low heat restores quadratic Fermi acts. Deformation, soft modes, and measured transport join quantitatively.
arxiv-2509-13562:
Yifan Liu and four co-authors improve dense passage retrieval in a 2025 information retrieval paper. Retrieval systems turn questions and passages into number lists called embeddings, then rank passages by distance. Straight-line distances work when embeddings lie flat, but the team finds they often curve along lower-dimensional surfaces, especially on unfamiliar topics.

Their method, MA-DPR, builds a nearest-neighbor graph of passages and measures distance by the shortest path through that graph, following the curved surface instead of cutting across it. On out-of-distribution tests it beat straight-line distances by up to about a quarter, with similar in-distribution results and little added query time. Borrowing context from neighboring passages helps even when direct word overlap is missing.
arxiv-2509-13662:
Yulan Guo and six co-authors propose replacing multiplications with lookups in a 2025 neural network paper. Multiplication is the most energy-hungry basic operation in convolutional networks. That blocks their use on small edge devices. Lookup tables, by contrast, answer precomputed results cheaply. The trick is long used on limited hardware.

The team builds lookup tables that can be trained end to end. Training strategies help them converge. Full lookup networks are then assembled from the operation. The tests cover image classification, image super-resolution, and point cloud classification. The networks matched ordinary convolutional networks on performance. In places they set the best reported results. They also used less energy and ran faster at inference time.
arxiv-2509-14062:
Saifur Rahman and eight co-authors estimate wireless channels for reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in a 2025 paper. These panels steer radio waves to boost sixth-generation network coverage. Their elements are passive, so the combined channel cannot be measured directly. The path runs base station to surface to user. Full pilot probing would be ruinously expensive.

Their framework groups surface elements. It rebuilds the full cascaded channel from partial pilot observations with a neural network. To fix poor reach, base station and users train a shared network together. The training data comes from across the network. A two-level design first classifies the propagation setting, then extracts setting-specific features. Pilot overhead and complexity fall, while standard estimators are beaten.
arxiv-2509-14362:
F. F. Braz and three co-authors study a one dimensional water like lattice model in 2025 with exact methods. The model mixes van der Waals attraction with hydrogen bond links on a chain. Particle number can vary under a chemical potential control.

Three ground state phases appear: gas, bonded liquid and dense liquid. Sharp borders separate them in the temperature and chemical potential plane. With the transfer matrix method the authors derive exact results at finite temperature. Entropy, density and energy then change sharply but smoothly, a pattern called a pseudotransition. Heat capacity and correlation length show finite peaks there too. Fixed density checks show how thermodynamic constraints reshape the behaviour.
arxiv-2509-15062:
Tianxin Hu and seven co-authors plan energy-safe routes for planetary rovers running on hybrid power in a 2025 space robotics paper. Future rovers may combine a steady radioisotope generator with variable solar panels. Most existing planners handle slope and smoothness but ignore whether power flow stays feasible moment by moment.

Their framework models translational, rotational, and resistive power draw plus baseline subsystem loads, all under the mixed power supply. Both total energy budgets and instantaneous power limits enter a polynomial trajectory optimization over the rover's planar motion. The result is paths that are geometrically sound and provably within what the power system can deliver at every instant. For long missions far from rescue, that feasibility guarantee is the difference between exploration and a stranded rover.
arxiv-2509-15262:
Monit Sharma and Hoong Chuin Lau let a learning agent tune a classical logistics solver in a 2025 operations research paper. The capacitated vehicle routing problem asks how a fleet with limited loads should serve customers at minimum cost, and it is NP-hard. Augmented Lagrangian solvers perform well only when their penalty parameters are tuned carefully, a chore that resists automation.

Their hybrid wraps deep reinforcement learning around the solver: a soft actor-critic agent reads instance features and constraint violations, then sets penalty values on the fly. Two solver variants are tested, a classical one and a quantum-enhanced one whose subproblems become binary optimization problems solved by a variational quantum eigensolver. On synthetic and benchmark instances, the learned tuning beats hand-tuned penalties with fewer iterations, and the agent optimizes feasibility and cost jointly.
arxiv-2509-15462:
Ryan Collette, Ross Greenwood, and Serena Nicoll squeeze speech into far fewer bits. Most speech codecs save space by using sameness over time, and they treat all sound traits the same way. New speech models, by contrast, split sound into distinct high level traits. The team use those split traits to send voice over very thin links.

Their method matches or beats known codecs on speech to text, mood checks, and speaker checks. It does this at two to four times lower bit rate. On sound quality and speaker checks it beats a known codec while using up to four times fewer bits. The work suits voice links where bandwidth is scarce.
arxiv-2509-15762:
Saikat Chakraborty and Piyabut Burikham test two cosmic histories inside a modified gravity theory. The theory, called f(R) gravity, tweaks how curvature drives cosmic expansion. One history mimics the standard model exactly. The other bends it slightly to allow a phantom crossing, as new sky data hint. The pair view each history as a flow in a two measure space.

For the mimicking history, they show the curvature part need not act like a fixed constant. Different theories that share the history give different matter shares today. Their flow study also shows these mimics wobble under small smooth shakes. That casts doubt on matching the standard history exactly in this theory.
arxiv-2509-15862:
Denise Boncioli, writing alone, reviews twenty years of results from the Pierre Auger Observatory. The observatory watches ultra high energy cosmic rays, the most energetic particles known to reach Earth. Its first phase set the field's agenda. Boncioli sums up what it found and what comes next.

Its measures of the energy spectrum are the most precise yet, with clear features marked. It also mapped what the rays are made of and where the strongest ones arrive from. The lack of matching high energy neutrinos and photons rules out the old all proton view. She lays out space based stories that fit the data. Phase two should sharpen the picture further.
arxiv-2509-16062:
Sampling methods that move in straight lines and bounce at random times offer a fresh way to draw from complex distributions. Sanket Agrawal and three co-authors study the early phase of such methods, when paths start in unlikely regions and head toward likely ones. They split each method's engine into fast and slow parts and derive plain equations for the early motion.

Counting jump events as a cost guide, they compare these methods with a classic random walk method. For bell-shaped targets the costs are alike, while for heavy-tailed targets the new methods can win. Some variants reach the likely zone in just a few jumps.
arxiv-2509-16162:
In some spread models on a grid, a link can open only if both its ends still have few open links. Ivailo Hartarsky and Roger W. C. Silva study when such a process stays small and when it can take off. Standard tools fail here, since links depend on each other over long range and lack key order traits.

The pair prove that below the critical point, the chance of reaching far falls off at an exponential rate. Their proof adapts a randomized algorithm method and a trick that boosts pivotal links. The result settles an open problem, and the trick may help in other dynamic spread models.
arxiv-2509-16362:
Phase changes in exotic number systems can be probed by turning a physics model into a dynamical system and watching its cycles. Farrukh Mukhamedov and Otabek Khakimov review and extend that approach for p-adic statistical mechanics, where numbers are measured by closeness to powers of a prime. Their focus is a lambda model on a branching Cayley tree.

They study broad families of quasi Gibbs measures for the model, each tied to recurrence equations that define the dynamics. The main aim is to check that forecasts made from the dynamical view actually hold. The paper links renormalization methods with p-adic phase behavior.
arxiv-2509-16462:
Scrubbing a model's inner bias may or may not make its later decisions fairer, and the two are usually studied apart. Mina Arzaghi and four co-authors bridge that gap with a method that unlearns stereotyped links while keeping skill intact. It balances the odds a model assigns to stereotyped versus counter-stereotyped word pairs, rather than just suppressing one side.

Across three open models and several bias and job-like tests, inner gender bias fell in a clear, measurable way. Fairer downstream calls followed in most settings, with no real skill loss. Pairing the method with fairer training data helped even more.
arxiv-2509-16562:
Baikang Yuan and Jiangbin Gong probe the edges of special lattices in a 2025 physics paper. In these materials, protected states travel along the edge and resist many kinds of flaws. The pair ask what happens when a moving impurity passes through. Does the edge state stay stable, and how do edge and bulk states mix?

Their study shows how motion can link bulk and edge behavior in new ways. They test the ideas across three kinds of systems. These include Chern insulators and a driven, time-based variant. The results add to what is known about how sturdy edge transport can be. They also hint at uses for future devices.
arxiv-2509-16662:
Eunjin Choi and co-authors clean a large music dataset in a 2025 paper. The Lakh MIDI set holds files scraped from many web sources. Scraping pulls in many duplicate files, which can skew training. The team set out to find and list those duplicates in a careful way.

They first tried rule-based checks and older search models for symbolic music. They then tested a learned model with varied tweaks to the files. From this work they offer three filtered lists, from careful to strict. Even the careful list removes tens of thousands of files. Cleaner data should give fairer tests for music models trained on this set.
arxiv-2509-16762:
Fayez Abu-Ajamieh and co-authors draw new limits from two gravity guesses in a 2025 theory paper. One guess says gravity must be the weakest force in a set sense. The other, with a Latin name meaning hurry slowly, caps how light some particles can be. The team combine both with models of early cosmic growth.

Joint use yields tighter caps than either guess alone. The caps touch searches for a fifth force in nature. They also touch tiny charged particles and the energy scale of inflation. Even the self-interaction of the Higgs field is bounded. Lab searches can use these caps to aim their hunts.
arxiv-2509-16862:
Rinka Nobukawa and co-authors turn drum sounds into vocal percussion in a 2025 audio paper. Singers in a cappella groups often mimic drums with their voices. That art is called vocal percussion. The team define a new task: converting a drum track into a vocal version of the same rhythm.

They build two baseline converters with a neural sound maker. One adds a quantization step, the other does not. Listeners judged both outputs plausible. The quantized version gave more consistent results. A shared task and test method could spur better tools for music makers who sketch beats with drums but perform them by voice.
arxiv-2509-17062:
Cristian Pérez-Corral, Antonio Garrido, and Laura Sebastia generate planning landmarks from learned graphs in a 2025 paper. Landmarks are facts that any valid plan must achieve along the way. They guide planning algorithms well. Classic extraction, though, is sensitive to the specific task at hand.

The team first learn a graph of landmarks for a whole domain. They then build a graph for a single problem. Merging the two by matching equivalences yields landmark orderings for that problem. Tests on well-known planning domains measure how much of the found information is correct and how much is found. Task-independent landmarks could make planners faster across many problems.
arxiv-2509-17562:
Yuxuan Li and six co-authors pretrain vision models with instructions so they fit specialist domains. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a gap in modern vision: perception, reasoning, and generation now feed each other, but high-level reasoning rarely shapes the low-level features a vision backbone learns first. Their method aims to close that loop from the top down.

Visual Instruction Pretraining, or ViTP, seats a vision transformer inside a vision-language model. It trains the pair end to end on visual instruction data drawn from the target domain. A companion method forces the backbone to learn robust, domain-relevant features while seeing only a sparse set of visual tokens. On sixteen hard benchmarks in remote sensing and medical imaging, the approach set new best scores across many tasks. The authors release their code for other domain teams.
arxiv-2509-17762:
Sitian Shen, Georgi Pramatarov, Yifu Tao, and Daniele De Martini rebuild large scenes from several sensors at once. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses 3D Gaussian splatting, the scene format that renders by throwing soft blobs of color and shape. Large-scale versions add LiDAR for geometry, but the team argues LiDAR's physical riches and semantic labels are still underexploited as mere side parameters.

Their framework, Neural-MMGS, fuses image, LiDAR, and semantic data into one compact, learnable embedding inside each Gaussian. Light neural decoders then map that embedding back to each modality's parameters, so the modalities share what they know. Memory overhead drops and scaling improves over appending separate parameter blocks. Tests on the Oxford Spires data set and other scenes judge the reconstruction. The authors pitch per-Gaussian fusion as the cleaner way to grow splatting scenes to city scale.
arxiv-2509-17962:
Jon Crowcroft and 4 co-authors ask a bold what-if: could a person swap their body-based ID for a new one? Their 2025 paper is a thought piece on biometrics, the body traits used to prove who you are. Such traits are prized since they are meant to be hard to fake at fair cost.

New bio tech might let folk rewrite those traits live, the authors suggest. That could help a user whose traits were stolen, since a fresh set could be set up. But fake traits may get cheap faster than real swaps do. The authors flag the threat as far-off and not yet real, yet worth thought now.
arxiv-2509-18462:
A model of quantum chaos called SYK has a hidden link to gravity in two dimensions. Andreas Blommaert, Damiano Tietto, and Herman Verlinde pin down that link in this 2025 paper. They connect the collective field theory of the double-scaled SYK model to the worldsheet theory of the complex Liouville string. That string theory is also known as sine dilaton gravity.

In the match, one Liouville field acts as a moving clock for the other. The second field is the SYK collective field itself, which gains a direct gravity meaning. The relevant geometry is a disk with set boundary rules, read off from the SYK side. The team computes the string amplitude on that geometry and finds it equals the SYK partition function. They preview a lift to three-dimensional gravity. SYK operators map to line operators in that setting.
arxiv-2509-18862:
Telling machine-written text from human text is a growing need, and richer features might seem the obvious route. Luyan Zhang and Xinyu Xie test that assumption head-on in this 2025 paper. Their system, MHFD, joins three feature kinds: meaning from a neural model, sentence structure, and statistical word patterns. An adaptive fusion merges them.

The headline result is negative. The multi-feature stack beat single models by only about half a percent in-domain. It cost over four times the computing to do so. Accuracy reached about ninety percent in-domain and held near eighty-four percent across domains. The authors argue modern neural models already capture most of the useful signals. Extra features mostly duplicate them. The study is a useful caution for detection research: measure the gain before paying for complexity.
arxiv-2509-19162:
A. Chervov and forty-eight co-authors release CayleyPy, an open-source Python library for computing with Cayley graphs, the maps that show how group elements connect through generators. This is the third paper from a project applying AI to group theory. Compared with established systems like GAP and Sage, the library handles far larger graphs, often hundreds of times faster. On top of the tool, the team announces about two hundred new conjectures.

Many conjectures concern diameters, the longest shortest path in a graph, and growth rates. For symmetric groups they observe near-polynomial diameter formulas and propose sharpened bounds. Other conjectures answer a question posed by Glushkov in 1968 and improve results on matrix groups. Some are stated as sorting puzzles that code can check. The team also published benchmark datasets for path finding, inviting others to test the conjectures.
arxiv-2509-19262:
Sankha Subhra Bakshi, writing alone, shows how a flash of light can make a material order more strongly, not less. Ultrafast light usually melts order in correlated materials, yet some experiments find new phases with higher ordering temperatures. Bakshi studies a model where localized spins and moving electrons interact on a square lattice, with two rival orders: antiferromagnetism driven by electron motion, and ferromagnetism from a direct exchange between spins. At half filling the two compete evenly.

Simulations that evolve the spins with quantum dynamics and the electrons in mean field reveal the trick. Light creates a long-lived population of excited carriers that refuses to settle. That population reshapes the energy landscape, tipping the balance from antiferromagnetism to ferromagnetism and raising the ordering temperature. Though model-specific, the pathway suggests a general route to optically engineered magnetism and other ordered states.
arxiv-2509-19462:
Primordial black holes may sit in the dense cores of dwarf galaxies, the smallest galaxy kind. Tadeo D. Gòmez-Aguilar, Encieh Erfani, and N. M. Jimènez Cruz ask what ripples in space those holes would send out. They model two sources: pairs of holes that merge, and pairs that swing past each other on open paths. Their model follows up to four rounds of mergers over the age of the universe.

Merged pairs give most of the total signal, the team finds. Near misses start sooner, though, and add a steady low hum. Each source leaves a distinct shape in the signal spectrum. The authors check the predicted hum against the reach of planned detectors such as LISA and the Einstein Telescope. Their code is posted in public for others to test.
arxiv-2509-19662:
A scheduler that cannot peek at job lengths must still finish work quickly on average. Ziyad Benomar and three co-authors give the scheduler a new sense: progress bars that estimate how much of each job is done. Bars may be honest, noisy, or even adversarial. The team designs algorithms for both hostile and random bar behavior.

Their bounds on worst-case delay are strong, and a surprise follows. The same ideas improve scheduling that uses predicted job sizes instead. A general method for merging algorithms adds further gains. A random model of bars yields a scheduler that is optimal in the long run. Cloud platforms already show progress bars to users. This work asks what a scheduler itself can learn from them.
arxiv-2509-19762:
Big reasoning models think long and loud, burning compute on verbosity and missed instructions. Yuanxin Wang and six co-authors argue that the model and its surrounding workflow should be designed together. They study the trade between capability and cost in test-time reasoning. Their workflow, named with the metaphor of a conductor guiding an engine, tightens that orchestration.

With the tuned workflow, smaller open models outperformed rivals several times their size. The team plans to release the workflow openly. The conductor metaphor names the split: an external guide shapes how the engine's power is spent. Co-design matters because prompting tricks alone cannot fix habits baked into a model. Cheaper strong reasoning would widen access to advanced AI help.
arxiv-2509-19862:
Open quantum systems watched continuously obey stochastic master equations with jumps and diffusion. Weichao Liang and three co-authors tackle a practical gap: the model's parameters, such as coupling strengths, are rarely known exactly. First they slim the filter that tracks the system. For an N-level system, the conditional state fits in a space of size order N, not N squared.

Stability of that filter survives both wrong starting states and wrong parameters, they prove. On that base they build an estimation framework for continuous parameter ranges, with near-certain convergence results. Quantum sensors and feedback control both lean on such filters. Knowing the filter forgives parameter error makes the estimator's job well-posed. The work serves measurement schemes based on nondemolition observations.
arxiv-2509-20462:
Electrons in a magnetic field form Landau levels, and some flat-band materials quantize them in anomalous ways. Soujanya Datta and Krishanu Roychowdhury study those anomalies under uneven magnetic flux in a 2025 arXiv paper. The unusual levels trace back to quantum geometry in singular flat bands. Their wavefunctions localize in odd patterns even in uniform fields.

The authors bridge continuum and lattice descriptions of the effect. Varying the flux inhomogeneity gives a handle for steering the anomalous levels deliberately. At special parameter values, the whole tower of levels collapses to zero energy. There, a form of supersymmetry emerges in parameter space, echoing a classic theorem about zero modes. The localized states partly resemble Aharonov-Bohm caging. Adding strong correlations could turn these controls toward exotic topological and charge-ordered phases.
arxiv-2509-20562:
Agents that learn from failure need better ways to reflect on it. Yubin Ge and four co-authors propose SAMULE, a self-learning framework, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Ordinary reflection often stays shallow because error analysis is weak and successes are rare. Their system trains a dedicated retrospective model to generate reflections at inference time.

The training data is synthesized at three levels. Single trajectories teach detailed error correction. Multiple trials of one task build an error taxonomy at the middle level. Failures across many tasks yield transferable lessons at the top level. A foresight mechanism extends the idea to live interaction, comparing predicted and actual replies. On three hard benchmarks for planning and tool use, the method beat reflection-based baselines clearly. The authors credit failure-centered learning, not reflection alone.
arxiv-2509-20762:
Many groups form around one key person, such as the sender of an email or the lead author of a paper. Fanchen Bu and three co-authors call such people group anchors in a 2025 paper for the IEEE ICDM conference. Their task is finding the anchor when labels are scarce.

The authors first document patterns of anchors across real co-authorship, email, and question-and-answer data. Based on those patterns, they build AnchorRadar, a fast method for identifying the anchor in a group interaction. The method is designed for cases with very few labeled examples to learn from. Finding anchors can help analysts understand how communities form, whom to credit, and where influence sits inside large interaction networks.
arxiv-2509-20862:
Muonium, an atom made of a muon and an electron, could serve as a sensor for axion dark matter. Feng Fang and seven co-authors lay out that idea in a 2025 paper set to appear in Physical Review Letters. The proposed experiment is called MASH, for muonium-based axion search.

Ultralight axions would nudge transitions between muonium's hyperfine states when the energies line up. High-intensity muon beams would supply enough atoms to see the effect. Combining theory with simulations, the authors show the method could tighten limits on the axion-muon coupling beyond those from the muon g-2 measurement. The gain covers a specific band of axion masses. The paper opens a new spectroscopic channel for hunting axion-like particles.
arxiv-2509-20962:
A supersinglet is a quantum state of many qubits with total spin exactly zero, prized for its symmetry. Saeed Ahmad and five co-authors design a way to purify such states in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Entanglement distillation takes several noisy copies and produces one cleaner copy.

Their protocol starts with three copies of a spin-zero state. Measuring each copy in the local total spin basis and keeping only selected outcomes yields a higher-fidelity supersinglet. The starting states can be prepared by distributing conventionally distilled Bell pairs to match the target symmetries. Only local operations and classical communication are needed. That restriction suits long-distance uses the authors name, such as quantum clock synchronization and cryptographic tasks.
arxiv-2509-21262:
One word with two meanings can make an image model draw both meanings at once. The work is by Evgeny Kaskov and 6 co-authors. Homonyms are words with one spelling but two meanings. When a prompt holds such a word, a model may draw both meanings at once. The authors call that homonym duplication. A bias toward English makes the flaw worse, since translation can create new homonyms.

The team built a way to measure duplication rates. They tested several diffusion models with auto scores and human checks.
