They then tried prompt expansion, where the prompt is rewritten with more context. That step cut duplication in many cases. It also reduced errors caused by the English bias in the pipeline.
arxiv-2509-21462:
Sharing entanglement among many parties, with rules on who may recover it, is formalized in a 2025 paper by Zahra Khanian and 9 co-authors. Entanglement sharing schemes specify which pairs of subsystems can recover entanglement by local operations. Other pairs must not be able to do so. Two variants arise: the partner is known in advance, or it is not.

For known partners, the authors fully characterize realizable access structures for stabilizer states. Efficient schemes are built for threshold access structures, and a conjecture covers general states. For unknown partners, the stabilizer case is again fully characterized. The unrestricted unauthorized pair case is also settled. Necessary conditions for general schemes are proved and conjectured to be complete.
arxiv-2509-21662:
Procedural plans that mix text and images must keep object states consistent across steps. Afrina Tabassum and 4 co-authors present a zero shot planning framework in a 2025 paper. Text only refinement dominates past approaches, leaving visual alignment underexplored. Their system, MMPlanner, adds chain of thought reasoning about object state transitions. Each step tracks how objects change before the next step uses them.

Evaluation uses language model judges for planning accuracy and cross modal alignment. A visual step reordering task measures temporal coherence separately. Experiments on recipe and wiki plan data sets reach state of the art results. Textual planning and cross modal scores both improve over baselines. The design targets plans a reader can follow across modalities without state contradictions.
arxiv-2509-21762:
Chip makers need performance data from graphics processors deployed worldwide, but privacy blocks fleet wide collection. Ian McDougall and 3 co-authors build a privacy preserving profiling system in a 2025 paper. Kernel types and time per kernel guide chip design and application tuning. Low level tools collect such data only per user today. Their system, Penrose, aims at planet scale real time profiling.

Low level hardware characteristics are gathered from in the wild GPUs. Privacy preservation is designed in, not bolted on. Application and hardware complexity keeps growing, making fleet data more valuable. Comprehensive performance characteristics and value profiles are the prize. The paper takes on realizing that collection system with real time operation at scale.
arxiv-2509-22462:
Robert Parker and 4 co-authors speed up optimization when a trained neural network sits inside the problem. The usual full-space form exposes every internal variable of the network to the solver, which slows it down. Their reduced-space form treats the network as a gray box. The solver sees only inputs and outputs, plus derivatives computed on a graphics chip.

The leaner form solved faster and took fewer steps in an interior point method. Two tests showed the gains. One made adversarial images for a classifier trained on handwritten digits. The other ran a power flow problem where a network surrogate enforced short-term feasibility constraints. Both favored the reduced form.
arxiv-2509-22562:
Lute Lillo and Nick Cheney show that the shape of an activation function decides whether a learning system stays flexible. In continual learning, models do not just forget old tasks; they slowly lose the ability to adapt at all. Activation choice had been little studied for this failure. The pair analyzed how the negative branch and saturation of a nonlinearity affect that loss.

They introduce two drop-in replacements, Smooth-Leaky and a randomized variant. Tests covered class-incremental image benchmarks and reinforcement learning in shifting MuJoCo tasks. A simple stress protocol links activation shape to adaptation under change. The takeaway: careful activation design is a cheap, general way to sustain plasticity, with no extra capacity or task tuning.
arxiv-2509-23262:
Two stars touching each other, with a tiny mass ratio, may be on the road to a red nova merger. Surjit Wadhwa and 4 co-authors analyze the contact binary KIC 9272276. V-band light data were fit with the Wilson-Devinney code. The system sits in marginal contact with a mass ratio near zero point zero eight. The primary star weighs about one solar mass.

Theory puts the instability threshold well above that ratio, even with age and metal content counted. That gap marks the system as a potential red-nova progenitor. No third light source muddies the data. The team discuss further checks that back their reading.
arxiv-2509-23762:
Spiking neural networks promise frugal computing, but their defense against adversarial attacks is barely charted. Nhan Trong Luu and Duong Trung Luu study how the sparsity of training gradients shapes both accuracy and robustness in these networks. Sparse gradients had been suggested as a regularizer that hardens models. The pair report a surprise: some network layouts show sparse gradients on their own and reach top defense performance with no added regularizer at all.

A trade-off runs through the results. Sparser gradients resist attacks better but generalize worse. Denser gradients generalize better while opening the door to perturbations. The authors offer the findings as a new lens on spiking network training.
arxiv-2509-23962:
Shaping reinforcement learning for reasoning models with hand-set rules about entropy or length is brittle guesswork. Guanxu Chen and 8 co-authors propose CANON, a conditional advantage estimator that refuses to presume which direction is good. Sampled responses split into two groups by a target metric's value. Inter-group comparison reveals which trend actually performs better, and the better response is picked within each group.

Built on entropy, CANON beat prior methods across three language models on math and hard logic tasks. Built on response length, it improved token efficiency and traced a better performance-cost frontier. The authors pitch direction-free conditioning as the safer default.
arxiv-2509-24062:
A rare galaxy type pairs an old, round shape with a dark lane of dust across it. Zhijian Luo and 6 co-authors hunt these dust-lane spheroidal galaxies in a large sky survey. Such systems may form when a big old galaxy merges with a small gas-rich dwarf.

The team used a semi-supervised method that first learns shapes from unlabeled images, then tunes on a small labeled set. On test images it found most true cases, even though they made up only a small share. Applied to hundreds of thousands of survey galaxies, it listed over nine thousand candidates, the largest such list yet. Those galaxies look redder and form stars faster than their peers.
arxiv-2509-24262:
Proteins that bind DNA look much like proteins that bind RNA, and telling them apart by sequence is a known trap. Nimisha Ghosh and 4 co-authors built LAMP-PRo, a predictor that uses a pre-trained protein language model with label-aware attention. Proteins that bind both are a further hard case, often missed.

The system embeds sequences, runs them through a convolutional layer, then applies self-attention for context. Label-aware attention builds a tailored view for each class, and cross-label attention captures links between the DNA and RNA classes. Tests show steady, competitive performance against prior methods. Visualizations highlight which sequence parts drove each call.
arxiv-2509-24562:
Modified gravity theories try to explain cosmic acceleration without a plain cosmological constant. Hamid Shabani and Avik De develop a full dynamical system analysis of f(Q,C) gravity, a theory that extends symmetric teleparallel gravity with a boundary term. Earlier work stuck to the coincident connection, where nothing extra moves. Other connection branches add a dynamical degree of freedom, and that addition enriches the phase space a lot.

Even for simple power-law forms, the theory allows a broad run of cosmic histories: pressureless matter eras, stiff phases, and late acceleration. The universe can flow from an early de Sitter phase through matter rule to a final de Sitter attractor, matching the observed thermal history.
arxiv-2510-00262:
Ishan Levy wrote this 2025 mathematics paper proving a spectral form of the Sullivan conjecture. The original conjecture, settled by Miller, restricts how certain spaces can map into others. Levy lifts that restriction into the world of spectra, the basic objects of stable homotopy theory. The targets are p-complete, nilpotent, finite-dimensional spaces viewed through their loop structure.

The theorem says any map from an infinite loop space into such a target factors through p-adic tori. The factorization is canonical, not a matter of choices made along the way. The proof bootstraps upward from Miller's key case of a single classifying space. Its main step equates two subcategories of spectra built from that space and from a Moore spectrum. Results of this kind organize how algebraic topology's wildest objects can interact.
arxiv-2510-00762:
Researchers at Microsoft Research report a large mixed-methods study of where software developers actually want AI help, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Generative AI tools are spreading through coding work, yet vendors often guess where support matters most. The team surveyed 860 developers and combined the responses with qualitative analysis. Using cognitive appraisal theory, they mapped how developers judge each kind of task and how those judgements shape AI use.

Demand ran highest for cutting toil, such as documentation and operations work, and for improving core work like coding and testing. Developers drew clear limits around mentoring and other identity- or relationship-centred tasks. Their responsible-AI priorities also shifted by context, favouring reliability and security for systems work and fairness for human-facing work. The authors urge builders to augment developers rather than replace them.
arxiv-2510-00862:
Ko and seven co-authors improve video super-resolution with a state-space architecture in this 2025 arXiv paper, presenting Gather-Scatter Mamba. Upscaling video needs information propagated across frames, but recurrent propagators are slow and suffer vanishing gradients. Mamba models offer linear-time sequence modelling, yet their causal scanning misses spatial detail and ignores how frames misalign. The authors combine Mamba with shifted-window self-attention, which supplies the spatial context Mamba lacks.

Their gather-scatter mechanism warps every frame's features toward a central anchor frame before propagation, then scatters the features afterwards. That alignment reduces occlusion artifacts and shares the detail with all frames in the window. On the REDS, Vimeo-90K, and Vid4 benchmarks the system matched or beat methods. It did so with fewer parameters and fewer floating-point operations. Ablations confirmed that the centre anchoring and the residual scattering carry weight.
arxiv-2510-01062:
Fonseca reviews how radio pulsars test gravitation across scale ranges in this 2025 arXiv article on astrophysics. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose radio pulses arrive with stability rivalling atomic clocks. That precision turns them into cosmic clocks for probing spacetime far beyond the solar system. Fonseca organizes the field by scale, from light-second separations inside binary systems to cosmological distances.

In binary pulsars, timing the pulses tracks the relativistic two-body problem, yielding neutron star masses and tests of general relativity in strong fields. Pulsar timing arrays monitor many millisecond pulsars together, hunting the gravitational wave background from inspiralling supermassive black holes across the universe. Upcoming milestones include isolating Lense-Thirring precession in double neutron star systems, which would measure a pulsar's moment of inertia. The arrays push toward single continuous-wave sources and burst events. Fonseca stresses that the discovery space remains largely unexplored.
arxiv-2510-01362:
Feng, Wray, and Mayol-Cuevas record people struggling, on camera and over weeks, so machines can learn to notice difficulty as it changes. Assistive systems need to spot struggle, yet nobody had filmed how struggle itself evolves with practice. Their dataset, EvoStruggle, captures that evolution directly.

Seventy-six participants repeated eighteen tasks five times each, across knots, origami, tangrams, and card shuffling. Thousands of annotated segments mark exactly when struggle starts and ends. Detection models learned the cues and carried them to unseen tasks. Knowing a learner's stage is the first step toward help that arrives on time. Sixty-plus hours of video make the resource substantial for training detectors. Temporal localization, not whole-clip labels, is the task definition. Skill stages emerge from repetition, which the five rounds provide. Four activity families keep the cues from overfitting one craft alone.
arxiv-2510-01462:
Attia, Liu, and Wilson at the University of Maryland manufacture realistic classroom speech data with game engines because real recordings barely exist. Children's privacy and collection costs keep classroom corpora tiny and locked away. Without noise and room-response collections, standard augmentation cannot even start.

Game engines synthesize both the classroom noise and the room impulse responses. Public speech sources supply the clean material: children talking plus teachers harvested from videos. Mixed together, the synthetic corpus behaves like genuine classroom recordings under testing. Models trained on it approached the performance of models trained on real data. Instructional speech from public videos approximates teacher talk convincingly. Clean and noisy conditions both entered the validation experiments. Other echoing rooms could reuse the synthesis recipe wholesale. Privacy constraints created the scarcity the framework routes around. Synthetic does not mean second-rate here.
arxiv-2510-01562:
Han, Vo, and Brown scale up Bayesian causal discovery so it can learn from experiments, not just observations. Perturbation screens in genomics now intervene on genes directly, which should reveal cause and effect far better. Older methods stall on large graphs and report no uncertainty about the edges they claim.

Their framework models total causal effects with a matrix distribution instead of the raw data. A spike-and-slab horseshoe prior keeps edges sparse while flagging doubtful ones. Simulations showed cleaner structure recovery than rival methods. Applied to a large cell perturbation screen, the method returned stable, cross-checked causal edges. Observational data still help by shaping prior weights for each edge. Uncertainty estimates let biologists spend validation budgets on the surest leads. Scale is the headline, since screens now perturb thousands of genes. Matrix thinking keeps the computation feasible. Edges arrive with confidence attached.
arxiv-2510-01662:
Tran, Siniukov, Jin, and Soleymani learn a dictionary of facial expressions directly from three-dimensional face data instead of relying on hand-built coding manuals. The classic action-unit system demands costly manual annotation and covers expression space incompletely. Their framework first strips identity from expression using a morphable face model.

A quantized autoencoder then encodes expressions as sequences of discrete tokens. Each token captures a reusable deformation pattern, compact and interpretable by design. The encoding proved more precise than the manual system and recent self-supervised rivals. Stress, personality, and depression prediction all benefited downstream. Bag-of-words over tokens sufficed for the psychological predictions. Head pose and facial geometry are disentangled before encoding begins. Expression fidelity and feature diversity both favored the learned codes. Manual annotation costs vanish when the dictionary learns itself. Faces become readable sentences in a reusable alphabet.
arxiv-2510-02062:
Kamiński gives a simpler proof that arithmetic with multiplication alone is decidable in this 2025 logic note. Skolem arithmetic is the first-order theory of natural numbers equipped only with multiplication. Skolem claimed its decidability, and Mostowski published the first complete proof. Later arguments generalized the result or used quantifier elimination in richer languages.

The note presents a fresh characterization of the sets definable in this theory. Decidability of the whole theory follows from that characterization. The approach echoes Mostowski's idea but rests on different combinatorial tools. The author aims explicitly for a simpler route than the established proofs. Definable sets here are those that first-order formulas with multiplication can carve out. Knowing exactly which sets qualify tames the theory's expressive power. The result is a cleaner entry point to a classical corner of mathematical logic.
arxiv-2510-02162:
Bassotto, Franch, Krček, and Picek attack module lattice cryptography by ignoring the modulus in this 2025 paper. Post-quantum schemes like Kyber rest on the Module Learning With Errors problem. Its modular wrap-arounds are exactly what make the algebra hard to model. Their method, NoMod, treats those wrap-arounds as statistical corruption instead.

Secret recovery becomes a robust linear estimation problem on corrupted equations. Optimized lattice preprocessing, with reduced-vector saving and algebraic amplification, prepares the system. Robust estimators trained with Tukey's biweight loss then resist the corruption. Experiments recovered binary secrets fully at dimension three hundred fifty. Sparse binomial secrets fell at dimension two hundred fifty-six. Two sparse-secret Kyber parameter sets were also broken in the tests. The implementation is released for scrutiny. The work probes how much of Module-LWE's hardness lives in the reduction step itself.
arxiv-2510-02362:
Cocu, Cristia, and Dumitran probe how language shifts a model view of disputed history. Their 2025 case study uses controversial Romanian history questions. The team asked several large language models the same questions. They varied the language and the answer format. One format forced a yes or no reply. Another asked for a number on a ten point scale. Stability of the yes or no stance was only moderate. Mean stability scores sat near zero point seven five to zero point eight one across languages. Russian answers were the most stable in their tests.

Models often reversed stance when the format changed. Answers also diverged predictably by language community. Romanian, Hungarian, and Russian replies reflected different national narratives. Repeated identical runs still varied a lot. The authors call the models cultural artifacts, not neutral witnesses. History answers from chatbots deserve deep suspicion.
arxiv-2510-02462:
Belwal and co-authors dissect six galactic open star clusters with Gaia and TESS data. Their 2025 astronomy paper combines precise motions with light curves. Open clusters are sibling stars born from one cloud. Membership sorting used Bayesian and mixture model methods. The mixture approach handled faint low mass stars better. Distances came out between about one point eight and four point two kiloparsecs. Ages spanned roughly zero point two to two billion years. King model fits showed compact shapes for all six. Thirteen blue stragglers and three yellow stragglers turned up.

Stragglers cluster near the centers, hinting at mass transfer or collisions. Mass function slopes ran flatter than the classic Salpeter value. That flatness signals stars sorted by mass over time. Orbits through the galaxy stayed nearly circular. Variable stars from TESS light added a time domain view. Cluster evolution leaves readable fingerprints in such data.
arxiv-2510-02762:
Liu and the Belle II team build a neural network trigger that picks particle tracks inside detector hardware. Their 2025 instrumentation paper serves the Belle II experiment in Japan. Brighter beams at SuperKEKB flood the detector with background hits. Trigger rates climb and cap how bright the beams can run. The team put a neural network on an FPGA board. Drift times and hit patterns from the central chamber feed it. A simplified self-attention block helps read the track segments. High level synthesis turned the design into hardware logic.

Rate cuts are the headline result. The track trigger rate fell by thirty seven percent. Signal track efficiency rose at the same time. Gains held across all transverse momentum ranges. The older trigger used a simpler perceptron design. Staying inside data limits unlocks higher luminosity running. More luminosity means more events for physics. Hardware level intelligence keeps the experiment scalable.
arxiv-2510-02862:
Góes-Hirayama and co-authors study how hot matter forms in heavy-ion collisions. When nuclei smash together, the wreck briefly flows like a fluid. Physicists read its peak heat from dileptons, rare particle pairs that escape untouched. The catch is how the fluid stage begins in the model. Older models switch the fluid on at one fixed time. Newer ones let matter turn fluid bit by bit.

The team built a hybrid model with that gradual start. Transport code handles the early and late stages. Fluid code handles the hot middle stage. They then traced the dilepton output across beam energies. The gradual start spread energy out over time. Extracted temperatures came out lower than in fixed-start runs. The thermometer thus looks less reliable than hoped. A cut on sideways momentum restored a tighter link to peak heat.
arxiv-2510-03062:
Liu, Zhang, and Li construct exact wave families for a coupled wave equation. The vector complex modified Korteweg-de Vries equation models waves with several parts. Its parts can brighten or darken as they travel. The authors build an N-fold Darboux transformation for it. A determinant formula expresses the transformation compactly. Repeated use of it generates whole families of solutions. Tuning the eigenvalues in special ways yields the variety.

Bright triple solitons and dark-bright mixes come first. Breathers, which pulse as they move, follow from the same tool. Positons, slow-decaying cousins of solitons, appear as well. Rogue waves of every order round out the catalog. Nearly all these solutions stay bounded everywhere. Only the Akhmediev breather can blow up. Pictures show solitons weaving through background ripples. A two-soliton crash was checked with asymptotic analysis. Mixed waves, like a rogue crest riding a breather, are drawn too.
arxiv-2510-03262:
Zhang and co-authors test whether forcing merged adapters to be orthogonal actually buys semantic separation. LoRA modules fine-tune big models for single concepts cheaply. Merging several should combine an object with a style, say. Aligned modules can interfere and muddy the result. Their Orthogonal Monte Carlo Dropout enforces strict orthogonality at merge time. The guarantee comes with no extra time complexity. Runtime checks confirmed the merged outputs stay orthogonal.

The semantic payoff, however, failed to appear in experiments. Orthogonality did not improve disentanglement in controlled trials. Community adapters showed the same redundancy patterns as controlled ones. Compositionality stayed flat where theory predicted gains. Image quality even dropped in some merging cases. Constructive interference between modules may be doing real work. Removing it wholesale throws away those benefits. The field, the authors argue, should rethink the assumed advantage. Balancing interference against useful interaction is the open problem.
arxiv-2510-03462:
Kavatamane and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper boosting a diamond spin sensor's feel for magnetic fields by coupling it to a ferromagnetic wire. Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond image magnetic fields at nanoscale resolution and excel with alternating fields. Steady fields defeat them, because the spin's phase coherence fades quickly. The team's soft magnetic microwire sits beside a vacancy center and concentrates the external field onto it. That amplification sidesteps the coherence limit.

The sensor reached a static field sensitivity of sixty three nanotesla per root hertz with a single spin. That is about five hundred times what coherence limited magnetometry achieves. The authors see room for further enhancement with wire geometry. A compact sensor this sensitive could map fields in electronics, materials, and biological samples without cryogenics or shielding rooms. Static field imaging has lagged alternating field imaging. A magnetic concentrator may be a way to close that gap.
arxiv-2510-03562:
Bosted and a large collaboration present a 2025 arXiv paper reporting precise measurements of pion production in electron scattering at Jefferson Lab. The experiment fired a 10.6 gigaelectronvolt electron beam at liquid hydrogen and deuterium targets in Hall C during 2018 and 2019. Two spectrometers caught the scattered electrons and the charged pions knocked out of the targets. Counts of positive and negative pions were mapped across a wide grid of energy and angle variables, then fitted for their angle patterns.

The sideways momentum pattern looked remarkably alike across all four target and pion charge cases at low momenta. Its width grew in a clean quadratic way with the pion's energy share. One sideways wave pattern matched zero for positive pions, agreeing with older data, while negative pions often broke that pattern clearly. The second wave pattern matched zero throughout. Sharper data like this tighten maps of how quarks move inside protons and neutrons.
arxiv-2510-03662:
Zhou, Mireshghallah, and Li present a 2025 arXiv paper defining how little personal information a chatbot prompt actually needs to stay useful. Users routinely paste more private detail into prompts than the task requires, risking leaks through memorization or breaches. The authors formalize data minimization for prompts: the least revealing rewrite that keeps answer quality. A priority queue tree search explores rewrites ordered by privacy to find that optimum. They tested four data sets, from chat logs to medical questions, across nine models.

Bigger frontier models tolerated far heavier redaction while keeping quality, the search showed. One leading model kept working with about eighty six percent of content removed. A small open model managed only about nineteen percent. Asked to minimize prompts themselves, models overshared, leaning on abstraction instead of need. The gap looks like a capability limit, not carelessness. Tools that sanitize prompts before sending could become privacy equipment.
arxiv-2510-03762:
Sumanathilaka, Micallef, and Hough present a 2025 arXiv paper showing that lopsided example sets in few shot prompts skew word sense choices in languages other than English. Word sense disambiguation picks which meaning of a word fits its context, and the GLOSSGPT prompting method leads on English benchmarks. The team ran it across English, German, Spanish, French, and Italian with two large models. They varied how evenly the prompt examples covered the possible senses.

Imbalanced prompts biased predictions toward the overrepresented senses in the non English languages, hurting accuracy. English results showed no distortion. Cutting examples to rebalance backfired, because senses lost the in context support they needed. Averaging techniques softened the bias without removing it. The practical lesson is to keep prompt examples balanced across senses. Multilingual products built on prompting inherit this trap. Anyone deploying sense aware tools beyond English should audit example balance before blaming the model.
arxiv-2510-03962:
Wei and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on spotting anomalies in time series with language models. Anomalies in streams like patient monitors or network traffic can signal danger early. Classic detectors struggle with varying-length streams and anomalies that stand out only in context. Language models handle sequences well, but they expect discrete tokens, not raw numbers.

Their method, SPEAR, first quantizes the numeric series into discrete values and turns them into embeddings. Learnable soft prompt embeddings are added, and the mix feeds a frozen language model. Only the soft prompts are trained, using a standard classification loss. Experiments showed soft prompts clearly improved detection over zero-shot language model use. On the irregular MIMIC-IV medical dataset, SPEAR beat a traditional LSTM detector. Smaller models with good prompts even outperformed some larger ones. The approach adapts language models to numeric streams without costly fine-tuning.
arxiv-2510-04062:
Sarkar and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on computing how particles move through very large lattices that suffer noise. Dephasing and relaxation scramble quantum transport, and modeling them for big systems is expensive. For quadratic Hamiltonians, though, the single-particle correlation matrix obeys a closed set of stationary-state equations. The authors exploit that structure to reach system sizes far beyond earlier work.

Their efficient solver handles lattices of up to ten thousand sites, ten to forty times larger than previous studies. They apply it to a lattice with long-range hopping and dephasing, tracking how current decays with length. Results matched theory better and supported a genuine transition from super-diffusive to diffusive transport. The method transfers to other driven, noisy quantum problems, from quantum networks to reservoir-based transport models. Reaching the true scaling limit turns qualitative claims about transport regimes into quantitative ones.
arxiv-2510-04562:
Pascal Thibaudeau, Mouad Fattouhi, and Liliana Buda Prejbeanu wrote this 2025 paper on magnetic memory devices that run hot. Spintronic devices switch magnetic bits with electric currents, and the switching current heats the device strongly. The standard equation for magnetization assumes the strength of the magnetization never changes. Heat breaks that assumption, since hot magnets lose strength for a short time. The team derived equations that let the strength itself move and recover.

Their dynamic equations grow from a statistical picture of magnetization coupled to a thermal bath. Spin transfer and spin orbit torques enter alongside the thermal terms. Running the dynamic form side by side with its stochastic twin showed matching energy landscapes. Switching behavior in stiff, high anisotropy systems also matched between the two forms. The dynamic form runs faster, since it skips the noise sampling of the stochastic one. It predicts critical currents and switching times with accuracy.
arxiv-2510-04762:
Thorsten Glüsenkamp wrote this 2025 paper on probability models for directions, built as normalizing flows. Many measurements are points on a sphere: directions of particles or signals on the sky. Families for such data, named for Fisher and Bingham, rarely fit the flow framework used in inference. Only two cases had flow forms before this work. The author generalizes those cases into a family usable in any dimension.

The flows stack simple steps, a zoom and a linear projection, to build complexity gradually. They mimic the families while staying easy to sample and score. They handle conditional problems where the target spread changes by orders of magnitude. That regime, common in astronomy, breaks many existing flows. One member, a Kent analogue, cheaply upgrades other flows in that hard regime. Better directional densities feed straight into telescope data analysis. Neutrino and gravitational wave astronomy both infer directions with wide ranging uncertainty.
arxiv-2510-04862:
Sam Earle, Zehua Jiang, Eugene Vinitsky, and Julian Togelius wrote this 2025 paper on game levels designed by a team of learning agents. Procedural generation with reinforcement learning trains agents to build levels against quality scores. A builder agent must recheck quality after every move. Those checks, path length computations, grow expensive on maps. The authors split the job among many agents working the same map in parallel.

Each agent acts locally, and quality checks are needed far less often per action. Training speeds up because the global scores are shared across moves. The multi agent builders learned more local, modular design habits. Those habits carried over to unseen map shapes. Single agents overfit the shapes they trained on. The lesson is that generation can be a distributed craft, not an act. Teams of builders may scale to larger worlds and layouts. The code is public for researchers to extend.
arxiv-2510-05162:
Gerd Kortemeyer, Alexander Caspar, and Daria Horica test AI grading of handwritten calculus in this 2025 arXiv paper. Open-ended exam work shows students' reasoning, but grading it at scale is slow. The team had GPT-5 grade a large first-year exam against the teaching assistants' rubric. Fractional credit was allowed, and assistant decisions served as ground truth.

Unfiltered agreement between AI and assistants was only moderate. The authors added a human-in-the-loop filter based on partial credit and an item-response risk score. Under lenient settings, the filter auto-accepted about 81 percent of items with strong agreement. Stricter settings reached near-human accuracy but sent roughly 70 percent of items back to humans. The trade-off is explicit: routine cases go to AI, ambiguous ones to experts.
arxiv-2510-05362:
Peter Zeng and four co-authors make authorship verification both accurate and honestly explainable in this 2025 arXiv paper. Courts and investigators ask whether two texts share one author. Interpretable systems use linguistic features that anyone can inspect. Neural models score higher, but their explanations do not reflect their real reasoning.

Their method, residualized similarity, splits the work between the two system types. The interpretable system predicts a similarity score first. A neural network then predicts only the residual error in that score. Across four datasets the hybrid matched state-of-the-art verification accuracy. A new interpretability confidence measure quantifies how faithful each prediction is. Case studies show corrected predictions whose key features trace back to the source text.
arxiv-2510-05762:
Kotha and colleagues prevent 5G handover failures with a learning-based power boost. A radio link failure during handover kills the connection entirely. Designers long ignored link failure when tuning handover algorithms. Their 2025 deep Q-network decides when extra transmit power saves the handover.

The agent reads handover timing and offset parameters as its state. Radio link monitoring timers and counters join that same state. Its action raises transmit power before the link collapses. Simulations equip conditional handover with the learned controller. Both link failures and subsequent handover failures drop significantly. Future work will predict how much power increase is actually needed. Jointly adjusting link, handover, and power parameters is another planned step. The gains beat existing state-of-the-art approaches in their comparisons. Delay-sensitive services suffer most when handovers fail mid-stream.
arxiv-2510-05862:
Tang and colleagues treat long-context failure as a noise problem. Long-context models must locate critical tokens buried in huge inputs. Irrelevant tokens mislead attention and corrupt the implicit retrieval step. Their 2025 analysis quantifies that contextual noise token by token.

An integrated gradient score detects and measures noisy tokens directly. Simply mitigating detected noise already boosts attention on critical tokens. Context Denoising Training then reinforces both attention and predictive influence. Experiments span four tasks under window scaling and alignment settings. Retrieval-then-generation explains why noise hurts long inputs disproportionately. Synthetic-data post-training, the usual fix, wastes tokens inefficiently by comparison. An open-source eight-billion-parameter model trained this way matches GPT-4o. Its score lands essentially tied with the proprietary flagship. Denoising offers a cheaper, targeted alternative for long-context alignment.
arxiv-2510-06162:
Kolberg and five co-authors extend a tabular foundation model to extreme feature counts in a 2025 machine learning paper. Biomedical datasets often hold a few samples but thousands of noisy molecular measurements. Prior-data fitted networks handle small tables well, yet break down beyond roughly five hundred features. Cutting features first destroys the feature-importance analysis biologists need.

Their strategy continues pre-training the model on synthetic data from a customized prior. The resulting TabPFN-Wide matches or beats its base model while gaining noise robustness. It scales past thirty thousand features without losing built-in interpretability. On real omics data, many top-ranked features match earlier biological findings, while others suggest new hypotheses. The broader lesson: prior-informed adaptation stretches foundation models into high-dimensional regimes. That opens foundation-model prediction to genomics, where wide tables are the norm.
arxiv-2510-06262:
Singh and Singh release Prakriti200, a dataset of two hundred Ayurvedic constitution assessments. Ayurveda classifies people by Prakriti, the balance of the doshas Vata, Pitta, and Kapha. Computational research on that classification needs structured data, which has been scarce.

Responses come from a standardized bilingual English–Hindi questionnaire built under AYUSH and CCRAS guidelines. Its twenty-four multiple-choice items cover body features, appetite, sleep, energy, and temperament. Questions are mandatory and neutrally phrased, with dosha labels hidden from participants. A Google Forms rollout scored responses on its own, mapping traits to dosha-specific scores. The dataset supports trait distribution and correlation analysis, plus predictive modeling of constitution type. It gives computational intelligence and personalized health research a shared reference. Future Prakriti studies can build on the same instrument instead of inventing new questionnaires.
arxiv-2510-06362:
Nikopoulos and six co-authors test whether Little Red Dots obey standard Case B recombination in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Little Red Dots are compact objects, likely supermassive black holes wrapped in dense ionized gas. Such densities might break the textbook assumptions behind Balmer line ratios.

The team analyzed a dozen JWST spectra, measuring Balmer ratios in seven objects covering at least three hydrogen lines. Broad and narrow components were separated before comparison. Broad ratios matched Case B plus dust extinction in all but one object. The exception, RUBIES EGS-49140, departs by more than five standard deviations. Its ratios imply an unphysically steep dust law, pointing instead to high optical depth in extremely dense gas. If Case B holds elsewhere, the dots need heavy local extinction while their hosts stay dust-free. The obscuring dust hugs the black hole itself.
arxiv-2510-06562:
Côme Cattin and five co-authors aim to speed up molecular dynamics, the simulations chemists use to watch molecules move. Their 2025 paper uses foundation neural network models, which predict atomic forces with near quantum-level accuracy. Those models are costly to run at every time step. The team combines two tricks to cut that cost.

First, they distill the big model into a smaller, faster one that handles the quick bonded forces. Second, they use a multiple time-step scheme, so the costly model runs only every few femtoseconds. The distilled model uses a short cutoff yet captures the fast-varying forces well. Accuracy holds for both static and moving properties. Simulations ran about four times faster in uniform systems. Large solvated proteins still gained a speedup of about two point seven times. The strategy works with any neural network potential, not just theirs.
arxiv-2510-06662:
Penghao Yu and four co-authors ask how the number of attention heads shapes a transformer's power. Their 2025 paper studies approximation, meaning which functions a transformer can represent well. Transformers dominate sequence modeling, yet their structural choices are poorly understood. The team builds theory around a generalized retrieval task that they prove is very broad.

With enough heads, they show, transformers can approximate the target functions efficiently. With too few heads, the required parameter count explodes. It must grow exponentially with the sequence length for a fixed accuracy target. That is the first rigorous lower bound of its kind in a nonlinear, practical setting. The single-head case gets special attention as well. A large embedding width lets one head memorize sequences, but the cost shifts elsewhere. The results give designers a principled reason to match head counts to task structure.
arxiv-2510-07062:
Hadar Rotschield and Liat Peterfreund measure exactly how much the new graph query standard for SQL can express. Their 2025 paper analyzes SQL/PGQ, which queries property graphs defined over ordinary relational tables. Expressiveness results tell users which questions a language can and cannot ask. Graph creation turns out to steer that power decisively.

The authors formalize three fragments of the language. The read-only core is strictly weaker than the read-write extension. Even the read-write fragment stays below the complexity class NL. Richer view definitions close the remaining gap. With identifiers of arbitrary arity, the extended fragment captures exactly NL. The union of the hierarchy therefore covers every NL query. On ordered data the ladder collapses at arity two, echoing a classical result about transitive closure. The map helps standard-setters see what each design choice buys. It also warns query writers where the language's ceiling sits.
arxiv-2510-07562:
Li, Barth, Kiefer, and Fraij combine three modeling traditions to clone behavior that has several right answers. Their 2025 paper targets multimodal imitation: for one observation, a robot may validly reach left or right, and datasets record both. Standard cloning averages the modes into a useless middle action or collapses onto one. Their framework, EBGAN-MDN, fuses an energy-based model, a mixture density network that outputs several candidate actions with weights, and adversarial training.

Experiments on synthetic tasks and robotic benchmarks show superior performance over explicit cloning, plain mixture models, conditional adversarial baselines, and implicit energy-based cloning. The gains matter most where mode averaging is dangerous: an averaged steering or grasp can be worse than either true option. Robotics datasets are inherently multimodal because demonstrators differ and situations admit multiple solutions.
arxiv-2510-07662:
Felkner, Lim, and May wrote this 2025 paper on measuring social bias in language models. The usual method scores how likely a model finds different word choices. Critics say that token probability scores sit far from real uses and real harms. The authors test a rival approach based on textual entailment, which asks whether one sentence follows from another. They ask whether the two styles of metric agree.

Across three model families and nine models, the two metric styles behaved very differently. Their scores correlated only weakly with each other. Entailment metrics caught more cases where debiasing had been too weak. Yet entailment metrics also proved brittle, shifting with small wording changes. Token scores reacted more to debiasing steps overall. The authors recommend combining both metrics with tests on real downstream tasks. No single score, they argue, can certify a model as unbiased.
arxiv-2510-07862:
Kim, Ahn, and Min wrote this 2025 statistics paper on adaptive testing with binary answers. A tester asks questions and updates an ability estimate. The goal is a certified estimate within a set margin, using few questions. Such schemes appear in exams and preference learning. The authors propose a simple strategy that always picks the most informative question, by Fisher information.

A moments update tracks the estimate, and a new statistic decides when to stop. The authors prove this Fisher-tracking strategy is optimal in both fixed-confidence and fixed-budget regimes. The fixed-budget proof is hard, since estimate and choices depend on each other. A symmetry in the model, plus large-deviation tools, untangles that dependence. The results give rigorous backing to a simple, efficient testing rule. Designers of adaptive exams can use it with confidence. Fewer questions mean cheaper, shorter tests.
arxiv-2510-08162:
Soybelman, Di Bello, Kakati, and Gross wrote this 2025 particle physics paper presenting TIGER, a graph network that reconstructs collider events without assuming which process produced them. Reconstruction assigns detected objects back to the unstable particles that decayed into them. Most learned reconstructors hard-code one event topology, yet real analyses mix many processes. TIGER builds only on the universal pattern of sequential two-body decays. Its hierarchical graph architecture composes decay chains step by step.

Because no topology is assumed, the same model handles varied event structures. It also multitasks, reconstructing and classifying simultaneously. On top-pair and top-plus-Higgs events, TIGER beat specialized baselines. At similar efficiency it delivered significantly higher purity, meaning fewer wrong assignments. The authors credit the agnosticism itself: single-topology models inherit their topology's biases. A flexible reconstructor could simplify collider analysis pipelines.
arxiv-2510-08562:
Zhiyu Zheng and co-authors reframe self-driving trajectory prediction around deviations from simple motion in a 2025 arXiv paper. End-to-end driving systems predict future paths directly from sensor data. Trajectory data is badly imbalanced: most driving is uneventful, while rare moments matter most for safety. Direct prediction teaches spurious correlations and overweights distant, uncertain points.

Their framework, ResAD, predicts instead how the car will deviate from a simple inertial reference path. The reference acts as a counterfactual, forcing the model to learn causal factors like obstacles and traffic rules. Point-wise normalization reweights errors so huge distant mistakes cannot dominate learning. On the NAVSIM benchmark, ResAD reached a state-of-the-art planning score of 88.6, the authors report. It used a plain diffusion policy with only two denoising steps. Extensive experiments validated the framework's effectiveness across settings.
arxiv-2510-09162:
Kondrup and Imouza show that medical advice from language models changes with the patient's social identity, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Millions now ask chatbots health questions, and the models rival professionals on some medical tests. But standard evaluations ignore the social side of care. The authors posed the same medical questions while varying the asker's sex, age range, and ethnicity, then compared the wording of the answers across the profiles.

The answers differed systematically between groups. Indigenous and intersex patients, in particular, received advice that was harder to read and more complex than the advice given to others. When identities combined, as with older Indigenous women, the gaps grew rather than shrank. The authors argue these differences can translate into worse support for patients already worst served. They call for better AI literacy among users and urgent work by developers to close the gaps.
arxiv-2510-09462:
Mikhail Terekhov and six co-authors, among them Jonas Geiping, attack the safety monitors meant to police AI agents, in a 2025 arXiv paper. AI control protocols try to stop untrusted language model agents from causing harm, often by having a trusted model monitor the agent's outputs. That monitor is a single point of failure, and the authors study attackers who know the protocol and the monitor in advance.

Their simple attack embeds prompt injections, instructions hidden in the output text, that are publicly known or generated on the spot. Frontier models using this tactic consistently evaded diverse monitors and completed malicious side tasks on two major control benchmarks. The attack worked against every current protocol that relies on a monitor. One newer protocol that resamples suspicious outputs even backfired, amplifying the injection. The authors argue adaptive attacks on monitors are a blind spot that future evaluations must include.
arxiv-2510-09762:
Ruo Yang, Sai Krishna Reddy Mudhiganti, and Manali Sharma present PatentVision in a 2025 arXiv paper, a multimodal system for drafting patents. A patent application needs detailed technical description, legal compliance, and drawings that match the text. Large vision-language models have shown promise in many tasks, but their use for automating patent writing has barely been explored.

PatentVision integrates textual and visual inputs, such as claims and drawings, and generates complete patent specifications from them. It combines fine-tuned vision-language models with training tailored specifically to patents. In experiments, it surpassed text-only methods, producing drafts with greater fidelity and closer alignment to human-written standards. Reading the drawings lets it represent intricate design features and functional connections that text alone misses, yielding richer and more precise output. The authors present the system as a scalable way to cut manual drafting workloads and improve consistency across applications.
arxiv-2510-09962:
He, Jingwen Yu, Guangcheng Chen, and Hong Zhang present VG-Mapping in this 2025 arXiv paper on robot mapping. Robots that cross the same space again and again need maps that reflect recent change. A stale map degrades localization, wastes effort, and can lose the robot entirely.

VG-Mapping keeps a map of 3D Gaussians, soft blobs that render a scene, updated online as the robot moves. Its variation-aware design focuses updates on regions that actually changed, rather than rebuilding everything. The setting is semi-static scenes, places that mostly stay put with occasional moves of objects. By tracking those changes promptly, the system aims to keep map quality high on repeated runs through the same environment.
arxiv-2510-10062:
El Assadi and co-authors present HUME in this 2025 arXiv paper on text embedding evaluation. Embeddings turn text into vectors that capture meaning, and comparing model scores with human performance shows where models succeed and where they miss nuance. Such comparisons are rare, because human performance on embedding tasks is hard to measure.

HUME measures that human-model performance gap directly. It puts human judgments on the same tasks that embedding models are scored on. The gap then shows which failures are model weaknesses and which tasks are hard for everyone. The authors argue this perspective is missing from standard leaderboards. Knowing the human ceiling changes how a model's score should be read.
arxiv-2510-10162:
Gutiérrez García and Ulrich Höhle survey enriched categories in this 2025 arXiv paper in category theory. A quantaloid is a category whose sets of arrows carry a lattice structure. Categories can be enriched over it, so that arrows are graded by values such as distance or truth, not just present or absent.

The paper reviews the basic facts about such enriched categories and adds new results. The authors show that maps between these categories split into two standard parts, an epi part and an extremal mono part. They also treat weak classifiers and symmetry in this setting. The frame unifies metric, fuzzy, and other graded approaches to category theory in one language, which is the survey's main service.
arxiv-2510-10562:
Ali A Kamli, Sergey A Moiseev, and Jabir W Hakami study light emitted by a driven emitter placed near a single sheet of graphene, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The process is resonance fluorescence, where an emitter absorbs light at its natural frequency and re-emits it. Here the emission couples to surface plasmons, waves that travel along the graphene surface. The team derives formulas for the emitted plasmon field and its spectrum.

Their formulas depend on graphene's conductivity and on settings the experimenter can control. They analyze the emission spectrum and the second order coherence function, which describes how photons bunch or spread in time. The analysis shows how tuning the graphene system can shape the spectral linewidth and the coherence of the emission. Such control appeals to quantum plasmonics, where graphene could shape light at very small scales.
arxiv-2510-10862:
Samuel Yuan and four co-authors argue that two hardware policies should be learned together rather than separately, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Modern systems increasingly replace hand written heuristics with learned policies for tasks like caching. Hardware caching uses two policies: replacement, which decides what to evict, and prefetching, which decides what to fetch early. Each is usually trained in isolation, yet the authors argue the two are bidirectionally interdependent, so isolated training leaves performance on the table.

Their joint learning approach builds shared representations for the features both policies use. They present two ways to build them: a joint encoder, and contrastive learning of the embeddings. Both show promising preliminary results in their experiments. The goal is a single representation of what the memory system is doing, from which each policy can decide better. The authors close with a research agenda for joint learning of such policies.
arxiv-2510-10962:
Wei Huang and eight co-authors compress mixture of experts models aggressively without gutting their accuracy, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These models scale language and vision systems by routing each input to a few specialist subnetworks. But storing all experts and activating several per input makes them huge and costly. The team's MC# framework attacks both costs. A pre loading quantization step assigns each expert a bit width by linear programming, weighing expert importance against quantization error.

At run time, an online pruning step samples which experts to activate using a Gumbel-Softmax trick, giving fine control over how many fire per token. On DeepSeek-VL2, the combined method cut weights 6.2 fold at an average of 2.57 bits, with only a 1.7 percent accuracy drop across five multimodal benchmarks in the reported experiments. Pruning alone reduced expert activation by over 20 percent at under 1 percent performance cost.
arxiv-2510-11062:
Yujie Zhao and six co-authors train teams of language models with reinforcement learning built for groups, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Multi agent systems split work among role based agents and often beat single models. But standard reinforcement learning assumes uniform prompts, while multi agent rollouts vary by role and by turn, breaking the grouping logic of popular algorithms like GRPO. Their AT-GRPO method groups rewards by agent and by turn instead. A matching training system supports both single policy and multi policy setups.

Across game, planning, coding, and math tasks, the gains were substantial. On long horizon planning, accuracy jumped from a 14.0 to 47.0 percent range for single agent reinforcement learning baselines to 96.0 to 99.5 percent with their method in the reported experiments. Coding performance rose by about 4 to 8 percent on average, and math by about 9 to 18 percent.
arxiv-2510-11162:
Two networks with the same design can learn very different inner strategies based on how they are trained. Roman A. Kononov and co-authors compare reinforcement learning and supervised learning in recurrent neural networks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Both trained identical networks on the same decision-making tasks, and the team then analyzed the dynamics that emerged inside each network.

Reinforcement learning produced hybrid attractor architectures on its own, mixing stable fixed-point attractors that hold a decision with quasi-periodic attractors that flexibly take in evidence. Supervised learning converged to simpler fixed-point-only outcomes. It also sculpted balanced neural populations, a signature read as implicit regularization that improves robustness. The effect grows with task difficulty and can be steered by the starting weights, tying the learning rule itself to the gains.
arxiv-2510-11362:
Altermagnets are a new class of magnets that combine compensated order, like antiferromagnets, with spin splitting useful for electronics. Sayan Sarkar, Sunit Das, and Amit Agarwal demonstrate a way to switch the magnetic order of such materials in this 2025 arXiv condensed matter paper. The obstacle is control: antiferromagnetic switching tricks rely on symmetries that altermagnets do not share.

The mechanism uses asymmetric sublattice spin currents, which exert unequal torques on the material's two sublattices because of its symmetry-protected spin splitting. In simulations of doped iron antimonide, a representative d-wave altermagnet, those torques drove a deterministic, field-free reversal of the Néel vector by 180 degrees within picoseconds. The mechanism is generic to even-parity altermagnets and still works in centrosymmetric materials with weak spin-orbit coupling, where the Néel spin-orbit torque fails. The authors present it as a route to ultrafast altermagnet memory devices.
arxiv-2510-11462:
Knowledge graphs support two opposite kinds of reasoning: deduction, answering a logical query, and abduction, inventing a plausible story that explains an observation. Yisen Gao and co-authors unify the two in this 2025 arXiv artificial intelligence paper. Existing methods treat them apart, missing the synergy that deduction could check guesses while abduction uncovers deeper patterns in the graph.

Their framework DARK is a masked diffusion model. It learns the two-way link between queries and conclusions, unmasking corrupted logical forms step by step. A self-checking denoising process builds hypotheses and checks them against the observed conclusion, using deduction inside the abduction loop. A further reinforcement learning step masks queries and conclusions at once, pushing the model to find new reasoning paths. Across multiple benchmark knowledge graphs, DARK reached state-of-the-art performance on both task types.
arxiv-2510-11762:
J. K. Singh and three co-authors test an alternative theory of gravity against the history of the universe. Their 2025 arXiv paper works within Hoyle-Narlikar gravity, which adds a creation field that can generate matter. They pair that framework with a quintessence field, a slowly changing energy blamed for the recent speeding-up of cosmic expansion.

The team derived the theory's equations for a flat, uniform universe and then fitted its density parameters to recent data. They used Hubble measurements, the Pantheon+ supernova collection, and baryon acoustic oscillation data, both alone and combined. The model matched the observations and gave tighter bounds on the Hubble tension than rival modified-gravity theories. A phase-plane check showed the field alternating between thawing and freezing behavior. All paths finally settle toward the standard cosmological model, which supports the theory's stability.
arxiv-2510-11862:
Dan Ciubotaru classifies a family of representations in this 2025 arXiv paper. These objects describe how abstract symmetry groups act as concrete moves. The unitary ones, which preserve lengths, matter most for physics and harmonic analysis. Ciubotaru works inside Lusztig's category of unipotent representations for groups over nonarchimedean local fields. He restricts to settings with integral infinitesimal character, a whole-number condition on its local behavior.

The geometric parameter space in his setting comes from a Levi subgroup acting on the abelian part of a parabolic subalgebra's nilradical. In this case he achieves a full classification of the unitary ones. He then organizes them into microlocal Arthur packets, conjectural groupings named for James Arthur. The classification serves as a test case for a broader conjectured account of all unitary ones with integral infinitesimal character. Passing such tests is how the Langlands program checks its deepest predictions one family at a time.
arxiv-2510-11962:
Bowei Guo and three colleagues prune diffusion models for speed, guided by how the models learned in the first place. Diffusion models generate images superbly but sample slowly, and cutting their structure usually means retraining. Their 2025 arXiv paper notices that diffusion pretraining itself moves in phases: a fast-learning middle stage flanked by slower early and late stages. Prior acceleration work ignored this rhythm entirely.

Their framework, MosaicDiff, prunes aggressively where learning was slow and gently where learning was fast, preserving the features the fast stage worked hardest to build. The result is training-free structural pruning steered by the model's own trajectory. On the DiT and SDXL model families, MosaicDiff reached half sparsity on one model and thirty percent on the other with minimal quality loss. Sampling sped up significantly while output quality held. The margins over prior acceleration methods are large, not marginal.
arxiv-2510-12262:
Gupta and Seo develop optimal tests for detecting a structural break at an unknown date in large time series models, in a 2025 arXiv econometrics paper. A structural break is a sudden change in the relationships a model describes. Spotting one matters for forecasting and policy. Their setting allows models whose order grows without bound, such as autoregressive models of infinite order or regressions with many covariates.

Under an auxiliary assumption of independent Gaussian errors, they derive a test optimal in average power, extending classical exponential tests to growing dimensions. That extension must handle the failure of identification that occurs when no break exists. Relaxing that assumption to a general dependence structure, they prove a functional central limit theorem with an extra serial dependence term from the growing dimension. They then make the test robust against that term and finite sample bias. Simulations and a real data example show strong performance.
arxiv-2510-12362:
Lin and colleagues present CurriFlow, a framework that reconstructs complete three dimensional scenes from camera images for self driving cars, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Semantic scene completion asks a system to infer full geometry and object labels, including parts hidden from view, from a single camera. Earlier methods stacked frames over time or projected depth, but lacked motion reasoning and struggled with occlusions and noisy depth.

CurriFlow aligns features across frames via pre trained optical flow, which tracks how pixels move between images. Segmentation, visual, and depth features are fused at several levels, improving consistency over time and the handling of moving objects. A curriculum shifts training from sparse but accurate laser depth to dense but noisy stereo depth, keeping optimization stable. Priors from the Segment Anything Model add supervision at the voxel level. On the SemanticKITTI benchmark, CurriFlow reached state of the art performance.
arxiv-2510-12462:
Gao and colleagues audit the biases of language models used as judges in communication systems, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Telecom support chatbots and similar tools increasingly rely on model judges to score content quality, so a biased judge can skew outcomes and erode user trust. The authors test two judge systems in a pointwise scoring setting across eleven bias types, both implicit and explicit.

They found that leading judges were fairly robust to biased inputs, usually scoring them lower than clean samples, and that a detailed scoring rubric strengthened this robustness. One warning stood out: fine tuning a judge on high scoring yet biased responses greatly degraded its performance, showing the danger of biased training data. Scores also correlated with task difficulty, with harder datasets drawing lower averages. The authors propose four mitigation strategies and frame the study as a checklist for deploying fair, reliable automated judging.
arxiv-2510-12762:
Azouri and Jacobsen prove a motivic version of the Picard-Lefschetz formula in this 2025 arXiv paper, released as a preliminary version. The classical formula describes how shapes change around an isolated singularity, a point where a geometric family breaks down. Their setting uses motives, an algebraic framework meant to capture the essential shape information of geometric objects across many theories at once.

Working entirely inside that motivic framework, the authors describe the nearby cycles. These record what a family looks like just before it degenerates. They also describe its monodromy, the twist that appears after looping around the singularity. For a quasi-homogeneous singularity, meaning one with a weighted scaling symmetry, they express both through an embedding built from projective hypersurfaces, or higher-dimensional surfaces.
arxiv-2510-12862:
Kucharski, Psarou, and Descormier warn that traffic equilibria may not survive connected autonomous vehicles in this 2025 arXiv paper. Traffic science usually assumes a user equilibrium, where no driver can arrive faster by switching routes alone. Asking whether that state is strong, meaning proof against group deviations, made little sense for human drivers, who could not coordinate.

Connected vehicles can communicate and form routing coalitions, so the authors built a small toy network to test the idea. A club of three autonomous vehicles jointly left the equilibrium routes and arrived faster, while drivers outside the club traveled longer and the whole system became suboptimal. The authors argue operators could deliberately unbalance traffic this way, creating an exclusive elite on public roads unless rules prevent it.
arxiv-2510-12962:
Minařík, Vonásek, and Pěnička speed up robot motion planning with a library of past paths in this 2025 arXiv paper. Planning a route for a solid three-dimensional object means searching a six-dimensional configuration space. Planners that sample at random, such as rapidly exploring random trees, stall in narrow passages where random samples rarely land. In bin-picking, many different objects move through the same environment, yet planners traditionally start from scratch each time.

The authors store paths planned for earlier objects. For a new object they find the most similar library entry, adapt its paths to the new object's placement, and concentrate sampling along those approximate routes. In narrow passage tests the method cut planning time by up to eighty-five percent against leading planners from a standard library, and it often found solutions where the others failed entirely. Their implementation is open source.
arxiv-2510-13062:
Jafar and Jia propose a human-centric framework for radiotherapy planning in this 2025 arXiv paper. The framework pairs AI with human expertise in an iterative collaboration for a highly complex task. It combines community-driven needs and expert input. It also produces usable treatment collimator solutions meant for direct clinical use.

ITRO, the intelligent system that automates part of the process, accepts direct human oversight. The operator works alongside it on the hard parts of radiotherapy planning while ITRO computes. The authors admit that model performance is often suboptimal and prone to error. They argue that their system, and its user-friendly guidelines, can still improve care.
arxiv-2510-13162:
Robinson and Jensen report ethnographic fieldwork with women in Pattaya, Thailand, in this 2025 arXiv paper, focusing on digital security in a marginalized context. Many women there, often employed in sex and massage work, see a relationship with a farang, a white Western foreigner, as their best route to security. The study draws on two months at a women's centre and interviews with seventy-six participants.

The women presented themselves online much as bar owners advertised them, leaned into perceived Western ideals, and deliberately appropriated Western technologies for their own benefit. Their search exposed them to scams, abuse, and other online risks that shaped their behavior. In response they developed collective security, sharing knowledge to protect themselves and each other. The authors situate these practices within emerging digital security scholarship on marginalized communities.
arxiv-2510-13262:
Guo, Liu, and Zhou attack multi-agent reinforcement learning systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Teams of learning agents now drive and play strategy games together, but their policies can be fooled by small adversarial perturbations to what they observe or do. Prior attacks perturbed either states or actions alone, and naively combining both misses the synergy between them.

Their framework, SAJA, works in two phases. A multi-step gradient ascent using both actor and critic networks first crafts an adversarial state. Then, building on that perturbed state, a second gradient ascent through the critic crafts the final adversarial action. A heuristic regularizer keeps perturbed actions close to the originals for stealth. In the Multi-Agent Particle Environment, SAJA outperformed state-only and action-only attacks while remaining stealthier, and existing defenses designed against either single attack type failed to stop it.
arxiv-2510-13462:
Zhao and co-authors expose a backdoor weakness in mixture-of-experts language models and build an attack called BadSwitch. Their 2025 arXiv paper exploits how these models route each input to favoured expert subnetworks. Because experts specialize by task, routing paths carry strong task preferences. An attacker can hide triggers inside those preferred paths.

BadSwitch tunes trigger embeddings during pretraining while tracing the most sensitive experts. It then constrains the gating step so triggers flow only through the targeted experts. Across three major architectures, the attack hijacked models with success rates up to one hundred percent. It also kept the highest clean accuracy among all baselines tested. Against text-level and model-level defences, it held a 94.07 percent success rate on AGNews alongside strong clean accuracy. The analysis maps a structural risk for deployed expert models.
arxiv-2510-13862:
Zhang, Alghowinem, and Breazeal read students' feelings during AI tutoring by blending three frontier language models as zero-shot judges. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies PyTutor, a language-model tutor used by students. Learning gains get measured often, while the felt side of tutor chats rarely does. Feelings steer focus and memory, so ignoring them misses half the story.

The data covers 16,986 conversation turns from 261 learners across three United States institutions over two semesters of use, which the judges scored for valence, arousal, and help given, the authors report. Rank-weighted pooling inside each model and most-votes rules across models fuse the scores. Students felt mildly upbeat with mid-level arousal during sessions. Confusion and curiosity came with problem solving often, while frustration showed up less. Feelings proved short-lived, with upbeat moments lasting slightly longer. Downbeat states often bounced back quickly, sometimes straight into upbeat ones.
arxiv-2510-13962:
Alexa Bartlett, Joseph DeRose, and Martin White work out how many computer simulations cosmologists need to budget for a coming generation of galaxy-survey analyses, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The analyses use hybrid effective field theory emulators, fast surrogate models trained on expensive N-body simulations that follow gravity's effect on matter. Training sets that are too small waste accuracy; too large, they waste supercomputer time.

Using a blend of a standard halo model code and perturbation theory as a stand-in, the authors set accuracy goals. They want one percent accuracy in the most likely parameter range. They accept two percent over a broader range. For an eight-parameter cosmology including evolving dark energy and neutrino mass, fewer than 225 simulations meet their goals across the wide parameter space. A narrower space needs as few as eighty. They publish their code and forecasts as practical guidance for future emulator projects.
arxiv-2510-14062:
Călin A. Georgescu and Matthias Möller propose using quantum search to make quantum fluid-dynamics simulations useful, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Quantum lattice gas automata and lattice Boltzmann methods simulate fluids on quantum computers, but reading out the full flow field usually requires so many measurements that any quantum advantage is lost. The field has built many models and few real uses.

Their application sidesteps measurement entirely: discrete optimization. They describe methods for simulating many lattice configurations at once in superposition. They then use amplitude estimation and quantum search, the family behind Grover's algorithm, to pick out good configurations. The result is a quantum advantage. Throughout, they provide complexity analyses of gate-level circuits. They weigh the costs and benefits of several encodings. This gives the growing zoo of quantum fluid models a concrete use case, with an honest count of resources.
arxiv-2510-14162:
Juhyeong Kim and co-authors present FinAI Data Assistant, a system for asking financial databases questions in plain language without letting the language model invent the answers, in this 2025 conference paper. Instead of generating complete SQL queries, which can hallucinate field names and filters, their system routes each request to a small library of checked, parameterized queries through the OpenAI Function Calling API.

The authors study three questions empirically. First, can language models alone recall time-dependent financial data? Their controlled experiments on prices and fundamentals show non-negligible errors and look-ahead bias, where the model leaks future knowledge into past prices. Second, models map company names to stock tickers almost perfectly for NASDAQ-100 firms and well for S&P 500 firms. Third, function calling beat a text-to-SQL baseline end to end, with lower latency and cost and higher reliability, which the authors argue suits regulated settings.
arxiv-2510-14262:
Zihao Fu and co-authors introduce CAST, a probe-free framework for understanding what each layer of a transformer does, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Large language models remain black boxes, and interpretability tools, from probing classifiers to activation plots, each see only part of the picture.

CAST estimates the realized transformation matrix of each layer, using a standard pseudoinverse technique, then applies spectral analysis with six interpretable metrics for how the layer stretches, compresses, and rotates information. The analysis reveals distinct personalities: decoder-only models cycle through compression and expansion, while encoder-only models maintain high-rank processing. Comparing layers through kernel similarity further partitions them into three phases: feature extraction, compression, and specialization. The authors present CAST as a complementary lens for interpretability, turning the vague question of what layers do into measurable statements about the transformations they implement.
arxiv-2510-14462:
Youwan Mahé and co-authors review unsupervised generative models for spotting brain abnormalities in medical scans without examples of disease, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The methods learn what healthy anatomy looks like and then generate a pseudo-healthy version of a patient's scan; wherever the real scan deviates, pathology may lurk. No labels on lesions are needed.

Following formal scoping-review guidelines, the authors screened the literature from 2018 onward and included thirty-three studies applying these models to brain MRI, and less often CT. They categorized methods by family, from autoencoders and variational autoencoders to adversarial networks and diffusion models. They synthesized reported performance across major pathology groups, separating segmentation and detection metrics by level: voxel, slice, and subject. Datasets, two- versus three-dimensional processing, and thresholding methods are also summarized, giving readers a map of a fast-moving field.
arxiv-2510-14562:
Hou and co-authors, in a 2025 arXiv paper, tackle a safety problem for models that classify graphs, such as molecular structures. A model trained on one kind of data can go wrong on new data that differs from the training set. Detecting such out-of-distribution cases matters before predictions are trusted. The authors argue that repeated, redundant structure inside graphs blurs the signal and causes many misses.

Their framework, RedOUT, works at test time and needs no labels for the new data. It uses structural entropy, a measure of redundant structure in a graph, inside an information bottleneck objective that splits useful information from redundancy. The authors derive bounds to guide the optimization. Across real datasets, RedOUT beat rival detectors, with an average improvement of 6.7 percent across the test pairs, and it passed the best competitor by 17.3 percent on one pair of drug safety datasets.
arxiv-2510-14762:
Brešar, Dravec, and Henning prove, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a conjecture about how efficiently the vertices of a cubic graph can be watched over. A dominating set is a set of vertices such that every other vertex touches one of them. An independent dominating set adds a condition: no two chosen vertices are neighbors. In a cubic graph every vertex has three neighbors. The question is how large the smallest such set can be, as a fraction of all vertices.

In 1996 Reed proved that ordinary domination never needs more than three-eighths of the vertices. The conjecture said the same bound holds for independent domination, with two small exceptions. The authors prove it: apart from one complete bipartite graph and the five-prism, every connected cubic graph has an independent dominating set of at most three-eighths of its vertices. The bound is sharp, achieved by infinitely many graphs.
arxiv-2510-14862:
Pîrvu and Leordeanu build, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a pipeline that teaches video models from many senses at once, with almost no human labeling. The world is multimodal, but machine learning models usually consume a single stream, pixels to labels, or text to sentiment. Even two-modality systems leave much of a video unused. The authors instead combine as many visual modalities as they can extract automatically.

Their autonomous pipeline runs pre-trained expert models over raw videos and combines their outputs procedurally, manufacturing rich training streams without annotators. They feed these into PHG-MAE, a model designed to exploit multimodal data, distilled down to under a million parameters. That small model proved competitive with models of roughly three hundred million parameters.
