The authors deploy it for real-time semantic segmentation from handheld devices and webcams on ordinary hardware, a setting where compactness and speed decide what is usable.
arxiv-2510-15262:
Zhiyuan Fan and four colleagues fix a practical headache in training large neural networks: tuning settings separately for every model width. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on maximal-update parameterization, a scheme that lets learning rates transfer from small test models to big ones. In modern networks, though, normalization layers make the effective learning rate drift with width once training settles down.

The team studied how each weight matrix's singular values, a measure of its strength, behave in that steady state. From the pattern they derived a simple rule: scale weight decay with the square root of width for matrix-like weights, and skip decay for vector-like ones. Together with the matching learning-rate rule, the recipe transferred both settings from small to large models with no fresh search. Tests on LLaMA-style transformers and a small synthetic setup confirmed the rule.
arxiv-2510-15762:
Antonio Remiro-Azócar and many fellow statisticians wrote a 2025 paper on meta-analysis. Meta-analysis pools results from many clinical trials. The authors want the estimand framework used in such pooling. An estimand states exactly what treatment effect a trial measures. It also covers events like patients switching treatment. Most pooled analyses still use the looser PICO framing. PICO names the population, intervention, comparator, and outcome.

The authors offer a practical framework for estimands in pooled work. Used systematically, estimands expose differences between studies. Those differences can distort pooled results. The paper follows estimands through the whole process. It runs from setting the question to sensitivity checks. The aim is conclusions that hold up better outside the trials.
arxiv-2510-15862:
Yi Wan works with five co-authors to rethink how reinforcement learning is set up for deep research agents. Such agents use tools to gather web facts. They then reason over those facts and combine them to answer hard queries. Open systems score well already. Yet the effect of basic design choices had not been mapped.

The team states deep research as reinforcement learning in a finite decision process. They build a strong baseline agent on that statement. They then vary training and test-time choices one by one. Four choices help a lot. AI feedback from a judge beats rule-based rewards. On-policy RLOO training beats off-policy GRPO. Filtering weak training samples helps. An error-tolerant rollout at test time also helps. Together, the choices set leading scores among agents of their size across ten benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-15962:
Zhuxuanzi Wang leads eight co-authors with a low-rank tuning method that decides where capacity goes by curvature, not by habit. Low-rank adaptation updates a small set of matrices to specialise a large model cheaply. Earlier methods, though, set the update budget apart from how training actually evolves, which wastes capacity or destabilises runs.

CTR-LoRA schedules rank by marginal utility estimated from light second-order proxies, so useful directions gain room first. A trust region built from Fisher and Hessian metrics then keeps each update stable. Across several open backbones in the seven to thirteen billion parameter range, on both familiar and shifted benchmarks, the method beats strong baselines consistently. Accuracy rises while memory use falls and throughput grows, placing the method on the performance and efficiency frontier, the team reports.
arxiv-2510-16062:
Guiyao Tie leads thirteen co-authors in a benchmark that asks if language models can truly fix their own mistakes. Self-correction is widely proposed to lift reasoning scores. Yet its methods had never been compared in a broad way. CorrectBench fills that gap in one place. It tests intrinsic, external, and fine-tuned correction plans across three tasks. Those tasks are commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation.

Self-correction does raise accuracy, the team finds. Complex reasoning tasks gain the most from it. Mixing strategies helps further but costs efficiency. Reasoning models gain little from added correction and pay heavily in time. A plain chain-of-thought baseline stays competitive on both accuracy and speed. The authors urge future work to target the balance of reasoning power and operating cost. A project page hosts the benchmark materials for other teams.
arxiv-2510-16162:
Chun Ho Lau and Taige Wang study waves governed by the Benjamin-Bona-Mahony-Burgers equation, a model mixing wave dispersion with dissipative Burgers-type behavior. On a finite interval with a time-periodic external force, they ask whether the system settles into solutions that repeat with the forcing period, and whether those solutions are stable.

The authors establish existence and stability of such periodic solutions in a first-order Sobolev setting, then push the analysis to higher regularity spaces where the solutions are smoother. They also treat a pseudo-parabolic regularized cousin of the equation under the same initial-boundary setup. Results of this kind anchor numerical studies of forced dispersive waves and clarify which periodic regimes a driven system can sustain.
arxiv-2510-16362:
Zohreh Hashempour and three co-authors study what happens when a strong laser wave plows through a magnetized plasma. In such extremes, electrons stream at near light speed, and the wave can turn unstable, breaking into modulations that grow. The team models the plasma with magnetohydrodynamic equations, the fluid math for charged matter in magnetic fields.

Treating the heavy ions as a still backdrop, they reduce the electron flow math to a nonlinear Schrödinger equation. That equation is a classic wave model. From it they extract the fastest growth rate of the instability and how it shifts with plasma traits and wave strength. They then refine the model with a perturbation method that adds nonlinear Landau damping, a quiet drain on the wave, alongside growth. The results give quantitative guidance for laser-plasma setups where such instabilities can help or hinder.
arxiv-2510-16462:
Emmanuelle Claeys, Elena Kerjean, and Jean-Michel Loubes model how bees choose food spots in a 2025 paper. Their model, MAYA, learns by copying past bee choices step by step. It rests on bandit tasks, where each choice is an arm that may pay off. Bees seem to hold only a short window of past trials in mind.

The best window is about seven trials, with a slight shift by weather. Tests use real bee data, fake data, and mouse data as a side check. MAYA beat both copy-based rivals and classic stats models. Its form also lets readers see each bee's style of learning. The model can fake new paths for eco studies as well.
arxiv-2510-16662:
Huyen N. Nguyen and Nils Gehlenborg define what makes two charts alike in a 2025 paper. Chart search tools need a clear sense of likeness to rank results. No shared frame for that sense yet exists in the field. Their frame, Safire, splits likeness along two axes. One axis lists what to compare: data, code, style, and more. The other lists how charts are stored for compare.

Storage forms run from flat images to full specs and word accounts. Each form sets what can be checked and what stays hid. They test Safire on past chart search tools to show its use. Form choice shapes search power as much as the score rule does. Their guide helps builders pick forms with eyes open.
arxiv-2510-16962:
Ama Bandara leads eight co-authors in testing wireless links inside quantum computers in a 2025 paper. Quantum machines work inside cryostats, chambers cooled to near absolute zero. Dense control wiring adds heat and tangles as machines grow. Wireless links could replace many of those cables.

The team designed tiny antennas meant to work at four kelvin. They modeled the antennas inside a realistic cryostat chamber. Simulations checked signal matching, field spread, and echoing off metal walls. Test receivers at several positions recorded the channel's response. Signals stayed strong with little sensitivity to receiver position. Echoes, though, spread signals notably in time. The study shows short-range wireless control inside cryostats is plausible.
arxiv-2510-17562:
Judging detectors that flag anomalies in time series turns out to be a swamp, because the scores used to grade them each capture only a sliver of what matters. Dennis Wagner, leading a team with twenty-six co-authors, puts that evaluation problem on formal ground. Missed anomalies can trigger disasters in chemical plants or power grids, so a misleading score is not a harmless academic flaw.

Wagner and his co-authors write down verifiable properties that any good metric should satisfy, then test thirty-seven widely used metrics against them. Most passed only a few properties, and none passed all, which explains years of contradictory rankings. To close the gap they propose a new metric that provably meets every property, plus a stricter variant for demanding uses.
arxiv-2510-17962:
Pablo A Cano, Marina David, and Guido van der Velde show that tiny changes to Einstein's theory can strongly shift the ringing tones of fast-spinning black holes. Near-extreme spinning holes have two mode families, one that fades slowly and one that fades fast. A boundary value separates the regions where each family exists.

Modes near that boundary proved very sensitive to small added terms in the theory. Their lifetimes grow as the boundary is approached, and the boundary itself moves. The upshot is that ringdown tones may reveal small breaks from standard gravity far better than a naive size count suggests.
arxiv-2510-18062:
Reshef Meir and Ganesh Ghalme revisit a famous jury result once voters may stay home. The classic theorem says a large majority vote picks the better option almost surely. Here voters weigh the cost of voting against a rough belief about how likely they are to swing the outcome.

One simple property of that belief decides the landscape. If the belief fades weakly, many stable near-tie outcomes appear. If it fades strongly, only zero-cost voters bother in the end. A sharp threshold marks where the jury effect survives. Voting theorists get a clean account of how abstention can freeze elections at a tie.
arxiv-2510-18162:
Yohei Ikenoue, Hitomi Tashiro, and Shigeru Kuroyanagi automate the craft of writing prompts for language models. Good prompting needs expert knowledge of many techniques and of the task at hand. Their method instead starts from a plain task description given by the user, with no template library in sight.

A knowledge base links clusters of similar tasks to the techniques that suit them. A new task is matched to its cluster, and a prompt is built from the linked techniques. Tests on twenty-three hard benchmark tasks judge the output. Casual users get a route to strong prompts without studying prompt engineering.
arxiv-2510-18262:
Da Zhang, with Chenggang Rong and five co-authors, builds UWBench in a 2025 paper on underwater vision. Vision-language models link pictures and words, but they are rarely tested underwater. Underwater photos suffer fading light, shifted colors, and floating particles that blur the scene.

UWBench holds over fifteen thousand high-resolution underwater images from oceans, reefs, and deep-sea sites. Human-checked notes include referring expressions, meaning phrases that point out one organism or structure, plus many question-answer pairs. The benchmark tests caption writing, object location, and question answering. Leading models still scored poorly, showing how much room remains for underwater understanding.
arxiv-2510-18762:
Jingyu Zhang and his eight co-authors present a first for open particle data. It is the first physics analysis built on DELPHI open data. DELPHI recorded electron-positron collisions at CERN. Event shapes summarize how energy spreads in collision debris. New theory and hadron-collider results revived interest in them. The cleaner electron-positron setting suits precision work.

Two quantities are measured in this note. Thrust says how pencil-like a collision's flow is. A track-based correlator compares energy flow at distinct angles. It uses charged tracks for the comparison. Both measures reach record resolution and precision. They are set against simulations and analytic predictions. DELPHI's geometry gives the correlator the best angular resolution of its kind. The results supply benchmarks for precision tests of quantum chromodynamics. They also template future work on this legacy data set.
arxiv-2510-19462:
Zhonghao Zhan and three co-authors present AegisMCP. It is an online intrusion detector for tool-using language model agents. Smart homes are a key setting. Agents can chain tools through the Model Context Protocol. Attacks can escalate privileges or leak data through tool chains. Malicious servers can be registered, and attacks can persist quietly.

A minimal attack suite defines the threats. An instrumentation layer records protocol activity as a streaming graph. Agents, servers, tools, and devices are its nodes. A detector on ordinary processors fuses novelty and session cues. Homes get near-real-time warnings without cloud defenses.
arxiv-2510-19562:
Runpeng Xie and nine co-authors tackle a basic snag for agents that follow language commands: the same command can mean two tasks, and two commands can mean the same one. Their method, DAIL, pairs a value-spread policy with a matching module. The module learns which action paths truly match which commands.

The team proves that scoring a spread of values, not a single value, makes tasks easier for the agent to tell apart. On tests with structured and visual inputs, DAIL cleared up command mix-ups better than baseline methods and scored higher. The goal is agents that follow human language well despite its loose ends.
arxiv-2510-19862:
Faizuddin Ahmed and three co-authors analyze an exotic black hole in anti-de Sitter space. It is dressed with a cloud of strings and a quintessence field, inside nonlinear electrodynamics. They study how small disturbances of three kinds move around it: scalar, electromagnetic, and fermion waves. For each kind they derive a wave equation. They also examine the potential barriers the fields must cross.

The Hawking temperature depends strongly on the horizon radius and the nonlinear charge. It departs from flat-space behavior because of the cosmological constant. Greybody factors, the odds that Hawking radiation of each type escapes, are computed for all spins. In the fermion sector, the two helicities transmit best at unlike quintessence strengths. Bosons show no such split. That asymmetry could, in principle, betray quintessence in radiation spectra.
arxiv-2510-20162:
Xudong Yan and Songhe Feng propose TOMCAT, a test-time method for compositional zero-shot learning, where a model must recognize new pairings of known attributes and objects. Performance usually drops at test time because the label space shifts to include unseen combinations. Their approach keeps learning during testing from unlabeled data, in both text and image forms.

The method updates multimodal prototypes at test time, with an adaptive weight controlling how far each prototype may move. A dynamic priority queue stores high-confidence images so visual knowledge from earlier test cases can inform later ones. Text and image prototypes are aligned through collaborative representation learning. Experiments show leading results on four benchmarks in closed and open settings.
arxiv-2510-20362:
Aritra Roy and three co-authors build ComProScanner, a multi-agent tool that pulls clean data from science texts. It reads journal texts and pulls out what things are made of, their traits, and how they were made. Such tools are still rare in a form that lay users can run, check, and plot. Their pack aims to fill that gap for dataset work.

The tool is tested on 100 journal texts with 10 language models, at a hard case: ceramic piezoelectric traits and their strain rates. One model, DeepSeek-V3-0324, tops the rest with the best score by a clear gap. The pack gives an easy route from buried print facts to clean sets for machine learning.
arxiv-2510-20462:
Piotr Stefaniak studies branch growth for elliptic systems set on domains with shape symmetry and with system symmetry as well. He proves full paths of non-plain solutions that split off from the plain branch set by a key point of the field. The proof uses the degree for maps that keep the symmetry in play. No nondegeneracy claim is made, which widens the reach.

All claims are phrased in terms of the right-hand side of the system, so checks stay clear. When the domain is a compact symmetric space, each split path breaks symmetry at each non-zero step. With more claims on the right-hand side, the paths run on without bound in place of a loop back.
arxiv-2510-20562:
Lingyu Guo, Victor Zhenyu Guo, and Mengyao Jing prove a new upper bound for exponential sums where the phase is a general polynomial, extending a classical topic long centered on monomials. Exponential sums connect to many central problems in number theory, and sharper bounds widen what can be proved about prime distribution. Their bound is the technical engine behind the applications that follow in the article.

As the main application, they study primes in Piatetski-Shapiro sequences, which are formed by taking integer parts of powers of consecutive integers. The admissible range for an asymptotic formula counting such primes improves over earlier work. They also study iterated versions of the sequence and prove an asymptotic formula for its prime counting function.
arxiv-2510-20862:
Nigel Higson and Emil Prodan build a universal model for topological behavior on any triangulated closed surface, placing simple resonators or artificial atoms at corners, edges, and faces. Hopping rules between near neighbors come straight from the boundary and duality maps of the triangulation itself.

Whatever the surface or mesh, the rules yield energy models with large clean topological gaps and nonzero Chern numbers as the mesh refines without limit. Simulations confirm the claim, and the models support protected edge modes on the surfaces of real world shaped objects. A metamaterial design whose dynamics copies the model is also described, bringing topological metamaterials closer to practical devices.
arxiv-2510-21162:
Varshika Srinivasavaradhan leads three co-authors on Quality of Coverage, a multi part measure of mobile network reach that goes beyond the bare speed floors shown on provider and regulator maps. A map that promises a minimum rate says nothing about ease of use or steadiness across place and time.

Their indicator set captures measured performance quality, ease of use, and steadiness in space and time from real measurements. Fine grained characterization exposes neighborhoods where nominal reach hides unusable service. Better reach truth supports consumer choice, infrastructure funding decisions, and honest public accountability for carriers nationwide.
arxiv-2510-21562:
Thomas Agugliaro proves a case of the standard conjecture of Hodge type, a deep expectation linking the algebraic cycles on a variety to its cohomological shadow. The conjecture is one of the standard conjectures on algebraic cycles, a family of statements that would tidy the foundations of how geometry counts its own sub-objects.

His proof covers all powers of abelian threefolds, products of a three-dimensional abelian variety with itself any number of times. Along the way he settles powers of simple abelian varieties of prime dimension over finite fields, plus related cases sorted by a notion called Frobenius rank. Two tools do the heavy lifting: a comparison between two ways of taking real fibers of tannakian categories. A fresh explicit description of simple Lefschetz motives over finite fields using enriched Frobenius eigenvalues.
arxiv-2510-21762:
Eric Jeangirard releases a multilingual corpus of scientific paragraphs sorted by what they are doing, raw material for teaching machines to mine the literature. From openly licensed papers in the French Open Science Monitor collection, processed with the GROBID document parser, he extracts eight hundred thirty-three thousand paragraphs.

Each paragraph lands in one of four categories: acknowledgments, mentions of data, mentions of software or code, and mentions of clinical trials. Every item also carries a language tag, assigned automatically, and a scientific domain label from OpenAlex. English and French dominate, with other European languages represented. The set, published openly under a permissive license, is built for training text classifiers and named-entity recognizers that can track how science credits its helpers, shares its data, and reports its trials.
arxiv-2510-22062:
Petros Prastakos, Kayhan Behdin, and Rahul Mazumder select a small set of useful variables from a mountain of candidates without leaking private data. Sparse selection aids both understanding and accuracy, and integer programming solvers can now find the best subset among millions of variables in minutes. Adding a formal privacy guarantee had largely been left undone.

The team introduces two estimators that are private in the strict, pure sense while still using modern integer programming machinery. Inspired by the exponential mechanism, their sampling procedures roam the jagged subset landscape in a structured way instead of searching it exhaustively. Theory backs the method with recovery guarantees for best subset selection, and experiments round out the evidence. The framework extends beyond regression to classification-style problems as well.
arxiv-2510-22362:
Jiazheng Li and four co-authors, Andreas Damianou, J Rosser, José Luis Redondo García. Konstantina Palla, check whether a reasoning model's written chain of thought is the real story or decoration. Prior work has shown the traces do not always mirror the computation, which is a problem for anyone overseeing models by reading their reasoning.

Their framework, Concept Walk, works inside the model instead of on its text. It learns a direction in activation space corresponding to a concept from contrastive examples, then projects every reasoning step onto that direction to watch the model's stance evolve. In a safety case study on a mid-sized open model, easy cases shrugged off tampered chains of thought almost immediately, marking that reasoning as decorative. Hard cases absorbed the tampering into lasting activation shifts, the signature of reasoning the model actually uses.
arxiv-2510-22462:
Abhijnan Nath and co-author Nikhil Krishnaswamy study how language model agents can learn to be partner aware collaborators in group tasks. Good teamwork needs shared common ground, yet standard training makes agents prone to ignore helpful interventions from partners. The pair model this problem with a two player decision process and draw on work about safe interruptibility.

They propose a learning method that trains an agent to use partner input to build common ground. Across several shared task settings, their trained agents reached agreement more often and finished tasks more successfully than standard agents. The work offers theory and a training recipe for better teaming.
arxiv-2510-22562:
Weather forecasts start from an estimate of the current atmosphere built from sparse observations. Jing-An Sun, with ten co-authors, proposes LO-SDA in 2025, a generative data assimilation method that avoids the simple Gaussian guess used by older approaches.

First, an autoencoder learns a compact hidden form that untangles complex air patterns. A diffusion model then learns realistic background states inside that hidden space. During generation, a latent optimization step forces outputs to match the sparse observations strictly. Idealized tests beat both traditional assimilation and earlier score based methods, suggesting learned priors can give less biased starting states.
arxiv-2510-23162:
Keisuke Kataoka and three co-authors study a quantum circuit that uses stabilizer measurements alone to build states with rich entanglement. The setup, reported in 2025, starts from the toric code, a known design for quantum memory, on a triangular lattice. Local Pauli terms act like added electric and magnetic fields and compete with the code terms.

They trace the changing states with a fast stabilizer method and map the phase changes. Three clues guide the map. One is entanglement tied to the shape of the system. Others are order measures for a broad symmetry, and logical operators that carry stored information. Unlike the square grid case, these changes do not line up, since the triangular pattern lacks the symmetry that forced a match. The team finds several separate transitions with their own critical exponents, and some sit close to a classic percolation change.
arxiv-2510-23762:
Raimondo Pala proposes Control VAR, a counterfactual method for drawing causal conclusions from vector autoregressions in macroeconomics. Giving VAR results a causal reading usually leans on independence assumptions that may not hold. Pala's earlier analysis shows those assumptions can deliver treatment effects or causal responses, depending on the policy's distribution, but economists often cannot rely on them.

Control VAR instead brings in control variables, much as a control group anchors an experiment. It can estimate effects on the treated for yes-no policies, or average causal responses over time for continuous ones. Pala demonstrates the approach on the economic impact of natural disasters in the United States, using Germany as the control. Against earlier literature, disasters show a clear negative effect with no compensating cyclical bounce-back. The author presents control-based VARs as a more credible route to causal estimates, with direct lessons for disaster policy design.
arxiv-2510-23962:
Hangil Jang and a co-author test an image-based way to tag b-jets, the sprays of particles that come from bottom quarks, inside heavy-ion collisions. Knowing a jet's flavor lets physicists probe how the hot, dense medium treats different quarks differently. Deep learning taggers already beat track-based methods, and this study asks what plain images around the collision point can add.

The images are built from charged particles inside the jet cone, as a silicon tracking system would record them, assuming detector performance for this first study. A convolutional neural network reads the images and classifies the jet's origin. The method reached eighty to ninety percent efficiency for b-jets with transverse momenta between twenty and one hundred gigaelectronvolts per c. The authors see room for the image approach to sharpen flavor tagging accuracy in heavy-ion experiments, once detector effects are folded in.
arxiv-2510-24062:
Erin S. Grant and fourteen co-authors report that tiny carbon dots can change their glow in response to spin effects at room temperature. Carbon quantum dots are popular because they are bright, easy to make, and safe for living tissue. Yet no one had clearly seen their light respond to spin under normal conditions before.

The team made dots from nineteen different amino acids and found a clear change in glow in a weak magnetic field, up to about one percent. They also detected an electron spin signal in the light itself. The result opens a path to small, low cost sensors that use carbon dots to image and sense quantum effects.
arxiv-2510-24362:
Gabriel Montes-Rojas and three co-authors study monetary policy when a central bank cares about a quantile of outcomes rather than the average. In their framework, the bank's risk attitude is set by a quantile index, giving a clear map between hawkish or dovish stances and attention to bad outcomes. They set up the infinite horizon problem with a Bellman equation using a quantile operator.

From an Euler equation approach, they derive Taylor rule style reaction functions for interest rates. Using indirect inference, they estimate the implicit quantile index that reveals the Federal Reserve's risk aversion. The empirical plan for the United States uses reduced form dynamics with changing volatility.
arxiv-2510-24562:
Alberto Chiarini and Emanuele Pasqui study a discrete Gaussian free field in a random environment pushed against a hard wall. The field lives on the integer lattice in dimension three or higher, with random conductances that are uniformly elliptic, bounded, and sufficiently mixing. They consider the event that the field stays nonnegative over a blown up bounded domain.

The authors establish a quenched large deviation asymptotic for this event's probability, with a rate set by the essential supremum of on site variances and the homogenized capacity of the domain. They then analyze the field's law conditioned on the wall event and determine its first order asymptotic profile, a classic entropic repulsion picture in a random medium.
arxiv-2510-24862:
Cesar Hilario and Karl Otto Stohr sort a class of curve families whose fibers are flat four degree curves in the plane. The fibers have set genus counts, three by count math and one by true shape, in a world where two is the prime. One move odd point is the sole such point they allow, with a set pull back trait.

Under those terms, they give a full sort of the families up to a loose form of same shape. The work rests on a close read of the plain fibers, whose shape they lay out in full. Each such family is shown to be capped by a family of genus one curves. The cap matches fiber by fiber, but twists the base in a pure inseparable way.
arxiv-2510-24962:
Zachary C Zelensky leads a team with nine co-authors who tracked a rare, sharp bend of radio waves from a pulsar. Such bends, called extreme scattering events, come from small dense zones in the gas between stars. Clips taken at high rate with a twenty metre dish let them track the bend in fine time steps.

In the bend, a pair of spikes showed, plus the set drop in wave spread that marks such an event. A side map showed a split trait like past twin lens cases. The team gauged the zone's range, its width at about fifteen sun to earth spans, and a span of about two hundred twenty days. Such events probe tiny gas forms.
arxiv-2510-25062:
Chul-Moon Yoo, Masashi Kimura, Akihiro Ishibashi, and Rikuto Ohashi study the ring down of a black hole that still grows, in a Vaidya space. For a still hole, the ring tone links to the speed and spread rate of light that loops at an unsafe ring path. A limit shape near that path backs the link.

Their case has a photon sphere that shifts with time, since the hole is not still. They ask how far the limit shape near that sphere can still mark the ring waves. To check, they match the shape based read with a full code wave form in the same space. The match shows where the old link holds and where it bends.
arxiv-2510-25162:
Frank C Porter, the sole author, replies to a comment by Robert Cousins on his past work on trust ranges for the Poisson count rule. That rule counts rare free events, and a trust range marks where the true rate most apt sits. Cousins holds that rates that can not be real should not sit in the chance form, even for count based stats.

Porter takes the other side. He argues it can be of use to let such rates in when one talks of these sketch stats. The note is short and set as a direct reply in a live method row. It holds no new data; its point is how the range should be framed and read.
arxiv-2510-25262:
Xiandong Zou, Jia Li, Xiaotong Yuan, and Pan Zhou propose IBNorm. Their 2025 paper offers a new normalization method. Normalization rescales values inside a neural network. It keeps training stable and smooth. Common methods include BatchNorm, LayerNorm, and RMSNorm. Those methods focus mainly on spread of values. They do not control what information representations keep.

IBNorm draws on the information bottleneck principle. That principle favors keeping facts that predict answers. It also favors dropping noise and useless variation. IBNorm adds bounded compression steps toward that goal. The authors prove stronger theory results for it. They claim tighter generalization bounds than rival methods. Tests cover language models like LLaMA and GPT-2. Tests also cover vision models like ResNet and ViT. In those tests, IBNorm beat the standard methods.
arxiv-2510-25362:
Georgios L Stavrinides and Helen D Karatza survey workload scheduling. Their 2025 chapter concerns large-scale distributed systems. Big data growth makes workloads more complex. Systems are growing in scale and capacity. Data-intensive apps differ in parallelism and locality needs.

Workloads also impose quality of service requirements. Time constraints and failure resilience matter greatly. Energy efficiency is another common objective today. The chapter proposes a classification of workloads. It overviews common scheduling methods used in literature. Novel strategies from recent work are presented too. The authors highlight open challenges for scholars. Future directions for large-scale scheduling are discussed. Readers get a structured map of the field.
arxiv-2510-25462: Manuel Garzon and Salvador Lopez-Martinez prove that the Lorentz force law has closed loop paths that repeat. Their 2025 paper works with a strong vector field term and no scalar term at all. They find the paths by making an action score as small as it can be. To make that proof work, the score must take scores below zero. They show this with the sign-changing part of the vector term. The result also holds when a scalar term is present, even a sharp one.
arxiv-2510-25662:
Gabrielle O'Brien led four co-authors on programming assistant misconceptions. Antonio Pedro Santos Alves, Sebastian Baltes, and Grischa Liebel helped. Marcos Kalinowski closes the five-author team. Their 2025 paper studies conversational language model assistants. Such assistants are widely ready to novice programmers. Web search, code execution, and retrieval may be absent.

Those gaps create user misconceptions and over-reliance. They screened over eleven thousand Python conversations. The WildChat dataset supplied those openly ready conversations. Hand annotation studied seven hundred fifty-four candidates closely. Four hundred fifty contained prompts with misconceptions. Eight likely misconception types were identified overall.
arxiv-2510-25762:
M I Gornostaev simulates an accreting X-ray pulsar polar region. A 3D, geometrically 2D model is used. Radiative transfer and region form are calculated self-always. An method developed earlier performs that calculation. Magnetic scattering cross sections depend on energy and polarization.

Second-order bulk Comptonization occurs over entire emitting region. Induced Compton scattering is also taken into account. Switching of polarization modes is included in model. A realistic channel shape and dipole field are used. Post-shock zone temperature is set by that effect. Within shock wave, higher electron temperature is reached. Bulk heating mechanism drives that shock heating. Photons gaining energy in shock form high-energy continuum. X-ray pulsar output modeling gains physical completeness.
arxiv-2510-25862:
Barbara J. Anthony-Twarog leads six co-authors in a detailed study of the star cluster NGC 7789. They combine precise ground based brightness measures with Gaia space data to map how dust reddens the cluster unevenly across its face. Spectra and model fits then pin down the cluster age at about one point five billion years, along with its distance and metal content.

Anthony-Twarog and the team trace lithium, an element that fades as stars age, from young dwarf stars to the tips of red giants. They also link the spread in the upper main sequence and the lithium dip pattern to how fast the stars spin. Comparisons with a sister cluster help explain why their diagrams differ.
arxiv-2510-25962:
Alvaro Velasquez, Susmit Jha, and Ismail R. Alkhouri survey work on training neural networks to solve optimization problems with no training data at all. In this dataless setting, a network re expresses a single problem, such as a linear program or an inverse problem, and its weights are tuned until the network output solves that instance. No data set of solved examples is needed.

Velasquez and the team sort methods by how the problem is encoded into the network, from architecture agnostic schemes to designs built for the problem class. They cover fully connected, convolutional, graph, and quadratic networks. Interest has grown because data driven learning still struggles on combinatorial problems and because data are scarce in fields such as medical imaging.
arxiv-2510-26162:
Sebastian V. Colom, Magnus A. Haw, and Jocelino Rodrigues design a fast sweeping Langmuir probe for measuring hot plasma flows. A Langmuir probe is a small electrode whose current, as voltage sweeps, reveals electron temperature, density, and plasma potential. Standard probes sweep too slowly to catch rapid fluctuations in dynamic settings such as an arc jet, a device that heats gas with an electric arc for testing heat shield materials.

Their system sweeps at up to two hundred kilohertz, resolving fast changes, and it is open source, low cost, and adaptable. They validate it in a thirty kilowatt miniature arc jet chamber, where it survived extreme heat conditions and gave time resolved temperature and density profiles across the flow.
arxiv-2510-26262:
Francesco Verde, Donatella Darsena, Marco Di Renzo, and Vincenzo Galdi find the best transmit field pattern for a radiating surface whose view is partly blocked. Near field communications focus energy at a finite distance rather than beaming it to infinity, and obstacles can diffract the waves. Their model uses knife edge diffraction, a classic approximation for waves bending around a sharp edge, to describe the blocked channel.

Cast as a maximization in Hilbert space, the problem has an optimal solution in matched filter form: the aperture field should match the shape of a diffraction induced kernel. The framework supports hardware built as continuous apertures, such as metasurfaces or lens antennas. It links wave physics with signal processing. The goal is efficient energy focusing in obstructed near field channels.
arxiv-2510-26562:
Sumit Mukherjee and Jonte R Hance probe a deep puzzle about quantum measurement. Wigner's friend paradoxes ask whether a measured event has one absolute result, or whether results can differ between observers. A recent no-go theorem, the Local Friendliness Theorem, turned one form of that puzzle into a firm clash with quantum theory.

Mukherjee and Hance build a time-ordered cousin, the Causal Friendliness Paradox. They swap the usual locality assumption for one about time symmetry, keep assumptions of absolute events, no backward causation, and screening by pseudo events, and derive a causal inequality. Quantum mechanics breaks that inequality, so at least one assumption must fail. They then show a weaker, working form of the absoluteness assumption still leads to clashes that quantum theory violates.
arxiv-2510-26662:
Tobias Wichmann, with twelve co-authors, reports giant magnetic effects at the buried interface between graphene and a layered ferromagnet. Stacking atom-thin materials lets interface effects reshape their traits, through orbital mixing and charge transfer. Direct spectroscopic proof of the new magnetic states that form at such interfaces has been lacking.

Wichmann and the team find electric-field tunable Zeeman effects at the graphene and iron-germanium-telluride interface. These are energy shifts in a magnetic field, with strength factors up to about two hundred thirty. The effect comes from local moments tilting together with travelling orbital moments. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy, working through a phonon gap in graphene, let them probe the hidden interface and measure screening. The findings open routes to electrically controlled interface magnetism for spin-based electronics.
arxiv-2510-26762:
Lin Htoo Zaw, with four co-authors, turns theory from a companion paper into lab-ready tests for genuine multipartite entanglement. Such entanglement links all parties of a many-part system together. Existing witnesses for continuous-variable systems rely on quadrature measurements, which are hard on platforms where the continuous degrees of freedom are read only through qubits.

Zaw and the team build five implementation schemes using controlled Gaussian unitaries, operations already available in qubit plus continuous-variable hardware. The schemes use controlled parity, displacement, and beam-splitter operations. They detect standard test states, including Dicke and N00N states and entangled cat states, and they hold up under realistic noise and finite resolution. One scheme needs only a single measurement on auxiliary modes, far fewer than full tomography.
arxiv-2510-26862:
Remi Abgrall, Yongle Liu, and Mario Ricchiuto design numerical schemes for shallow water flows that keep their balance. Shallow water models, such as the Saint-Venant system with friction, mix moving water with source terms from terrain and rotation. A good scheme should preserve steady states exactly and never predict negative water depth.

Abgrall and his two co-authors build PAMPA schemes, a point-average-moment method, around a global flux quadrature that folds source terms into an added flux. The method preserves a large family of smooth moving equilibria, both supercritical and subcritical, with super-convergent accuracy, and it preserves still water exactly. Blending with a first-order scheme near shocks keeps depth positive and handles wet-dry fronts. Extensive numerical tests back the claims.
arxiv-2510-26962:
Zecheng Zhang, Hao Liu, Guosheng Fu, Hayden Schaeffer, and Guang Lin propose a learning method for equations that describe change across space and time. Operator learning maps an input function to an output function, often by writing the output as a sum of basis functions, meaning fixed building-block shapes. Global blocks can miss sharp local features such as shocks.

Their network, called FERN, builds local blocks in the style of the finite element method, a classic way to solve such equations piece by piece. With simple activation rules, the blocks form exactly inside the network and can shift to match local features. Tests on seven families of equations show good accuracy with fewer trainable values than deep global methods.
arxiv-2510-27162:
Ruifei Huang leads eight co-authors in dissecting a solar flare that showed two ribbon shapes at once. Flare ribbons are bright arcs where energy strikes the solar surface. Parallel ribbons and circular ribbons usually point to different magnetic reconnection models, so seeing both together is rare and informative.

Multi-wavelength observations of the strong September 2023 event show parallel ribbons brightening in two episodes matching two hard X-ray peaks. The semi-circular ribbons brighten in the lull between peaks instead. Field reconstruction reveals an incomplete dome structure with two sets of field lines. Standard reconnection explains the parallel ribbons, while interaction with the dome drives a second reconnection type for the round ribbons and delays the second peak.
arxiv-2510-27662:
Xiangjiang Bao, Zheng-da Hu, Lucas Kreiss, Josh Lerner, and Roarke Horstmeyer build a mobile phase microscope in 2025 from a phone sensor. Phase imaging shows clear samples by mapping how light slows as it passes through them. Classic tools need many shots or complex optics, which keeps them in labs.

Their method uses a quad-pixel sensor made for fast focus in phones. Each tiny lens covers four pixels, and a sample's phase slope shifts the focus spot, which unbalances the four readings. From that imbalance, one shot yields a full phase map. Tests on beads and on living samples confirm the maps are sound. A phone-grade part could bring phase views to clinics and field work.
arxiv-2511-00062:
An NVIDIA-led team introduces Cosmos-Predict2.5, a generation of world foundation models that simulate video of physical environments for Physical AI. A flow-based architecture unifies text-to-world, image-to-world, and video-to-world generation in one model. A physical AI vision-language model, Cosmos-Reason1, provides richer text grounding and finer control of the simulation.

Training used two hundred million curated video clips, refined by reinforcement learning post-training, with substantial gains over the previous generation in quality and instruction alignment. Robotics readers get a simulator-grade generator for training embodied systems. World models let robots practice in generated environments before facing real ones.
arxiv-2511-00262:
Romina Etezadi, Sallam Abualhaija, Chetan Arora, and Lionel Briand target a costly chore in software projects: when one requirement changes, which others are affected? Doing this by hand is slow and error-prone, and missed links can cause serious downstream failures, above all in regulated fields. Their tool, ProReFiCIA, uses large language models to flag affected requirements automatically.

Across several models and prompt designs, the best setup recovered most affected items on an unseen industrial dataset, while engineers only had to review a tiny share of all requirements. Adding domain knowledge through retrieval raised recall further, at slightly higher cost. The study shows language models can cut the price of change analysis without flooding engineers with false leads.
arxiv-2511-00662:
Bagun Shchamkhalova and Vladimir Sablikov study how electrons move in two-dimensional topological insulators whose energy bands bend like a Mexican hat. That shape gives a singular density of states and a ring-shaped Fermi surface, exotic features that make charged impurity scattering, the main brake on electron motion in quantum materials, unusually rich. Electron-electron interaction and jumps between energy contours become central actors.

The authors compute the screened potential of Coulomb centers within the random phase approximation. Those factors reshape both the potential's spatial profile and how mobility depends on temperature and density. Transport is handled without the usual relaxation time shortcut: the energy-space distribution obeys a two-equation system. The results guide what to expect in a class of materials where standard transport intuition fails.
arxiv-2511-00862:
Deepak Patel and Praveen Srivastava compute properties of a rare nuclear decay called two neutrino double electron capture in barium-132 and krypton-78. In this process a nucleus captures two of its own electrons and emits two neutrinos, and measuring it is extremely difficult.

Using large scale shell model calculations with established effective interactions, they first check that the models reproduce known spectra of the parent, intermediate, and daughter nuclei. They then track how the nuclear matrix element builds up across excited states of the intermediate nucleus. The krypton results update earlier estimates of the matrix element and half life, while the barium results give a first baseline prediction to guide future experiments.
arxiv-2511-00962:
Dongheng Lin and colleagues propose a unified framework for analyzing anomalies in video without any task specific training. Most systems only score frames as normal or abnormal, saying nothing about where the event is or why it counts as strange. Newer explanation methods still depend on their training data.

Their approach chains reasoning steps at test time: first refine the timing of detections, then pass the results onward to locate the event in space, then explain it in words. Careful prompt design ties the stages together on top of foundation models. With no extra data or training, the framework reaches state of the art zero shot results across detection, localization, and explanation benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-01462:
Peng Xia, Junbiao Pang, and Tianyang Cai prepare neural networks in advance for aggressive quantization, the compression step that shrinks a trained model to a few bits per weight for cheap deployment. Post training quantization of vision transformers is efficient, but ignoring how the full precision model relates to its quantized twin leaves large errors.

Their starting discovery is that a flat full precision network, one sitting in a wide, shallow minimum, quantizes far better. They model activation and weight quantization errors as independent Gaussian noises, disentangle the error sources, and study noise injection training methods that steer the network toward such flat minima. Experiments support the approach, and the authors flag the work as ongoing, with more results to come.
arxiv-2511-01562:
Jack Stade settles a complexity question about the art gallery problem, the classic puzzle of placing the fewest guards so every wall of a polygonal gallery is watched. In the boundary-boundary variant, guards stand on the boundary and only the boundary must be seen, but guards' sight lines must stay inside the polygon, holes included.

Neighbors of this variant were known to be NP-complete or complete for a larger real-number class, leaving boundary-boundary stranded somewhere between NP and that class. Stade shows it is in NP. The proof builds a constraint-propagation procedure for continuous constraint satisfaction problems. In these problems each constraint involves at most two variables. An example is needed first, to show the solution cannot simply be reduced to a discrete set-cover instance.
arxiv-2511-01862:
Vanessa Sochat and Daniel Milroy write on what the cloud's pricing shift means for science. Computing innovation once answered to scientific needs; as industry and consumer use exploded, vendors served a multipolar customer base. Now artificial intelligence demand dominates, innovation has centralized in the cloud, and cost and resource models are being rebuilt around AI workloads.

That leaves scientific computing, the cloud's original driver, poorly served by models not designed for it. Suppose one dominant class of customer makes contended resources harder for scientists to reach. Then a likely future is research workloads running in environments never intended for them. The authors trace the past and present of cloud cost models and sketch possible futures, arguing for arrangements that keep discovery science viable on commercial infrastructure.
arxiv-2511-01962:
Marcin Płodzień and Jan Chwedeńczuk show that one extra qubit is enough to both create and certify deep quantum correlations in a many-body system. As quantum technologies grow, verifying that a complex device truly holds entanglement and many-body Bell correlations, the strongest form of nonlocality, becomes essential and difficult.

Their method couples a single probe qubit pairwise to an N-qubit system. Two results carry the paper. First, pairwise interaction suffices to induce genuine many-body quantum correlations in the system. Second, the probe can then serve as the readout. It extracts all information about those correlations from measurements on the single qubit alone. Single-qubit measurements thus reveal multipartite entanglement and N-body Bell correlations, offering a rapid route to certifying non-classicality in complex quantum hardware.
arxiv-2511-02062:
Yuting Yang leads a team of eight co-authors building infrastructure for machine learning services that must answer within strict time limits. Interactive users, and AI agents acting for them, increasingly need guaranteed response times, known as service level objectives. Existing platforms such as TorchServe and Ray Serve group requests into batches for throughput, which makes the slowest responses unpredictable.

Their system, Vortex, is designed around latency targets first. Across a wide range of workloads its pipelines gave lower and steadier response times than the two established platforms, often handling more than twice the request rate at the same target. When high-speed RDMA networking was available, the advantage grew further, the authors report.
arxiv-2511-02162:
Alexander Htet Kyaw and ten co-authors connect three technologies so a person can describe an object in words and watch a robot build it. Generative AI first produces a 3D mesh from the text prompt, but real objects mix structural parts with flat panels, and the mesh alone does not say which is which. A vision-language model examines the generated mesh and, reasoning about its geometry and function, assigns regions to predefined structural and panel components.

In user evaluations, people preferred the model's assignments about 90.6 percent of the time, far ahead of rule-based and random assignment. Users could also correct the plan through conversational feedback before assembly. The authors present the pipeline as a way to give non-experts more control over fabricating multi-part objects with generative AI and robotics.
arxiv-2511-02262:
Diptajit Roy, Nitin Saxena, and Madhavan Venkatesh study how hard it is to count points on curves and surfaces over a finite field. It is a basic problem in number theory whose difficulty is unresolved. No subexponential algorithm is known, and it is unclear whether the problem is NP-hard. Instead of computing the count outright, the authors show it can be certified. They give the first Arthur-Merlin protocol that convinces a verifier of a curve's point count, its Jacobian group structure, and its Hasse-Weil zeta function.

For a smooth projective surface they certify the first factor of the zeta function, tied to the first Betti number, using a point-counting oracle. An algorithm computes that factor in time polynomial in the logarithm of the field size for fixed surface degree, and in quantum polynomial time. The proofs reduce surfaces to curves through pencils of hyperplane sections.
arxiv-2511-02662:
Jean-Marie Mirebeau and Erwan Stampfli study how to compute two hard evolution equations by turning them into optimization problems. The porous medium equation governs slow spreading, as in gas through rock, while Burgers' equation models shock-like flow. Their 2025 paper uses a ballistic variant of the Benamou-Brenier formulation, borrowed from optimal transport theory.

The pair discretize the whole space-time problem at once, using harmonic interpolation for the densities, a choice they note is new here. They prove the scheme stays stable for any step sizes and converges at a quadratic rate for the dual solution. A proximal splitting solver with fast Fourier transforms makes it practical. Numerical tests back the theory on both equations, in several dimensions for the porous case.
arxiv-2511-02762:
Xun Wang and four colleagues want teams of learning agents to start from solo practice instead of costly group data. Training a team from scratch in multi-agent reinforcement learning is slow, they note in a 2025 paper, like asking beginners to play a symphony at once. Solo demonstrations, by contrast, are cheap to gather in coding, housework, and rescue tasks.

Their framework, SoCo, first pretrains one shared solo policy from single-agent demos. During team training, a gating selector and an action editor fuse that solo skill into joint behavior. Across varied cooperative tasks, SoCo raised both training speed and final scores for the base algorithms it was added to. Solo experience, the results suggest, scales well as a training aid.
arxiv-2511-02962:
Ezequiel Santos and eight colleagues build fast surrogate models for multiphase flow underground, the kind that governs oil and water moving through rock. Full simulations of these systems are notoriously heavy. Neural operators promise cheap stand-ins, but used alone they strain memory and handle time poorly. Their 2025 paper builds hybrid DeepONet surrogates that mix several network types inside one design.

Fourier operators, plain multilayer networks, and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks share the branch and trunk parts, with space and time learning split between them. Tests ran from steady two-dimensional Darcy flow to a standard three-dimensional reservoir benchmark. The hybrids stayed accurate with far fewer parameters than plain designs. The authors pitch them for large reservoir studies where full solvers are too slow.
arxiv-2511-03462:
Enzo Francisco, Julien Lambret, and Sebastien Aumaitre make the first direct maps of energy loss at the wall of a turbulent flow. A light-scattering method called diffusing-wave spectroscopy reads tiny motions near the boundary and turns them into the local dissipation rate over space and time. The flow is stirred by an impeller inside a square box.

Even at the wall, dissipation tracks the injected power and follows the classic turbulent scaling with Reynolds number across a wide range. No extra logarithmic fix is needed near the flat wall, a point theory had debated. Fine maps of where energy dies at boundaries can sharpen models of drag, heat transfer, and mixing in real devices.
arxiv-2511-03562:
Ana Mitrasinovic warns that the edges of a famous galaxy simulation quietly corrupt some of its galaxies. Cosmological boxes wrap around at their faces, a practical trick that can fake or strip matter when galaxies cross the seam. Galaxies oddly starved of dark matter serve as tracers for the damage.

Their numbers grow as box size shrinks, and they cluster near the edges, with the smallest box hit hardest. Hand checks confirm abrupt, unphysical mass losses right at boundary crossings. In a mid-size box, telling seam damage from true tidal stripping in crossing clusters stays genuinely hard. The author closes with concrete safeguards for anyone mining that irreplaceable simulation for galaxy structure claims.
arxiv-2511-03862:
Giulio Del Felice and Ludovico Theo Giorgini combine score-based learning with neural differential equations to build reduced models of chaotic systems with fast and slow parts. Such systems pair slow parts, which set long-term statistics, with fast chaotic processes that drive short bursts and rare switches.

Slow dynamics follow a Langevin equation whose drift comes from a learned score function, keeping the invariant measure. Fast forcing is handled by a neural differential equation trained on delayed leftover signals instead of plain Gaussian noise. Tests on metastable systems driven by Lorenz dynamics, including bistable and tristable cases, kept long-run stats while predicting rare transitions better than standard reduced models.
arxiv-2511-04362:
Chiara Telli, Oleg Antropov, Anne Lonnqvist, and Marco Lavalle map forest structure at high resolution over Asturias in northern Spain using L-band interferometric radar time series and deep learning. Nine dual-polarization satellite radar images at near-zero spatial baseline form the input stack, with airborne laser scanning supplying reference data.

Several U-Net family models were tested with different polarimetric and interferometric feature mixes. Adding model-based inverted interferometric features or coherence layers beat backscatter intensity alone. Attention and nested-fusion variants beat a vanilla U-Net and traditional machine learning. Forest height errors landed in the low single metres at twenty-metre resolution in the reported ranges, supporting radar time series as a forest monitoring source.
arxiv-2511-04862:
Catrin Harris leads five authors imaging unstable drainage as gas invades brine-filled rock. Fast four-dimensional synchrotron X-ray scans watch both pore and sample scales at once. The layered sandstone holds one thin layer with similar pores but poorer connections.

That centimeter-scale layer acts as a capillary barrier, stalling and redirecting the gas. Small upstream differences then send gas down different downstream paths in repeated runs. Breakthrough times vary by up to a factor of four between repeats. The message is stark: subtle connectivity contrasts can make underground gas flow genuinely unpredictable.
arxiv-2511-04962:
Zihao Yi and co-authors test whether large language models can play villains well in made-up scenes. Models are now asked to act as many kinds of characters, yet their skill with dark or hostile roles had not been checked.

The team built a Moral RolePlay test set with a four-step scale from hero to pure villain. As a role grew more immoral, model play grew less true, most of all for traits like deceit and sly control. Models swapped subtle menace for plain rage. Skill as a chat bot also did not predict skill at villain play.
arxiv-2511-05062:
Yu-Chen Hua and co-authors search for a break in Lorentz invariance in the light of a huge gamma-ray burst seen by LHAASO. Some quantum gravity ideas say light speed should shift a bit with energy, which would smear arrival times over vast distances.

Using the dispersion cancellation method, which seeks the shift that sharpens the burst profile, they join data from two detectors that span a wide energy range. They fold in doubts from energy and time bins. The null result sets firm lower bounds on the energy scale where such an effect could start.
arxiv-2511-05162:
Jan-Thorsten Peter and co-authors warn that translation slips and scoring details can skew tests of language models across languages. They take math as a test domain and grade models in tongues from German and Chinese to Swahili and Telugu.

A clear, steady score gap showed up across languages. To their surprise, the gap hit both rich-resource and low-resource tongues. Then the twist: parts of the gap trace to flawed translations of test items and to scoring choices. Their point is stark: cross-language league tables need care before they guide research or product calls.
arxiv-2511-05462:
Xiaodong Wang and co-authors recast deep unsupervised learning methods that use clustering as classic mixture models from statistics. Clustering-based self-supervised methods work well, but their use was mostly heuristic, with no clear rule for the best form.

Through the mixture lens, the authors find upgrades to those methods and build a new model, SiamMM. It reaches top scores on several self-supervised tests, by their report. A look at its learned clusters shows what the model groups and why, which ties a modern trick back to a firm statistical base overall.
arxiv-2511-05562:
Sanghyun Lee and colleagues propose a way to spend extra compute at generation time to improve discrete diffusion models. Such models build text or images step by step, but reward-guided methods for them remain little studied. Their method, IterRef, uses reward signals to refine each intermediate state where it stands.

IterRef runs cycles of noising and denoising steered by a reward score. The authors cast the process in a formal sampling framework and prove it converges toward the reward-aligned distribution. Across text and image models, quality rose in test after test. Gains were largest when the compute budget was small, where the method far beat prior baselines.
arxiv-2511-05662:
Nathan Roth leads a team observing comet C/2017 K2 with the ALMA radio array in Chile. They caught the comet near the inner edge of the zone where water ice starts to boil off in earnest, a shift that changes which gases dominate the comet's coma. The observations ran over three days in September 2022.

The team mapped emissions from five molecules plus dust. Some gases came from within a short distance of the nucleus, possibly with help from icy grains. Others needed sources spread through the coma, and one traced back to breakdown of a parent molecule by sunlight. They also bounded the nucleus size and weighed the dust in the coma.
arxiv-2511-05762:
Diana Cohen, Roy Friedman, and Rana Shahout ask how network nodes can rebuild lost summary data after crashes. Switches and routers keep sketches, compact summaries of traffic statistics, and losing them blinds network analysis. Their work lets the nodes cooperate so a sketch can be recovered even when any subset of nodes fails.

They focus on linear sketches for counting frequencies, such as the Count-Min Sketch. Several recovery designs are compared for space use, runtime cost, and traffic during repair. A key choice is how nodes share updates: full periodic refreshes versus small incremental ones, with compact ways to encode the latest changes. The system is modular, so other data structures can plug in through a shared interface.
arxiv-2511-06062:
Diego Cifuentes and Zhuorui Li recover a rank-one tensor from a handful of its entries using semidefinite programming. A tensor is a multi-dimensional array; completing one from few observations is a core data problem. Their convex relaxations solve the exact case and stay robust when observations are noisy.

The guarantees rest only on the pattern of observed entries, not on randomness or on hidden assumptions about the tensor. For special patterns, barely more entries than the dimensions sum are enough. For random patterns, their bound beats naive scaling by a wide margin. For matrices, their condition matches unique solvability exactly. Early experiments needed far fewer observations than rival methods, which the authors highlight.
arxiv-2511-06562:
Saannidhya Rawat asks whether gaining official municipal status actually improves life in fast-growing Indian towns. Many urbanizing villages meet the census criteria for town status yet wait years for statutory recognition as urban local bodies. Towns just above and below the eligibility thresholds form a natural comparison for a fuzzy regression discontinuity study.

Qualifying in 2001 sharply raised the odds of recognition by 2011. Recognized towns gained many more government schools at every level, extra hospitals and family welfare centers, and deeper financial access through cooperative banks and farm credit societies. Sports facilities shrank, likely as urban land was reallocated. The evidence favors prompt town status for emerging urban areas.
arxiv-2511-06662:
Franklin Lee and Tengfei Ma predict dangerous drug pairings for medicines a knowledge graph has never seen. Drug-drug interactions cause preventable harm, and many mechanisms remain unknown. Graph-based models fail on new drugs, while hospital record models are noisy and site-bound, so the authors fuse both sources during training.

A teacher model scores graph relations conditioned on each patient's record context, learning mechanism-level patterns where both data types exist. A distilled student then works from records alone, making zero-shot predictions for new or rare drugs. Alerts name the specific mechanism instead of a bare risk score. Hospital tests across institutions kept precision high and missed fewer real interactions than earlier methods.
arxiv-2511-06762:
Rui Lu and four co-authors tackle a common software maintenance problem: Java projects reuse open-source libraries, but old versions carry fixed bugs and security holes. Their tool, DepUpdater, upgrades those libraries automatically. It aims to cut technical lag, the gap between the version in use and the newest release, without breaking the project.

Upgrades often fail because new versions clash with current code or drag in redundant dependencies that bloat the project. DepUpdater balances fresh versions against compatibility and prunes unneeded dependencies as it goes. In comparisons with current tools it reduced lag more effectively, and the authors also studied how upgrading indirect dependencies affects the programs that rely on them.
arxiv-2511-06862:
Huan Sun and five co-authors present a verification tool for proving that secure software stays secure as it is refined into real code. Information flow security is hard to guarantee for concurrent systems like multicore operating system kernels. Their generalized refinement method handles complex policies, including intransitive noninterference, where some indirect flows are allowed by design.

The key idea is a step-mapping relation pairing each implementation step with an abstract step, so the policy can be checked pair by pair. All proofs are mechanized in the Isabelle/HOL prover. Applying the method to two case studies, the authors confirmed that two covert channels known from the single-core ARINC 653 standard also exist in its multicore version. The authors then proved a revised mechanism correct.
arxiv-2511-07262:
Qile Jiang and George Karniadakis let a team of AI agents do scientific machine learning research. Designing designs, loss functions, and training plans for physics-based learning is expert work requiring long experimentation. Their system, AgenticSciML, fields more than ten specialized agents that propose, critique, and refine solutions through structured debate, a retrieval-augmented memory of methods, and ensemble-guided evolutionary search.

On physics-informed learning and operator learning tasks, the agents discovered methods beating single-agent and human-built baselines by up to four orders of magnitude in error reduction. The plans they invented, including adaptive mixture-of-expert designs, decomposition-based physics-informed networks, and physics-informed operator models, did not appear in the curated knowledge base the agents could search. The authors present this as fresh methodological innovation from collaborative machine reasoning.
arxiv-2511-07362:
Kai A Horstmann, Maxim Clouser, and Kia Khezeli generate synthetic infrared images without needing a foundation-scale infrared dataset. Infrared cameras enable temperature-based scene understanding when visible imaging fails, but labeled infrared data is scarce because labeling it takes specialized expertise. Training a big generative model from scratch is therefore out of reach. The authors instead adapt FLUX.1-dev, a leading text-to-image diffusion model, to infrared with parameter-efficient fine-tuning on a small sample.

Quality is then scaled at inference time: a domain-adapted CLIP-based verifier guides the diffusion sampling toward generations that better match the prompt and the infrared domain. On the KAIST multispectral pedestrian benchmark, guided sampling cut the FID score by ten percent against unguided baselines. The authors argue inference-time guidance is a promising way to bridge domain gaps wherever data is limited.
arxiv-2511-07462:
Mahid Mangontarum, Norlailah Madid, and Asnawi Campong derive integral formulas for a family of special polynomials. The noncentral Tanny-Dowling polynomials generalize older geometric and exponential polynomials used in counting problems. Integrals give flexible ways to compute and compare such sequences.

Each new formula is shown to extend a known result for the classic geometric polynomials. That link places the newer family firmly inside an established theory rather than beside it. The work is aimed at researchers in combinatorics and special functions. Readers gain tools for proving identities and for studying growth and structure in related polynomial families.
arxiv-2511-07562:
Giovanni Tedeschi-Prades, Til Birnstiel, and Klaus Dolag speed up drag physics in planet formation simulations. Gas drags on dust grains of many sizes, and stiff coupling makes time steps painfully small. A solver must stay stable without slowing the whole code.

Their General Implicit Runge-Kutta scheme fits Strang splitting, so outside forces and fluid motion slot in cleanly. An analytic drag solution keeps cost growing only linearly as grain sizes multiply, beating matrix methods that grow cubically. Standard benchmarks check accuracy. Faster dust handling lets modelers follow grain growth and drift over the long spans planets need to form.
arxiv-2511-07662:
Owen Lailey, Dusan Sarenac, and Charles Clark shape neutron beams into structured patterns. Neutrons carrying orbital angular momentum, and Airy beams that curve and self-focus, opened new probes for materials and fundamental physics. Single-mode beams, though, carry limited information per measurement and suffer grating losses.

Multimode beams pack several spatial and angular momentum modes into one shot. More selection rules and scattering details become readable from a single exposure. The demonstration pushes structured neutron science toward richer experiments on topological materials. Facilities gain a way to extract more from scarce neutron beam time.
arxiv-2511-07762:
Shakibul Chowdhury speeds up tracking how polarized light twists around a spinning black hole. Near Kerr black holes, gravity bends photon paths and rotates their polarization angle. Modelers need that rotation computed accurately to read telescope images, but strict integrators run slowly.

A compact reproducible integrator advances photon momentum and polarization together. Median angle errors stay near a tenth of a degree across spins up to ninety percent of maximum, with a fivefold or better speedup. Only near the extreme spin limit do errors grow modestly. Faster transport lets simulation grids cover more black hole and plasma cases per study.
arxiv-2511-08162:
Stefan Hetzl and Johannes Kloibhofer prove an abstract fixed point theorem for Horn formula equations in first order logic. These equations restrict how predicate variables may appear, and they show up across computer science applications. Their theorem concerns equations equipped with a least fixed point operator, a standard way to express definitions that build up in stages.

The result is abstract because it works for a general semantics that includes the standard one as a special case. That generality pays off in several corollaries across computational logic. Applications range from the logical foundations of program verification to inductive theorem proving, giving those fields a shared fixed point principle.
arxiv-2511-08262:
Ezra Gayawan and co-authors examine how women's empowerment relates to childhood vaccine reach across Nigeria over space and time. Vaccination prevents much child illness and death, yet gender gaps can limit mothers freedom in health choices. Four waves of the Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey supply the data behind two women power indices, covering household choice participation and personal health care choice.

A structured spatio temporal model estimates how much regional vaccine disparity follows from empowerment and predicts reach at a fine administrative level. Five indicators are tracked, from BCG and measles doses to zero dose and complete basic reach. Women power generally raises uptake, though effect sizes vary geographically.
arxiv-2511-08362:
Gordon Ma and Dimitris Angelakis recast qubit lean quantum tuning as a question about the minimal geometry an objective function truly needs. Quadratic binary tuning problems depend only on one and two body statistics, yet standard variational quantum algorithms wander exponentially large Hilbert spaces with far wider circuits than the variable count demands. The authors ask what representation the objective itself requires, independent of any algorithm.

Enforcing consistency among pairwise statistics defines a convex body, the level two Sherali Adams polytope, capturing exactly the needed information. Their pipeline uses a logarithmic width circuit for pairwise moments, a differentiable projection for local feasibility, and a maximum entropy decoder. On large Max-Cut instances it reaches near optimal ratios at shallow depth.
arxiv-2511-08462:
Claire Wang, Ziyang Li, Saikat Dutta, and Mayur Naik present QLCoder, an agent system that writes CodeQL security queries automatically from vulnerability records. Static analysis can hunt vulnerable code patterns, but writing good queries demands rare combined expertise in security and program analysis. QLCoder places a language model inside a synthesis loop with execution feedback, guided by a custom interface to a language server for syntax help and a retrieval database for examples and documentation.

Evaluation covers one hundred seventy six known vulnerabilities across one hundred eleven Java projects. For over half of them, the system produces a correct query that flags the vulnerable version and not the patched one. A plain agent baseline manages only about a tenth, showing the value of the structured guidance.
arxiv-2511-08862:
Justin Hom and thirty co-authors vet the guide stars that future space telescopes will lean on to photograph Earth-like planets. The Roman Coronagraph alternates between its science target and a bright reference star. It is a technology demonstrator for the planned Habitable Worlds Observatory. The dark hole it digs is only as good as that star.

Reference stars must be very bright, tiny in apparent size, and single, criteria that shrink the candidate pool to massive stars, which often have companions. From a literature review of ninety-five stars the team lists forty primary and eighteen reserve candidates usable by both missions. Fresh adaptive optics imaging and speckle interferometry find no new companions among them. The authors stress that deeper high-contrast checks are still needed before launch planning can rest.
arxiv-2511-09562:
Hannah Park and Dasaem Jeong present WaveRoll, a browser library for comparing several automatic music transcriptions side by side. Transcription systems turn audio into MIDI, and judging them means contrasting multiple outputs from the same recording. Existing viewers rarely align several piano rolls for direct comparison.

WaveRoll displays multiple MIDI tracks on one time-aligned grid with synchronized playback. Users can compare pitch and timing, spot missed or extra notes, and see onset and offset differences and section-level patterns. The authors expect the tool to aid model evaluation and error analysis, and to help readers understand model behavior better. The library is open source, so transcription researchers can adopt it directly in the browser.
arxiv-2511-09862:
Yi-Ming Zhu and eight co-authors introduce CPISM, a simulation program for the Cool Planet Imaging Coronagraph aboard the China Space Station Telescope. High-contrast imaging aims to photograph planets beside bright stars, and good target selection plus observation planning are essential. CPISM models targets, imaging, observational effects, detector response, and data products in separate modules that can be swapped and combined.

Simulations of a bright star matched theoretical expectations, confirming the tool's accuracy. The program can include instrumental noise, cosmic rays, and other effects, and supports signal-to-noise analysis and high-contrast photometry. Its outputs are meant to improve observation planning and scientific return for the coronagraph mission, aiding future exoplanet discovery and characterization work.
arxiv-2511-10062:
Muhammad Kashif, Shaf Khalid, Alberto Marchisio, Nouhaila Innan, and Muhammad Shafique present FAQNAS, an architecture search approach for hybrid quantum neural networks that counts classical computing cost as a design goal. These hybrids pair parameterized quantum circuits with classical layers, and in the current noisy era they are mostly trained on classical simulators, where floating point operations set the runtime. Ignoring that cost produces designs that are accurate but impractical.

FAQNAS treats design as multi-objective optimization over accuracy and operations, using a genetic method. On five benchmarks from handwritten digits to medical and wine data, quantum operations drove accuracy gains while classical cost stayed roughly fixed.
