Pareto-optimal designs often matched heavier baselines at far lower cost, making cost-awareness a practical rule for hybrid quantum design.
arxiv-2511-10262:
He Zhang and seven co-authors introduce MTR-DuplexBench, a benchmark for full-duplex speech models that can talk and listen at once across many conversational rounds. Existing benchmarks test single exchanges, while real full-duplex dialogue has blurred turn boundaries and context that drifts during inference. The new benchmark segments continuous dialogue into discrete turns so each round can be scored separately.

Evaluation covers conversational features, dialogue quality, instruction following, and safety, rather than fluency alone. Current full-duplex models struggled to hold performance steady across rounds and dimensions, which the authors take as evidence the benchmark is needed. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2511-10362:
Joel Wendin and Claudio Altafini survey what is known about training deep linear neural networks, in an article accepted by SIAM Review. These are networks built only from matrix multiplication, with no activation functions, trained on a simple squared error loss. Stripped down this way, training can be studied exactly as a set of differential equations.

The survey describes the loss landscape in detail, with its many global minima and saddle points but no local minima. It explains how the training equations preserve certain quantities and how a quotient space view tidies the picture of critical points. Readers also get results on stability at saddle points and on what a training run actually learns.
arxiv-2511-10562:
Emmanuel Asiedu Brempong leads a team of ten introducing Oya, a deep learning system that estimates rainfall across most of the globe in real time. The need is sharpest in the Global South, where ground rain gauges are sparse and existing satellite products, often built on a single infrared channel, can err badly at short timescales.

Oya uses the full visible and infrared spectrum from geostationary satellites and works in two stages, with one U-Net model detecting rain and a second estimating how much fell. Training used high-resolution radar-radiometer data from the GPM mission, with pretraining on an established satellite product for robustness. Drawing on several satellites for quasi-global coverage, Oya beat competitive regional and global baselines in the team's tests.
arxiv-2511-10662:
Tamas Almos Vami and Danyi Zhang report a search for microscopic black holes and electroweak sphalerons in proton-proton collisions recorded by the CMS detector from 2016 to 2018. Both phenomena would produce distinctive bursts of many jets and leptons, and both remain unobserved predictions of speculative theories.

The analysis uses a new tool that identifies events by their kinematic features, based on distances between events in phase space. No signal appeared, so the team set model-independent limits on new physics producing multiple jets and leptons. In models with large extra dimensions, semiclassical black holes below roughly 9 to 11 TeV in mass are excluded, well beyond earlier sensitivity. A dedicated sphaleron search also capped how often the transition can occur above its energy threshold.
arxiv-2511-10762:
Nikolaos Tsagkas and six co-authors address a robustness problem in robot vision. Policies trained on features from large pretrained vision models inherit everything those features encode, including distractors, so a change of scenery can break a policy that performed well in training.

Their mechanism, Attentive Feature Aggregation, is a lightweight trainable pooling layer that learns to attend to task-relevant visual cues and ignore the rest, even semantically rich distractions. Experiments in simulation and on real robots show policies using it significantly outperform standard pooling when scenes are perturbed, with no expensive dataset augmentation and no fine-tuning of the vision model itself. The authors conclude that discarding extraneous visual information is a crucial step toward dependable visuomotor policies.
arxiv-2511-11062:
Dor Shmilovich, Tony Wu, and their colleagues present LiteAttention, a way to speed up the transformer models that generate video step by step. Attention cost grows fast with size, so these models can be very slow. Guessing which parts to skip at each step costs time and can err, while fixed skip patterns cannot adapt as the steps unfold.

The authors found that skip patterns stay alike across nearby steps: blocks judged useless at one step tend to stay useless at the next. LiteAttention marks such blocks early and carries the skip choice forward. Built on a fast attention kernel, it gave large speedups on real video models.
arxiv-2511-11162:
Zhanpeng Wang, Shuting Cao, and their colleagues present OT-ALD, a faster way to translate an image from one style domain to another using paired diffusion models. The standard bridge adds noise to a source image, then denoises it in the target style, but the two latent spaces do not line up, which skews the path and slows sampling. Keeping cycle consistency while fixing that mismatch is the challenge.

Their method first computes an optimal transport map, the cheapest way to reshape one spread into another, between the two latent spreads. Denoising then starts from the mapped spread. Error analysis confirms the mismatch is removed, and tests show faster, better translation.
arxiv-2511-11362:
Prabodh Katti, Houssem Sifaou, and their colleagues analyze fine-tuning large models directly on edge devices without backpropagation. Edge systems must adapt to new tasks under tight memory, but standard training stores layer activations and optimizer states, which caps the model size that fits on a chip. A zeroth-order method called MeZO estimates gradients from forward passes alone and drops that storage entirely.

The authors first derive how model size limits compare under the two training styles. Simulations then confirm that MeZO holds an accuracy edge under fixed on-device memory, as long as enough wall-clock time is allowed for the slower fine-tuning to finish.
arxiv-2511-11462:
Kevin Chen, Kenneth Parker, and Anish Arora present MoCap2Radar, a transformer model that synthesizes micro-Doppler radar signatures from motion capture data. Radar can sense movement without cameras, but radar data are scarce, while motion capture of human movement is plentiful. Their process treats the translation as a windowed sequence-to-sequence task, with the model jointly reading spatial links among body markers and motion over time.

Real-world tests produce visually and numerically plausible radar spectrograms, and the model generalizes to new cases. Ablation tests show it learned both how body-part motion maps to Doppler shifts and how body parts relate in space. The method costs far less compute than physics-based radar simulation.
arxiv-2511-11562:
Afra Feyza Akyürek and twenty-three co-authors introduce PRBench, a benchmark that grades AI models on real professional work in finance and law instead of academic exam questions. Open-ended, high-stakes tasks in these fields are where errors carry real economic cost, yet most evaluations ignore them.

PRBench holds eleven hundred expert-written tasks and more than nineteen thousand scoring criteria, written by one hundred eighty-two professionals with law degrees, finance credentials, or long experience. Tasks span one hundred fourteen countries, reflecting actual workflows. As the largest public rubric-based benchmark for both fields, it gives model builders a harder, more honest test of professional reasoning.
arxiv-2511-11762:
Ben Zelenskiy and four co-authors present the Sumudu Neural Operator. It learns to solve differential equations, using the Sumudu transform. That transform is a lesser-known cousin of the Laplace transform. Neural operators learn maps between whole families of equations. The transform's polynomial structure gives a fresh way to build them.

Inputs are split into coefficients and moved into Sumudu space. The operator works there, then returns the result. Tests cover ordinary equations, such as the Duffing oscillator and the Lorenz system. They also cover partial equations, including Burgers, diffusion, and the Brusselator. The method beats the Fourier neural operator on several partial tasks. It posts the lowest error on beam and diffusion problems.
arxiv-2511-11862:
Jiafeng Chen and four co-authors design selection rules that choose many items at once from noisy measurements, borrowing strength across the whole list instead of judging each case alone. In their Gaussian sequence model, each candidate has an unknown value, a known noise level, and a known cost, and the decision maker wants the subset with the best total payoff.

Inspired by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, they build ASSURE, an almost unbiased estimator of any proposed rule's expected utility. Optimizing the estimate over a class of rules yields compound decisions with asymptotic guarantees. Hiring, screening, and funding panels all face compound selection under noise, and principled borrowing of strength beats case-by-case gut calls.
arxiv-2511-11962:
Carlos Mosquera and four co-authors study virtual object handling on tabletops in mixed reality. Bare hands are compared with a physical proxy shaped like a knob. Tasks cover translation, rotation and scaling. Combined three-degree moves and full four-degree compound tasks are included. All work happens on real surfaces.

Hand interaction needed repeated corrections on compound tasks. Completion times grew as a result. Yet rotation errors were oddly smaller there than in rotation-only tasks. The cylindrical tangible rests stably on the table. It showed clearly distinct performance patterns. Designers of mixed reality workspaces gain hard evidence here. A cheap physical prop can beat empty-hand control for precise work.
arxiv-2511-12162:
Shuo Yin and five co-authors improve deep hashing, a method that turns images or other items into short codes so similar items can be found fast. Methods that assign a fixed target code to each class work well, but random targets ignore how classes relate in meaning. Two-stage fixes add cost and mismatch.

Their method, Center-Reassigned Hashing, learns the neural hash function and reassigns target codes from a preset codebook at the same time, in one end-to-end process. The targets thus adapt to the data and carry semantic links without a separate phase. A multi-head design also lets the centers capture richer structure.
arxiv-2511-12262:
Mario Bertaina, Matteo Battisti and the JEM-EUSO collaboration report what Mini-EUSO, a telescope on the International Space Station, implies for watching ultra-high-energy cosmic rays from space. The instrument has viewed Earth through a window in the Russian segment since 2019, mapping the night side in near ultraviolet light.

Mini-EUSO uses Fresnel lenses and thousands of photon-counting channels to record faint flashes at several time scales. Its observations test whether a space detector can study cosmic rays, air showers and related events from orbit. The authors draw lessons for larger planned missions, including how background light and instrument response affect what such a telescope can see.
arxiv-2511-12462:
Yuzhou Liu, Jiarui Liu and Wanfu Gao propose a feature selection method. It is for data that carry several views and several labels at once. An item may be described by text, image and sound, and tagged in many ways. Choosing which features to keep is hard because features, views and labels interact, and redundant features can hurt the final subset.

Their network uses multiple attention heads: each head models links inside one view, while cross-attention between heads captures how views complement each other. Feature-label links are modeled directly, and a redundancy term penalizes keeping features that repeat each other. The goal is a smaller subset that keeps the useful, distinct information for learning.
arxiv-2511-12562:
Suhaib Ardah, Francisco J. Profito and Daniele Dini develop a three-dimensional numerical method for problems at interfaces, where several physical effects meet and geometry can be irregular. Standard discretization often forces a trade between flexible meshes and strict conservation of flow. Their method aims to keep both.

The framework adapts the element-based finite volume method. That method merges the geometric flexibility of finite elements with the conservation focus of finite volumes. New scheme tools handle unstructured meshes. They also handle parametric shape functions, flux integrals and body-fitted curved coordinates. Lubrication-driven benchmark problems show the method capturing intricate transport, strong coupling between fields and large scale differences at interfaces.
arxiv-2511-12662:
Hongbin Huang and ten co-authors present Hi-Reco, a system for digital humans that can hold a conversation in real time. The system joins three parts: a realistic three-dimensional avatar, speech synthesis that carries a persona and emotion, and dialogue generation grounded in stored knowledge. A pipeline that runs its parts in parallel keeps delays low, so the avatar can answer without awkward pauses during live interaction.

Hi-Reco supports wake word detection, expressive prosody in its voice, and context-aware replies. Two retrieval ideas help it stay on track: past conversation history is folded into new answers, and questions are routed by intent to the right knowledge source. The authors aim the system at immersive uses in communication, education, and entertainment, where a digital person must look convincing and respond quickly at the same time.
arxiv-2511-12762:
John R. Thorstensen and nine co-authors report new observations of five little-studied cataclysmic binary stars in the southern sky. In these systems a white dwarf pulls gas from a companion star, causing outbursts and flickering. Their data come from the South African Astronomical Observatory, backed by archival space telescope photometry. Each of the five stars gets a fresh classification, an orbital period, or both, from spectra and light curves.

One is a dwarf nova with a five-hour orbit and a visible mid-M companion. Another is confirmed as a magnetic system. A third behaves like an SW Sextantis novalike with a superhump period, and a fourth is an eclipsing novalike whose light dips every hour and a half. The fifth cycles between high and low states and lately mimics a U Gem dwarf nova. Such studies fill in the census of interacting binaries.
arxiv-2511-12962:
Daniel Cavadia builds EndoSight AI, a system that finds and outlines gastrointestinal polyps while an endoscopy is still running. Polyps are the precursors endoscopists hunt because removing them prevents colorectal cancer, yet small or flat ones are easy to miss on a moving video feed. EndoSight both localizes polyps and delineates their boundaries, trained and tested on the public Hyper-Kvasir dataset. It reached a mean average precision of about eighty-eight percent for detection and a Dice score up to sixty-nine percent for segmentation.

Speed is the other half of the design: over thirty-five frames per second on graphics hardware, fast enough to overlay guidance live. Training used clinically relevant metrics and a thermal-aware procedure intended to keep the model robust and efficient. Cavadia presents it as a deployable assistant for endoscopy suites.
arxiv-2511-13462:
The DUNE Collaboration reports first results on charged pion interactions with argon in the ProtoDUNE Single-Phase device at Fermilab. A beam of positive pions with kinetic energy in the mid hundreds of mega-electronvolts struck liquid argon. Results cover absorption, charge exchange, and the remaining inelastic channels as separate outcomes.

No group had measured pion-argon absorption in this energy range before, and charge exchange had never been taken at all. The data feed directly into models for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment and the Short Baseline Neutrino program. Better pion modeling sharpens how event generators handle final-state effects and secondary pion collisions inside liquid argon.
arxiv-2511-13562:
James Hallam and João Magueijo ask what happens to unimodular gravity when matter couples to a second metric instead of the gravity metric itself. Unimodular gravity turns the cosmological constant into a fixed integration constant set by a volume rule. Here both metrics, linked through a scalar field, carry their own volume constraint.

In the two-metric theory the scalar does not propagate, yet it still drives a non-trivial expansion history. Rewritten with one metric, the vacuum term need not stay constant, and the expansion can cross the phantom divide by a purely frame-dependent effect. Formalisms that agreed for one metric split apart once the second metric enters.
arxiv-2511-13662:
Benoît Jeanson, Mathieu Tanneau, and Simon Tindemans tackle optimal transmission switching with de-energization, a power grid problem that allows for local blackouts after failures. Grid operators switch lines to ease congestion, but losing elements can cut connectivity in ways standard models miss. The problem matters for real sub-transmission work at the French operator RTE, yet barely appears in the literature.

Their new mixed-integer formulation captures post-failure loss of connectivity without extra binary variables. That lean model seeds a fast iterative heuristic. Where top solvers often failed to find even trivial answers in fair time, the heuristic found high-quality feasible plans one hundred to one thousand times faster in their experiments.
arxiv-2511-13862:
Ryan J. French and six co-authors examine fast downward flows seen in the ribbons of an X9-class solar flare, the strongest class of solar eruption. Using the IRIS spacecraft, they tracked flows of 150 to 217 kilometers per second during a flare on October 3, 2024. The speeds stayed high for over fifteen minutes after the flare began.

The team splits the event into two stages with different causes. Early downflows match peaks in hard X-ray and ultraviolet light, pointing to dense plasma condensing as energy dumps into the lower atmosphere. Later flows persist after those signals fade, matching rain falling along flare loops instead. Pulsations near fifty seconds run through both stages, likely from waves in the magnetic arcade.
arxiv-2511-14362:
Hang Ding, Yilun Zhao, Tiansheng Hu, and two co-authors built SciRAG, an open tool that writes answers from the science literature. Papers pour out so fast that sound sums of what is known are hard to make. The usual fetch-and-write tools skip the cite graph, cope poorly with hard queries, and give chopped answers that are hard to check. SciRAG adds three parts aimed at those gaps.

First, its fetch step can switch between one-by-one and side-by-side search as the query needs. Next, a cite-aware step uses the cite graph to sort and sift the source papers. Last, an outline-led write step plans the answer, picks at it, and polishes it. On tests such as QASA and ScholarQA it beat past tools on facts and on sum quality.
arxiv-2511-14562:
Wei-Juan Zhang and Dimitri Leemans give group theory conditions for a coset geometry to be a chiral hypertope. Hypertopes are highly symmetric incidence structures. Checking chirality used to require building the full incidence graph, which grows too large for many cases. The authors work instead with maximal parabolic subgroups of the geometry.

Their conditions let researchers test chirality from group data alone. Computers can then handle much larger coset geometries than before. The result also raises hope for general theorems about chiral hypertopes. Readers get a practical test and a theoretical shortcut in one. The paper serves specialists in incidence geometry and group theory.
arxiv-2511-14862:
Phuong N. Hoàng, Kevin McGoff, and three co-authors propose a transport-based way to compare networks. Their joining of two graphs glues them into one product graph that keeps each graph's degree structure intact. The cheapest joining, under a cost for matching vertex labels, gives a distance-like score between the two networks.

That best joining problem turns out to be a linear program with a well-shaped solution set. The authors prove basic properties and tie the problem to the famous graph isomorphism question, working out when families of graphs can be told apart this way. The method offers a principled tool for fingerprinting networks in chemistry, biology, and security.
arxiv-2511-15262:
Tomas Espana, Yadh Hafsi, and two co-authors train a reinforcement learning agent to execute large trades inside a simulated order book. Optimal execution means dribbling a big order into the market slowly enough to avoid moving the price against yourself. Historical data cannot answer what-if questions about different pacing, so a simulator must supply the feedback.

The team uses a queue-reactive model, which reproduces how order flow responds and how price impact fades, to generate realistic book dynamics. A double deep Q-network agent, watching time, inventory, price, and depth, learns the pacing policy there. Its performance is checked against established execution benchmarks, testing whether model-free learning beats parametric rules.
arxiv-2511-15362: R. V. Romanik and four co-authors present results for the pair distribution function of the cell fluid model with Curie-Weiss interaction. The pair distribution describes how particle positions correlate in the fluid. As supporting results, the authors also calculate one particle and two particle densities for the same model. The work contributes exact style statistical mechanics results for a mean field fluid model that serves as a test case for theory.
arxiv-2511-15462:
Amir Hossein Kargaran, Nafiseh Nikeghbal, Jing Yang, and Nedjma Ousidhoum analyze how peer review worked at ICLR, a leading machine learning meeting, in 2024 and 2025. Peer review decides which papers are accepted, and rebuttal is the stage where authors answer reviewer doubts. With submissions rising fast, the team wanted hard evidence on what actually moves scores.

They studied score changes, timing, engagement, and the text of reviews and replies. First scores and the scores of fellow reviewers best predicted later changes. Rebuttals helped most for borderline papers, where a careful reply could shift views. The findings offer practical guidance for authors and for fairer review design, with data shared openly.
arxiv-2511-15662:
Kostiantyn Drach, Zhi Fu, Vadim Kaloshin, Zhiqiang Li, and Carlangelo Liverani prove a central-limit style result for expanding circle maps, smooth maps that stretch the circle so distances grow. A Lyapunov exponent measures that average stretching rate along an orbit. For periodic points, points that return to their start after a fixed number of steps, the exponents vary from orbit to orbit.

Collecting the exponents of all periodic points of a given period gives an empirical distribution. The authors show that distribution sits close to a normal, bell-shaped distribution. The gap shrinks as the period grows. That gives a version of the Central Limit Theorem for these finite periodic orbits.
arxiv-2511-15962:
Zichuan Wang interprets a change-of-weights operation for triangulated modules in p-adic Hodge theory. These modules, built from a Frobenius map and a Galois group action, encode Galois representations, and changing weights shifts a key parameter of the family. An existence result for the operation in families was shown by Zhixiang Wu, and Wang revisits it in the trianguline case, where representations split into triangular steps.

In that case the operation is interpreted as a pullback, with a discussion of the related stacks that parametrize such objects. Wang then proves the operation intertwines well with translation functors, through a one-to-one correspondence defined by Yiwen Ding, in the non-critical crystabelline case.
arxiv-2511-16062:
Yoonhyuk Choi, Jiho Choi, and Jiwoo Kang propose GESC, a graph neural network for graphs where neighbors often differ. Graph networks excel when neighbors are alike. Under heterophily, mixed signals reinforce themselves and clash in phase, hurting results. Past magnetic and gauge-based networks still mix messages additively. The authors name that mixing as a main driver of oversmoothing under gauge transport.

GESC swaps additive mixing for projection-based interference cancellation. A phase step first aligns signals. A rank-one projection then suppresses parts parallel to a node own signal before attention, and a sign-aware gate regulates neighbors aligned against it. Across diverse graph benchmarks, GESC beat recent leading models throughout.
arxiv-2511-16162:
Yuting Lu, Ziliang Wang, and five co-authors propose a training method that keeps medical image segmentation stable under distribution shifts and attacks. Clinical models must not collapse when scans differ from training data, but the standard fix, adversarial training, trades clean accuracy for robustness and is costly to tune. Their method instead injects small zero-mean noise at multiple layers during training.

That noise teaches a frequency-bias prior that steers internal representations away from noise-sensitive directions. A selective wavelet reconstruction step then suppresses noise-sensitive frequency bands, enhances directional structures and shape cues, and stabilizes boundary responses in the input or feature branch. The backbone-agnostic framework adds little inference cost and improved clean and robust scores on CT and ultrasound data.
arxiv-2511-16362:
Félix Benoist and Pablo Sartori model how protein complexes assemble accurately and quickly inside the cell, where many shared parts must find the right partners despite thermal noise. Energy-based toy models miss the role of kinetics, so the authors extend a heteropolymer growth model to the retrieval of two-dimensional structures.

In the extended model, assembly runs into strong speed and encoding bottlenecks: structures either form slowly or cannot be specified reliably. Raising the connectivity of just a small fraction of components suppresses both bottlenecks at once. Controlling a few critical binding events kinetically thus explains how large complexes assemble on time, and points to a unifying role for the assembly factors that guide real protein construction.
arxiv-2511-16462:
L. J. Milligan describes the systems that detect and measure backgrounds for SABRE South, a dark matter experiment hunting the annual rate modulation reported by DAMA/LIBRA. SABRE runs twin detectors in both hemispheres so seasonal and site effects can be separated from a true dark matter signal, and the southern detector sits in Australia's Stawell Underground Physics Laboratory.

Knowing the background is essential, and SABRE South doubles as the first large detector in its laboratory, measuring radiogenic and cosmogenic radiation there. Its veto system pairs a 12-kiloliter liquid scintillator vessel read by 18 photomultiplier tubes with a plane of plastic scintillator modules above it. The plane catches cosmic-ray muons and locates them to about five centimeters.
arxiv-2511-16662:
Eddie Pokming Sheung and five co-authors present TriDiff-4D, a pipeline that generates animated 3D avatars from text descriptions in seconds rather than hours. Earlier 4D generation methods suffered from flicker, geometric drift, awkward motion, and heavy optimization costs, which kept controllable 4D content out of practical reach.

TriDiff-4D first creates a canonical 3D avatar and a motion sequence from the prompt. A second diffusion model then re-poses triplane representations of the avatar frame by frame, following the motion in an autoregressive way that allows sequences of arbitrary length. Learning separate structure and motion priors from large 3D and motion datasets gives temporal consistency and accurate geometry. Experiments show clear gains over existing methods in speed, motion quality, and visual fidelity.
arxiv-2511-16762:
Mohamed Amin Loualidi, Salah Nasri, and Maximiliano A. Rivera present a model in which neutrino masses arise radiatively at three loops and dark matter comes along for free. Two new scalar doublets couple asymmetrically to vectorlike lepton doublets, and one doublet's neutral components supply the dark matter candidates.

The mass splitting between those neutral components feeds the neutrino mass generation, while the singly charged scalars of both doublets mix and are essential to the loop. A single generation of vectorlike leptons already yields two nonzero neutrino masses, thanks to the asymmetric Yukawa structure. The authors test the model against dark matter phenomenology, neutrino oscillation data, and the flavor-violating decay of a muon to an electron plus a photon. They find compatibility with current bounds and predictions within experimental reach.
arxiv-2511-17162:
Sara Zuppiroli and eight co-authors formalize the Belief-Desire-Intention model of rational agents as a reusable ontology, a structured vocabulary for the semantic web. The BDI model, which explains action through beliefs, desires, and intentions, is a cornerstone of artificial intelligence and cognitive science. Yet it had rarely been expressed in interoperable knowledge formats that machines can share and reason over.

The ontology is built as a modular design pattern, aligned with foundational ontologies, and captures how the three mental components relate and change. Two experiments test it in action. In one, the ontology grounds a large language model's reasoning, improving its coherence. In the other, it plugs into the Semas platform, where data triples and agent mental states convert into each other. The authors offer it as a bridge between declarative knowledge and agent behavior.
arxiv-2511-17362:
Linxiang Su and András Balogh defend CLIP, the widely used image-text matching model, against adversarial images, without retraining it. Adversarial fine-tuning is prohibitively expensive, and earlier test-time defenses gave limited protection. Their method, ATAC, works inside CLIP's embedding space at test time. It measures how the embedding drifts under image augmentations, infers the direction that restores the true semantics, and corrects the embedding, guided by how consistent those drifts are in angle.

Across a wide range of benchmarks, ATAC raised robustness well above previous test-time methods, by nearly 50 percent on average in the authors' comparisons, at minimal extra computing cost. It kept state-of-the-art robustness in extreme settings and even resisted adaptive attacks designed against it. The authors present embedding-space correction as a new, efficient paradigm for test-time defense.
arxiv-2511-17462:
Ryan Engel and three co-authors scale up a popular approach to building investment portfolios from asset-pricing factors. Conditional autoencoders estimate latent factors from firm characteristics in an interpretable way, but studies usually cap the factor count near five, fearing that more factors hurt performance. The authors pair a high-dimensional autoencoder with an uncertainty-aware selection step. Three quantile forecasting models each rank the factors by how predictably they behave, and only the most predictable subset is kept for portfolio construction.

Pruning this way delivered substantial gains in risk-adjusted performance for every forecasting model tried. Because the models' predictions were largely uncorrelated, a performance-weighted ensemble of them beat each individual model on the Sharpe, Sortino, and Omega ratios. The paper offers factor selection by forecast uncertainty as a general tool for data-driven portfolio design.
arxiv-2511-17962:
Ziheng Jia, Linhan Cao, Jinliang Han, and six co-authors pre train large multimodal models to judge image and video quality. In that task, earlier models each handled one job and were fully fine tuned, making them brittle. Their VITAL series centers training on the vision encoder instead.

They build a training set of millions of image text pairs with machine made labels checked by a scrutiny process, the largest for this task. Multi task training improves both numeric quality scores and written quality explanations. New model variants then need only a tiny warm up to match fully trained ones, making the family cheap to extend.
arxiv-2511-18162:
Sheridan Feucht, Byron Wallace, and David Bau show that language models keep meaning and surface form in separable parts of their internal activations. Earlier work found attention heads that copy word meanings and others that copy the literal token, and the authors use those heads to transform hidden states into concept and token subspaces.

In the concept subspace, classic analogy arithmetic works far better, with much higher nearest neighbor accuracy than raw activations. In the token subspace, similar arithmetic reveals surface relations, such as verb form changes. The results give a concrete way to read and manipulate what kind of information a model carries at a given point.
arxiv-2511-18562:
Xunlei Qian and Yue Xing test how split conformal prediction holds up when inputs are attacked. Conformal methods give coverage pledges with no distribution claims, but they rest on data being exchangeable — a state attacks break. The team study both pledge validity and set size when test inputs face adversarial tweaks.

Theory ties pledge shifts to the attack strength used at calibration time. Coverage moves in a steady, one way fashion with that strength, so a set nonzero attack at calibration can tune coverage under attack at test. Model training with attacks gets the same check. Tests back the theory, and target coverage can hold across a range of test attack strengths. The work gives knobs for sound sets under attack.
arxiv-2511-19462:
E. J. Thompson builds a dark matter sector inside a grand unified framework based on the SU(5) symmetry group. The dark matter ignores the unbroken Standard Model forces and couples only to the broken directions, the heavy X and Y leptoquark bosons. An exact twofold symmetry keeps the dark matter particle stable.

Careful projector definitions separate the unbroken and broken parts of the theory, and the heavy bosons are then removed to leave effective interactions. A loop effect links the dark matter to gluons, while color neutrality is proved. Production in the early universe runs through ultraviolet freeze-in or weaker channels, consistent with cold dark matter behavior.
arxiv-2511-19562:
Abraham Itzhak Weinberg lets simulated agents teach each other a shared language, guided by trust. In multi-agent learning, communication usually emerges slowly as each agent learns alone, and the resulting protocols can be poor. His framework, TSLEC, adds explicit teaching, where agents pass successful strategies to peers.

Learned trust scores weight whose lessons get accepted, filtering out bad teaching. Across one hundred episodes and thirty random seeds, trust-based learning reaches convergence about twenty-four percent faster than independent emergence, a strongly significant gap. The protocols stay compositional and keep decoding accuracy high when goals shift, and trust scores track teaching quality closely.
arxiv-2511-19662:
Eric R. Bittner analyzes two coupled oscillators, each in contact with a squeezed bath, a reservoir engineered to carry nonclassical noise. Squeezing is a tool for controlling irreversible quantum dynamics, and the Gaussian formalism lets him solve the covariance motion in closed form. Entropy flow between the modes is the central quantity.

Squeezing creates entropy only at second order in the unusual correlations, a nonlinear effect absent with ordinary heat baths. The dynamics also show a fan of exceptional points separating a narrow zone of oscillatory motion from broad zones where one mode is purely damped. Symmetry survives only when the two baths squeeze opposite quadratures.
arxiv-2511-19762:
Jeremy Sakstein and Bhuvnesh Jain recount how the first joint detection of gravitational waves and light from a merging pair of neutron stars, in August 2017, transformed the study of dark energy. Telescopes worldwide caught the event, and the two signals arrived almost together after a journey of over a hundred million light years. That near-simultaneity shows the speed of gravity and the speed of light agree to within one part in a quadrillion, an extraordinarily tight match.

Many theories that explained cosmic acceleration by modifying gravity predicted a mismatch in those speeds. So whole classes of them were excluded at a stroke, along with models coupling dark energy to matter in those ways. Written as a congress proceeding, the piece explains how one event redrew the map of viable dark energy theories.
arxiv-2511-19962:
Manoj Kummini and Abhiram Subramanian study when a special variety inside projective space must be a complete intersection. Their objects are codimension-two subcanonical local complete intersection varieties, whose canonical bundle is a power of the hyperplane bundle. The question is what extra conditions force such a variety to be cut out in the simplest possible way.

Working with the ideal sheaf and a chosen integer shift, the authors give sufficient conditions on the first deficiency module that ensure the variety is a complete intersection. They also prove that smooth codimension-two varieties with the 3-Buchsbaum property, inside projective spaces of dimension at least six, are complete intersections. The results sharpen known structure tests for these varieties.
arxiv-2511-20062:
Fierobe, Kaloshin, and Sorrentino ask whether a billiard table's shape is fixed by its bounce lengths. Their 2025 paper studies convex tables close to an ellipse. A billiard ball travels straight, then reflects off the boundary. The set of closed path lengths is called the length spectrum. Kac's 1967 question asks if sound or lengths determine shape.

The team restricts to dihedrally symmetric domains. Such tables are symmetric across both axes and centrally. They deform a near-ellipse while keeping every length unchanged. The only allowed results are slides and rotations of the original. Any other symmetric reshaping must alter some path length. That is deformational spectral rigidity in their terms. The boundary topology used is finitely smooth Whitney type. Earlier compactness results for isospectral sets frame the work. The theorem pins down ellipses as locally unchangeable impostors. Symmetric tables near an ellipse cannot secretly differ.
arxiv-2511-20362:
Solé, Mosella-Montoro, Cardona, and colleagues build a crystal predictor that respects repeating structure. Their 2025 paper introduces PRISM for crystal property prediction. Crystals repeat their atom patterns endlessly through space. Graph networks often ignore that periodic nature. Multiscale interactions also slip past standard models.

PRISM splits the job among expert modules. Four experts encode atoms, similarity, scale, and the cell. Periodicity enters both geometry and feature encodings. Local and global information fuse inside the network. Benchmarks covered JARVIS, Materials Project, and MatBench suites. Results reached state of the art on most targets tested. Competitive baselines fell behind across those properties. The method screens candidate materials far faster than quantum calculations. Limits remain for non-periodic molecular tasks. Only one unit cell feeds the similarity expert today. Larger supercells would need retraining to include. Materials search gains a periodicity-aware engine. Code release is promised on acceptance.
arxiv-2511-20662:
Hen-Hsen Huang argues in 2025 that the famous tricks for making large language models cheaper to run were built for giant tech firms and mostly fail everyone else. Methods such as mixture-of-experts routing, speculative decoding, and retrieval pipelines assume huge graphics-card clusters and specialist teams. A hospital, school, or small company has neither, so the savings collapse into overhead, fragile setups, and wasted energy, leaving a few big providers with the gains.

Huang's agenda favours robust simplicity over squeezing out an extra 5 percent of speed at giant scale, starting with ways to retrofit trained models into leaner shapes without retraining. He also calls for light fine-tuning that keeps safety training intact, cheaper handling of long reasoning chains, and knowledge updates that skip heavy retrieval pipelines. His proposed benchmark, Overhead-Aware Efficiency, would grade methods on adoption cost, energy use, and fairness alongside raw speed.
arxiv-2511-21362:
Ulf Danielsson and Suvendu Giri draw testable predictions from dark bubble cosmology in 2025. In this string-theory picture, our universe is an expanding bubble wall inside a five-dimensional space, and dark energy emerges naturally. Most extra-dimension models make gravity stronger at short distances. The dark bubble does the opposite: below a scale near ten micrometers, gravity should fade below Newton's prediction.

Danielsson and Giri compute explicit deviations that tabletop experiments can measure at scales around 10 to the minus 5 meters. The same weakening at high energy densities drives a period of early cosmic inflation powered by radiation alone, no extra inflaton field needed. A five-dimensional black hole seeds the bubble's birth and explains today's matter content. The model predicts a small positive cosmic curvature, about 5 ten-thousandths in density terms, addressing why dark energy matters now.
arxiv-2511-21462:
M. Ablikim and the BESIII Collaboration fire antineutrons brewed inside a collider at the collider's own plumbing, in a 2025 particle physics paper. Antineutrons are superb probes of nuclear forces, free of electric-charge distortions, but they are notoriously hard to produce as a beam. The team's trick: harvest antineutrons from J/psi particle decays inside their detector, and let them strike protons in the hydrogen-rich cooling oil of the beam pipe.

Using about 10 billion recorded J/psi events at the BEPCII collider in Beijing, the collaboration measures three reactions where an antineutron hits a proton and produces three or four pions. The antineutron momenta span 200 to 1174 MeV per c, giving the first experimental data above 800 in those units. The method pioneers antineutron-nucleon studies at an electron-positron collider, opening a new supply of a rare projectile for hadron physics.
arxiv-2511-22062:
Gorji, Jana, and Petrov, physicists in Korea, hunt for black hole solutions in mimetic gravity. Mimetic gravity is a modified theory of gravity where a constrained field can mimic dark matter. It is coupled to Yang-Mills fields, the gauge fields behind the strong and weak nuclear forces. They ask which black holes exist when the Yang-Mills term is forced to stay constant, separately in the Abelian case and the richer non-Abelian SU(2) case.

In the simpler Abelian case they find a static, spherically symmetric family containing the Schwarzschild and charged Reissner-Nordström black holes as special cases. They find a stealth Schwarzschild solution carrying electric hair, extra field structure invisible in the geometry; magnetic hair proves impossible there. The non-Abelian stealth solutions, by contrast, sustain both electric and magnetic hair with arbitrary integer magnetic parameter, unlike conventional Einstein-Yang-Mills black holes.
arxiv-2511-22362:
Orazaly, Temirkhanova, and Park shrink a transformer for stress detection until it runs on modest hardware without losing accuracy. Transformers read physiological signals well but are heavy, so the team takes the multimodal Husformer architecture, which fuses body-sensor streams. Runs a structured hyperparameter search over its layers, attention heads, and dimensions, checking which modality combinations actually earn their cost on the WESAD and CogLoad datasets.

The best configuration is strikingly small: a single layer, three attention heads, and roughly 30 thousand parameters total, yet it scores 88.41 percent accuracy on WESAD and 92.61 percent on CogLoad, improving on the original Husformer by 13.83 and 6.98 points respectively in their experiments. The winning sensor pairings combine the strongest modalities rather than all of them. For wearable stress monitoring, the message is that careful tuning beats model size.
arxiv-2511-22462:
Baum, Visscher, and Förster speed up a standard calculation in quantum chemistry. GW calculations give quasiparticle energies, corresponding to the ionisation potentials and electron affinities measured in photoemission experiments. Their accuracy suffers because results converge slowly as the basis set, the functions describing the electrons, grows toward the complete basis set limit, and huge basis sets are expensive.

The authors propose a simple linear model predicting an orbital's remaining basis set error from its kinetic energy alone. They fitted it for three GW variants, including a vertex-corrected one, on a large set of molecules spanning ten elements, using reference values extrapolated from basis sets up to hextuple-zeta quality. Triple-zeta results corrected by the model land within 20 to 30 millielectronvolts of the complete basis set limit, beating the common extrapolation scheme, which errs more even from a larger quadruple-zeta start.
arxiv-2511-22562:
Bang-Jensen and colleagues study a bulk operation on directed graphs: an inversion picks a vertex set and reverses every arrow with both ends in it. When can repeated inversions of fixed set size untangle a directed graph into an acyclic one, and how many does it take? They connect this to feedback arc sets, the classic deletion route to acyclicity, and map out which versions are easy or hard.

For set size one less than the vertex count, deciding invertibility is NP-complete. For every other size, a polynomial-time algorithm decides it. Any invertible graph needs at most as many inversions as arcs for size at least two. For even sizes the count is bounded by a linear function of the feedback arc set number, while no bound exists for odd sizes. Whether a given budget suffices is NP-hard even in tournaments, though polynomial kernels exist.
arxiv-2511-22662:
Smith, Chughtai, and Nanda argue that the hard part of catching a deceptive AI is not building the detector but knowing when it is right. A detector would flag when an AI is being deceptive on purpose. It would read internal signals rather than behaviour. To test this tool, we need cases we can label with confidence as deceptive or honest. The authors contend such cases do not yet exist in usable form.

They set out the labelling obstacles, drawing on past studies and new case studies. A transcript that looks deceptive may reflect confusion, role-play, or test artefacts, not intent. Setups built to elicit deception often fail to prove the intent that defines it. Existing benchmarks blur strategic deception with neighbouring categories. Proposed fixes, such as planted-deception sandboxes, are valuable but insufficient alone. The blocker is the lack of settings where the label is beyond doubt.
arxiv-2511-22762:
Hu, Wang, and Feng build a hypothesis test for an awkward corner of modern statistics: checking whether a high-dimensional mean vector is zero when observations arrive as a dependent time series. Classical tests assume independent data, and existing high-dimensional versions lean on restrictive conditions such as Gaussianity or dependence dying after a fixed lag. Finance, biomedicine, and geology all produce such data, dependent across time and components.

Their sum-type statistic is proved asymptotically normal as dimension and sample size grow together, without Gaussian or finite-lag assumptions, making the theory portable to other high-dimensional problems with temporal dependence. The method is also far cheaper computationally than competitors, and simulations confirm the speed and performance gains. The test is powerful when departures are dense across many variables. A max-type companion for sparse signals, and its asymptotic independence from this test, is flagged as the next step.
arxiv-2511-22862:
Li and Feng adapt multimodal models to new data on the fly, when each sense has drifted differently. Test-time adaptation updates a deployed model using only unlabelled test data, but multimodal inputs suffer a coupling effect: each modality's features shift, and high-level meanings fall out of alignment across modalities. Unimodal methods, applied naively, improve some modalities while leaving the cross-modal mismatch untouched.

BriMPR attacks the problem divide-and-conquer in two stages. First it decomposes the task into unimodal alignment sub-problems, using modality-specific prompt tuning to calibrate each modality's feature distribution back toward its source distribution, for a semantic re-alignment. Then it assigns pseudo-labels to combinations of masked and complete modalities and applies inter-modal contrastive learning, with masked embedding recombination feeding information into modalities. Across corruption and domain shift benchmarks, BriMPR outperformed state-of-the-art methods; the code is released.
arxiv-2511-23162:
Nørskov and colleagues attack a bottleneck in brain research: the event-related potential, a brain response to a stimulus. It is normally recovered only by averaging many EEG trials to beat down noise. Their model, EEG2ERP, is an uncertainty-aware autoencoder that maps any number of trials to the response. It is trained with bootstrapped targets and a decoder that estimates how uncertain each recovered waveform is.

Tested in the zero-shot setting of generalizing to new subjects, the method gave substantially better estimates than conventional and robust averaging whenever only a few trials were available. This held across three public datasets. The largest, ERP CORE, holds over 50,000 trials across six paradigms from 40 subjects. The tests also covered a P300 speller brain-computer interface dataset and a face-perception dataset recorded with both EEG and MEG, pointing to shorter experiments for clinical and basic neuroscience.
arxiv-2511-23262:
Li and colleagues give vision-language models a human trick they normally lack. The models learn how to play while being tested at test time, through a framework modeled on metacognition, thinking about one's own thinking. Their MCTR splits the model into a meta-reasoning module that gradually writes down task rules, environmental patterns, and action-outcome lessons as plain-language memory. An action-reasoning module retrieves that memory to choose moves.

The action module also keeps improving its policy during play through a metacognitive test-time reinforcement learning scheme, so strategy updates as the memory grows rather than staying frozen after training. Across 45 Atari games the system adapted robustly to games it had never trained on, taking the top score in 9 of the 12 unseen games against baseline agents. Trace analysis showed its strategies maturing from trial-and-error exploration toward structured, goal-directed play.
arxiv-2512-00262:
People judge their own social mistakes by watching bystanders: a raised eyebrow, a laugh. Maria Teresa Parreira and a large team ask whether robots could use the same cues, in a 2025 study. Robots struggle to perceive such nuanced reactions.

The team explores robot error detection using instrumented bystander reactions, measuring how people respond when a robot slips up. Social competence in humans depends on decoding these subtle signals quickly. If robots can read them too, service and classroom robots could notice their own errors and repair them gracefully. Instrumented reactions turn fleeting expressions into data a robot could actually learn from.
arxiv-2512-00362:
Two-dimensional fullerene networks link carbon cages into sheets with varied bonding patterns. Qing Li, Haikuan Dong, Penghua Ying, and Zheyong Fan study monolayer carbon-24 networks in 2025, using machine-learning molecular dynamics. They examine two phases, one quasi-hexagonal and one quasi-tetragonal.

The team develops an accurate machine-learned potential within the neuroevolution potential framework. With it, they compute elasticity, both anisotropic and isotropic, and thermal transport for the two phases. Such sheets are mechanically robust, and knowing their heat and stiffness behavior guides uses in nanoelectronics and thermal management. Machine-learned potentials run far faster than direct quantum calculations at similar accuracy. Monolayers are all surface, so their transport behavior differs sharply from bulk carbon.
arxiv-2512-00462:
Drones avoiding moving obstacles must react fast with limited onboard computing. Dnyandeep Mandaokar and Bernhard Rinner present a distributionally robust acceleration control barrier filter for drone obstacle avoidance in 2025. The method keeps the drone inside safe regions while it flies.

Their filter builds a second-order control barrier function as linear half-space constraints on commanded acceleration. Distributional robustness means safety holds across a family of plausible uncertainty distributions, not just one guess. Efficient safety filters like this are a building block for drones operating near people, vehicles, and buildings. Acceleration-level control suits drones because their motors command acceleration most directly. Safety regions give the filter a clear rule: never command a move that leaves them.
arxiv-2512-00762:
Zhiyuan Gao and seven coauthors ask a striking vision question in a 2025 paper: can you see the wind in a falling leaf? Computer vision usually models how things move in video. The forces behind the motion, which are invisible, get far less study.

The team works on recovering those hidden forces from what a camera sees. A leaf twists and drifts as air pushes on it, and that path carries news about the wind field around it. If vision systems can read forces this way, they could infer weather, loads, or contact from plain video. That would widen what cameras can measure.
arxiv-2512-00862:
Ningning Chen, Weicai Ye, and Ying Jiang present HBLLM in a 2025 paper on shrinking large language models. Quantization stores model weights in fewer bits, making models cheaper to run. At the extreme of one bit per weight, quality usually drops badly.

HBLLM is a post-training method that aims to keep quality high at one bit. It uses Haar wavelet transforms, which split data into frequency layers, to add expressive power at little cost. Two grouping strategies sort weights by frequency and by importance before compression. High-fidelity one-bit models could run on much smaller devices.
arxiv-2512-00962:
Sandro Fonseca de Souza and Gilvan Augusto Alves survey Brazilian work on gaseous detectors in a 2025 report. Many particle detectors sense charged particles by the ionization they leave in gas. Resistive plate chambers are a workhorse kind of such detector, used widely in high energy physics.

The report centers on the CMS experiment at the CERN Large Hadron Collider, a huge detector that uses these chambers to catch muons. It summarizes the chambers' design, performance, maintenance, and upgrades, including improved chambers for the high-luminosity era. It also covers work on alternative gas mixtures with lower global warming potential.
arxiv-2512-01062:
Seokhyun Chin, Junghwan Park, and Woojin Cho present PIANO in a 2025 paper on forecasting rain. Precipitation nowcasting predicts rain in the next few hours and underpins early disaster warnings. Current methods are computationally expensive and restrictive, which limits access for many countries.

PIANO is a physics-informed dual neural operator that nowcasts from satellite imagery. Neural operators learn maps between fields, like cloud images to rainfall fields. Adding physics constraints aims to improve accuracy and keep predictions physically consistent. A cheap, satellite-based system could bring timely rain warnings to regions that cannot run heavy weather models.
arxiv-2512-01462:
Daniele Proverbio, Rami Katz, and Giulia Giordano review robustness in biological networks. Living systems keep key traits under stress and change. They do so in hostile, shifting settings. That strength is called robustness and resilience.

Studying it is hard due to nonlinear, complex dynamics. The review maps methods and open gaps in biology and epidemiology. It links cell networks to disease spread networks. Shared math across those scales could guide drug design and outbreak plans that hold up when conditions turn bad. The review stresses early warning traits, network signs that a system is near a flip from health to collapse or outbreak.
arxiv-2512-01562:
Simon Leszek presents TimePred, a fast way to find shift points in big data streams. Streams with many channels are hard to scan. Tests must be sound, fast, and clear to read. TimePred learns to guess each sample's time index in normalized form.

That trick turns a multi-channel hunt into a one-channel mean-shift hunt. Old proven tools can then finish the job offline. The method scales to high-volume data. It serves in fields like factory watch and finance, where a shift in regime must be caught and explained.
arxiv-2512-01662:
Amelia Hankla and co-authors explain millimeter emission from quiet active galaxies. Recent views show such emission from near the central black hole. Its source was unknown. The zone lies within parsec scales of the core.

The team says an outflow from the X-ray corona makes the signal. The outflow zone is magnetically tied to the compact corona. That tie mirrors the solar wind and corona link. If right, the signal gives a new probe of winds that feed back on galaxy growth. Millimeter data from quiet galaxies are growing fast with new arrays, so a source model now will shape how those data get read.
arxiv-2512-01862:
Game theory studies how players reason about each other's beliefs, beliefs about beliefs, and so on without end. Stuart Zoble's 2025 paper revisits the Fundamental Theorem of Epistemic Game Theory, which ties these belief hierarchies to what players can rationally do, and pushes the theorem into harder territory.

Zoble extends the result to games whose payoffs are Baire class one functions played on locally compact Polish strategy spaces. Under an assumption called Projective Determinacy, he goes further, covering payoffs that are only analytically measurable and arbitrary Polish strategy spaces. The extensions widen the range of games for which belief-based reasoning rests on proven ground.
arxiv-2512-02062:
Deep learning models drive safety-critical systems like automated driving and face recognition, yet tiny, crafted changes to an input can flip their answers. Issa Oe and four co-authors present the Superpixel Attack in 2025, a method for finding such misleading perturbations without access to the model's internals.

Attacks that work in this black-box setting are the realistic threat, since real adversaries rarely see a model's weights. Stronger attacks are also a defensive tool: they expose weaknesses before deployment so defenses can be built against them. The work belongs to the ongoing contest between those who fool vision models and those who harden them.
arxiv-2512-02162:
A cancer scan shows where a tumor is, but choosing treatment increasingly depends on the tumor's genetic mutations, which require separate testing. Rahul Mehta, Yang Lu, and Muge Karaman study in 2025 how medical images of lesions can be mapped to the somatic mutations behind them.

Imaging is the clinician's first tool, giving fast intervention and a more reliable prognosis, while genetic results arrive later in the diagnostic path. Linking the two could let image features hint at mutations before sequencing returns. Work in this direction aims to shorten the road from first scan to a treatment plan matched to the patient's tumor.
arxiv-2512-02362:
Economies are webs of firms buying from firms, but the full web is rarely observed directly. Ashwin Bhattathiripad and Vipin Veetil develop in 2025 an algorithm that reconstructs large weighted firm-to-firm production networks from two kinds of scraps: firm sizes and sector-level input-output flows.

Their four-step procedure first builds connection probabilities between all firms, using an augmented gravity model inside a logistic function where firm size plays the role of mass. Reconstructed networks let economists simulate how shocks ripple through supply chains. Getting the web right matters for judging which firms are systemically important.
arxiv-2512-02462:
Shengheng Liu and eight co-authors study phone networks that can also sense the world around them. Future mobile networks aim to mix communication with sensing in one system. A single access point sees only part of a scene, so several points working together can sense more widely.

Shared sensing across access points can be more accurate, and it keeps working if one point fails. The team blends what each point reports using Bayesian probability fusion, a principled way to weigh uncertain evidence. Better shared sensing supports location based services that need steady, trustworthy readings of people and objects nearby. The same blend of reports could serve cars, drones, and rescue teams in the field too.
arxiv-2512-02562:
Salman Ghori and three co-authors study self driving cars crossing a junction with no traffic lights. Junctions are a hard point in traffic control, where safety and smooth flow both matter. Gains in speed often come at the cost of fairness, which users need to trust the system.

Their 2025 study asks when a central controller should step in to guide autonomous agents. Timing that intervention changes safety, efficiency, and fairness at once, under strict safety limits. The findings speak to city planners who must balance fast traffic with equal treatment for every driver. The right time to step in may shift with load, speed, and the mix of cars on the road that day.
arxiv-2512-03262:
Letting AI agents write code with little oversight is now common. Songwen Zhao and co-authors ask whether that code is safe in this 2025 work. The style, called vibe coding, has engineers instruct language model agents to finish complex tasks.

The team benchmarks how often agent-made code has security flaws on real-world tasks. Such flaws could put production systems at risk if no one checks. Their results give firms a clearer view of the trade-off. Speed from agents may need review steps to stay safe in practice. Benchmarks give teams a shared yardstick before vibe coding spreads further into production code.
arxiv-2512-03462:
Malicious web links remain a top route for attacks. Berkani Khaled and Zeraoulia Rafik propose a hybrid framework to classify them in this 2025 work. Phishing and malware often arrive through crafted URLs shared by mail or chat.

Their system combines n-gram analysis of the link text with data balancing and anomaly filtering. A lightweight neural network then makes the final call in real time. Fast, accurate filters can block harmful links before users click. That protection matters for firms and home users alike. Real-time scoring is vital, since a filter that lags cannot block a click in time.
arxiv-2512-03862:
Big vision models are usually credited to sheer scale, but Oli Bridge and colleagues test what happens when the model stays small. Their 2025 preprint studies a five-million-parameter Vision Transformer trained for semantic segmentation. They ask how self-supervised pre-training, an intermediate fine-tuning stage, and final task training interact when capacity is scarce.

Across several data scales, masked image modelling pre-training and downstream fine-tuning both helped, though gains shrank as supervision grew. The surprise was the middle stage: adding classification fine-tuning reliably hurt the final result, worst exactly where pre-training helped most. Looking at the geometry of patch representations, the authors show classification training collapses spatial structure that dense prediction needs. Their lesson is pointed. In small models, whether a training stage's objective fits the final task matters more than how many stages are stacked together.
arxiv-2512-04262:
Usability flaws are cheapest to fix before launch, but expert heuristic evaluation is slow and subjective. Nolan Platt, Ethan Luchs, and Sehrish Nizamani ask whether a large language model can do the evaluating, in a 2025 software engineering preprint. Their test applies Nielsen's ten usability heuristics to real websites at the development stage.

The team ran GPT-4o over thirty open-source websites, generating more than eight hundred fifty evaluations, three independent passes per site. For detecting whether an issue exists, the model was moderately consistent, with exact agreement of eighty-four percent across passes. Severity judgments were shakier: exact agreement fell to fifty-six percent, and one reliability statistic sat near zero. The verdict is split. The model is consistent enough at spotting problems to be useful early, but its severity calls vary enough to require human oversight.
arxiv-2512-04562:
Siddharth Betala, Samuel Gleason, Ali Ramlaoui, and co-authors launch LeMat-GenBench, a shared yardstick for models that dream up new crystals. Generative models promise to speed materials discovery by proposing crystals no one has made. Yet each team grades its model its own way, so claims cannot be compared. Their 2025 arXiv paper supplies one framework, an open scoring suite, and a public leaderboard.

The bench grades models on stability, novelty, and diversity at once. The team ran a dozen recent crystal generators through the suite. A clear tension emerged: models that chase stability tend to propose safer, less novel crystals. Diversity drops as stability climbs. No model led on every axis. By making the trade-off plain, the bench steers builders toward balanced designs. It also gives experimental teams a fair map of which generator suits a given hunt.
arxiv-2512-04662:
Vittoria Mazzini, Paolo Cardarelli, Andrew Coathup, and co-authors introduce a way to measure calcium build-up inside joint cartilage without cutting the tissue open. The test tissue is the hip labrum, a fibrocartilage ring, taken from patients with osteoarthritis and hip impingement. Standard checks rely on histology, which slices the sample and sees only thin sections. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses spectral micro-CT, an X-ray scan that reads energy as well as shape.

A photon-counting detector with two energy thresholds captures two scans at once. A decomposition algorithm, tuned to the scanner's spectral response, splits calcium-like from water-like material. The result is a three-dimensional map and a volume measure of calcified zones inside intact, wax-held samples. Seeing the whole volume at once beats slicing for tracking how calcification spreads, which may guide earlier care for damaged hips.
arxiv-2512-04862:
Maria-Paola Forte, Nikos Athanasiou, Giulia Ballardini, and co-authors present BioTUCH, a method that sharpens three-dimensional body pose estimates by listening for skin touching skin. Video pose tools are strong, yet they stumble when a hand meets a face or arms cross, since cameras cannot see the contact. Wearable bioimpedance sensors measure self-contact cheaply and without cameras. Their 2025 arXiv paper fuses the two sources into one pose pipeline.

The method starts from a standard video estimate. During moments when sensors report self-contact, an optimization step refines the pose: it keeps the image fit close, stays near the first estimate, and pulls touching body points together as constraints demand. Validation shows cleaner poses in contact-heavy motion. Better ground truth for touch-rich movement could improve training data for animation, rehabilitation, and robot learning from human demos.
arxiv-2512-04962:
L. Andrew Wray, Cheng-Ju Lin, and Vincent Su test how a hybrid quantum-classical chemistry algorithm scales on chains of copper oxide plaquettes, the building units of cuprate superconductors. Sample-based quantum diagonalization draws configurations from a quantum device, then diagonalizes classically in that sampled space. It does not always converge in practical time. Their 2025 arXiv paper varies the chain from two to six plaquettes and hunts what unblocks the sampling.

Three levers mattered: wiring the qubits with all-to-all connectivity, raising the expansion order of the method, and using orbitals beyond the plain Hartree-Fock choice. Each lever eases bottlenecks, at costs that must be weighed against real hardware. Runs on the Quantinuum H2 trapped-ion machine show how device noise enters the picture. The lessons guide near-term quantum chemistry on materials that matter.
arxiv-2512-05162:
C. M. Wyss builds a mathematical theory of how meaning moves inside a large language model. The model is treated as a continuous state machine: a smooth system whose inner states evolve under probabilistic rules, with a transfer operator describing how clouds of meaning spread and settle. Under mild assumptions — compactness, thorough mixing, controlled stretching — that operator has a tidy, discrete spectrum of modes.

Wyss proves a Semantic Characterization Theorem: the leading modes carve the state space into finitely many basins of stable meaning, each describable in a logically tame language. In other words, the continuous machinery collapses into a finite, interpretable set of concepts, which may explain how discrete symbols emerge from smooth computation. The theorem is then extended to noisy versions and to slowly drifting ones, where the basin structure survives — a bridge between dynamical systems, logic, and machine learning theory.
arxiv-2512-05262:
Daniel Nezamabadi, Magnus Myreen, and Yong Kiam Tan rebuild two of Dafny's core tools so their correctness is proved, not merely trusted. Dafny is a programming language designed for verification, shipping with a compiler and a static verifier — but neither tool was itself proved correct, and soundness bugs have surfaced in both. The authors ask what it takes to give Dafny programs foundational guarantees from source code down to machine code.

They define a precise big-step semantics for a substantial imperative subset of Dafny, including recursive method calls, loops, and arrays. On it they build a verified verification-condition generator and a verified compiler targeting CakeML. Programs proved correct with the generator keep their guarantees through compilation, and CakeML's own verified compiler carries them to executable code. Everything is mechanized in the HOL4 theorem prover, and the subset is strong enough for teaching examples like McCarthy's 91 function.
arxiv-2512-05562:
Shaikh Saad and Qaisar Shafi work out what a supersymmetric grand unified model predicts for the lightest particles we barely know: neutrinos. In their SO(10) model — one gauge group embracing all forces — the leptonic sector must give the observed neutrino masses. It must also give the cosmic excess of matter over antimatter through non-thermal leptogenesis, and consistency with JUNO's recent precision measurement. The model ties those demands to a supersymmetric hybrid inflation scenario.

The authors estimate all three light neutrino masses and the three heavy right-handed masses, and the leptonic CP-violating phase. They also estimate the expected rate parameter for neutrinoless double beta decay, the process that would prove neutrinos are their own antiparticles. A statistical analysis turns estimates into likelihood ranges, and the fit agrees with JUNO's first results. The paper shows a grand unified model making itself vulnerable to experiment on several fronts at once.
arxiv-2512-05862:
Jörn Venderbos, Paola Gentile, and Carmine Ortix predict that topology sets the magnetoelectric response in two dimensional antiferromagnets. Magnetoelectric materials answer electric fields with magnetism, and magnetic fields with polarization. In flat insulators whose electrons behave like massive Dirac particles, the authors find a native effect, encoded in a quantity they call spin multipolization. Unlike the famous three dimensional version, this effect belongs to two dimensions.

They compute the response in detail in two minimal lattice models: a Néel antiferromagnet with spin-orbit coupling, and a noncollinear one with a doubled magnetic pattern and none. The effect traces back to the response of two dimensional semimetals, and so to an invariant living one dimension lower. One dimensional versions of both models show the signature too. The work suggests a design rule: build flat magnets from Dirac-like electrons, and a protected magnetoelectric coupling may come free.
arxiv-2512-06062:
S. M. Mustaqim, Anantaa Kotal, and Paul Yi demonstrate that synthetic data, the privacy conscious substitute for sharing real records, can still betray the people behind it. Institutions release generated datasets hoping the fakes protect the originals. The authors' attack needs no access to the model or the real data. The adversary collects synthetic samples, clusters them, and studies the densest neighborhoods. Those neighborhoods mirror crowded regions of the training data, enabling membership inference.

Across healthcare, finance, and other sensitive domains, the leakage is measurable, and it persists even when the generator was trained with differential privacy or other noise defenses. The weakness is structural: the distribution's shape remembers where real people were dense. The authors argue guarantees must cover neighborhood level inference too. Institutions publishing synthetic data should read it first.
arxiv-2512-06262:
Vivek Bhartiya, John Tranquada, and their co authors untangle two kinds of magnetic order hiding in one crystal of a chromium telluride. Materials like this one, built in thin layers, draw interest for magnetic states that survive at room warmth and can be tuned. Early tests hinted that two rival orders, one with spins aligned and one with spins opposed, might share the same crystal.

Using neutron beams on a single crystal, the team finds the two orders live in two slightly distinct forms of the crystal, mixed at a very fine scale. One form orders with aligned spins at high warmth, the other with opposed spins when cold. A crystal with a bit less chromium shows only the aligned form. Shape changes at each shift, and microscope views back the fine mix. The work shows that rival phases in such crystals may sit side by side, not blend.
arxiv-2512-06462:
Eugenio Gambari and nine co authors clear up a puzzle about moire patterns, the big ripples that appear when two fine grids overlap at a slight twist. In stacks of atom thin sheets, such patterns shape electronic and magnetic behavior. Diffraction tools see many ripple spacings at once, yet microscope scans often show just one main spacing, making the two views seem at odds.

The team scanned a twisted single sheet of chromium chloride on gold with a tunneling microscope. Several ripple patterns shared the same patch at one fixed twist, and which one stood out changed with the voltage used to probe. Wave analysis revealed faint higher order ripples hidden in the surface maps, and energy maps showed each pattern shifting weight with electron energy. The microscope, they conclude, samples distinct ripples by electron confinement. That view unites the real space and diffraction pictures of these stacks.
arxiv-2512-06562:
Dung Thuy Nguyen and five co authors present SUGAR, a way to make an image generator forget specific people. Modern generators can mint near perfect faces of real identities, which raises a consent problem: a person should be able to have their likeness removed from a model's range. Retraining the whole model for each removal is out of the question, and crude fixes swap in fake looking or stock faces.

SUGAR instead learns, for each identity to be removed, a personal surrogate in the model's inner space. Requests for the removed person are diverted to that surrogate, giving a coherent stand in face that keeps the image quality and variety intact. A further goal guards the model's general skill as removals pile up. The team reports top results removing up to two hundred identities at once, with far better retention than rival methods.
arxiv-2512-07462:
Trung-Kiet Huynh and fifteen co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on how language models behave as strategic players. Models now act as decision-makers in shared systems. Knowing what they output is not enough; their underlying intentions matter.

The team extends a testing framework called FAIRGAME for repeated social dilemmas. One new test scales the payoffs in the Prisoner's Dilemma to probe sensitivity to stakes. Another adds a public goods game with shifting payoffs and shared histories. Across models and languages, clear habits appear in the games. Models cooperate more when incentives grow, differ by language, and drift toward defection near the end. To read intentions, the team trains classifiers on classic repeated-game strategies. Applied to model play, the classifiers reveal systematic, model-dependent intentions. Language framing can sway behavior as strongly as the model's design. Such audits, they argue, should guide how agent systems are governed.
arxiv-2512-07862:
Aleksey Turchanov wrote this 2025 physics paper proposing an experiment on superconducting weak links. A thick SNS bridge joins two superconductors through a normal metal layer. Textbooks say magnetic control of its Josephson phase should be negligibly weak.

That belief forces engineers toward bulky SQUID loops for phase control. Turchanov argues the standard view is far too restrictive. His design sets a tiny on-chip coil directly above the bridge. Near the Josephson plasma resonance, phase and flux couple surprisingly strongly. Realistic bridges reach a large share of an ideal SQUID's efficiency. Circuit theory traces the strength to two ordinary causes working together. A large kinetic inductance in the thick bridge does part of the work. Resonant amplification around the plasma frequency does the rest. He proposes comparing Shapiro steps driven two ways to measure the effect. Compact phase elements could then serve dense superconducting quantum circuits.
arxiv-2512-08062:
John Alexander Cruz Morales, a mathematician who works on mirror symmetry, posted a tentative proposal on arXiv in December 2025. His starting point is Aganagic work on mirror symmetry, in its equivariant form, for certain Coulomb branches of a three dimensional gauge quiver theory. He asks how that proposal might extend to Hitchin systems, a central family of objects in geometry and mathematical physics.

Cruz Morales advances two main points. First, the equivariant mirror of a Hitchin system should be a Landau Ginzburg model with twisted masses. Second, a known split between additive and multiplicative varieties, seen for Nakajima quiver varieties, should also be considered for Hitchin systems. He presents the note openly as non rigorous, inviting comments from the community. For researchers in geometric representation theory, it sketches a concrete direction for testing how far equivariant mirror symmetry can reach.
arxiv-2512-08662:
Kashif Ammar Yasir and Gao Xianlong propose a way to read the topology of light inside a single optical cavity.
