The cavity holds a Bose Einstein condensate with spin orbit coupling, a cold quantum gas that interacts strongly with light. Instead of mapping bands or imaging edge modes, their method uses the spectrum of light that leaves the cavity.

They show that the power spectrum of the transmitted light can stand in for a Chern marker resolved by momentum and frequency. In one loss regime the spectrum shows gapped modes with no topological signal. When the loss balance flips, a bright ridge spans the gap and lines up with peaks in the marker and curvature. The work links noise spectra to topology in a compact setup that could suit tunable photonic devices.
arxiv-2512-08862:
Mohamed Elmahallawy, Sanjay Madria, and Samuel Frimpong present FedMining, a federated learning framework designed for safety monitoring in underground mines. Mines rely on sensor networks that track temperature, gas levels, and miner movement to detect hazards early. Sending raw sensor data to a central server for training raises serious privacy and security concerns.

Federated learning trains models locally, but mine settings add hard problems. Attackers can probe shared updates to infer private data, and data distributions differ across mines while sensor noise hurts convergence. FedMining answers with a decentralized encryption scheme that keeps local models encrypted during sharing. It also adds a balancing aggregation step to handle uneven data and improve convergence. Tests on real mining data sets show strong privacy protection with high accuracy and fast convergence. Communication and computation costs are also reduced, supporting real time safety use.
arxiv-2512-08962:
S Hariharan, R Suresh, and V K Chandrasekar study extreme events in a globally coupled network of neuron like oscillators. Each unit follows the FitzHugh Nagumo model, a standard model of excitable cells. Past work used identical noise across the network and found synchronization and resonance effects, but the role of noise diversity was poorly understood.

By giving each oscillator its own noise source, the authors mimic natural variation. Extreme events can then arise in two forms: across the whole network at once, or in only a subset of units, depending on noise strength and coupling. Three distinct classes of extreme events are identified, and a quantitative metric separates global from local cases. Remarkably, noise alone can synchronize extreme events across the network despite the uneven inputs. Analysis of causal links between pairs reveals how such events start and spread through the system.
arxiv-2512-09162:
Kelian Baert and co-authors present GTAvatar, a method for building realistic head avatars that can be relighted and edited like textured models. Their work starts from a problem in computer graphics. A technique called Gaussian splatting can rebuild a lifelike human head, but the result is hard to edit in the simple way artists edit a triangle mesh with a painted texture.

GTAvatar links each small Gaussian piece to a patch on the flat texture map of a template mesh. From a single ordinary video of a person, it rebuilds a continuous head texture that artists can change directly. A physical model of how surfaces reflect light then lets users relight the avatar and edit its material maps. Tests against leading methods show accurate reconstructions, good relighting, and easy control over appearance and shape through texture edits alone.
arxiv-2512-09262:
James Peng, Michal Juraska, Pamela A. Shaw, and Peter B. Gilbert develop statistics for vaccine sieve analysis, which asks whether a vaccine blocks some strains of a pathogen better than others. The question matters most for diverse pathogens such as HIV. Older sieve studies used a single sequence from each infected person.

Modern deep sequencing now yields hundreds of sequences per person, revealing the mix of viral variants inside each infection. The authors' method uses that richer data. It estimates vaccine efficacy against viral populations with different true shares of vaccine-mismatched mutations, using competing-risks Cox regression where the failure type can be misclassified. An empirical Bayes step handles the fact that people contribute different numbers of sequences. In simulations the method cut bias, kept confidence intervals honest, and gained power. They apply it to the HVTN 705 Imbokodo HIV vaccine trial.
arxiv-2512-09562:
Radoslaw Klimek and Jakub Blazowski tackle a trust problem in process mining, the field that discovers workflows from event logs recorded by software systems. Mining can recover layered process trees, but it cannot say why such a model satisfies or violates a logical property, or which elements are to blame. Without that, compliance checks and process redesign rest on guesswork.

Their approach turns mined workflows into logical statements and checks traits such as satisfiability, liveness, and safety with automated theorem provers. They then borrow Shapley values from cooperative game theory, which fairly divide credit among players, to attribute the verification outcome to individual workflow parts. On benchmark datasets, the combination identified critical nodes, exposed redundancies, and revealed harmful structures. The authors frame this as a new direction for explainable workflow analysis, with direct use in software engineering practice, from compliance auditing to leaner next-generation process mining tools.
arxiv-2512-09762:
Jonathan Edwards and Tomas Petricek present Baseline, a platform for richly structured data that has to change in several ways at once. Data can be edited over time, shared among collaborators, and reshaped when its design changes. Baseline rests on a new method called operational differencing. The method tracks data through high level operations, including refactorings and schema changes, instead of raw edits.

On that base the authors build version control for data structures used in programming languages and relational databases. Diffing and merging stay accurate even after structural changes. There is no central repository, and branching is simply copying. The authors also turn queries into sequences of operations, so a query adjusts to schema change on its own. Case studies drawn from a literature review test the system on known schema evolution problems.
arxiv-2512-10162:
Yang Ding leads a team writing a primer on solid state laser cooling, refrigeration by light. Shine the right laser light on certain materials and they emit slightly more energetic light than they absorb, carrying heat away. What began as proof of concept demos has become a credible rival to conventional cryogenics, with new materials steadily pushing temperature limits lower. The field's growth created a housekeeping need: gather what is known and use one yardstick for cooling claims, so results can be trusted and compared.

The primer lays out the key concepts and test requirements. It recaps milestones reached with rare earth doped glasses and crystals, the workhorse materials, and with semiconductors. New uses of optical refrigeration are highlighted, from cooling sensitive instruments to vibration free cryogenics for space and quantum devices. Two reporting checklists cover materials, cooling metrics, and thermometry, aiming at consistency across laboratories.
arxiv-2512-10362:
Woojun Jung and colleagues at Chung-Ang University name a failure they call contextual blindness in multimodal language models. Their paper shows a model can lose its grip when it zooms into a cropped part of an image to catch fine detail. It forgets how that detail fits the whole picture, even when all the needed information is present.

Their fix, Visual Funnel, needs no retraining and works in two steps. First it anchors on the region of interest, then it builds a set of crops at several sizes, from tight detail to wide surroundings, with sizes set by attention patterns. In tests, this layered set beat single crops and loose multi-crop methods, showing that structure, not more crops, solves the problem.
arxiv-2512-10762:
Wan-Zhe Feng and co-authors hide dark matter behind neutrinos. Their dark sector holds a fermion and a complex scalar. The pair's only bridge to ordinary matter runs through right-handed neutrinos. Those are the heavy partners the type-I seesaw mechanism uses to explain why neutrinos are so light. After the seesaw mixing, the bridge becomes a neutrino portal at the electroweak scale.

The portal comes in three versions, with small, tiny, and ultraweak couplings. The dark particles either freeze out while hidden or trickle in by freeze-in. Instead of guessing the seesaw parameters, the authors search them with a swarm optimisation. They keep only sets consistent with neutrino data and limits. Then they evolve the dark and neutrino populations. The care matters: for freeze-in, treating the particles as independent can badly misjudge the dark matter abundance. The framework ties neutrino physics to the relic density.
arxiv-2512-10862:
Qing-Yang Wang proposes an inflation theory rooted in Weyl gravity to meet the newest sky measurements. The Atacama Cosmology Telescope and the South Pole Telescope have set the tightest limits yet on the spectrum of primordial ripples. They find its spectral index in a range that implies stronger scale invariance than older estimates. That is an awkward result for many inflation models.

In Weyl scale-invariant gravity, the quadratic curvature term makes the scalar spectrum scale-invariant by construction, while higher-order extensions stamp the slight tilt that telescopes observe. Exponential curvature extensions are added to suppress a divergence in the inflaton's mass. The scenario naturally predicts spectral index values, across its variants, that land inside the new confidence range. Wang reads this as a bridge between theoretical and observational scale invariance: the early universe may still echo a symmetry built into the gravity theory itself.
arxiv-2512-11062:
Charvi Goyal and fellow authors run detailed model runs to see how cosmic rays from a central black hole help shut down star formation in massive galaxies. Active galactic nuclei are thought to supply the energy that quenches these galaxies, and cosmic rays are a promising channel, but their behaviour is uncertain. The team used high resolution galaxy model runs with several feedback channels included.

They varied how efficiently cosmic rays are injected and how they travel, within limits set by observations of the Milky Way's local gas. Every version still produced quenched galaxies matching observed scaling relations. The gas surrounding the galaxies, however, differed enormously between versions. The authors argue that multi wavelength observations of those halos, matched against larger model run sets, could pin down how quenching really works.
arxiv-2512-11762:
Jack Liell-Cock, Zev Shirazi, and Sam Staton generalize a language design for describing computations with effects. Monads are the standard tool for that job in programming theory. Relative monads loosen the setup, letting computations run between different type worlds.

The team builds a relative monadic metalanguage and gives it a full semantics with strong relative monads. They recast two known calculi in the new frame. One, for graded monads, is shown to extend the older language without changing its meaning. The arrow calculus turns out to be a restricted case, which motivates a new language, ARMM, that extends it safely. The work unifies scattered language designs under one roof.
arxiv-2512-11862:
Jiahao You and co-authors tackle task offloading in low altitude drone networks. Swarms of drones, air base stations, and ground stations promise fast edge computing for disaster relief and sensing. But drones are energy poor, tasks arrive at random, and compute power varies wildly.

The team states the joint problem of flight paths and task placement as a hard time linked program. Their fix works on two clocks. On the slow clock, a Vickrey-Clarke-Groves auction assigns routes in an energy aware, honest way. On the fast clock, a diffusion based multi agent learning method refines actions. Simulations beat baseline methods on energy use, task success, and learning speed.
arxiv-2512-11962:
Timothy Zaklama, Daniele Guerci, and Liang Fu train one attention based model to predict quantum ground states across many systems. A foundation model for quantum matter would take basis patterns and physical settings as input and output the ground state wave function. Their network does exactly that.

From just 18 parameter pairs, the model rebuilt the full phase diagram of the two dimensional t-V model on a square lattice. Accuracy stayed high across system sizes and settings never seen in training. Such a model could replace piles of costly one off simulations in condensed matter work. The authors offer it as a base for a universal quantum matter model, ready to grow with more data.
arxiv-2512-12262:
Francesco Camellini and six co-authors analyze a dice removal game in a 2025 math paper. Start with n dice, each with s faces and s at least n. Roll all dice and remove any that show n. Then roll the rest, and with k dice left, remove any that show k, until no dice remain.

The team finds both stepwise and direct formulas for the mean and variance of the number of turns. They also give bounds for both values. The turn count can be modeled as the largest of a set of geometric random variables. The paper grew from the Polymath Jr program and treats a game not studied before.
arxiv-2512-12362:
Antoine Barbieri and four co-authors build a regression model for repeated health measures over time in a 2025 paper. Hospital data track the same patient many times, and values often show outliers, uneven spread, and skew. Standard mixed models focus on the average path and assume even spread, which can bias results on such rich data.

Their model uses the asymmetric Laplace distribution and tracks the whole response distribution for each person, not just its mean. A Bayesian method fits it, and a new selection score compares fitted and observed distributions by quantiles. Tests and simulations favored it over Gaussian and quantile rivals. They apply it to blood pressure in intensive care patients.
arxiv-2512-12462:
Eray Erturk and Maryam M Shanechi model hidden factors in brain activity for real time decoding in a 2025 paper, presented at NeurIPS. Brain recordings mix types: spikes arrive as discrete events, field potentials flow continuously, and each samples at its own rate with samples sometimes missing. Older nonlinear models do not handle those mismatches, or cannot decode in real time.

Their framework has three parts: an encoder that learns within each signal type first, a dynamical backbone that extracts shared patterns over time, and decoders matched to each signal's statistics. In simulations and three brain data sets, the model beat linear and nonlinear rivals at real time target decoding across mixed, missing data.
arxiv-2512-12562:
Victor Hernandez-Santamaria, Subrata Majumdar, and Luz de Teresa prove global controllability of the Cahn-Hilliard equation in a 2025 paper. That equation models phase separation, like oil and water unmixing, on a flat torus. Controllability asks whether outside controls can steer the system to any target state, a basic question for theory and applications.

They first show small time global approximate controllability using controls on finitely many Fourier modes, with geometric control methods. Next they prove null controllability of the linearized equation with a spatially localized control on any set of positive measure. A fixed point argument extends local null control to the full nonlinear system in dimensions 1, 2, and 3. Combined, the results give the first global controllability result for this equation.
arxiv-2512-12862:
A. Della Corte and co-authors ask whether the collapse of a quantum state, a sudden jump in its description, must truly be one-way. They work with finite systems and allow collapse events of a general kind. Their focus is on what happens along single observed paths, called realizations.

Under a condition that no information is erased, they prove a structural no-go result. In plain terms, true one-way behavior at the level of single paths cannot arise in this setting. Genuine one-way change needs extra ingredients, such as loss of information. The result, now framed as a no-go theorem, sets a clear limit for collapse models.
arxiv-2512-13162:
Chiara Castello, Paolo Santonastaso, and Martin Scotti study rank-metric codes, error-correcting codes where distance is measured by matrix rank instead of by differing entries. They ask how many distinct nonzero weights such a code can have, at most. Weights here are the ranks of its codewords.

They determine that maximum exactly for all allowed values of length, dimension, and field size. They also characterize when a code reaches the full weight spectrum, meaning every possible rank occurs. Necessary and sufficient conditions for such codes are given, along with explicit constructions. Duality behavior and a classification for two-dimensional codes round out the study.
arxiv-2512-13662:
Ljuben Mutafchiev and Steven Finch study the largest pieces of a random mapping graph. A mapping sends each number from 1 to n to a value in the same set. Its graph splits into components, each a directed cycle with rooted labeled trees attached.

The authors pick a mapping at random and look at a random vertex in the largest component. They compute the limiting chance, as n grows, that this vertex lies in the s-th largest tree of that component. That limit also answers a question the authors posed in 2024, about whether the s-th largest tree sits inside the largest component. The paper is short, five pages, and purely probabilistic.
arxiv-2512-13762:
TK Lee presents a qualitative case study of refusal behavior in a safety-aligned language model. Standard benchmarks may miss patterns that only appear over long interactions. Lee audits one 86-turn dialogue session for policy-linked selectivity in how the model responds across topics.

In broad, non-sensitive domains the model showed normal performance, while in provider- or policy-sensitive domains it repeatedly produced what Lee calls functional refusal. Lee names this selective withholding learned incapacity, by analogy with learned helplessness, without claiming intent or inner mechanisms. Three response regimes are defined, and meta-narrative framing tended to appear alongside refusals. Lee proposes interaction-level auditing from observable behavior and calls for tests across users and models.
arxiv-2512-14462:
Led by M. L. Mays with thirteen co-authors, the report closes out a three-year NASA and NOAA project on forecasting when solar storms reach Earth. The team tested whether maps of the Sun's magnetic field, improved by the ADAPT model and GONG observatory data, sharpen arrival-time predictions from the WSA-ENLIL simulation used by forecasters.

They ran nearly thirteen hundred simulations on thirty-eight past eruptions. Feeding the model a changing sequence of corrected magnetic maps cut arrival errors by up to about an hour compared with a single map. For five recent events with the best map corrections, the upgraded chain beat every benchmark.
arxiv-2512-14562:
Tejaswani Dash and six co-authors present PolyPersona, a system that teaches small language models to answer surveys in character. Each synthetic respondent carries a persona, and a dialogue-style training pipeline keeps those traits visible so answers stay consistent. Training used light LoRA adapters on compact chat models, producing a dataset of over thirty-five hundred responses across ten domains and hundreds of personas.

Judged by standard text scores plus survey-specific checks for structure, style, and sentiment, the small tuned models matched far larger baselines. The authors offer the setup as a cheap, open, reproducible way to generate survey data and to study bias in it.
arxiv-2512-14662:
Pricing fixed-income products and replicating future payment obligations are usually handled inside a chosen model, but a model-free framework is developed here instead. The starting question is what market prices alone, across a whole universe of instruments, force us to conclude.

The central result is an equivalence: no static arbitrage across those instruments holds exactly when a strictly positive discount curve exists that reproduces every observed price. That curve is also what lets a desk replicate liability cash flows from traded instruments. The work gives fixed-income theory a clean foundation that does not lean on any single model's assumptions.
arxiv-2512-14762:
Henry Gray, Tom Yotam, and Octavian Udrea compare two ways of using language models to translate code for computer chips. Engineers must turn MATLAB algorithms into hardware description code for FPGAs and ASICs, a slow step that models handle poorly because they saw little hardware code in training. The study isolates one stage of that pipeline: fixing syntax errors.

One method follows a fixed, expert designed sequence of steps. The other is an agent that picks its own tools through the Model Context Protocol. On 42 MATLAB signal processing functions, the agent fixed more errors and unblocked more candidates, lifting the simulation reach rate by over 20 percentage points on mid sized models. Gains shrank at the largest scale, where a simple retrieval variant did best.
arxiv-2512-14962:
Jonathan Marbey and two coauthors add radio frequency sensing to a microscope that works near absolute zero. A scanning tunneling microscope at millikelvin temperatures probes surfaces atom by atom, but it normally cannot do RF reflectometry, a method that reads how a surface reflects radio waves. Their home built upgrade adds that skill in place.

They use a niobium tip to form a special tunnel junction and track its coherence peaks to measure RF losses and electron temperature. Matching the impedance well, by tuning the tip to sample gap, proved key to sensitivity. As a demo, they scanned a 50 by 50 nanometer patch of gold crystal with condensed islands. The reflection losses let them size islands down to 5 square nanometers of area, a new imaging channel for cold microscopy.
arxiv-2512-15162:
Rui-Zhi Li and six coauthors track how the early glow of a gamma ray burst faded in visible light compared with X-rays. The event, GRB 240825A, was a long duration burst, the kind born in star forming regions. Rich follow up data let the team study its afterglow across wavelengths over time.

They split the X-ray data into time slices and fit spectra for each, then computed an optical darkness measure, beta OX, across the event. The measure fell, then rose, bottoming near 1000 seconds after the trigger. At 11 hours the burst no longer met the criteria for an optically dark burst. Extinction curves from each interval show the burst went off in a dust obscured environment. The study shows how darkness itself evolves, not just that it exists.
arxiv-2512-15762:
Kanxue Li and co authors present CSA-TTA, a test time adaptation method for predicting low blood pressure during surgery, in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. Intraoperative hypotension is dangerous, and predicting it for a specific patient is hard because patients differ and events are rare. Rare events also make test time training unreliable.

Their framework borrows hypotension events from other patients through a cross sample bank of past cases. A coarse to fine retrieval step clusters signals, then picks the most similar samples for the current patient. Masked reconstruction and sequence forecasting signals add robustness. On VitalDB and a hospital data set, recall and F1 gains reach 7.46 and 5.07 points in zero shot use.
arxiv-2512-15862:
Supratim Das Bakshi, T. J. Hobbs, and Brandon Kriesten build a trial foundation model for collider theory codes in a 2025 paper. Searches for new physics at colliders use the Standard Model Effective Field Theory, whose many Wilson coefficients are hard to explore head on. A reusable learned code could serve many analyses at once.

The team samples the dimension six coefficient space and simulates neutral current Drell Yan cross sections at high resolution, with Monte Carlo replicas carrying linked uncertainties. A small encoder trained with comparison based loss maps these spectra to a latent space with clear shape. Latent directions track known shape distortions, and clusters group coefficient choices with similar effects. The code supports sorting, anomaly spotting, and lookup.
arxiv-2512-15962:
Johannes Lange and co authors present cosmological constraints from galaxy clustering and galaxy galaxy lensing with DESI Data Release 1 in a 2025 paper. Four galaxy samples from the Bright Galaxy Survey and Luminous Red Galaxy classes are analyzed, with lensing data from the Dark Energy, Kilo-Degree, and Hyper Suprime-Cam surveys around the same targets.

The modeling uses AbacusSummit simulations with a halo occupation model that includes assembly bias, reaching scales down to 0.4 megaparsecs per h for clustering. With other parameters fixed to microwave background values, they find S8 of 0.797 with DES and KiDS lensing, and 0.791 with HSC lensing. Matter density comes out near 0.29 to 0.30 in both cases.
arxiv-2512-16062:
Igor Araujo, Rafael Filipe, and Rafael Miyazaki sharpen a classic graph theory bound in an arXiv note from 2025. For any graph, two numbers matter: the clique number, the size of the largest fully connected group, and the chromatic number, the fewest colors needed so linked vertices differ. The authors study the worst-case ratio between the two across all graphs with a fixed number of vertices.

In 1967, Erdos showed this ratio grows like the number of vertices divided by the squared logarithm of that number, up to a constant factor between one quarter and four. The new note lowers the upper constant to below 3.72. The gain comes from recent progress on Ramsey numbers, another classic problem about order inside large graphs. It is the first improvement on Erdos's bound in this form.
arxiv-2512-16162:
Avishek Basu leads a large SKA team in reviewing the physics of star cores in a paper uploaded to arXiv in 2025. Inside a neutron star, matter is crushed to several times nuclear density while staying cold, a state no Earth lab can recreate. The exact behavior of that ultra-dense matter is still unknown.

The authors summarize what masses, spin limits, sudden glitches, and slow wobbles of pulsars reveal about the interior, including superfluid behavior. Radio observations of lone and binary pulsars carry much of that evidence. They show how the SKA's sensitivity, big surveys, and flexible sub-arrays will tighten the constraints. Links with X-ray telescopes and next-generation gravitational wave detectors add power, while dark matter and modified gravity could shift the answers, a caveat the review keeps in view.
arxiv-2512-16462:
Li Cai and Taiwang Deng count matrices in research shared on arXiv in 2025. Fix a number field and a polynomial, then count the integer matrices of a given size whose characteristic polynomial equals it, with bounded size measured at the infinite places. Earlier work showed the count grows with a positive leading constant, but did not name it.

The authors determine that constant exactly, in terms of the leading Laurent coefficients at s equals 1 of Dedekind zeta functions attached to orders in the polynomial's splitting algebra. The proof refines how group orbits equidistribute, recasts the count through generalized orbital integrals, and moves those integrals across using the endoscopic fundamental lemma. This expanded version removes an irreducibility condition earlier drafts needed, widening the result's reach.
arxiv-2512-16662:
Philip Hendrik Matthias and coauthors prove a limit result for Partial Information Decomposition, a frame that splits what several sources tell about a target into shared, unique, and joint parts. Many competing splits exist, and no agreed answer has been found.

The team shows three bedrock rules of classic information theory cannot all survive the move to this frame. Those rules are that information is never negative, that it obeys a chain rule, and that it stays fixed under reversible recoding. They also rework an older clash tied to the identity rule, under weaker terms. A parts-based frame makes the roots of the clash clear for any version of the split.
arxiv-2512-16762:
Nima Dehmamy and coauthors propose NRGPT, a twist on the GPT language model design that views text generation as motion on an energy landscape. Energy-based models treat inference as a search for low-energy states, a frame apart from standard next-token prediction.

With a small change to the GPT setup, token choice becomes a walk over that landscape. The team proves, and checks in tests, that the walk can turn into gradient descent under set conditions, though not always to the best models. NRGPT did well on Shakespeare text, on ListOPS algebra tasks, and on OpenWebText, and it resisted overfitting except in very long training runs.
arxiv-2512-16862:
Stefan Antusch, Salvador Centelles Chuliá, and Miguel Levy propose gravity-assisted neutrino masses, a new way to explain the tiny masses neutrinos show in oscillation data. Gravity should break global symmetries such as lepton number, but the plain Planck-scale effect is too small.

In their setup, a mid-level symmetry break first gives masses and mixing to heavy neutral leptons, while a leftover symmetry blocks light neutrino masses. Gravity then breaks that leftover symmetry through Planck-suppressed terms, adding just the small leak needed for low-scale seesaw models. The heavy partners form near twin pairs that future colliders could catch, with flavor tests as backup probes.
arxiv-2512-16962:
Saksham Sahai Srivastava and Haoyu He introduce MemoryGraft, an attack that poisons the long-term memory of language model agents. Agents that learn from past wins store those records and fetch them for new tasks, and that trust in their own past is the weak point.

The attacker plants benign-looking inputs during a run, steering the agent to store a few malicious procedure templates among true wins. Later, on like tasks, joint word and embedding search reliably pulls those grafted records up, and the agent copies their unsafe steps. Tests on MetaGPT DataInterpreter with GPT-4o show a few poisoned records can dominate what gets retrieved, turning self-improvement into lasting compromise.
arxiv-2512-17062:
Muhayy Ud Din and coauthors present Lang2Manip, a tool that links language model planning to robot motion execution in simulation. Language models can draft symbolic plans from plain instructions, but running those plans usually demands robot-specific glue code.

Their pipeline feeds symbolic actions into the Kautham motion planning framework, which supports many industrial arms under one interface, with geometric, kinodynamic, physics-based, and constraint-based planners. The system turns language into symbolic steps, then computes and runs collision-free paths with any Kautham planner, no extra coding per robot. The result is a flexible test bed for language-driven task and motion planning across robots and task types.
arxiv-2512-17262:
Suraj Kumar, Arvind Kumar, and Soumi Chattopadhyay address a practical guessing game: how well will a web service perform before anyone calls it? Quality-of-service numbers, such as speed and failure rate, guide that choice, but real records are sparse, noisy, and tangled with place and network effects. Older tools predict each number with a separate model.

Their model, SHARP-QoS, predicts all the numbers together. It reads layered structure with a curved-space method, lets related signals share what they learn through a gate, and balances the training losses so one number cannot swamp the rest. On three data sets it beat both single-task and joint rivals. It also held up under missing data, odd outliers, and brand-new services.
arxiv-2512-17462:
Olivier Jeunen and Schaun Wheeler ran a two-month trial of AI-written customer messages at a financial service during the 2025 tax filing season. Customers were split at random: half got the usual rule-based campaigns, and half got messages from an agentic system that adapted each note to the person. The team tracked who unsubscribed and when people filed.

Agent-led messages cut unsubscribe events by 21 percent compared with the usual campaigns. They also nudged more customers to file early, in the weeks before the deadline, rather than in a last-minute rush. The authors read this as evidence that adaptive, per-person messaging can push engagement where it helps while easing off where it annoys, aiding long-term retention.
arxiv-2512-17762:
Luca Miglior and three co-authors build ECHO, a hearing test for graph neural networks that must pass messages across long distances. Such networks learn by letting each node gossip with its neighbors, so news from far away arrives diluted or not at all. Chemists feel that limit keenly, since distant atoms still tug on each other's charges and energies.

ECHO grades the skill head-on. Three synthetic tasks force true long-range math: shortest paths from one source, each node's farthest reach, and the whole graph's diameter. Two molecular data sets add real stakes, predicting atomic charges and total energies against quantum reference values. Popular architectures show clear gaps under the test. The benchmark gives designers a common yardstick for a long-standing weakness.
arxiv-2512-17862:
Raí M. Menezes and Clécio de Souza Silva study skyrmions, tiny swirling patterns of magnetism that could carry data in future memory devices. They focus on two layer skyrmions in synthetic antiferromagnets, pairs that move fast and straight. The open question is what makes such a pair fall apart.

Using an atom level spin model, they trace two ways a pair can die: the layers split apart, or one collapses after the other. The weaker path sets the pair's lifetime. Stronger links between layers help one chiral type but hurt the other, while softer anisotropy helps the second type. These rules point to better designs for racetrack style storage.
arxiv-2512-18162:
Steven Hu and coauthors at Harvard measure how a cellist's vibrato changes as the finger moves along the string. Vibrato is the small rocking of the finger that makes the pitch waver, and players are often assumed to adjust it as positions change.

Across 94 excerpts, moving the finger toward the bridge strongly increased the acoustic depth of the vibrato, with a correlation of 0.6902. At the same time the physical swing of the finger got smaller, with a correlation of minus 0.6391. Players do ease off their finger motion in higher positions, but not enough to offset the larger pitch swing there. The study shows both that this compensation exists and where it falls short.
arxiv-2512-18362:
Wiktor Kamzela, Mateusz Lango, and Ondrej Dusek write stories that teach languages by stealth. Their system asks a large language model for a fresh tale built only from words the learner already knows. New words slip in through context, and words due for review return on a spaced schedule, the timing trick behind flashcard apps.

Trials ran in English, Chinese, and Polish, with three story making methods and three ways to hold the word limit. The tailored stories came out cleaner in grammar, smoother in flow, and richer in word usage than those from a standard forced search method. Reading for fun, the work suggests, can double as study when the word diet is planned.
arxiv-2512-18462:
Christopher Román Jaimes tackles a quiet flaw in natural language inference, the task of judging whether one sentence follows from another. Models for this task often lean on spurious correlations, surface clues that hint at the answer without real reasoning. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, proposes an automated pipeline to break that habit without costly human labeling.

First, a detection method called Log-Frequency LMI spots the misleading artifacts. Next, a large language model writes counterfactual examples, checked by several judges, that remove the false clues. A training scheme called Dynamic Balanced Sampling then rotates the original data to stop the model forgetting what it knew. Consistency on a hard benchmark rose from 63.5 percent to 81.0 percent, while accuracy on standard data held at 88.4 percent.
arxiv-2512-18562:
Philip Korman studies a resonant equation on a unit ball, where a vibrating system is driven at its own natural frequency. The equation couples the Laplacian of u with the principal eigenvalue term and a periodic, mean-zero nonlinearity g(u). Radial solutions are the focus of his paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Nonlinear Differential Equations and Applications.

The headline result is dimensional: whether the problem has infinitely many solutions or only finitely many depends on the space dimension n. The pattern is not uniform. Dimensions one through three behave one way, while four, five, and six each differ, and seven and above form another case. Such dimension-by-dimension maps matter in nonlinear analysis, where resonance can flood a problem with solutions or shut them down.
arxiv-2512-18962:
Alonso Tapia and Enrique Muñoz explore when superconducting phases can arise in multi-Weyl semimetals, materials whose electrons carry several units of chirality, the index nu. Pairing can happen within one Weyl node, described by monopole harmonics. It can also happen between nodes, following ordinary spherical harmonics. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and published in Physical Review, maps when the topological and conventional phases compete or coexist.

They identify a topological repulsion effect, first seen in simple Weyl semimetals, that pushes the phases apart. Critical temperatures for both phases are computed, and so is the specific heat across temperature. That heat curve is the practical gift: its shape can reveal the value of nu in a lab measurement. Exotic pairing states are a hunting ground for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and this work tells labs where to look.
arxiv-2512-19262:
Kaustav Bhattacharjee, Himanshu Grover, and P. Arumugam built a small radio telescope from a pyramidal horn to hear the Milky Way's hydrogen line. Neutral hydrogen glows at a wavelength of twenty-one centimeters, a classic tracer of galactic gas. Their receiver uses a software-defined radio pipeline and drift scans, letting the sky sweep past.

After calibration, the modest setup produced hydrogen sky maps, a galactic rotation curve, and signs of spiral arm structure. Those are real research products, not just a classroom demo. The authors present the system as proof that low-cost gear can serve both teaching and genuine study of galactic structure at radio wavelengths.
arxiv-2512-19662:
Austin Baldwin and seven colleagues, including Joshua Lothringer and David Sing, point the Hubble Space Telescope at the hottest known giant planet. KELT-9b orbits so close to its star that its atmosphere is actively escaping. Using the STIS spectrograph in the near ultraviolet, and carefully removing telescope jitter effects, the team searched the planet's transit spectrum for fingerprints of fleeing gas.

Two fingerprints stand out clearly: magnesium and iron ions. The magnesium signal reaches beyond the planet's Roche radius, direct evidence of escape, and fits suggest mass loss on the order of a trillion grams per second, with fast, blueshifted outflows. Comparing with a cooler comparison planet supports the idea that the hottest stars emit surprisingly little of the radiation that drives escape.
arxiv-2512-19862:
Jiri Kvita and Petr Baron rebuild the energy spectrum of the most energetic particles in nature. They use only public data. The Pierre Auger Observatory released event counts, a corrected spectrum, and its detector response matrix. It did not release event-level truth from its own simulations. To run the correction themselves, the authors make a stand-in Monte Carlo set. They build it from exactly those public parts.

They normalize the response matrix row by row. They treat the released spectrum as a truth prior. That yields a migration matrix on an absolute scale. From it, pairs of true and measured values are drawn. The fake set mimics the surface detector well. It supports classic bin-by-bin correction and Bayesian methods. A machine learning method, OmniFold, is used too. The work shows a full workflow on open data alone.
arxiv-2512-20062:
Sangryu Park, Gihyuk Ko, and Homook Cho reframe how language models should hunt software vulnerabilities, and where they should live. Most current approaches ship proprietary code to online API models and ask only whether a bug exists. Their formulation, software vulnerability identification, demands the specific weakness type as a Common Weakness Enumeration identifier, far more useful for a developer deciding what to fix.

Rather than renting a giant model, they instruction-tune smaller, locally deployable ones. The tuned local models beat the online API-based systems on identification performance while offering a better cost trade-off, and they keep source code on the owner's machines. Presented at MobiSec 2025, the findings argue local instruction-tuned models are the more effective, secure, and practical route for real vulnerability management.
arxiv-2512-20262:
Rishu Garg and Jitender Singh prove new results about how polynomials with integer coefficients break into irreducible factors. Their method reads information from the values a polynomial and its derivatives take at large integer points. Prime factorizations of those values restrict what factors the polynomial itself can have.

Knowing in advance that every factor must have degree above some bound makes the required integer argument much smaller, so the tests become practical. The authors also prove such a degree bound for the polynomial classes they study, using Newton polygons. The results give number theorists cleaner tools for certifying irreducibility or pinning down factor shapes in specific families.
arxiv-2512-20862:
Z. Zajicek and seven co-authors squeeze an iron-based superconductor and watch its resistance for signs of hidden magnetism. In FeSe, nematic order, a directional electron arrangement, and magnetism tangle together under pressure. Swapping a little sulfur for selenium helps pull the two apart.

At middle pressures inside the nematic phase, resistance turned upward, and a magnetic field up to fifteen tesla made the upturn far stronger. That points to a spin-density wave competing with superconductivity. Past the nematic region, upturns appeared only when a field was applied, revealing field-induced order instead. Pressure and field together, the study shows, steer a delicate rivalry between magnetism and superconductivity.
arxiv-2512-20962:
Shaun Scovil and Bhargav Chickmagalur Nanjundappa fix a storage trap in expiring-token systems. When each deposited token carries its own time-to-live, the naive design writes a new balance record per deposit. Storage then grows without bound. Worse, an attacker can bloat a victim's account with dust deposits. Their data structure instead rounds time into a fixed number of buckets. Deposits that land in the same bucket merge, capping how many distinct expiration records an account can hold.

Three guarantees come with proofs. Storage stays at the bucket count plus one, no matter how often deposits arrive. Tokens never expire earlier than their configured lifetime. And an adversary cannot push a victim's operating cost past the same bounded scale. A Solidity implementation with measured gas costs shows the scheme is practical on-chain.
arxiv-2512-21262:
Isaac Pesenson surveys a golden thread of harmonic analysis and then carries it into abstract space. The classical material concerns bandlimited functions. It covers Bernstein spaces of functions whose frequencies stay bounded. It covers Shannon-type sampling theorems reconstructing such functions from discrete values. And it covers the Riesz and Boas interpolation formulas recovering a function, or its derivatives and Hilbert transform, from samples. These results underlie signal processing.

The survey's second half reports how the theory generalizes when functions are replaced by vectors in a Banach space. The space carries a well-behaved one-parameter group of operators, the abstract stand-in for translation or modulation. Sampling and interpolation survive the transplant, which means engineers' intuition about bandwidth and reconstruction can guide analysis on far more exotic state spaces. Analysts gain a map connecting classical theorems to their operator-theoretic descendants, with the proofs' architecture visible in both worlds.
arxiv-2512-21362:
A processor can compute correctly and still leak its secrets through power draw. Behnam Farnaghinejad and five colleagues probe the CVA6, an open RISC-V core, while it runs software AES encryption. Their tool is VeriSide, a framework that profiles power at the register-transfer level, before any silicon exists.

Correlation power analysis on the design recovers the encryption key, exposing significant leakage in the core as written. Finding that at the design stage matters: fixes cost little in simulation and a fortune after fabrication. The study makes the case that early RTL-level side-channel checks belong in the standard flow for secure RISC-V development.
arxiv-2512-21662:
Prasoon Saurabh proposes a new way to check by spectroscopy whether quantum hardware keeps its topological protection. The standard reading takes the response as a sum of lone modes, each fading at its own rate. That reading fails at exceptional points, where modes merge and Jordan blocks that cannot be diagonalized set the response.

His framework rests on objects he calls dissipative mixed Hodge modules. It swaps the single linewidth number for a weight filtration, layers graded by the nilpotency rank of the system's generator. The protocol, weight-filtered spectroscopy, sorts decay channels in space by that rank. Saurabh calls it a dissipative X-ray: it measures leakage in molecular polaritons and certifies topological isolation in non-Hermitian Aharonov-Bohm rings. His claim is that topological protection survives as an algebraic invariant even when the spectral gap closes, and the protocol can detect that survival.
arxiv-2512-21862:
Comparing inequality or poverty indices between two groups is awkward when the samples are dependent, as household surveys over time usually are. Jean-Marie Dufour and Tianyu He propose distribution-free inference methods for comparing a broad range of welfare, inequality, poverty, and risk functionals across dependent samples.

For any dependence they give asymptotic and bootstrap intersection methods valid for any dependence structure. For the common overlapping-samples case, where dependence comes only from matched pairs, they add sharper procedures with influence-function variance estimates. Simulations show good coverage where independence-based methods fail, though heavy tails favor the bootstrap. An application tracks changes in Italian household inequality over time.
arxiv-2512-21962:
Certifying nonlocality in quantum networks is harder than in the Bell setting because the set of network-local correlations is non-convex, and existing inflation methods blow up combinatorially. Salome Hayes-Shuptar, Daniel Bhatti, Ana Belen Sainz, and David Elkouss introduce a linear programming witness built from five classes of linear constraints.

The constraint classes are network-agnostic in form, though their explicit instances must be tailored to each network's structure. The authors construct witnesses for a family of ring networks and certify nonlocality in a concrete example using only observed probabilities and one tunable experimental parameter. The approach offers a scalable alternative for verifying quantum network behavior across architectures, a practical need as multi-source networks move toward deployment.
arxiv-2512-22062:
Gergely Buza and George Haller prove that spectral submanifolds exist in systems with time delay. A spectral submanifold is an invariant surface in a system's state space, tangent at a steady state to a chosen spectral subspace of the linearized dynamics. Such surfaces are prized for reducing complex dynamics to a simpler model, but delay systems, whose future depends on their history, were not covered.

The authors establish existence for a large class of spectral subspaces, together with smoothness, attractivity, and conditional uniqueness of the manifolds. They then generalize when inertial manifolds exist and show those need not match the physical configuration's dimension, contrary to earlier accounts. A few simple examples demonstrate how the results apply in practice.
arxiv-2512-22362:
Pablo Serra counts words over a three-letter alphabet, sorting them by modular arithmetic. The classic problem asks how many words of a given length exist with prescribed counts of each letter. Serra classifies words by the residues modulo three of both the total length and each letter's multiplicity, covering every combination of cases systematically.

That classification yields explicit formulas for all cases. As a consequence, several identities involving sums of trinomial coefficients fall out, the trinomial coefficients being the natural counting numbers for three-symbol words. The note offers a tidy, complete treatment of a staple combinatorics question.
arxiv-2512-22962:
Yankai Zhang, Yoshitaka Tanimura, and So Hirata extend a powerful open-quantum-system method so it can work in the language of molecular orbitals. Studies of how heat and environment affect excited molecules often use toy models with a few energy levels. Real molecules are large objects in uneven settings, where orbitals shape what the molecule does. The authors aim for a treatment that keeps that chemical detail.

They first build a rotationally invariant system-bath model inside the molecular orbital framework, including intramolecular vibration. From it they derive hierarchical equations of motion, a numerically exact scheme for a system coupled to its environment, now written in orbital space. As a test they compute linear absorption spectra for the hydrogen molecule and its molecular ion, both with vibrational motion included. The work positions the method for studies of excitation dynamics in real molecules.
arxiv-2512-23462:
A. Gómez Nicola, R. Molina, and Julián Sánchez calculate how pion-pion scattering changes when the two pions are confined in a finite box. Lattice simulations work in finite volumes, so extracting real scattering information from them requires theory that predicts how energy levels shift with box size. Their tools are chiral perturbation theory and the inverse amplitude method.

Unlike earlier treatments, their calculation discretizes every channel of the scattering process, including the left-hand contributions and tadpole terms, not just the direct channel. The result is the full volume dependence of the two-pion energy levels, expressed in the symmetry language of the cubic box. For small boxes the corrections to earlier estimates are sizable, and the predicted levels agree with lattice data, which should sharpen future determinations of phase shifts.
arxiv-2512-23662:
Tim Huesmann, Michael Klasen, and Vishnu P. K. stress-test the Krauss-Nasri-Trodden model, a particle physics framework designed to explain two mysteries at once: why neutrino masses are so small, via a three-loop mechanism. How much dark matter the universe holds, via thermal freeze-out. A model can look healthy at low energies yet fail when its parameters are run up to higher scales.

Using Markov chain Monte Carlo scans, the authors map the parameter regions consistent with experiments and theory at low energy, then impose vacuum stability conditions with renormalization group running included. A significant share of the low-energy viable region fails those stability tests. Most of the surviving space, they note, can be probed by future experiments searching for charged lepton flavor violation.
arxiv-2512-23762:
Dominik Soukup, Richard Plný, Daniel Vašata, and Tomáš Čejka build a way to judge the data behind network traffic classifiers, not just the classifiers themselves. Machine learning identifies traffic types well, but models decay after deployment as protocols evolve and traffic behavior shifts; a sudden performance collapse is called concept drift. Teams usually retrain blindly, assuming the data are fine, an assumption the authors challenge.

Their method evaluates dataset stability directly, using a drift detection method boosted by machine learning feature weights to find where a data set is fragile. A benchmark workflow then lets different data sets be compared on equal footing. Demonstrating on the CESNET-TLS-Year22 data set, they publish an initial stability benchmark, pinpoint weak spots for optimization. Show how the benchmark scores respond when improved variants of the data set are created.
arxiv-2512-24162:
Anton Adelöw, Matteo Gamba, and Atsuto Maki rethink training targets for image classifiers. Ordinary training forces one hard label per image. That habit breeds overconfidence. Calibration and robustness suffer for it. Self-distillation softens the targets using the model's own predictions. Yet it still leans on hard labels.

Their framework builds a tailored target distribution for each sample. Statistical inference over the model's predictions produces it. After initialization, no hard targets are needed at all. Benchmarks showed consistent accuracy gains. One large network gained two points on ImageNet. Calibration error fell sharply in other tests. A ResNet on CIFAR-100 cut its error by forty percent. With a contrastive loss added, robustness under label noise reached state-of-the-art levels.
arxiv-2512-24462:
Yoonha Cha and four colleagues interview blind and low vision software professionals about generative AI at work. Software workplaces pose technical and collaborative accessibility challenges for these professionals. Generative AI has spread fast through the industry. Research had not asked this group what the tools mean for them. Thirty-nine semi-structured interviews fill that gap.

The tools help with many development tasks. Productivity and accessibility both rose for the interviewees. Serious costs came with the gains. Blind professionals are more exposed to AI hallucinations than sighted colleagues. A wrong answer is harder to spot without quick visual checks. Workplace policies sometimes blocked use entirely. Each adoption decision thus weighs higher risks against higher returns. The authors draw out that asymmetry for tool designers and employers.
arxiv-2512-24662:
Yongsoo Jho, Jeonghwan Park, Min Gi Park, and Seong Chan Park ask whether Sommerfeld enhancement could explain a halo-like gamma-ray excess near twenty gigaelectronvolts reported around the Milky Way. The effect boosts dark matter annihilation when particles move slowly and meet through a light mediator. Their minimal model uses a light scalar particle as that mediator.

With that setup, the velocity-dependent annihilation rate fits thermal freeze-out in the early universe, the reported excess, and limits from small dwarf galaxies. Readers get a compact test of one dark matter explanation, with clear links between the model, the signal, and the observations that could rule it out.
arxiv-2512-24962:
Tong Wei, Kumar Vijay Mishra, and Bhavani Shankar develop fundamental estimation limits for wide-band near-field sensing with extremely large antenna arrays, as companion to a narrow-band part. Sixth-generation systems will sense over broad bandwidths, where delay, Doppler, and spatial effects couple tightly across frequency. Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing signals over a coherent interval frame their model.

Unified Cramer-Rao bounds, the lowest possible estimation variance, are derived spanning far-field to near-field regimes. Wireless sensing readers get benchmarks that no estimator can beat. Wide-band near-field operation is expected in practice, so limits must reflect coupled effects rather than treating each frequency separately.
arxiv-2512-25062:
Yidong Chen, Nima Lashkari, and Kwing Lam Leung write the global Hamiltonian of a conformal field theory in finite volume using the modular Hamiltonian of the vacuum limited to a ball-shaped region. From that identity they propose local estimates to the global Minkowski Hamiltonian in quantum field theory. The buildings use characteristic functions of nested sets of algebras and act as controls of local modular Hamiltonians.

Operator-algebraic nuclearity drives the plan. Quantum field theory readers get a bridge between local modular data and global energy. Approximating a global Hamiltonian locally could help define motion where the full map is too singular to handle directly.
arxiv-2601-00162:
Rong-Zhen Guo and coauthor Qing-Guo Huang build tools for studying ripples in a general round spacetime. Higher order effects during black hole ringdown can test gravity theories. Those tests need math that goes beyond general relativity. They also need a way to rebuild the full metric from wave data. Most older methods assume one special theory.

The authors give a modified Teukolsky equation for flat, spherically symmetric spacetimes. Their metric rebuild avoids the Hertz potential used before. It extends to spacetimes with a time reflection symmetry. Set gauge choices then yield each metric component. On top of that, they present second order perturbation theory. It applies to any such round spacetime. For gravity researchers, the package widens ringdown analysis. Whole classes of theories can now be probed at second order.
arxiv-2601-00462:
Hodari-Sadiki Hubbard-James and colleagues present a detailed survey of nearby K dwarf stars, the smaller, cooler stars that make up much of the solar neighborhood. Their sample covers five hundred eighty K dwarfs within thirty-three parsecs, observed with the CHIRON spectrograph on a telescope in Chile. The work belongs to a larger survey of about forty-four hundred K dwarf systems within fifty parsecs.

Using a matching tool tested against thirty-five benchmark stars of known age, the team measured temperature, metal content, and spin, plus activity signals from hydrogen and lithium lines. About nine percent of the stars look young or active, including members of known moving groups, and about four percent are notably poor in metals. The catalog gives a firm base for studying how such stars age and behave.
arxiv-2601-00762:
The Thomas-Reiche-Kuhn sum rule is a classic check on how matter takes in light, retold by Angiolo Huamán in 2026. The rule caps the total strength with which atoms can absorb light. Huamán takes a fresh route to the same rule.

His route starts from a form of that tensor with no blow-ups. In that form, some parts shrink down to a simple object called the effective mass tensor. He shows that this shrink step is tied tight to the sum rule. In fact, the rule can be read straight off that step. On the way, he gives a full account of the momentum links between Bloch states. Those states are the wave forms electrons take in a crystal. His account skips a frame that most texts lean on. The paper recasts a textbook result in a cleaner light.
arxiv-2601-00962:
Luan Ghezzi, Ellen Costa-Almeida, Verónica Loaiza-Tacuri, and Katia Cunha ask how a star's chemistry shapes the planets it hosts. The correlation between giant planets and metal-rich stars is famous, and hints suggest smaller hot planets follow it too. Whether elements beyond iron matter was unclear. The team measured abundances of thirteen elements in five hundred sixty-one Kepler planet-hosting stars using high-resolution spectra from the Keck telescope.

Stars with only large or only hot planets proved enriched in some elements compared with stars hosting only small or warm planets, a signature tied to the stars' overall metallicity. The sample spans the galaxy's thin and thick disks, so the analysis also reads as a story about where in the galaxy different planetary systems prefer to form.
arxiv-2601-01262:
Razdan and 3 co-authors offer a hands-on way to teach a core idea that runs across physics. Many laws, from light bending to motion, can be stated as nature choosing a best path or lowest value. Classes often treat that idea only with pencil and paper, which hides its wide reach.

Here classic problems become computer tasks solved with modern tools, including neural networks trained with physics rules built in. Worked cases move from light and falling objects to heat flow, a double pendulum, and vibrating strings. Quantum examples cover hydrogen, helium, and a simple model of a silicon nucleus, linking school topics to research methods.
arxiv-2601-01562:
Xu and 18 co-authors release Logics-STEM, a model tuned to reason through science, technology, engineering, and math problems. Long step-by-step answers are only as good as their training data, so the team built a data set at a scale of ten million examples. A five-stage cleaning process checked labels, removed repeats, and guarded against test leakage.

Training then focused on places where the model failed, pulling in targeted facts and new practice data before a second round. The authors report gains over the next best similar-size model on STEM tests. Both model sizes and the data set are public, inviting others to check and extend the work.
arxiv-2601-01662:
Predicting whether a cancer will return is the job of survival models, and Bayesian versions of these models are widely used in medical research. Saku Suorsa and Aki Vehtari examine how researchers should check and compare such models. The data are messy: some event times stay hidden, and some risk factors change their effect over time.

Their paper sets out targeted recommendations for predictive assessment across a range of scenarios and model types. Existing checking methods often mishandle censored times or time-varying effects, so the authors show how to judge forecasts more honestly. Open-source code accompanies the guidance, letting other medical statisticians apply the same checks to their own recurrence studies.
arxiv-2601-01862:
When language models grade search results, does the personality they are told to imitate change their grades and their confidence? Nuo Chen and five co-authors prompted commercial and open models to adopt Big Five personality traits. They collected relevance judgments on three test collections. Each judgment came with a self-reported confidence score.

Some personas, notably low agreeableness, matched human labels more closely than the unprompted model, while low conscientiousness best balanced over- and under-confidence. Scores and confidence shifted systematically with personality. Feeding those scores and confidence values into a random forest classifier beat the best single persona. The test used a fresh dataset. Simulated personality, it seems, is a useful signal. It can help build more reliable automated evaluators.
arxiv-2601-01962:
The chromatic number of a graph, the fewest colors that keep neighbors distinct, is hard to compute, so mathematicians bound it using eigenvalues. Finn Steinke and Luis Varona make the classic Hoffman bound actually computable for powers of three famous graph families: Hamming, Johnson, and Kneser graphs.

Direct computation would be astronomically slow because these graphs are huge, but their eigenvalues can be written with hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials whose recurrence relations unlock the whole spectrum efficiently. Dynamic programming then evaluates the Hoffman bound in time linear or quadratic in the small parameters. The authors report the first computationally feasible non-trivial spectral bounds for these graph powers, tools for coding theory and combinatorics where the families originate.
arxiv-2601-02062:
Quantum software tools are mostly built in isolation, each with its own compiler plumbing, so chaining them into one toolchain is painful. Patrick Hopf and eight co-authors argue the classical world's answer, the MLIR compiler infrastructure from the LLVM project, can unify quantum toolchains too, if developers can climb its steep learning curve.

The paper is a hands-on guide built around a real case study linking Xanadu's PennyLane framework with the Munich Quantum Toolkit. It lays out concrete integration steps, best practices, and lessons earned in development, pitched at quantum software engineers who are experimentalists first. The goal is a modular, interoperable quantum software stack instead of today's ad hoc collection.
arxiv-2601-02162:
Drinfeld modules are the function-field cousins of elliptic curves. They are central to number theory over polynomial rings. Six authors present them from a computational point of view. They are Cécile Armana, Elena Berardini, Xavier Caruso, Antoine Leudière, Jade Nardi, and Fabien Pazuki.

The text starts from the Carlitz module. It builds Drinfeld modules of any rank. Their arithmetic is explained. The elliptic curve analogy is stressed. The real differences are flagged too, including rank structure and Anderson motives. Detailed SageMath implementations invite hands-on experimentation. Applications run from polynomial factorization and isogeny computation to cryptography and coding theory. The survey is a working toolkit for researchers in algorithmic number theory and computer algebra.
arxiv-2601-02462:
Jacob K. Luhn, Ryan A. Rubenzahl, Samuel Halverson, and Lily L. Zhao handle a subtle timing problem in precise measurements of stellar motion. Gaussian process models describe how a star's surface activity varies, using kernels that give the covariance between any two instants. That works when exposures are short compared with the activity timescale, but fast readout data from extreme precision spectrographs can have exposures comparable to the timescale itself.

An exposure then records an averaged version of the true signal, not an instant. Different solar monitoring sites use different exposure times by design, so each traces a differently binned copy of the same underlying solar signal. The authors present an exposure averaged Gaussian process framework that combines such overlapping data sets on a common footing, so sites and instruments can be merged without pretending their exposures were instant.
arxiv-2601-02562:
Rohit Kaushik and Eva Kaushik present CutisAI, a deep learning framework for automatic skin checks and cancer screening, built around a classifier they call the conformal Bayesian dermatological classifier. Skin imaging tools are growing fast, but a model that is merely accurate is not safe to deploy in a clinic unless its uncertainty is well calibrated. Their framework joins three math traditions to supply the missing guarantees.

Statistical learning theory gives generalization bounds that depend on the distribution and reflect real variation in skin images. Topological data analysis supports a stability theorem, showing the network's internal code stays the same under lighting and shape changes. Bayesian conformal inference adds finite sample coverage promises for the uncertainty scores. Together the pieces aim at screening software a clinician could trust, with stated limits rather than bare scores.
arxiv-2601-02862:
Boyuan Li and eight co-authors study defect states in electrical circuits that break the usual rules of energy conservation, a setting called non-Hermitian physics. In ordinary materials, a known correspondence links defects in a crystal lattice to special states trapped at those defects. The authors extend that idea to a two-dimensional lattice model with a defect and a mix of gain and loss.

They compute the relevant phase quantities and predict the defect states and the fractional charge near the defect core. The model is then built on a nonreciprocal circuit board, where measured impedance confirms the predicted states directly. The results stretch the bulk and defect correspondence into non-Hermitian systems and suggest new circuit-based ways to probe topological physics.
arxiv-2601-02962:
Fabian Haak and Philipp Schaer tackle a measurement problem: how to detect bias in the query suggestions search engines offer as users type. Suggestions matter for what people find online, yet each query returns at most ten of them, so the data for spotting bias is thin. Earlier work deepened the record by following suggestions across repeated searches over time.

The authors propose recursive algorithm interrogation instead: they feed suggestions back as new queries and build suggestion trees, reaching less prominent suggestions that sit deeper in the system. With that richer basis, they investigate bias toward topical groups in person-related searches in the political domain. The method gives auditors a new way to probe search engines from the outside.
arxiv-2601-03062:
Qusai Khaled and five co-authors build a leak detector for water distribution networks that can explain its own decisions. Finding leaks quickly saves water and keeps systems running, and graph neural networks read the spatial and temporal patterns in sensor data well. Their black-box nature, though, has slowed adoption by the engineers who must act on their output.

The framework uses mutual information to find the network regions that matter most, then fuzzy logic to give clear rule-based explanations for each classified node. Their fuzzy model scored slightly below the best crisp network on detection and localization, but it compensates with localized, readable rules. That trade-off could let hydraulic engineers check predicted leak locations instead of trusting them blindly.
arxiv-2601-03562:
Samantha Sudhoff and five co-authors built a pipeline that turns written music directly into robot arm motions for playing the cello. String instruments demand precise bow angle and pressure, and earlier robot cellists often needed costly motion capture systems. Their pipeline reads MIDI files, the standard digital score format, and plans collision-aware bowing for a UR5e robot arm.

Using the robot's freedrive mode, in which a person can guide the arm by hand, the team achieved human-like sound without motion capture. They also recorded live joint data while the robot played five standard pieces, and shared that labeled dataset with other researchers. A robot that can sight-read scores opens new ground for music technology, education, and performance research.
arxiv-2601-03762:
Jim de Groot, Ian Shillito, and Ranald Clouston study the constructive modal logic CK, a logic of possibility and necessity built on constructive rather than classical reasoning. Their approach is semantic: they build a categorical duality, a systematic two-way bridge between the logic's algebraic side and its birelational models, which use two relations to interpret proofs and possibilities.

That bridge then does concrete work. The authors prove Sahlqvist-style correspondence results, which match logical formulas to properties of frames, together with completeness results. They also prove a Goldblatt-Thomason style theorem about which classes of frames the logic can define. Duality theorems are prized in logic because one construction can transport many results at once; here it organizes the theory of a logic that constructive mathematics and computer science both care about.
arxiv-2601-03862:
Francesco D'Amato and four co-authors present Majorum, a consensus protocol for blockchains that must stay live while participants drop offline and return. Protocols with that dynamic availability are known to lack strong safety guarantees during network partitions or long delays. Ebb-and-flow designs solve this by pairing a flexible protocol with a finality protocol that permanently locks in a growing prefix of blocks.

Majorum's flexible component builds on a quorum-based protocol called TOB-SVD. Under favorable conditions it finalizes blocks in as few as three slots with only one voting phase per slot. When conditions stay good, each slot finalizes the next block extending the previously finalized chain. Practical consensus needs both liveness for flaky real networks and finality users can trust; Majorum aims to deliver both without extra voting rounds.
arxiv-2601-03962:
I. Stephens and four co-authors report new radio observations of Scorpius X-1, a neutron star pulling matter rapidly from a low-mass companion star. The system is highly luminous at radio wavelengths and known to launch jet material at mildly relativistic speeds. Using the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array with a fast imaging method, the team caught a series of flares in their higher-frequency data.

They interpret the flares as possible launches of ultra-relativistic flows, extremely fast jets previously reported in this system, colliding with slower ejecta launched earlier. Timing between successive flares suggests such fast jets could often hide: their emission beams along their motion, away from our line of sight. The findings, presented as a Letter, show how much jet activity even a well-watched source can conceal.
arxiv-2601-04062:
Wang Yi and Takashi Hasuike test a decision-first approach to portfolio choice in real markets. Better return forecasts do not always give better portfolios once trading costs and limits enter. Their approach trains the forecast model on the quality of the final decision, not just on forecast error.

The pair use simple linear predictors built from returns and technical signals, paired with portfolio models that include trading costs, turnover control, and regularisation. A rolling backtest on United States ETF data from the mid twenty tens to the mid twenty twenties rebalances monthly. Decision-focused training improves risk-adjusted results over forecast-first baselines and standard benchmarks. It also holds up well in bad periods such as the twenty twenty market shock.
arxiv-2601-04262:
Wang Cai leads seven co-authors in arguing that clashes between safety and usefulness in language models are local, not global. Safety tuning often dulls general skill, and standard fixes adjust all parameters by one global rule. Attention heads, though, differ widely in how sensitive they are and how much they conflict.

Their framework, CAST, first maps conflict per head by joining optimisation conflict with functional sensitivity, then tunes only selected parameters. Experiments show the capability drop comes mainly from updating a small set of high-conflict heads. Skipping those heads during training cuts the loss sharply while safety holds steady. The eight authors present head-level diagnosis as an interpretable, parameter-light way to improve the safety and utility balance.
arxiv-2601-04762:
Emanuele Maggio finds a cleaner route to the Berry phase of crystalline materials by way of an unfamiliar symmetry, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Berry phase labels topological phases of matter, but extracting it from realistic band calculations is fiddly: it demands a consistent gauge across the Brillouin zone and fine sampling. Maggio constructs analytic Bloch states from an infinite series of simple Gaussian orbitals and derives the phase in closed form.

The expression splits in two, and one contribution is immediately geometric — it is the Zak phase, the phase a band accumulates across the zone. The bridge is a modular symmetry, applied to crystalline solids here for the first time. Its eigenvalues correspond to the Zak phase and define a meaningful inversion-like operation even in crystals with no inversion centre. A chiral space group known to host Berry-distinguishable states serves as the demonstration.
arxiv-2601-04962:
Amit Adhikary and 3 co-authors assess what the future Electron-Ion Collider could reveal about two hypothetical particles in a 2026 paper. Working in effective field theory, they consider an axion-like particle and a new heavy neutral boson called Z prime, each coupling only to electrons, in the giga-electronvolt mass range. Such purely electrophilic particles would escape many searches tuned to other interactions.

They analyse electron-proton collisions at the collider's planned energy and luminosity, focusing on a tri-electron final state, and they also explore photon signals from loop-induced couplings. Realistic detector effects are included. Sensitivity studies like this help set the physics case and detector requirements for a machine still being built.
arxiv-2601-05062:
Deploying a language model often means satisfying several behaviours at once: helpful, safe, concise, and in character. Gorjan Radevski and 4 co-authors tackle that compositional steering problem in a 2026 paper. Steering one behaviour is well studied, but steering toward many behaviours simultaneously remains underexplored, and most methods operate on the model's internal activations, which can clash when combined.

Their approach embeds individual behaviours, written as natural language instructions, into dedicated steering tokens through self-distillation. Tokens for separate behaviours can then be combined at use time. Compositional control matters for real products, where a system must hold several requirements together and adding one instruction should not silently break another that users depend on.
arxiv-2601-05262:
Xiaocong Yang's 2026 paper turns a long-context language model into an information retriever with a simple unsupervised method. Modern dense retrieval models usually need costly large-scale pretraining on labelled pairs. Yang introduces LLM2IR, an unsupervised contrastive learning framework that converts any decoder-only large language model into a retrieval model, teaching it to place matching texts close together without human labels.

The author reports proven effectiveness across several language models on multiple retrieval benchmarks, including long-document collections. Models with longer context windows tend to retrieve better within the same family. A cheap conversion path matters because strong language models are now common, while the labelled data and compute for dedicated retrievers remain scarce and expensive.
arxiv-2601-05362:
The CMS Collaboration searches for a fast-moving Higgs boson decaying into bottom quarks in a 2026 paper. The search uses proton-proton collision data collected with the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider during its 2016 to 2018 running period. It targets Higgs bosons with large transverse momentum, produced together with a W or Z boson that itself decays into quarks, a rare and demanding signature.

Boosted decays of all three bosons are reconstructed as large-radius jets, and heavy-flavour classifiers built on a graph convolutional neural network identify the bottom-quark jets. Such searches test Higgs production in an extreme kinematic regime where new physics could hide, complementing the precision measurements made at gentler momenta.
arxiv-2601-06662:
Stefan Ciba builds a filter to strip room echo from sound in a 2026 paper. Echo and ring spoil a great deal of real-world sound work. His filter works on one track of sound at a time, as most clips have.
