The only other open channel is a charmonium-eta pair, and they track the coupled-channel scattering matrix as light-quark mass varies. Across that scan, only weakly interacting meson pairs appear, confirming weak near-threshold D-pair interactions.
arxiv-2602-09962:
Neutrino masses and dark matter are two open puzzles that may share one explanation. A 2026 paper by Pritam Das revisits a model that gauges muon-minus-tau lepton number in a Dirac neutrino framework. Breaking that symmetry yields a new gauge boson, while added fermions, right-handed neutrinos, and scalars complete the picture.

One added fermion serves as the dark matter candidate, reaching the right cosmic abundance through a resonance effect that also forces early kinetic decoupling. After current bounds on the new boson and its coupling are applied, the surviving parameter space is narrow but still open to present and near-future experiments. The framework lets neutrino masses, dark matter, and cosmic observables be studied together.
arxiv-2602-10062:
Spotting inputs unlike anything a model was trained on is essential for safe deployment. A 2026 paper by Amey P. Pasarkar and Adji Bousso Dieng offers a third way beyond confidence scores and likelihood estimates: judge novelty by diversity. The Vendi Novelty Score measures how much a test sample raises the diversity score of the in-distribution feature set.

The score needs no density modeling, runs in linear time, and is non-parametric, blending local class-conditional and global data set signals. Across image classification benchmarks and architectures, it reaches leading detection performance. Remarkably, it keeps that performance using only one percent of the training data, easing memory- and access-constrained deployment.
arxiv-2602-10162:
Power grid operators detect false data injection by checking measurement residuals for physical mismatch, but that check has limits. A 2026 paper by Chenhan Xiao and Yang Weng shows that tampered readings can stay on the manifold defined by AC power flow links and measurement redundancy. In that case, residual-based checks may fail to tell attack from normal operation. The limitation belongs to the measurement surface itself, not to the attacker's knowledge of the system model.

To make the gap visible, the authors present a data-driven constructive mechanism that uses the generic structure of AC power flow to build physically consistent, surface-bound nudges. Tests on multiple AC test systems map the cases where detection turns challenging and illustrate failure modes. The results motivate extra shields beyond consistency checks.
arxiv-2602-10262:
The AMD MI300A chip pairs CDNA3 graphics units with high-bandwidth memory and advanced features: FP8 matrix cores, async compute engines, and two-to-four structured sparsity. A 2026 paper led by Aaron Jarmusch, with two co-authors, profiles how those features run using targeted microbenchmarks. Fill thresholds, fairness, and speed trade-offs under joint runs are measured, along with setting-dependent sparsity benefits.

Sample cases spanning transformer-style, joint, and mixed-precision kernels show how these effects shape app speed and run timing. The results offer practical tips for fill-aware scheduling, concurrency choices, and sparsity use on MI300A-class unified nodes, helping HPC and HPC-AI workloads use the hardware well.
arxiv-2602-10362:
Altermagnetism is a straight, overall balanced magnet order breaking spin-rotation symmetry while keeping zero net magnetization. A 2026 paper led by Jia Wang, with three co-authors, investigates a weakly interacting two-part Bose-Einstein condensate in the miscible regime under altermagnetism. In Bogoliubov theory, quasiparticle spectrum and coherence factors are derived, showing altermagnetic order usually induces angular dependence of low-energy excitations.

As a result, sound speed, momentum-resolved magnetization in quantum loss, and density-spin response functions gain anisotropic parts. Those anisotropic contributions fade after angular averaging, matching altermagnetism's key feature of striking local spin polarization without global magnetization. Finally, the Lee-Huang-Yang shift to ground-state energy in the altermagnetic phase is worked out, with results open to cold-atom tests.
arxiv-2602-10462:
Adrian Ka-Wai Chung constructs spacetimes for spinning black holes wrapped in massive scalar fields in a 2026 paper. Such fields appear in extensions of general relativity and particle physics, yet exact spacetimes for rotating holes with scalar hair have been hard to build. The paper develops spectral methods that handle spins up to four-fifths of the maximum.

The methods cover three coupling types and resolve scalar fields whose wavelengths run as short as five times the black hole mass. Residual errors stay tiny, and the paper reports leading-order shifts in surface gravity and related quantities. The constructed spacetimes give teams concrete backgrounds for testing how scalar fields would alter black hole views.
arxiv-2602-10762:
Muhammad Imran proposes a layered security system for the Internet of Things in a 2026 paper. IoT systems operate in heterogeneous settings, and security problems keep growing as devices multiply. The paper systematically analyzes architectural patterns from more than twenty recent works and current standards.

The new system integrates trusted execution environments with meaning middleware and blockchain technologies. Hardware-rooted trust anchors the peripheral level, zero-trust principles govern the network level, and meaning security tools operate at the application level. The paper emphasizes useful build. It gives system architects a coherent design for the fragmented IoT landscape. Hands-on and operational hurdles are addressed jointly, rather than one layer at a time.
arxiv-2602-10862:
Marco Marengon and Clayton McDonald give an alternative proof about slice links in a 2026 note. They show there exist links that are not smoothly slice in the product of two two-spheres. That reproves a result of Miyazaki and Yasuhara by other means. A follow-up to a similar note for another four-surface, the paper also discusses possible uses.

The uses concern detecting exotic copies of the product of two spheres: smooth structures that are topologically standard but smoothly distinct. Slice obstructions serve as sensitive probes for such exotic phenomena. The note is short, but its alternative argument may transfer where the first does not, giving topologists another tool for four-sized questions.
arxiv-2602-10962:
A short 2026 note by Shmuel Friedland widens a known integral formula. The formula, due to Frenkel, concerns traces of tools. Friedland extends it to a broader class of tools than before.

The new version holds for bounded self-adjoint positive tools and for compact positive tools in the p-Schatten class. In plain terms, it gives one trace rule that covers both settings. The value lies in that wider reach. A single formula now serves cases that once sat apart. Later work can build on it without re-deriving the trace step each time.
arxiv-2602-11062:
Recommenders fail new items that lack user history. Jialin Liu and two co-authors recast multimodal recommendation as discrete tokenization with MoToRec, a frame built on a sparsely regularized quantized autoencoder. It turns item content into a compositional code of clear tokens, untangling mixed signals.

Three parts work jointly. The regularized autoencoder is joined by a rarity boost that favours learning for cold-start items. A layered graph encoder then fuses content with collaborative signals. Tests on three large sets show gains over leading methods overall and for cold starts alike. The work argues that discrete codes offer a scalable path past the long-standing cold-start trap.
arxiv-2602-11162:
Recall heads in language models were treated as fixed parts. Yuping Lin and eight co-authors show they shift over time instead. Through fine-grained analysis of autoregressive making, they establish three claims about these heads.

First, recall heads vary across timesteps. Second, moving heads at each step cannot be swapped for static ones without loss. Third, the model's hidden state carries a predictive signal for future head patterns, hinting at internal planning. Tests on needle-in-a-haystack and multi-hop question tasks, plus a moving recall-augmented making frame, confirm the picture. The work reframes recall as a moving, planned process.
arxiv-2602-11262:
Some phases of matter may be fundamentally hard for machines to learn. Tarun Advaith Kumar and four co-authors show that nontrivial mixed-state phases resist unsupervised learning by autoregressive networks. The obstacle is local indistinguishability: global traits hide from local views.

Conditional mutual information diagnoses that hiding, since long-range values imply a locally indistinguishable partner for classic spreads. In a restricted numerical query model, phases with long-range values, such as strong-to-weak symmetry breaking, prove hard to learn. Tests on toric and surface codes under bit-flip noise confirm the pattern across recurrent, convolutional, and model nets. Hardness itself becomes a diagnostic for phases and error thresholds.
arxiv-2602-11462:
Longest runs in digit sequences obey precise laws. Ying Wai Lee, writing alone, pairs two measures: a single chosen value's longest run, and the longest run across all values. Under measured mixing and exponential cylinder values for constant words, a general theorem is proved.

Measured almost-sure logarithmic growth follows, with eventual two-sided bounds carrying double-logarithmic error terms. Applied to continued-fraction partial quotients, the work pins down explicit centring constants and double-logarithmic error bounds for each measure. The paper supplies sharp, measured longest-run laws where earlier work gave only orders of magnitude. The bounds are measured throughout, not merely asymptotic in form.
arxiv-2602-11662:
UMAP is one of the most widely used tools for flattening high-dimensional data into pictures, yet its exact relationship to classical spectral methods has stayed informal, despite its presentation through algebraic topology. Yang Yang closes that gap with a proof that UMAP performs spectral clustering on the fuzzy nearest-neighbor graph. The argument runs in three steps, linking stochastic optimization with negative sampling to a contrastive objective on the similarity graph.

A known result then equates that contrastive objective with spectral clustering, and a final check shows UMAP spectral initialization computes the exact linear solution to the spectral problem. The equivalence is exact for Gaussian kernels and holds as a first-order approximation for the default Cauchy-type kernel. The result unifies UMAP, contrastive learning, and spectral clustering in one framework, grounding several empirical observations about UMAP behavior in theory.
arxiv-2602-11762:
Low-energy quantum chromodynamics in a magnetic field, at finite baryon and isospin chemical potentials, produces a rich phase map. Yu Hamada and two co-authors build that map from chiral perturbation theory at leading order. The phases include the vacuum, a chiral soliton lattice, uniform charged pion condensation, an Abrikosov vortex lattice of charged pions, and a baryonic vortex lattice whose linking number gives the baryon number.

A hybrid phase mixing chiral soliton and vortex lattices also appears, with intersections carrying baryon number. The chiral soliton lattice demands ultra-strong fields, but the intersection phase appears at fields a hundred times weaker, a range more realistic inside neutron stars. The map thus ties exotic field-driven phases to settings astrophysics might actually reach.
arxiv-2602-11962:
Harmful political content during elections can mislead voters and corrode democratic trust, so catching it early matters. Qile Wang and five co-authors build USE24-XD, a large-scale dataset of nearly 100,000 posts from X during the 2024 United States presidential election cycle, enriched with location and time metadata. To cut annotation cost, they employ six large language models to label posts across five categories: conspiracy, sensationalism, hate speech, speculation, and satire.

Model labels were checked against crowd workers and human annotators, showing comparable agreement patterns, with models more internally consistent and reaching up to 90 percent recall on speculation. A wisdom-of-the-crowd blend across models yields a robust multi-label dataset, with 60 percent of posts carrying at least one label. The authors also show how annotator politics shape labeling, exposing systematic subjectivity in judgments of harmful content. The dataset is publicly released.
arxiv-2602-12162:
Designing a better molecule usually means restarting a costly search for each new starting shape, which scales poorly when shapes or tests are dear. Muhammad bin Javaid led this work with seven co-authors, presenting AMORTIX, a graph transformer that learns the whole task once and then answers in a single pass, with no test-time oracle calls.

The hard part is that some starting shapes are far tougher than others, and plain training wobbles under that spread. The team steadies it by scaling rewards within groups that share one starting shape. Tests on kinase inhibitor design and a prodrug case show it beating rival learned and per-case methods, and a learned rule even transfers to unseen drug shapes.
arxiv-2602-12562:
Rising atmospheric carbon dioxide drives the search for stable, efficient, tunable materials that can capture and activate CO2. Jakkapat Seeyangnok led this work with three co-authors, using first-principles DFT to study CO2 uptake on 2D six-sided metal layers, M2B2, where M spans Sc, Y, Ti, Zr, and Nb.

Uptake values, shape bends, and bonding traits show how the metal centre governs switching on. Found values sit near minus 2 eV, with Ti and Sc layers binding strongest, while Y, Zr, and Nb layers show fairly strong sticking. Uptake stretches C-O bonds to about 1 point 3 angstroms and bends O-C-O angles to about 130 degrees, against a linear gas-phase shape. Charge transfer from layer to CO2 weakens internal C-O bonds, and tiny motion shows most faces stay stable at 300 kelvin, while Ti layers drive sudden CO2 split into CO and O.
arxiv-2602-12662:
Large language models deployed as self-run agents for multi-turn choice jobs typically rely on fixed thought patterns. Non-thinking models give instant replies, while thinking models use deep thought uniformly. Ruihan Yang led this work with twelve co-authors, noting that rigidity is wasteful for long-horizon jobs. Thought needs vary from step to step, with some needing strategic planning and others only routine execution.

Their frame, CogRouter, trains agents to adapt thought depth at each step. Grounded in ACT-R theory, four ranked thought levels are designed, ranging from instinctive replies to deliberate planning. A router picks the level per step, balancing hit rate and compute. Tests on multi-turn agent tests show CogRouter beating fixed-depth rivals in job success with lower average thought cost.
arxiv-2602-12962:
On-device language models need accelerators that fit tight power and memory budgets, yet transformer sizes keep growing while setting reuse stays low. Jonghun Lee and seven co-authors propose TriGen, a neural processing unit built through software-hardware co-design for resource-limited fitting. It uses microscaling low-sharpness arithmetic to open tuning room while preserving closeness, and handles the final issues explicitly.

Non-linear operations, usually needing special hardware, run on fast, close lookup tables, and scheduling techniques lift utilisation under limited on-chip memory. Jointly, the choices jointly tune linear and non-linear work without extra specialised units. On varied language models, TriGen averages 2.73 times the baseline speed with 52% less memory transfer and negligible closeness loss, a strong result for on-device deployment.
arxiv-2602-13162:
Moduli spaces of sheaves hide irreducible components that are hard to find, and code can help locate them. Aislan Fontes and Maxwell Santos provide Macaulay2 code that computes the dimension of the tangent space to the moduli space B(e, c2) in certain cases. With that code, they find components holding singular points and work out the dimension of the component M4 of B(-1, 6), whose existence was proved earlier.

They further prove infinite families of new irreducible components of B(0, c2) exist. The combination of computation and proof is the point: code does not merely illustrate known components, it guides discovery of new ones and measures their size. For algebraic geometers, the work supplies both a tool and fresh components in a classical moduli problem.
arxiv-2602-13262:
Giving a language model more thinking time helps, but running one long chain or many blind samples wastes compute under a fixed budget. SELFCEST teaches a base model to split itself into clones, copies with the same weights that work in parallel contexts and share what they learn. A learned controller divides both text output and context space across branches, trained end to end under one overall task reward.

Across hard math tests and long-context questions needing several hops, the clone approach beat single-model baselines at the same compute budget and held up on new task types. The idea reframes test-time compute as a delegation problem: one model that learns to manage its own team of copies. Darren Li leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13562:
Safety alignment for reasoning models faces a trade-off: strict safety rules protect users but can blunt reasoning, since training data built by context distillation ties rule memorization to refusal. Adaptive Safe Context Learning reframes alignment as a multi-turn tool-use process, letting the model decide for itself when to consult safety rules and how to carry reasoning forward. That decoupling keeps reasoning alive while rules stay available on demand.

To counter a bias toward rule consultation during reinforcement learning, the authors add Inverse Frequency Policy Optimization, rebalancing advantage estimates. The combined method beats baselines on overall performance, showing safety and utility need not be traded so steeply. Yanbo Wang leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13862:
Eduardo Vera Pichardo, writing alone, presents a 2026 arXiv paper on a circular flaw in machine-made survey data. When one model family both writes survey answers and scores them, the scores may flatter the model. The paper calibrates a fix called Semantic Similarity Rating, which scores text by its closeness to preset anchor statements.

In pilots and cross-checks across eight domains, plain behavioral anchors beat jargon by 29 points, with 65 to 67% exact matches and 91% within one point. A pre-registered test of 345 cases found model self-rating compressed error variance fourfold, a bias that held across models. The method trades a little accuracy for independence, the author argues.
arxiv-2602-14462:
Hong Li and six co-authors spot a 2026 arXiv hidden flaw in data-parallel fine-tuning. Sync all-reduce training ensures matching weights after each round, but it does not ensure matching worker-level optimization dynamics before gradient pooling. The paper names that latent mismatch silent clash: cross-worker gaps in losses and gradients can hide under pooled watch signals.

A light, model-free check setup gauges worker match from old training signals, using three gauges: loss spread, gradient-norm spread, and gradient-direction match via inter-worker cosine likeness. The gauges add tiny overhead and need no shifts to design, sync, or tuning. Checks on fine-tuning runs show the gauges surfacing mismatch that pooled loss alone would miss.
arxiv-2602-14862:
Pierre-Alexandre Mattei and Bruno Loureiro examine temperature scaling, the simple method that tunes uncertainty in probabilistic models and stochasticity in large language models. Despite its popularity, rigorous theory has lagged, and the authors supply some of it: for classification, raising temperature increases uncertainty in a very general sense, including entropy.

For language models, however, they challenge the common claim that higher temperature increases diversity, showing the picture is subtler than folklore suggests. A beloved knob gains a partial user manual, with one popular belief corrected. Practitioners learn when temperature truly loosens a model, and when it does not.
arxiv-2602-15562:
Lee works alone against a famous slogan. It says a confidence interval either covers the true value or it does not, so coverage odds after the data are in are out of bounds. Neyman justified intervals by long-run coverage alone. On that view, a single realised interval admits no sensible coverage chance. Lee argues that reading is not the only fair one, and he makes the case in two ways.

First, thought experiments show one joint model giving both forward and backward chances for events that have happened but stay unobserved. Second, infinite trial sequences with zero-or-one coverage markers recast design coverage and data-conditional coverage as different conditioning levels of one model. Lee then sketches confidence as a forecast about coverage, with a rule for when middle chances for single intervals are allowed.
arxiv-2602-15962:
Yu and colleagues solve a farmyard recognition problem: telling Holstein Friesian cows apart when they crowd together. Standard detectors cope when animals stand apart, but they break down in dense groups, and the breed broken coat patterns make outlines hard to read. A working dairy farm needs a system that keeps working in the crush, with no hand holding.

Their pipeline first locates animals with open vocabulary methods, segments them, and only then runs re identification networks, tested on nine days of farm CCTV. Detection accuracy reaches nearly ninety nine percent, far ahead of oriented box and segment anything baselines. Unsupervised contrastive learning then lifts re identification to about ninety five percent on test data, and the team releases code and data so others can reproduce the result.
arxiv-2602-16162:
Peiqi Sui argues that uncertainty is a neglected clue to writing quality in large language models. Model prose is often called trite and cliche-ridden. Literary theory treats doubt as necessary for creative expression. Yet current alignment steers models away from doubtful outputs to protect factuality and curb hallucination. Sui formalizes this tension by measuring a gap between human-authored stories and model-generated continuations.

Through a controlled analysis of twenty-eight language models on high-quality storytelling data sets, human writing consistently shows much higher doubt than model outputs. Instruction-tuned and reasoning models widen it versus their base counterparts. It runs larger in creative writing than in functional domains, and it tracks writing quality closely. Sui concludes that human-level creativity needs new alignment that is aware of doubt. It must tell destructive made-up bits apart from constructive vagueness.
arxiv-2602-16262:
P. Amiot and coauthors extract photometric properties of protoplanetary disks in the Orion Nebula Cluster from high-resolution NIRCam images. Combining PDRs4All images with those of another program, they measure disk radii in silhouette, identify dissociation and ionization fronts, and derive near-infrared spectral energy distributions. From those diagnostics they define a typology of Orion disks.

Type I sources show merged ionization and dissociation fronts close to the disk surface. Type II sources have dissociation fronts at the surface and ionization fronts tens of astronomical units away. Type III sources show a dissociation front at the surface but no ionization front. Disk radius grows with projected distance to the ionizing source, consistent with disk truncation by photoevaporation. Infrared disk radii exceed millimeter radii, suggesting radial dust segregation. Spectral energy distributions of candidate Jupiter-mass binary objects resemble Type III disks, except one case resembling Type I or II.
arxiv-2602-16662:
Richard Willis and co-authors build a frame for judging the group behavior of hundreds of language model agents. Assistants acting for users can yield poor group outcomes at scale. The frame tests emergent play in social dilemmas across three iterated games: Public Goods, Collective Risk, and Common Pool Resource. Each model first writes a plain-language plan, then turns that same plan into code.

That split aims to isolate plan quality from input parsing, allows pre-deployment checks, and scales to large groups. Three checks follow: behavioral fingerprints over foe histories, self-play robustness under Selfish or Collective mixes, and cultural evolution under payoff-biased imitation. Tests on three top models find wide gaps in self-play welfare, and evolution tends toward low-welfare, Selfish-led states in larger groups.
arxiv-2602-16762:
Ayush Roy and co-authors add attention to routers for indoor Wi-Fi positioning. Machine learning positioning still struggles in varied indoor spots. A key flaw is that most codes weight router info equally when merging it. That yields slow convergence and weak accuracy. Old weighted triangulation, by contrast, weights sources by worth.

The paper adds attention layers to a standard positioning net. Each router's share is then weighted by worth when triangulating. Tests on open sets show the new design beating the base net by over thirty percent in accuracy. Builders of indoor positioning get a simple, well-motivated gain from weighting what each router truly adds.
arxiv-2602-16862:
Andy Au solves the entropy-tuned mean-variance portfolio problem under Bayesian drift uncertainty. Continuous-time Bayesian filtering is joined with stochastic policy optimization. The main finding is negative. The two mechanisms are orthogonal. Posterior dynamics do not depend on policy. Entropy regularization thus cannot speed learning about the unknown drift.

The mean control matches the fixed Bayesian Markowitz feedback exactly. Entropy enters only through policy variance. On the technical side, the optimal policy is Gaussian. The value function is quadratic in wealth. The leading belief-dependent coefficient closes in exponential shape. The frame recovers both parent models as limiting cases. Portfolio theorists get a clean negative result that clarifies what entropy regularization can and cannot do.
arxiv-2602-17062:
Yonghyeon Jo led a three-author team fixing a rigidity in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Value decomposition methods usually commit to a single best action, which leaves them stranded when the value landscape shifts during training and they settle on poor policies. The paper proposes Successive Sub-value Q-learning, or S2Q, which learns several sub-value functions so that strong alternative actions stay alive.

Fed into a Softmax-based behavior policy, those sub-values keep exploration going and let the total value adjust fast when the best action changes. Tests on demanding multi-agent benchmarks showed S2Q beating a range of rival algorithms, with better adaptability and overall scores. The approach offers teams of learning agents a way to stay flexible instead of locking in early.
arxiv-2602-17162:
Ariel Larey led a large team rethinking how genomic foundation models learn. Current models lean on masked language modeling or next-token prediction, which capture local sequence syntax well but prize token recovery over functional meaning. The paper adds JEPA-DNA, a continual training add-on that works with any base model and pairs a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture with the usual generative goals.

By guiding global sequence vectors in latent space, JEPA-DNA makes models predict functional profiles of masked genomic segments, shifting the signal from token recovery to meaning match. Across seventeen varied genomic test tasks, it lifted linear probing and zero-shot scores for varied base models and goals, setting a new best mark under linear probing. Ablation tests confirm the generative and latent goals work better as a pair than apart.
arxiv-2602-17262:
Kensuke Okada led a three-author team measuring a quiet bias in language model questionnaires. Self-report inventories now benchmark and audit models for persona, safety, and bias, yet they assume honest answers. In evaluative settings, models may drift toward socially preferred replies, a pattern called socially desirable responding, which skews scores and downstream conclusions. The paper builds a psychometric framework to quantify and curb that drift.

To measure it, the same inventory runs under honest versus fake-good instructions, with the gap scored as a direction-corrected effect size from item response theory latent scores. For mitigation, the team builds a graded forced-choice Big Five inventory from desirability-matched item pairs. Across nine instruction-following models on synthetic personas, Likert formats showed large drift, while the matched forced-choice format cut it sharply while largely preserving persona recovery.
arxiv-2602-17462:
Gabriele Cobucci led a four-author team asking whether quantum measurements can be simulated without superposition devices. Superposition is the core feature setting quantum theory apart. The paper asks whether sets of quantum readings can be modeled with devices limited to jointly diagonalisable measurements. It introduces classical models, where many such devices connect through shared randomness and post-processing.

Such models sit between commutative measurements and joint measurability. The team identifies exact noise and loss rates at which all projective measurements admit a classical model. They propose number-based methods to build classical models for finite sets of measurements, and show how to build witnesses that rule out classical models. Classical models also matter for non-disturbance tasks, where ordered quantum readings run with shared side-information. The work gives a new approach to superposition in quantum measurements, pinning down when plain devices suffice and when they provably cannot.
arxiv-2602-17562:
Georg Hartl led a three-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on when nonlinear control systems can be made linear by prolongation. The paper studies differentially flat systems with more than two inputs, asking when a minimal number of prolongations of well-chosen inputs, after a static input transformation, yields a static feedback linearizable system. It derives sufficient conditions that guarantee such prolongations work.

For two-input flat systems, prior work already linked relative degrees, the highest derivative orders in the flat parameterization, and the minimal size of a linearizing dynamic extension. Those links gave necessary and sufficient criteria for systems that become linearizable after at most two prolongations. Building on the structure of time derivatives of a flat output, the present work extends the analysis to systems with three inputs. The result widens a precise linearization toolkit from two-input to three-input flat systems.
arxiv-2602-17662:
Ashutosh Tripathi and team study how well the Variational Quantum Eigensolver prepares eigenstates of the transverse-field Ising model. The solver is a leading hybrid quantum-classical method for many-body systems in the NISQ era. Its power hinges on faithful state prep, which grows hard in degenerate and strongly entangled regimes.

The team tests the model with periodic edges in one, two and three dimensions, on systems of up to twenty-seven qubits. They compare designs: the hardware-lean EfficientSU2, the physics-led Hamiltonian Variational Ansatz, and that design with symmetry breaking. Energy variance, entanglement entropy, spin links and magnetization serve as the benchmarks for how much each design can show.
arxiv-2602-18262:
Aaron Louis Eidt and one co-author built ELIA, a web app that makes language model internals readable to non-specialists. Their 2026 paper starts from an access gap: mechanistic interpretability tools are powerful but so complex that only specialists use them. ELIA folds in circuit tracing, attribution analysis, and function vector analysis, then adds auto-generated plain-language explanations from a vision-language model.

A mixed-methods user study found a clear preference for interactive, explorable views over static pictures. The AI explanations helped novices most: comprehension scores showed no meaningful link to prior language model experience, suggesting the app levels the field. The paper concludes that AI can indeed simplify model analysis, but only when paired with user-centered design that prizes interactivity, specificity, and narrative guidance.
arxiv-2602-18362:
Emanuel Castelo and three co-authors chart when redundant and irredundant sets can be listed efficiently in incidence graphs. Their 2026 paper starts from a hardness result of Boros and Makino: no output-polynomial algorithm lists maximal irredundant or minimal redundant sets of a hypergraph unless P equals NP. The graph case was left open, with only few tractable cases known.

For maximal irredundant sets, the team shows co-bipartite graphs stay as hard as general graphs, while split and strongly orderable graphs admit tractable listing. For minimal redundant sets, split and co-bipartite graphs prove intractable, settling the open question, while graphs free of cycles of length three, five, six, and eight prove tractable. That last class generalizes chordal bipartite graphs and is incomparable with strongly orderable graphs.
arxiv-2602-18662:
Nikolaos Kougioulis and six co-authors build one model for many causal tasks. Their 2026 paper notes causal discovery for cross-sectional and temporal data has followed a dataset-specific pattern, fitting a new model per dataset. That approach limits multi-dataset training. Large causal models picture pre-trained neural nets for temporal causal discovery, but prior methods handle only small variable counts, worsen with larger inputs, and lean on synthetic data.

The team proposes a principled framework mixing synthetic generators with realistic time-series datasets, enabling scale learning. Broad tests on synthetic, semi-synthetic, plus realistic benchmarks show the models scale to higher variable counts and deeper nets while keeping performance. Trained models match or beat classical and neural baselines, notably out-of-distribution, with fast runs. The results present large causal models as a promising foundation-model approach for temporal causal discovery, with experiments and weights open.
arxiv-2602-18862:
Weakness on one side of the body makes walking lopsided, but testing assistive devices on patients is slow and risky. Yifei Yuan, with two co-authors, builds a reinforcement learning musculoskeletal simulation in 2026 to study gait asymmetry from unilateral weakness and ankle assistance.

Weakness is induced by cutting right-leg muscle strength to three levels below baseline. Asymmetry is measured through toe-off timing, max contact forces, and joint symmetry metrics. Greater weakness brings progressively larger temporal and kinematic asymmetry, worst at the ankle. Load shifts toward the unimpaired limb. At half strength, ankle exoskeleton assistance improves kinematic symmetry, though peak loading stays biased. The framework supports controlled testing before any patient experiments. The goal is safe testing. No patient is put at risk while controllers are tuned.
arxiv-2602-18962:
Communication trouble between neurodivergent and neurotypical people is often framed as a deficit on one side. The double empathy view instead treats it as mutual misunderstanding. Albert Tang, with seven co-authors, presents NeuroWise in 2026, a multi-agent LLM coaching system for neurotypical users. It offers stress visualisation, reading of inner experiences, and situational guidance.

In a between-subjects study of thirty people, all rated NeuroWise as helpful. NeuroWise users reduced deficit-based framing, while baseline users moved toward blaming autistic deficits following hard interactions. NeuroWise users also finished chats more efficiently, with about a third fewer turns. The findings suggest AI reading can support attributional change, helping users see communication challenges as shared rather than one-sided. Both sides must be heard. That is the double empathy point.
arxiv-2602-19262:
Operator networks learn how whole systems evolve, but the physics-informed versions usually demand either a known governing formula or huge piles of training data. Many real systems offer neither: only a few experiments, or partial mathematical clues. Jieming Sun and Lichun Li design a network for exactly that thin-data case, learning nonlinear dynamics without a preset formula.

Their framework is data-driven and model-free, yet still informed by physics in how it treats the data. It first studies short-term dependence in the available measurements, learning how the near past shapes the near future, and then uses a surrogate model to extend that knowledge. The goal is a practical tool for systems where experiments are costly and equations are out of reach.
arxiv-2602-19362:
Reinforcement learning for large language models usually assumes on-policy data, yet distributed training breaks that assumption. Daniel Ritter and five co-authors embrace the resulting off-policy data instead of disguising it. Their algorithm, Optimal Advantage-based Policy Optimization with Lagged Inference policy, or OAPL, breaks from prior approaches. It needs neither importance sampling fixes nor changes to the inference engine.

OAPL beats GRPO with importance sampling on competition mathematics benchmarks. It also matches a public coding model, DeepCoder, on LiveCodeBench while using three times fewer generations in training. Models trained with OAPL scale better at test time under the Pass@k metric. The method stays effective with lags beyond 400 gradient steps, far more off-policy than prior work allowed.
arxiv-2602-19462:
When assets outnumber samples, the minimum variance portfolio interpolates training data and reports a pathological zero in-sample variance. Jinyuan Chang and three co-authors show that a portfolio whose weights are learned by a new Ridgelet estimator generalizes out of sample, despite that interpolation. It exhibits double descent and can reach optimal risk in the overparametrized regime where assets dominate sample size.

In contrast, a Ridgeless estimator using the pseudoinverse fails at in-sample interpolation and drifts away from out-of-sample optimality. Broad simulations and empirical studies show the Ridgelet method competing well in high-dimensional portfolio optimization. Readers get a surprising lesson: with the right estimator, a zero-variance fit need not be a useless one.
arxiv-2602-19562:
Linking words to what we see is a core puzzle for mind science and AI. Joseph Bingham offers a computer framework that models how people read references, by joining spoken phrases with sense-based pictures from large crowd-sourced image sets. Humans pin down references in noisy, unclear settings, yet the gears behind cross-sense matching stay poorly grasped.

The system nears human sense-based sorting by joining scale-free feature transform matching with the Universal Quality Index. It gauges likeness in a true-to-life mind-like feature space. Speech prep and query-change steps catch real-use shifts in phrases that refer. Tests check how well the framework mirrors human matching between descriptions and visual data.
arxiv-2602-19662:
Stress-limited topology optimization is well studied for structures, yet metamaterials with top mechanical performance still lack a solid design framework. Yanda Chen and three co-authors add local stress limits to topology optimization for metamaterial microstructures, aiming to dodge stress pile-ups in the optimized shape. They stretch the Augmented Lagrangian method to handle local minimization under combined local and global limits.

Beyond static loads, the study designs microstructures under cyclic loading as well. A run of two- and three-dimensional benchmark problems shows the approach works. Readers get a stress-aware design route for metamaterials that keeps local stress in check while chasing mechanical performance.
arxiv-2602-19962:
Parity violation in atoms offers a window on weak interactions and possibly on new physics, and highly charged ions sharpen that window. A 2026 arXiv paper by A. V. Viatkina and four co-authors calculates parity-violation-induced transition amplitudes for hydrogen-like and lithium-like ions of two calcium isotopes and a lead isotope.

The analysis takes neutron skin effects and nuclear uncertainties into account for each nucleus. It covers the spin-independent weak contribution of the standard-model neutral boson, plus effects of a hypothetical heavier neutral boson across a range of masses. For the calcium isotope pair, neutron-skin corrections can mostly be ignored when hunting the hypothetical boson, an advantage for new-physics searches. For lead, the neutron skin effect matters, and so does sensitivity to the hypothetical boson.
arxiv-2602-20062:
Models learn features during pretraining and refine them during fine-tuning. Theory has lagged behind practice on how the starting point shapes that refinement. A 2026 arXiv paper by Nicolas Anguita and six co-authors develops a theory of the pretraining and fine-tuning pipeline in diagonal linear networks.

The theory gives expressions for generalization error in terms of initialization parameters and task statistics. Initialization choices place the network in one of four fine-tuning regimes. Regimes differ in whether they support feature learning and reuse, and in which task statistics they suit. A smaller scale for initialization in earlier layers proves favourable: the network reuses and refines its features, improving generalization when fine-tuning tasks draw on only part of the pretraining features. Initialization effects appear in residual networks on image tasks and in transformers on modular arithmetic. Data and initialization interact across layers to shape fine-tuning.
arxiv-2602-20262:
The Milky Way's central zone funnels gas from the disk toward the nucleus, but its bulk molecular gas had not been mapped in fine detail, despite the region's extreme conditions. A 2026 arXiv paper by a large team led by Cara Battersby uses Band 3 data from the ALMA Central Molecular Zone Exploration Survey. It maps that gas in fine detail, at three arcseconds or a tenth of a parsec.

Visual inspection across the whole zone turns up at least two broad kinds of thread-like structures. Some threads stretch about ten parsecs, spanning large scales. Others, about one parsec long, appear everywhere. The paper details shape and motion for three examples of each kind, giving a census of filaments across the Galaxy's central gas store. Readers gain a first fine-grained map of how central gas organizes itself into threads.
arxiv-2602-20362:
Robin Jeanne Kirschner and six co-authors build the first energy-based Injury Protection Database for hand and finger contact. Collision avoidance is a staple of robotics research, yet in tight spaces and future humanoid systems, contact cannot always be avoided. Energy-limiting control is the usual safeguard, but its thresholds came from blunt-impact data that do not cover edged or pointed collisions. Without broad, clinically grounded data, safety checks stay limited.

Earlier work set surrogate-based velocity and mass limits for perpendicular impacts across shapes. This study adds shearing contacts in unconstrained collisions and reexamines all prior porcine surrogate data. Collision angle turns out to matter greatly: unconstrained shearing contacts cause fewer injuries than perpendicular ones. The resulting energy thresholds span shapes and contact types, giving controller designers a realistic basis for limiting energy across many collision events.
arxiv-2602-20762:
Keigo Oka shows that GNU find, a humble file-search command taught to beginners, can in fact compute anything a computer can. He proves three versions of this claim, each turning file names, paths, and search steps into a working machine.

First, find plus mkdir can mimic tag systems by storing states as paths and copying text with pattern tricks. Next, find alone, from version 4.9.0 onward, can mimic a two-counter machine by reading and writing files as it walks. Even without those pattern tricks, find plus mkdir still reaches full power by hiding patterns inside directory names.
arxiv-2602-20962:
Light pulses that carry information in time and frequency face a quantum limit on joint measurement. Patrick Folge and six co-authors derive and test that limit in this 2026 arXiv paper. When detection is confined to finite time windows, the problem behaves like a quantum rotor, which puts the familiar Heisenberg relation out of reach.

The authors propose an optimal detection scheme that saturates the new bounds, sampling the Q-function to rebuild the Wigner function beyond the harmonic oscillator. An implementation based on a quantum pulse gate confirms the scheme approaches the ultimate quantum limit. The result offers a fresh framework for joint time-frequency detection in precision measurement and quantum information work.
arxiv-2602-21262:
Language models advise in high-stakes calls, so two social skills matter: watchfulness about which facts to trust, and sway to convince a user. Sasha Robinson, Katherine Collins, Ilia Sucholutsky, and Kelsey Allen study how those skills link in this 2026 arXiv paper. They use a multi-turn puzzle game, Sokoban, with models swaying and fending off other models.

Puzzle skill, sway, and watchfulness prove separable: solving well does not mean spotting trickery, even when trickery is named outright. Yet models tune token use steadily, thinking with fewer tokens for kind advice and more for mean advice, even when still swayed into failure. Watching all three skills on their own emerges as key for AI safety work.
arxiv-2602-21462:
Alan F. Karr and one co-author run extensive numerical experiments on how training-data quality shapes classifier performance, a factor often neglected in classifier analysis. The scientific setting is metagenomic assembly, joining short DNA reads into longer contigs. Four models are tested: Bayes classifiers, neural nets, partition models, and random forests.

Training data are degraded by several mechanisms, and both single-model behavior and agreement among models are tracked. A breakdown-like pattern holds for all four. As degradation grows, models shift from mostly correct to only coincidentally correct, because they go wrong in the same way. A patchy picture also emerges. As training data drift farther from analysis data, decisions degenerate, the boundary grows less dense, and agreement among models rises.
arxiv-2602-21662:
Wenjie Huang and five co-authors propose Hybrid-PCGC for hybrid lossless point cloud geometry compression. It bridges pretrained and implicit neural models for 3D sensing uses like driving and digital twins.

Hybrid-PCGC frames compression as a joint geometry-and-model bitrate problem, optimizing instance weight offsets as rate-constrained variables. Four parts split prior modeling from instance adaptation: a Frozen General Module, a Dual Trainable Adaptive Module, an Adaptive Scope Controller, and a Supervised Offset Compression Module. The frozen module captures global regularities and the adaptive module adjusts to single clouds, with scope and offset modules handling updates. Tests cut bitrate over G-PCC by about 14 percent lossless and about 16 percent lossy, and save up to about 12 percent over the leading hybrid method on dense clouds.
arxiv-2602-21862:
People forget parts of their lives. They also mix up events. A tool that helps them recall past events would help a lot. Past tools used deep learning. Those tools need much training data. But personal logs are small, so data is scarce. As logs grow, a tool must learn fast from new entries. Large language models do well on many tasks. They look like a good fit for personal use.

Chia Cheng Chang and three co-authors built a frame that uses large language models for proactive info access. It links personal knowledge graphs to spot when a user needs help. The choice step is refined. The frame is flexible. Teams can swap the base model. They can also change how facts are fetched. Tests show it finds lost events well. It helps users recall the past with less effort.
arxiv-2602-21962:
Meng-Yun Mao, Zhixiang Sun, and Wen-Long You study quantum many-body scars, rare states that refuse to thermalize and keep coherent motion alive in strongly interacting systems. How long such scars survive under small disturbances was poorly understood. Their 2026 arXiv paper derives tighter lower bounds on that survival time for local perturbations.

Exact scars, they show, thermalize slowly thanks to a protective algebraic structure, beating prior bounds by a clear margin. Strangely, approximate scars can last even longer under generic disturbances, through second-order effects that arise precisely because they lack that protection. The two cases together clarify when scarred motion stays long-lived, a question that matters for controlling quantum matter.
arxiv-2602-22462:
Breast screening is high volume, time sensitive, and paperwork heavy: radiologists must turn subtle findings into consistent assessments, density categories, and structured reports. Raiyan Jahangir and three co-authors present MammoWise, a local multi-model setup that turns open-source vision-language models into breast-scan report writers and multi-task classifiers. It runs on any Ollama-hosted model and breast-scan dataset.

The setup supports zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting, with optional image-and-text search help from a vector store for case-specific context. Trials on three medical vision-language models across two breast-scan datasets assess report quality, assessment calls, density, and key findings. Hospitals gain a private, repeatable reporting aid that keeps patient images local.
arxiv-2602-22562:
Taoran Li and two co-authors study why erasing knowledge from language models fails across languages. Facts removed in one language often resurface in another, and the cause was unclear. Through layer-by-layer tests they find intervention depth decides the outcome. Shallow edits erase the fact but damage multilingual skill. Deep edits preserve skill but fail to erase even in the source language.

Their fix, MUTE, hunts for middle layers where languages share representations. It uses centered kernel alignment and a linguistic regions score to find them. Then it limits unlearning updates to those layers. Across three model architectures and three unlearning methods, MUTE removed target knowledge across languages while sparing general ability. Logit-lens probing confirmed real removal rather than surface-level suppression of outputs.
arxiv-2602-22662:
Gaoyang Pang and six co-authors sketch wireless human-machine teamwork for the 6G era. Industry 5.0, the coming factory wave, pairs human ideas, judgment, and hand skill with machine strength, finesse, and speed. 6G radio would link far-flung partners at low cost and large scale.

The article lays out a generic design and key parts for such teamwork, surveys network shapes and sector uses, and offers fresh success metrics and design methods. It sums up radio needs, reviews leading tools that could carry the load, and closes with a proof-of-concept case study plus open problems for research teams and builders.
arxiv-2602-22962:
Yuejiang Yu and three co-authors map how weather-model skill scales with size, data, and compute. Across a range of models, Aurora shows the strongest data scaling: a tenfold larger training set cuts validation loss by more than threefold. GraphCast proves the most parameter-efficient yet uses hardware poorly.

Under fixed compute budgets, spending on more training data beats growing model size. Weather models also break from language-model habits, favouring wider shapes over deeper ones. Future weather models should therefore prize wide designs and large effective training sets for the best forecasts.
arxiv-2602-23062:
Gabriela Anna Kaczmarek and four co-authors build a dataset for automatic Case Report Form filling from Italian emergency-department notes. Case Report Forms collect patient data at the core of clinical research, and language technology now promises automatic filling from clinical notes, mostly with large language models. Progress is limited by scarce annotated CRF data for training and testing.

The new dataset annotates clinical notes from an Italian Emergency Department against a predefined form with 134 items. It adds an analysis of the data, a defined task and evaluation metric, and pilot experiments using an open-source state-of-the-art model. Results show zero-shot CRF filling from real Italian clinical notes is feasible, though model biases, such as a cautious tilt toward unknown answers, need correction.
arxiv-2602-23262:
Jasmine Bayrooti and five co-authors propose a private route to image making based on coarse-to-fine wavelets. Models trained on sensitive images can recall and copy single cases, so strong privacy pledges matter. Standard private fine-tuning often wrecks image quality, above all in fine detail, because it adds noise to all weights.

The key idea is that the most private image content lives in coarse wavelet parts, such as facial traits and object shapes, while fine parts are largely generic and public. The method fine-tunes a spectral code model in private on low-detail wavelet numbers, then sharpens with a ready-made super-resolution model. Keeping the privacy budget to global structure yields better quality and style capture than rival private methods on MS-COCO and MM-CelebA-HQ. Later detail steps add no new leak, by a standard privacy rule.
arxiv-2602-23662:
Kohei Obata and four co-authors propose AnomalyFilter, a spot cleaning spread model for time series anomaly spotting. Anomaly spotting has counted for decades, with rebuild-based methods, mostly making models, gaining favor and success. Spread models lately drew notice for strong making powers.

Current spread methods for anomaly spotting rely on a guided plan, redoing inputs from white noise with a guide. That poses hurdles in redoing normal parts well, yielding weak spotting. AnomalyFilter instead acts as a spot filter that only cleans anomaly parts while keeping normal parts. Building it needs masking Gaussian noise during training and cleaning without adding noise to cases. The synergy of these two simple parts greatly lifts naive spread models. Tests on five data sets show notably low rebuild error on normal parts, backing its worth. AnomalyFilter pioneers focus on noise design for time series anomaly spotting.
arxiv-2602-23762:
Mengzhong Ma and two co-authors study how price jumps on one blockchain tend to drag down prices on other chains. The 2026 paper uses on-chain data from five major chains over four years, a period that covers sharp booms and falls in crypto markets.

The authors find a pattern unlike stock markets, where assets usually move together. Here a surge on one chain often came with falls elsewhere, and the effect grew stronger during bursts of attention. The pattern held after allowing for stock returns, interest rates, and Bitcoin. They argue that attention-driven shifts of funds, not shared news, drive the link. That matters for spreading risk, for measuring system-wide danger, and for rules on new token launches.
arxiv-2603-00062: Schons and colleagues estimate the pool of technically strong machine-learning research talent inside ML consulting firms. They screen 2,121 organisations, find 403 offering broad ML consulting, and score staff LinkedIn resumes with keyword filters and language-model classifiers, feeding a bootstrap probit model. Their middle estimate puts highly technical talent at 1,121 people, twice the alumni count of the MATS training program. In a three-day work trial, 97 firms were approached, 20 applied, 8 were invited and 5 of 8 earned at least a conditional recommendation.
arxiv-2603-00162: Wu and colleagues present GazeXPErT, a 4D eye-tracking dataset of expert decisions for tumour spotting and sizing on 346 dual-read FDG-PET/CT scans. It holds 9,030 gaze-to-lesion trajectories drawn from 3,948 minutes of 60 Hz gaze recordings, stored in COCO-style format. The dataset captures how experts reason when adjudicating suspicious lesions. Baseline tests suggest gaze signal carries usable information. A 3D nnU-Net reaches higher Dice with gaze than without, gaze-trained vision transformers aid dynamic lesion localisation, and expert intent proves partly predictable from raw gaze.
arxiv-2603-00262: A study by de Soto and colleagues calls AT 2024ahzi, a flash found by the Vera Rubin Observatory's test camera, a Type IIP supernova. Its plateau length, brightness and colour match a large set of Type II supernovae. Matching multi-band light curves against model fits pins down the progenitor, explosion dynamics and nearby gas. The progenitor likely has a wide density profile much like a slowly speeding wind of nearby star matter. The same workflow can spot and sort future Rubin Type II supernovae.
arxiv-2603-00362: Pogoncheff and colleagues present a percept-aware plan for surgery for visual cortical prostheses, which restore sight by driving early visual cortex. Current plans stress coverage and anatomical rules, not the predicted results for sight under safety limits. Their plan treats electrode spots as learnable values, tuned with a differentiable model of prosthetic vision, cutting perceptual error while keeping vessel avoidance and grey-matter fit. On mock reading and image tasks, percept-aware tuning beats coverage-based plans, and vessel-safety limits remove margin breaches without hurting results.
arxiv-2603-00962: Gong and Ye propose a penalty plan for non-self-adjoint topology optimization, shown with compliant devices. A convex nonlocal edge-length scheme backs proofs that answers exist and that fine grids tend to the smooth problem, while a gradient scheme lowers the goal each step. The plan also covers heat flow with a broad material-mix rule for link control, and tests on both tasks confirm it works.
arxiv-2603-01562:
Qiyuan Zhang, Junyi Zhou, Yufei Wang, and colleagues ask whether AI-written grading rubrics can match human ones. Their 2026 work starts from a shift in how reward models judge AI output: rubrics now guide scores more than surface traits do. Yet no shared test checked if model-made rubrics are in fact sound.

Their test set, RubricBench, holds more than a thousand paired cases picked to be hard and bias-prone. Each case carries expert rubrics built strictly from the given instructions, split into small checkable points. Wide tests show a large gap between human rubrics and model-made ones. Even top models lag far behind human-guided scores when they must set their own criteria. That gap marks rubric writing as a skill AI still lacks.
arxiv-2603-01762:
Yingjie Tan, Quanming Yao, and Yaqing Wang teach neural solvers to solve physics equations with far less training data. Their 2026 work covers partial differential equations that change over space and time, core tools in science and engineering. Neural solvers promise speed, yet they need many costly simulated runs and fail on new source terms.

The team builds physics structure into the network through Green function theory, a classic way to build solutions from point responses. Their network, DGNet, turns that theory into a graph form and bakes in the superposition rule. Superposition says total response equals the sum of part responses, a deep fact models usually must learn. With structure supplied, tens of training runs reach top accuracy in their tests. The solver also handles unseen source terms with no retraining.
arxiv-2603-01962:
Milton Aguilar, Franklin Rodrigues, and Eric Lutz measure the work of quantum engines without wrecking the coherence they run on. Their 2026 work tackles measurement backaction, the disturbance any probe causes in a quantum system. A standard two-point scheme can distort average work so badly that an engine stops acting like one under watch.

Their scheme builds measurement into a dynamic Bayesian network that preserves coherence inside each cycle. Averaged over one full cycle, the measured state matches the unmeasured state exactly. That match makes the probe minimally invasive in a precise, provable sense. The frame thus supports general study of energy exchange statistics in quantum machines. They also show that recently proposed universal fluctuation bounds need not hold for coherent machines.
arxiv-2603-02162:
Aniek Eijpe, Soufyan Lakbir, Melis Erdal Cesur, and colleagues tackle cancer survival forecasts in this 2026 paper. Models that mix tissue images and gene data can forecast well, but doctors cannot see why. Their framework, DIMAFx, splits what it learns into parts tied to one source and parts shared across sources. That split is meant to keep forecasts sharp and also readable.

Across several cancer groups, the model matched the best scores and split its parts more cleanly. A standard tool then traced which parts drove each forecast. In breast cancer, shared parts carried the most weight, linking tumor shape with gene response. Single-source parts flagged signals from fat and support tissue nearby. The work shows accuracy and clear reasons can coexist.
arxiv-2603-02462:
Semih Cantürk, Thomas Sabourin, Frederik Wenkel, and colleagues test transfer across hard graph problems in this 2026 paper. Neural solvers learn to tackle combinatorial problems like clique and cover finding. Training one solver per problem is wasteful if skills overlap. The authors ask whether reducibility, the classic map between problems, can guide transfer.

Their solver uses strong message passing with an energy-based unsupervised loss. Trained alone, it matches leading results on several problems. Pretraining strategies drawn from reduction theory then move skills between tasks. Leaving one task out, pretraining on the rest sped fine-tuning on it almost always. No harmful transfer appeared in that setting. Shared representations across graph problems look viable, a step toward foundation solvers.
arxiv-2603-02862:
Davide Maran, Davide Salaorni, and Marcello Restelli exploit a simple fact: in many systems, the agent controls only part of the state. Weather, demand, and other outside forces evolve on their own and supply most of the randomness. Their 2026 paper studies reinforcement learning for such Markov decision processes with exogenous dynamics.

By using the split structure, they prove learning guarantees where only the outside state space size drives the main cost terms. A matching lower bound shows no method can do fundamentally better, so the dependence is optimal. Tests on classic toy problems and realistic settings confirm large gains in sample efficiency over standard algorithms. The lesson is to stop paying learning costs for parts of the world the agent cannot touch.
arxiv-2603-03062:
Sabhyata Gupta, Piotr Sierant, Luis Santos, and Paolo Stornati find perfectly simple states hiding inside a complex quantum system. Their 2026 paper studies the Rokhsar-Kivelson model, a two-dimensional lattice gauge theory used to probe how excited quantum states behave. Most excited states are wildly complex, yet scarred states stay unusually simple.

The team identifies a family called sublattice scars, born from gauge-obeying zero modes that are exact stabilizer states, the kind quantum engineers find easy to describe. The host Hamiltonian is not a stabilizer model, yet its spectrum hosts these states naturally. The scars show structured entanglement and zero stabilizer entropy, allowing efficient classical simulation. The authors even give explicit circuits that prepare them.
arxiv-2603-03262:
Rémi Di Guardia and three colleagues revisit a classic problem in linear logic: turning a proof net back into a step-by-step derivation. Proof nets are graph-like proofs, and a correctness test decides which graphs count as valid. Sequentialization then recovers the ordered proof. Their 2026 paper finds the right level of abstraction in a theorem from graph theory, Yeo's theorem, restated with colorings of half-edges.

A key lemma, cusp minimization, shows how to shrink certain color patterns around cycles until a splitting vertex appears, one that unlocks the inductive recovery. Different color choices then yield different recovery styles in a modular way, with no change to the graph itself. The method also covers proof nets with mix rules and the unit-free multiplicative-additive fragment, and it subsumes several older graph results.
arxiv-2603-03362:
Xin Li proposes a theory of how the brain splits the work of intelligence between two systems. The world’s meaning structure is tangled and keeps shifting, so no single smooth inner geometry can represent it all. His 2026 framework, Metric-Topology Factorization, separates two jobs: picking which context applies, and reasoning smoothly inside that context once picked.

In the brain, the hippocampus supplies sparse context signatures that index the right setting, while the neocortex untangles sensory input step by step, stripping away shifts in position, size, and rotation. Replay in sleep recalibrates the system offline, and Li reads dreaming as sampling of the memory graph during rest. Consciousness, on this view, marks states whose embedding is not yet fully settled. Five great evolutionary transitions, from navigation to language, each expanded the split further.
arxiv-2603-03562:
Dieter Bothe and Matthias Köhne rebuild a cornerstone theorem of fluid mechanics for flows with a moving boundary between phases. The Reynolds transport theorem converts between following a moving volume and watching a fixed one. In two-phase flows with evaporation or condensation and slip at the interface, the velocity field jumps across the boundary, and the equations tracing fluid elements become ill-posed in general. Their 2026 paper fixes the foundations.

A motivating example, fully consistent with mass, momentum, and entropy balances, shows the pathology is real, not pedantry. The authors then borrow differential inclusions from analysis to define co-moving sets rigorously inside such discontinuous fields. On that basis they prove a natural extension of the transport theorem to the sharp-interface, phase-changing case. The result firms up the mathematics beneath interface-resolving simulation methods.
arxiv-2603-03762:
Junhan Chen and five colleagues build an agent that identifies fine visual categories the way an expert would: by gathering evidence, not guessing labels. Fine-grained understanding is leaving closed lists behind, and models must now justify their calls in open settings where categories were never predefined. Their 2026 agent, KFRA, runs a three-stage loop that mimics expert analysis.

Open-vocabulary detection plus web-scale retrieval first proposes candidate categories. The agent then retrieves textual knowledge for each candidate and aligns it with the image, hunting the discriminative regions, a color patch, a structure, a behavior, that separate look-alikes. A large multimodal model finally weighs the grounded evidence into an interpretable verdict. A new benchmark, FGExpertBench, grades reasoning depth across six knowledge dimensions. KFRA beats standalone models and rival agents, gaining up to about a fifth in reasoning accuracy.
arxiv-2603-04162: Jakub Prejzner presents Bielik-Q2-Sharp, a comparative study of extreme 2-bit quantization for a Polish 11-billion-parameter model. He compares six post-training quantization methods calibrated on a Polish corpus with shared Hessian matrices. On eq_bench it scores higher, suggesting better preservation of higher-order reasoning, while QTIP matches VPTQ quality at 35% smaller size. He also documents a dissociation where rotation-based methods keep log-likelihood quality yet fail at autoregressive generation.
arxiv-2603-04562: Thomas and Sreevalsan-Nair compare fusion and grouping strategies for local climate zone classification. Local climate zones map urban structure, land use, and urbanization effects on local climate. Multimodal remote sensing aids classification through fusion. The study tests convolutional models: baseline hybrid fusion, self and cross attention variants, multi-scale Gaussian filtered variants, and weighted decision level fusion. Ablations probe pixel, feature, and decision level effects, plus band grouping and label merging. On So2Sat LCZ42, baseline hybrid fusion wins overall, reaching 76.6 percent accuracy with band grouping plus label merging.
arxiv-2603-04962: Yan Tong and team offer a dynamic virtual power plant coordinating mixed resources across many timescales with grid-forming control. Grid-following converters use a phase-locked loop that can undermine balance in weak grids, while their design applies virtual synchronous generator control for inertia and damping. A participation factor method gauges each device's contribution through the loops linking rate to active power and voltage to reactive power. Fast resources deliver rapid reply and damping, middle resources smooth shifts, and slow resources handle steady state and low-rate regulation.
arxiv-2603-05062: Bui Minh Tuan and colleagues present a deep learning framework for securing the physical layer of multicarrier ISAC systems under imperfect channel information. Unlike friendly jamming needing Eve's channel data or angle estimates, their method uses radar echo feedback to guide jamming. A radar-aware network jointly optimizes beamforming and jamming with a nonparametric Fisher estimator based on f-divergence, meeting Cramér-Rao bound constraints despite noisy angle estimates. A tensor-train encoder shrinks model size more than 100 times with little loss, and dedicated sub-bands serve communication only.
arxiv-2603-05262: Hieu Pham Dinh and team present VietJobs, the first large public Vietnamese job-ad corpus, with 48,092 postings and over 15 million words from 34 provinces. It covers titles, categories, salaries, skills, and employment conditions across 16 domains and employment types. On job sorting and salary estimation, instruction-tuned models gain notably under few-shot and fine-tuned settings. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-SEA-LION-v3-8B-IT lead those gains. Multilingual and Vietnamese-given ordered guess remains hard. VietJobs sets a Vietnamese processing benchmark and a base for recruitment and labor research.
arxiv-2603-05462: Eyasir and colleagues build NCTB-QA from 50 school textbooks issued by Bangladesh's National Curriculum and Textbook Board, yielding 87,805 Bangla question-answer pairs. Reading comprehension systems for low-resource languages often answer unreliably when the correct answer is absent from context. The dataset keeps a balanced mix of answerable and unanswerable questions, plus adversarial items with plausible distractors, and fine-tuning lifts BERT by 313% in relative F1 score.
arxiv-2603-05562: Ozaki and Ribeiro look at changing a description logic concept given models as pointed interpretations, a setting they call model change. They tell apart three kinds: eviction, removing models only; reception, adding models; and revision, joining removal with adding in a single step. They define revision in a formal way and argue, against gut feeling, that it is not merely eviction plus reception. Results follow on whether eviction and reception fit for EL and ALC concepts, and whether revision fits for ALC concepts.
arxiv-2603-05662: Angus and team develop an orderly framework for using vertex labels of graphs and digraphs to build digraph-defined outside gap families. The approach combines fitting vertex labels, wider versions of alpha-values, via a graph blow-up trick. New groups abound, including a clear first build of an endless 2-CEDF group, hitting all setting sets with m matching 0 modulo 4. New results also arise for graph labels themselves, including circle-based near alpha-values for trees without alpha-values, and an alpha-value for sun graphs.
arxiv-2603-06162: Dong and colleagues study the lightest two Higgs bosons near 95 and 125 GeV in the CP violating NB-LSSM. CP violation in the Higgs potential mixes CP even and CP odd fields, forcing a ten by ten neutral mass matrix. The neutral bosons mix strongly with each other, shifting masses and changing fermion and gauge boson couplings. Model parameters and CP violating phases shape mass and signal strength predictions. Predictions for Standard Model like channels plus excess signals near 95 GeV fit data well.
arxiv-2603-06262: Wang characterizes real laminations for cubic polynomials on tame edges of bounded hyperbolic components of types A, B, and C, per Milnor's four types. For such maps, the real lamination is the smallest one holding the maps' real laminations in the component plus a relation made by a single characteristic class. As a use, the work shows every hyperbolic cubic polynomial except type D fails to be combinatorially rigid.
arxiv-2603-06362: Impiö and colleagues present two image only approaches for invertebrate dry mass estimation, avoiding destructive dry weighing. One fits a linear model with novel predictors from an imaging device, and the other trains deep networks in single view, multi view, and metadata aware designs. Area and sinking speed serve as predictors, calculated with BIODISCOVER, a system imaging specimens sinking in ethanol. With automatic taxonomic classification, the approach gives accurate group level dry mass estimation even for complex diverse morphologies, with median error of 10 to 20 percent for individuals.
arxiv-2603-06662: Nguyen and team address continual VideoQA, where tuning causes task clash and storing task-specific prompts grows heavy. They bring DynaTokens, a token generator making fine-tuning tokens on demand for prompt updates through generation weights. Meta-learning-inspired rules look ahead to avoid sharp update directions while tying it to prior-task ways, picking flatter cross-task minima. Slope-free routing from ready token and visual codes reduces router drift. Across such VideoQA benchmarks, It beats baselines on accuracy and forgetting and enables cross-modal transfer.
arxiv-2604-00062: Kar and Koranga treat sterile neutrinos as a cosmic fluid whose pressure-to-density ratio changes over time. Standard accounts often freeze that ratio as a fixed radiation-like shift, but incomplete thermalization lets it drift instead. Their model tracks the fluid through radiation-like, transitional, and matter-like stages. For neutrinos near giga-electronvolt masses, the matter-like stage at matter-radiation equality shifts that epoch in line with their small energy share.
arxiv-2604-00262: Dean and Diamant show that orientational dipolar fluctuations in polar liquids yield a large share of shear viscosity, expressible through dielectric response values. With a Green-Kubo approach built on dipolar body-force correlations, they derive a direct link between the share and static permittivity and Debye relaxation time. Fixing one tiny cutoff length from one temperature, the theory predicts how it varies with heat for water and alcohol, using data from elsewhere. Slow polar motion thus adds a further, often main, share, bridging dielectric tests and rheology.
arxiv-2604-00462: Sar and colleagues train a neural network, SAT3-NN, to predict turbulent transport saturation from linear gyrokinetic inputs. The network maps linear data onto saturated potential sizes in the nonlinear regime, giving total energy and particle fluxes. Its training set comes from high-resolution CGYRO turbulence runs built for the SAT3 model. Against that dataset, SAT3-NN beats SAT3 on one-dimensional saturated potentials, with lower errors at peaks in both place and size. Its fluxes sit closer to nonlinear CGYRO results than the SAT0 through SAT2 models.
arxiv-2604-00862: Sapoutzoglou and colleagues propose a compact, object-specific way to represent shapes with Gaussian process mixture models, instead of bulky point clouds and meshes. Their light method learns smooth distance fields that point in each direction from thinly sampled point clouds, anchoring local priors at reference points drawn from structural decomposition. Tests on ShapeNetCore and IndustryShapes show it captures complex geometries well and fast.
arxiv-2604-00962: Zhang and team show mass inequalities for hadrons with heavy quarks arise mainly because binding values are concave in the quark model. That curve reflects short-range Coulombic forces and long-range confinement. Fitting two-body bindings from data as functions of reduced mass reveals a key confinement length of 1.34 fm where bindings turn above zero. Promoting them to exact matches, they predict masses for unseen heavy baryons and spot favored quark-exchange channels.
arxiv-2604-01062: Bertrand and team track how squeezing changes FeSe's superconductivity onset. Up to 0.6 GPa, onset rises under in-plane, out-of-plane, and uniform squeezing, matching loss of nematic order. Once nematic order is lost, angle matters: out-of-plane squeezing rises sharply like the uniform case, while in-plane squeezing kills superconductivity. Math suggests in-plane squeezing shifts a Se-iron band across the Fermi level along the Gamma-Z line, adding a metal band. This makes the charge setup more 3D, maybe a Lifshitz-type Fermi surface change.
arxiv-2604-01462: Dalirrooyfard, Makarychev and Mitrović revisit the random greedy algorithm for maximal independent sets, first analyzed by Yoshida, Yamamoto and Ito in 2009. Yoshida, Yamamoto and Ito showed that, on average per vertex, expected calls are bounded by the average degree of the input graph. While that analysis is clever and intricate, the authors provide a significantly simpler alternative with the same guarantee. It adapts the authors' 2024 potential-function argument for correlation clustering. Applied to maximal sets, it yields a more direct and transparent analysis.
arxiv-2604-01562: Yang and colleagues compare standard and strong-accent Mandarin speech and their voice clones, using machine and people tests. Machine tests show bigger source-clone gaps for strong-accent speakers, but this gap goes away after own spread is taken into account. In people tests, clones rate closer to sources for standard than strong-accent speakers, and clarity rises from source to clone, with a bigger gain for strong-accent speech. Accent spread thus shapes how well clones match speaker and clarity even when baseline machine distance shows no effect.
arxiv-2604-02162: Hinduja, Kaur, Bilalpur, Cohn and Canavan show that cross validation itself adds noise to facial action unit scores. Repeated subject exclusive splits on BP4D+ produce a measurable noise floor in average F1, larger for rare action units, and model rankings can flip with fold assignment. F1 swings more than threshold free measures like AUC.
