The paper supplies both halves. Scalable qLDPC on ordinary chips moves from hope to blueprint.
arxiv-2606-06162:
Can Savcı studies how fair agent teams can resist exploitation in this 2026 arXiv paper on multi-agent reinforcement learning, where several agents learn together by trial and error and share rewards. An egalitarian team works to raise its worst-off member, but a self-interested free-rider can pocket the surplus the others give up. The known fix needs a central allocator, which he wants to avoid.

CAN watches how teammates behave through cross-attention and infers how many free-riders are present. When a contested resource still delivers part of its value, pushing back beats yielding. CAN therefore contests just enough and otherwise takes turns. Trained against an adversarial league, it kept exploitability close to a centralized oracle. Its measured ratio stayed near one and a half rather than growing with team size, at almost no efficiency cost. Rival fair-learning objectives collapsed even with the same training.
arxiv-2606-06462:
Shiyun Xiong and co-authors build a machine that builds benchmarks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Benchmarks, the standardized tests used to grade language models, are slow to construct by hand. They also saturate quickly: top models cluster near the ceiling and stop being distinguishable. The team asks whether an AI agent system can run the whole construction pipeline itself, from reading a user's request to designing subtasks, annotating data, and controlling quality.

Their Benchmark Agent produced fifteen representative benchmarks spanning text understanding, multimodal understanding, and domain specific reasoning. Human evaluation, model judges, and consistency checks rated the generated samples as high quality with minimal human involvement. The fresh tests also exposed real weaknesses: current models struggled with certain domain specific reasoning tasks that older benchmarks no longer separate. Rapidly rebuilt benchmarks, the authors argue, are the sustainable way to keep measuring fast moving models.
arxiv-2606-06662:
Writing the files that automate software testing and release is slow, error prone work. Aboelfotoh and co-authors present AutoPipelineAI in this 2026 arXiv paper, a system that turns plain language requests into ready pipeline files. It reads the layout of a code project, then uses a large language model, a program trained to work with text, to draft setups for tools such as GitHub Actions and GitLab.

The paper lays out the system design, how it was built, and a plan for judging its output. The authors tested four models, among them GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o, on jobs of rising difficulty, from a Python project to a Go based website build. Their checks found that the models handled overall pipeline structure well, but made more mistakes in logic and step links as the workflows grew more complex and joined up.
arxiv-2606-07062:
When several judges rate the same items, researchers measure agreement with the kappa statistic. Gai and co-authors wrap that whole workflow into one friendly tool in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their R package, CATEKAPPA, targets a common pain point. Planning and analyzing agreement studies usually demands programming skill.

Two existing packages handle the halves separately. One plans sample size; the other computes kappa values. CATEKAPPA merges them behind a Shiny web interface. Users with no coding background can point and click. Cohen's kappa covers two raters, and Fleiss' version covers three or more. Light's kappa is included as well. Results come with automatic interpretation on the classic Landis and Koch scale. Command line functions remain available for scripted work. The package is free on the CRAN archive.
arxiv-2606-07262:
Materials that compute like neural networks, instead of merely housing electronics, are the vision in this 2026 arXiv perspective by Charles de Kergariou and co-authors. They define engineering material neural networks as load-bearing structures whose physical parameters can be trained, much as software networks adjust their weights. Intelligence would sit inside the structure itself, offering change without power-hungry graphics processors.

The authors survey candidate material families that might realize the idea soonest. Composites and architected materials, solids with designed internal geometry, lead the list. Living and bio-inspired materials also show promise because they adapt and repair on their own. The paper maps needed properties, such as reversibility and adaptive response, against what each family already shows. It closes with research directions, arguing that linked adjustable nodes inside a solid could approach the function-fitting power of software networks.
arxiv-2606-07562:
Cazenave designs RNA molecules with a Monte Carlo algorithm, Montparnasse, in this 2026 arXiv paper. RNA design means finding a nucleotide sequence that folds into a secondary structure or optimizes properties like paired-base count, with applications from synthetic biology to drug design. His framework builds on generalized nested rollout policy adaptation, a Monte Carlo technique that learns move preferences. It adds a problem-specific prior, slow and long tuning at the top level, and a lexicographic evaluation ranking solutions by tests in fixed order.

On the Eterna100 benchmark of 100 folding puzzles, Montparnasse solved every puzzle faster than DesiRNA, the best prior method, at every time limit. It reached coverage 3 times faster. A test optimized messenger RNA for hemoglobin alpha, where Montparnasse found sequences with more paired bases than the energy-optimal solution from a linear-time method. The results argue Monte Carlo remains competitive for molecular design.
arxiv-2606-07662:
Neishtadt studies a subtle timing puzzle in dynamical systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a parameter drifts slowly through the point where a steady state loses stability, the system often clings to the now-unstable state for a long while before departing. This delayed loss of stability is known, but how long the delay can possibly last is the sharper question.

Working with slow-fast systems near a Hopf bifurcation, where steady behaviour gives way to oscillation, Neishtadt confirms a maximal delay exists. Systems leave the unstable state almost together, near a threshold called a buffer point, and no longer delay is possible for ordinary starting data. The new result pins the size of that maximal delay to a hidden complex singularity, a breakdown point off the real number line. Its Stokes lines, curves tied to that singularity, meet the real axis exactly at the thresholds that set the delay.
arxiv-2606-07962:
Bin Zhu and co-authors ask whether multimodal AI models understand physics or just talk as if they do, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model can answer physics questions by exploiting language priors, statistical patterns in text, while barely looking at the images. Standard question-answering benchmarks cannot tell genuine visual reasoning from that shortcut.

Their benchmark, ChronoPhyBench, is built to block the shortcut. Models watch historical video with captions and must deduce what happens next. They select the correct next image, or sort several frames into chronological order, a task punishing guesses from words alone. The companion dataset holds more than ten thousand long-form videos with careful captions, totalling about five million tokens. Experiments on the benchmark quantify hallucination rates and expose how much apparent physical understanding collapses when language priors are neutralised. The authors offer it as a transparent yardstick for physically grounded AI.
arxiv-2606-08062:
Isaac Ortega Romero and Ioannis Zografopoulos argue that power grid resilience cannot be scored one dimension at a time, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Decarbonisation has made power systems sprawling cyber-physical infrastructures. Studies usually assess it dimension by dimension: physical, operational, digital, climatic, economic. The couplings between them go unexamined.

Following a PRISMA review across five axes, the authors show three things. Single-dimension scores miss the damage from failures hitting several axes at once. Joint compromise of the physical, operational, and cyber dimensions amplifies harm out of proportion. Climatic and economic stressors intensify the effect. They build a Multidimensional Resilience Index giving one combined score, and test it under real-world attack scenarios. The point: interactions between axes are themselves a first-class risk. Grid operators can use the index to compare systems and to check whether fixes help over time.
arxiv-2606-08262:
Kexuan Zhang and co-authors improve language-model forecasting of time series in this 2026 arXiv paper. Large language models can forecast by aligning temporal patterns with pretrained word embeddings, letting text knowledge inform prediction. But time series are mixed: each variable blends changing dynamics with stable meaning. The dynamic parts act as confounders, factors that distort the alignment and mislead the forecast.

Their framework, CVAformer, disentangles each variable into invariant and dynamic components just before alignment. It then applies causal intervention, a deliberate step that breaks the confounding influence of the dynamics. To support alignment variable by variable, it replaces the standard causal attention of language models, which only looks backward, with non-causal attention that can weigh the whole sequence. The authors argue that cleaning the alignment this way is the key to trustworthy forecasts.
arxiv-2606-08562:
Busigin and Pinter open up a language model to watch it assemble words from fragments, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Transformer models receive input as subword fragments, but meaning lives at the level of whole words. Detokenization is the internal process reconciling the two. Prior work located this mostly in early-to-middle layers without pinning down the exact mechanics. Using activation patching, swapping internal activations between paired runs, the authors isolate the contribution of individual components.

They localize English detokenization in a widely studied seven-billion-parameter model to a two-stage process at a single early layer. Attention first transmits a token-specific signal from the non-final subwords of a word. The feed-forward network then composes that signal with the local embedding to form the word representation. The two-stage structure generalizes across twelve models from eight families.
arxiv-2606-08662:
Malavolta and Rosen prove uncertainty principles for a transform at the heart of computer algebra and cryptography, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The number theoretic transform is the finite-field analogue of the Fourier transform, used for fast polynomial multiplication. An uncertainty principle says a function and its transform cannot both be concentrated on few points. The authors show strong sparsity tradeoffs: for suitable primes, the support sizes of a nonzero function and its transform sum to at least the domain size plus one.

Their main technical contribution is a probabilistic version of the principle, averaged over the choice of prime, in a regime where the prime is polynomially bounded in the domain size. The motivation comes from polynomial identity testing with exponentials, deciding whether an algebraic expression is identically zero. As an application, they obtain a black-box identity test for sparse exponential polynomials with vanishing soundness error.
arxiv-2606-08762:
Martin Andričik and colleagues study how many empty convex polygons a set of points can form without allowing a slightly larger one, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A k-hole is a convex polygon with k corners whose vertices come from the point set and whose interior contains no other points. The team asks for the largest number of k-holes in an n-point set with no empty convex (k plus one)-gon.

When the point count barely exceeds k, the maximum number of k-holes is two raised to the power a. This holds when n equals k plus a, with a at most half of k minus one. Each extra point doubles the achievable count in that range. Beyond it, they prove upper and lower bounds for two regimes: when n grows in proportion to k, and when k stays fixed while n grows without bound.
arxiv-2606-08862:
Kammoun and colleagues use X-ray polarization to test what lights up the center of the galaxy NGC 4151, in this 2026 arXiv paper. It hosts an active galactic nucleus, a feeding black hole whose surroundings glow. Earlier observers measured polarized X-rays and credited a wide, flat corona, the cloud of hot electrons above the accretion disk. The authors instead test whether it comes from disk reflection, X-rays bouncing off the disk, lit by a compact corona above the black hole like a lamp post.

Fitting two IXPE observations from 2022 and 2024, they find the lamp-post picture works. The corona must sit lower than nine gravitational radii above the black hole. Disk reflection supplies about twenty percent of the flux in the two-to-eight kilo-electronvolt band, where the polarization reaches six to seven percent. A separate soft component is polarized above ten percent at a different angle.
arxiv-2606-09162:
Yang and colleagues keep drone video segmentation steady with a routing trick costing no learned parameters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video semantic segmentation labels every pixel of every frame. Low-altitude UAV footage is dominated by flat regions, roads, roofs, fields, where motion follows a simple homography, one geometric warp. Standard temporal methods warp predictions with dense optical flow, whose flat-area noise is spatially structured and makes boundaries flicker.

Their gate uses RANSAC homography inlier ratios on a 16 by 16 grid, routing each region to homography or flow warping by a median-threshold decision, then fuses results by semantic similarity propagation. Diagnostics: flow residuals in planar regions are spatially autocorrelated, Moran's I of 0.32, and predict boundary instability. Rigidifying valid regions lifted temporal consistency from 62 percent to 92 percent. On synthetic UAVid data the method improved mIoU by 4.24 to 4.91 points across two architectures, adding 211,000 trainable weights on a frozen backbone.
arxiv-2606-09362:
Eduardo Borges and his colleagues ask whether vision-language models can recognise the same vehicle or person across camera views without any task-specific training, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task is re-identification, matching an object seen in one image against a gallery of images from other moments. Their zero-shot pipeline skips the usual training on labelled examples entirely.

Instead, a vision-language model writes a plain description of the object in each image, and a text encoder turns those descriptions into numeric vectors. Gallery entries are then ranked by how closely their vectors match the query object's vector. On the KITTI driving data, the strongest pairing reached a mean average precision near seventy-two percent and ranked the correct object first in about eighty-three percent of queries. Notably, the smallest text encoder tested, with three hundred million parameters, produced the best overall scores.
arxiv-2606-09562:
Atul Bhat and his co-authors report odd sideways drift in bright lanes inside sunspots in this 2026 arXiv paper. These lanes are called light bridges. They cut through the dark core of a sunspot and mark where hot gas forces its way up. Past work sorted bridges by shape, but their motion got less study.

Using images from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, the team tracked two cases of rare bridge motion. In one case, an S-shaped bridge formed, shifted, and faded within a span of twenty-four hours. The authors argue that such drift is not true travel of the lane itself. It is an apparent effect of change deep in the spot's core. Signs in the hot upper layers back this view. The bridge shifts line up with loops in the corona, the Sun's outer halo, and with how those loops move.
arxiv-2606-09762:
Andries Rosseau, Robert Müller, and Ann Nowé trace why networks grow stiff with age, and how to keep them limber in this 2026 arXiv paper. In continual learning, tasks shift over time. A network that once learned fast can lose plasticity, its power to pick up new skills. The team links that power to the neural tangent kernel, a map of how outputs react to tweaks.

The key trait is dynamical isometry: each layer's stretch factors stay near one, so signals pass without blow-up or fade. Some net families keep that trait by build, yet stay strong at hard fits. For plain nets, a cheap penalty pulls each layer toward it. The penalty can even wake dead ReLU units, which had gone dark. A new optimizer, AdamO, splits the push from the gradient steps, like AdamW does for weight decay.
arxiv-2606-09962:
Popov and colleagues ask which way of chopping speech into tokens works best for a newer generative model, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Continuous diffusion for categorical data generates discrete items, like tokens, through gradual noising in a continuous space. The team studies the latent structure behind tokens using divergence measures and correct-token prediction accuracy. Candidates include FSQ, finite scalar quantization.

Through rigorous theory and numerical experiments, they find the FSQ latent structure best suited to this diffusion framework. To test the claim in practice, they trained several text-to-speech diffusion models that use speech tokens as intermediate acoustic features. The FSQ-based model performed best among them. It also outperformed a strong language-model-based counterpart while being significantly smaller and faster, a practical win for speech synthesis. The authors present FSQ as the natural token choice when diffusion replaces autoregression for discrete data.
arxiv-2606-10062:
Chen and colleagues study a privacy problem created by AI agents that remember their users, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning privacy. Long-lived foundation-model agents store memories across interactions, so memorization happens at deployment time, not only inside model weights. The team frames agent memory as a frontier between personalization utility and extraction risk, measured by personalization recall and an adversarial extraction rate.

On the LongMemEval benchmark, key-fact summarization cut canary extraction, the leaking of planted secrets, by seventy-six percent on one model and sixty-four percent on another, while preserving nearly all personalization. The same compression, however, broke deletion: raw-only deletion left derived summary copies recoverable in about twenty percent of cases. Only full-pipeline purges or tombstone redaction drove residue to zero, so memory must be audited for recall, leakage, and true erasure.
arxiv-2606-10162:
Panda and his team report the first atom-scale look at superconductivity in a copper-cobalt sulfur compound, in a 2026 arXiv paper on condensed matter physics. The team used muon spin rotation and relaxation, a technique implanting short-lived particles to sense internal magnetic fields, alongside magnetization and heat-capacity measurements. The temperature dependence of the superconducting signal indicates a fully gapped order parameter, meaning the energy gap for excitations never closes.

Their extracted gap ratio, just under four, exceeds the classic BCS weak-coupling value of about three and a half, placing the material in the intermediate electron-phonon coupling regime. None were observed within resolution, though a ferromagnetic impurity phase reduced reach for weak fields. The authors conclude there is no evidence for such symmetry breaking, while noting it cannot be ruled out for sure.
arxiv-2606-10262:
Hafiz and colleagues simulate how heat and electric current conspire inside phase change memory cells, in a 2026 arXiv paper on device physics. Phase change memory stores data by switching a germanium-antimony-tellurium alloy between amorphous and crystalline states in a mushroom-shaped cell. Their two-dimensional finite-element electro-thermal study covers Reset and Set operations, including spatial variations in activation energy and phase-change dynamics.

Running current from the top electrode to the narrow four-nanometer bottom electrode required about three times less energy and power. It also needed about half the current, to reach the same Reset resistance as the opposite polarity. Filamentary conduction, electrical breakdown, thermal runaway, and local crystallization all depend on polarity and thermal boundary conditions. Together they fix the programming region's location, shape, and volume, which can be far smaller than the mushroom region.
arxiv-2606-10362:
Chen and colleagues introduce a family of invariants for knotoids, the open-ended cousins of knots, in a 2026 arXiv paper on low-dimensional topology. Knotoids are diagrams of curves with two endpoints, and polynomial invariants help distinguish them, with some constructions using crossing signs. Their coloring-allowed invariants are defined through the coloring number, a count of valid colorings of the diagram's arcs under set rules. The paper demonstrates several basic properties of the coloring number and gives examples of the resulting invariants.

Among the examples, the four-phases functions are discussed in detail, including proofs of their invariance and their properties. Working through Gauss diagrams, the combinatorial encodings of knotoid diagrams, the authors place coloring-allowed invariants within the growing toolkit for planar knotoids. Such invariants support tabulation and comparison of knotoid types arising in applications from polymer physics to protein folding.
arxiv-2606-10462:
Aoki and Fukaya defend their earlier work on hot quantum chromodynamics in this short 2026 arXiv reply to a published comment by Giordano. Quantum chromodynamics, or QCD, is the theory of the strong force. The dispute concerns chiral symmetry restoration at high temperature and the axial anomaly. The original argument leaned on analyticity: above the transition temperature, every gluonic observable should vary smoothly with the squared quark mass.

The reply makes three points. The counterexamples all break that smoothness assumption, as the comment itself acknowledges, so they cannot refute an argument built on it. The disputed quantity is well defined when the theory is regularised on a finite lattice with the overlap Dirac operator. They also flag a concrete algebraic mistake, a wrong equality in the comment's handling of averaged quantities. Their verdict is blunt: the criticisms are invalid and the original conclusions stand.
arxiv-2606-11062:
Akarsu and three co-authors present a 2026 arXiv essay on cosmology, the study of the universe. The standard model gives dark energy a fixed positive density, yet expansion measurements disagree enough to trouble it. The authors build a physical version of the sign-switching cosmological constant idea, where dark energy flips from negative to positive late in cosmic history, near redshift two.

Their engine is a phantom scalar field, whose kinetic energy carries the wrong sign. That flaw becomes the mechanism. The field climbs its bounded potential, lifting the vacuum from negative-energy anti-de Sitter space to positive-energy de Sitter space. It pushes outward even while its density stays negative. Total energy stays positive, the end state is calm de Sitter space rather than a Big Rip, and the dynamics stay safely infrared, at low energies. The honored essay offers one mechanism bearing on several tensions at once.
arxiv-2606-11262:
Sivaramakrishnan and three co-authors test what causes interference between language model adapters in a 2026 arXiv paper. Access control for large models needs modular adapters, small trained add-ons carrying domain knowledge, composed only for authorized users. A common hypothesis blames interference on overlap in the adapters' weight updates, implying that forcing orthogonality, updates at right angles, should fix it.

Using DoRA-RBAC, a composition framework built on weight-decomposed low-rank adaptation, they compare plain Euclidean merging with a geometry-aware Riemannian strategy across QA benchmarks including GPQA and PubMedQA, on LLaMA-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B. Single-domain performance matched LoRA, but geometry-aware merging gave no consistent advantage in multi-domain settings. Diagnostics further showed angular alignment is a weak predictor of merging performance. They conclude the effect is not governed mainly by weight-space shape, but by interactions in shared nonlinear features.
arxiv-2606-11462:
Usman Gohar, Hunter, Purandare, Rios, Cohen, and Lutz propose a documentation tool for safety arguments in a 2026 arXiv paper, from Iowa State University. Safety assurance cases give structured cases that safety-critical systems meet their requirements. Defeaters, challenges to a safety argument such as overly strict claims, unreliable evidence, or reasoning gaps, rigorously test validity. Yet they remain ad hoc and hard to review.

Their Defeater Cards are a standard artifact for describing and managing defeaters. A literature survey and theme analysis yield criteria shaping the card, built on the 5W1H framework: who, what, when, where, why, and how. The cards support informed analysis, improve traceability and auditability, and let defeater knowledge be reused across systems. Two cross-domain case studies show the cards expose hidden assumptions and surface reasoning gaps. The team also releases an open-source repository of defeater cards.
arxiv-2606-11562:
Peng, Jiang, Gu, Fan, and Yang benchmark whether language models can infer from graphs in a 2026 arXiv paper. Many real answers cannot be looked up in a single record or retrieved along a path. Laundering rings, drug repurposing, user preferences, and scientific themes are all inferred from a node with its neighborhood. Existing graph question-answering protocols cannot test this, since their answers are retrievable from a single node or path.

Their GraphInfer-Bench defines five tasks along two axes, Description, what a region is, and Comparison, how regions differ. Each task is built so the truth lives in no single node. It asks models for open-ended answers no node supports and no path retrieves. They contrast it with algorithm simulation, node classification, knowledge-graph QA, and GraphRAG, which admit retrievable answers. The release targets a gap current evaluations miss: genuine graph inference, synthesizing a neighborhood into a judgment.
arxiv-2606-11762:
Tan Min Sen leads a Raffles Institution team measuring the creativity of language models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Judging creativity is usually welded to one task, which blocks fair comparison across domains. Their framework separates the measuring apparatus from the task itself, so the same yardstick applies to any open-ended work.

Creativity is split in two. Divergent creativity, the spread of novel and varied ideas, is scored by semantic entropy, a reference-free measure of how spread out meanings are, checked against human annotations. Convergent creativity, actually fulfilling the task, is judged by a retrieval-based panel of model agents, which the authors say improves efficiency by over sixty percent. They validate the framework in three domains: improvised problem solving, research ideation and creative writing. Results show how model size, temperature, recency and reasoning style each shift creative performance, giving a reproducible standard for comparing models.
arxiv-2606-11862:
Meysam Bagheri Tagani and Carmine Autieri show how to switch a topological material with an electric field in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chern insulators carry dissipationless edge currents, counted by a whole number called the Chern number, and are prized for low-power devices. Altermagnets, a newly recognised magnetic class with no net magnetisation, resist hosting this effect because opposite spin states stay degenerate at one key point.

Starting from a standard model of topological bands, the authors combine an external magnetic field, a tilting of spins called canting, and ferroelectric coupling. Together these lift the degeneracy. Their minimal two-dimensional model becomes a Chern insulator whose phase the polarisation controls reversibly. Switching it flips the system between states with Chern numbers of plus or minus one and two. The orbital magnetisation is likewise sizable and electrically tunable, a property the authors link to orbitronic devices.
arxiv-2606-12062:
Abhinav Naga and three colleagues work out when a raindrop can clean a dirty surface in this 2026 arXiv paper. Dust and soot particles degrade solar panels, windows and microelectronics, yet how a drop captures and carries off a particle was unclear. The team combined lattice Boltzmann fluid simulations with confocal microscopy experiments. When a drop meets a particle on a surface, at least six distinct removal scenarios emerge from capillary and friction forces.

Capillarity plays a dual role: its sideways component always pushes the particle toward removal, while its vertical component can pin the particle down. The authors condense the physics into one dimensionless capillary capture parameter that predicts removal across many surfaces. A practical subtlety matters: for water-loving particles on a thin water film, the friction coefficient drops sharply and must be measured in liquid. The results give quantitative design principles for easy-to-clean surfaces.
arxiv-2606-12262:
Strobel and co-authors fabricate Josephson junctions without the organic films that usually limit them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Josephson junction is a sandwich of two superconductors around a thin barrier, the core switch of superconducting quantum circuits. Standard production uses organic resist masks, which burn at high temperatures and leave residues tied to decoherence, lost quantum behavior. High-melting superconductors like tantalum and niobium stay hard to use, despite better temperature and speed limits.

Their technique patterns a three-dimensional, low-loss substrate instead, so no organics touch the junction area. Electrodes come out free of added oxides and residues. The team builds niobium trilayer junctions in several sizes and shapes, all underdamped, their current-voltage curves showing the sharp hysteresis of high quality. Flexible deposition opens quantum circuits to a wide range of materials. Faster circuits running at higher temperatures become realistic targets.
arxiv-2606-12362:
Wang and co-authors teach cancer models to work with whatever patient data exists, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-omics profiles combine gene expression, methylation, protein levels, and more for one patient. In practice some assays are always missing, through cost, failure, or mismatched study protocols. Filling in fake values for missing modalities risks propagating errors. Their Latent World Recovery framework instead treats each modality as a partial view of one underlying state.

Each modality gets a variational encoder mapping into a shared latent space. Neighbor-based alignment keeps the views consistent without forcing exact coordinate matches. A fusion step combines only the modalities present for that patient, at training and at prediction time alike. Nothing is imputed or reconstructed for absent channels. On incomplete multi-omics benchmarks, the approach supports cancer phenotype classification and survival prediction. Availability-aware learning, the authors argue, beats pretending the data were complete.
arxiv-2606-12462:
Coquand reports what happened when he let an AI write machine-checked proofs of the incompleteness theorems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Autoformalisation turns human mathematics into proofs a computer can verify. Working in Agda, a strict proof language, the author wrote not a single line himself. Claude, the language model, formalized Chaitin's proof of the first incompleteness theorem, then the Kritchman-Raz surprise-examination version of the second.

The hard part was computation itself: no internal evaluation function exists at this arithmetic level. Claude autonomously built a continuation-stack evaluation machine over ternary-string code, plus a parser, with no suggestions from the author. A majorisation argument the author proposed was followed without trouble. The result is a machine-checked development inside Church's Basic Recursive Arithmetic, clarifying details the original papers left implicit. Coquand's verdict is measured: today's models are excellent tools for dissecting proofs, but they need constant supervision.
arxiv-2606-12662:
Martins Gomes and Capman present BASENet, a speech enhancement network designed around how human hearing actually works, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speech enhancement means recovering clean speech from a noisy recording, a task used in hearing aids and voice calls. Most models spend equal computing effort on every frequency, yet hearing resolves low frequencies finely and high frequencies coarsely. BASENet therefore splits sound into Bark-scale bands, a scale matching that uneven resolution.

Deeper branches handle the perceptually dense low bands, while lighter branches handle high bands, and a cross-band attention module tracks harmonics, related tones spread across bands. On the VoiceBank plus DEMAND test set, BASENet reaches strong quality scores with under a million parameters, the fewest among methods of comparable quality. A causal variant, which cannot peek at future sound, still beats several non-causal rivals, suiting it to live streaming on small devices.
arxiv-2606-12762:
Roseman and colleagues compare 2 cloud microphysics schemes in regional weather runs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Microphysics schemes represent how cloud particles form, grow, and fall as precipitation. The team used the MPAS-A model on a mesh refined to 1 kilometre. It ran convection-permitting hindcasts over 3 subtropical and tropical regions, Houston, Taiwan, and Hawai'i, under strongly and weakly forced weather regimes.

The 2 schemes, NSSL and TEMPO, both captured the timing and placement of convection but produced distinct structures. TEMPO made more numerous, weaker convective cores with earlier, more widespread rain and cooler surface conditions. NSSL favoured fewer, stronger cores and updrafts, with denser, more intense rainfall. Both schemes differed from observations more than from each other, producing scattered cells with weak order and too little stratiform rain. Rainfall was underestimated in strongly forced regimes and overestimated in weakly forced ones, where forecast skill was lower.
arxiv-2606-12962:
Liu and Patey study the reverse mathematics of the Ordered Variable Word theorem, a combinatorial principle used in the proof of the Dual Ramsey theorem, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reverse mathematics measures which set-existence axioms a theorem requires, by proving it from a weak base theory and showing the axioms cannot be weakened. Variable word theorems concern colourings of words with placeholders, and their strength relative to classical Ramsey principles was unclear.

The authors prove that the Ordered Variable Word theorem does not imply Ramsey's theorem for pairs, separating it from a principle it was suspected to match. They show that every computable instance of the theorem admits a solution of low-2 degree, a computability-theoretic weakness property. The paper answers open questions standing for some 40 years and clarifies dual Ramsey theory's position in the reverse-mathematics hierarchy.
arxiv-2606-13062:
Ariga and colleagues optimise sweeper magnets to suppress the forward muon background at the Forward Physics Facility of the High-Luminosity LHC, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The facility will enable high-statistics measurements of TeV-scale neutrinos in the far-forward region, but the intense flux of forward muons threatens the neutrino detectors. The team studies magnet configurations with a simulation framework combining SIBYLL event generation, BDSIM beam transport, Geant4 particle tracking, and realistic magnetic field maps.

Starting from a muon flux of 3.8 thousand per square centimetre per inverse femtobarn without magnets, a single magnet in the LHC tunnel alone achieves the target level of 2 thousand. Additional magnets at the TI18 tunnel and at the facility entrance further reduce the flux to 1.5 thousand per square centimetre per inverse femtobarn in the optimised configuration.
arxiv-2606-13162:
Pan, Skandera, and Wang prove permanental inequalities for a class of totally nonnegative matrices arising from unit interval orders, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The permanent of a matrix resembles the determinant but sums over permutations without signs, and totally nonnegative matrices, those whose minors are all nonnegative, satisfy inequalities in their entries. The matrices studied are 0-1 antiadjacency matrices of unit interval orders, shown by intervals of unit length on a line.

For each such matrix, the authors prove a family of inequalities comparing products of permanents of submatrices. A split of the index set at any cut position dominates, in permanent product, the split into even and odd indices. The proof connects to permutation combinatorics. They construct a map between a Young subgroup and the permutations such that each permutation lies below its image in the Bruhat order. That is checked for sizes up to 13 and conjectured for all sizes.
arxiv-2606-13262:
Yang and colleagues present ProFact in this 2026 arXiv paper, a system that learns how to check facts step by step. Automated fact verification usually runs as a fixed pipeline: split a claim into parts, gather evidence, then issue a verdict. Most systems tune each stage separately or follow rigid rules, so the stages cannot adapt to each other. ProFact instead trains one policy with reinforcement learning, meaning the system improves by trial and reward. The same policy handles breaking down claims, searching for evidence, drafting answers, and giving the final verdict.

Because the only natural reward arrives at the very end, the authors add process-aware rewards that grade each intermediate stage as well. Tests on the AVeriTeC benchmark, a standard set of real-world claims, show ProFact beating strong systems. It also used less computing effort than those baselines.
arxiv-2606-13362:
Beccaria and Ternes test whether neutrino oscillations fade with distance in this 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrinos change flavour as they travel, a quantum effect called oscillation. Several mechanisms could damp that pattern: the neutrino wave packets could separate and lose coherence, the system could leak coherence to its surroundings, or the neutrinos could decay invisibly. The authors confront three scenarios with data from JUNO, a reactor neutrino experiment in China. JUNO's first release, based on 59 days of data, gives the most precise values of two key parameters.

Fitting the damping scenarios to that data yields bounds matching older experiments. The open quantum system treatment lets the authors vary how the decoherence scales with neutrino energy. Invisible decay, where a neutrino disappears without visible products, is constrained. The standard oscillation parameters remain measured in every scenario, so the physics search does not undermine the experiment's goals.
arxiv-2606-13662:
Amy Xin and colleagues argue that designing agent environments matters more than scripting agent workflows in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language model agents can automate scientific discovery: given a measurable objective and an execution setting, they propose, test, and refine solutions, sometimes beating human-designed approaches. The authors contend that as models improve, the bottleneck shifts to environment design, the tools, limits, and links that shape agent behaviour. Good settings boost behaviours such as open-ended search, careful artefact handling, and teamwork between agents, while suppressing harmful ones.

Their system, EurekAgent, embodies this philosophy for self-directed science. Rather than scripting the agent's steps, the setting is built so that good scientific practice is the path of least resistance. The framing mirrors a lesson from human institutions: outcomes depend less on instructing people and more on designing the setting they work in. The paper provides the argument and a working system.
arxiv-2606-13762:
Abbasi and the IceCube Collaboration report real-time neutrino searches tied to gravitational-wave alerts in this 2026 arXiv paper. IceCube, a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, detects high-energy neutrinos from cosmic accelerators. When the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA observatories issue a gravitational-wave alert, IceCube searches its data around the alert time for coincident neutrinos. Such neutrinos would identify the source as a hadronic accelerator and sharpen its localisation. The paper describes these searches during the fourth observing run and the pipelines that execute them within moments of an alert.

Multi-messenger astronomy lives on such coincidences: neither messenger alone gives the full picture of an event. The collaboration's system scans the sky maps against neutrino arrival directions and times. Even non-detections constrain the sources, limiting how much energy they can channel into high-energy particles. The report documents the programme's methods as observing runs grow longer.
arxiv-2606-13862:
Xiong and colleagues speed up the step-by-step reasoning that large language models write out before answering. This chain of thought improves accuracy but costs time, since each token is produced one after another. Pure latent reasoning, done inside the model's hidden states, trains poorly without token-level guidance. Their 2026 arXiv paper, SuperThoughts, blends the two: pairs of consecutive reasoning tokens are packed into single latent units, then decoded two tokens per step.

A light multi-token prediction module does the paired decoding, while training keeps ordinary token supervision. A confidence check falls back to standard decoding when the model seems unsure. The team fine-tuned three Qwen math models, at one point five, seven, and fourteen billion parameters. On MATH500, AMC, OlympiadBench, and GPQA-Diamond, reasoning chains shrank by about twenty to thirty percent. Accuracy mostly held, dropping one to two points on most tasks.
arxiv-2606-14062:
Shimamoto makes a computer out of knitted fabric, where logic lives in the stitch pattern, not the material's shape. Mechanical computers built from origami or metamaterials encode states in geometry, so stretching corrupts them. His 2026 arXiv paper instead encodes information in topology: a circuit knitted from one yarn, each bit a pair of stitches, computation proceeding by controlled unraveling. Splitting the textile into cells yields propagation rules for the unraveling front.

The rules implement universal logic: NOT, AND, OR gates, plus a half-adder. Sample circuits ran six to ten stitches wide and six to twenty rows tall, hand-knitted from rubber-cord yarn. Experiments showed output stays correct under deformation; mechanical factors decide only whether the computation can run, not what it computes. This split of logic from mechanics is the claim. The framework might extend from textiles to buildings: computation needing no power, tolerating heat or radiation.
arxiv-2606-14162:
Xiang and co-authors keep generated videos geometrically honest, no reconstruction pipeline needed. Video diffusion models produce realistic frames but drift in 3D structure over time, above all under viewpoint change. Prior fixes condition on explicit geometry, depth maps or point clouds, propagating upstream errors at heavy compute cost. Their 2026 arXiv paper proposes VideoWeave: features from an implicit geometry model become 3D latents, modeled jointly with video latents in one shared denoising space.

They built GeoVid-80K for training, eighty thousand videos with paired appearance and 3D data. The joint prior is then distilled into a compact student generator. At inference the student needs no 3D encoder or renderer, yet keeps the prior. Experiments on text-to-video and image-to-video tasks showed much better coherence and stability, with fidelity preserved. Implicit joint modeling, they argue, is a scalable path to world-consistent video.
arxiv-2606-14362:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a 2026 arXiv search for dark photons, hypothetical particles that could carry a hidden force. The team looked for Higgs bosons decaying into one ordinary photon plus one dark photon, which would leave missing momentum in the detector. Data came from proton collisions at thirteen point six teraelectronvolts at the Large Hadron Collider.

The analysis used one hundred thirty-five inverse femtobarns of Run 3 data from twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four, with a new trigger lowering photon thresholds to fifty gigaelectronvolts. A boosted decision tree cleaned events with faulty vertex reconstruction. No significant excess over Standard Model expectations appeared. The branching ratio for the decay is capped near one point four percent, and combining with earlier Run 2 searches tightens the cap below one percent.
arxiv-2606-14662:
Ines Nolasco and co-authors probe what pretrained audio models actually encode in a 2026 arXiv paper on bioacoustics. Sound embeddings are standard tools for studying animal calls, yet nobody knew which acoustic features they capture or which suit a given task. The team regressed model embeddings against eighty-eight speech-science features across six taxonomic groups, using linear and nonlinear probes.

No single model captured the full feature space, confirming a no-free-lunch pattern, while concatenating embeddings from several models performed best, suggesting complementary coverage. Loudness features were recovered best, with an explained-variance score near zero point seven six, while pitch was hardest at about zero point three three in the same units. Cross-referencing feature recoverability with per-species salience gave data-driven guidance for choosing a model for a new species or scarce-data task.
arxiv-2606-14762:
Abelarde and Garrido-Lestache Belinchon propose a multi-level scheme for semantic video study in a 2026 arXiv paper. Video keeps growing in schooling and fun media. Current AI summarizers mostly give coarse views from transcripts. They miss a video's structure, theme flow, and meaning links. Their scheme, Scribby, balances the big picture with sentence-level detail.

The first stage indexes the video at micro level in three ways. It studies the full transcript. It studies single sentences. It groups sentences by likeness of meaning, with a language model as judge. Sentence-level prompts include the global study and nearby sentences. That keeps context that lone processing would lose. The authors frame Scribby as a base for tools that picture semantic chunks and matches. Heatmaps of relevance are the planned display. They also note current limits and planned growth.
arxiv-2606-15162:
Zhao and coauthors present GeoStream, a 2026 framework for camera-controlled streaming video generation. Streaming generators build a video frame by frame, and users steer the camera as it runs. Most systems learn camera motion loosely, so requested moves drift from the true path. Fixed 3D caches help, but they fail once the view leaves the first frame's area. GeoStream instead rebuilds its geometric guidance from its own newest output.

The system estimates depth from the latest generated frame and reprojects points into the target view. Those reprojections condition the next frames, keeping control at metric scale. Training uses the same trick: conditioning comes from the student's own frames, not ground truth. This on-policy training matches the errors the model meets at run time. On the RealEstate10K benchmark, GeoStream cuts camera-pose errors sharply against strong baselines. It keeps accurate control far outside the training range of camera paths.
arxiv-2606-15262:
Meoto and Lekala show that four-momentum conservation alone fixes mesonic decay momenta, in a 2026 nuclear physics paper. Their case is the hypernucleus helium-5-lambda, whose lambda particle decays into a pion and a nucleon. Inside a nucleus, that decay competes with Pauli blocking of the outgoing nucleon. The authors treat both two-body and three-body decay channels with relativistic kinematics. Two-body decay is constrained, forcing a monochromatic pion momentum.

For three-body decay, conservation laws no longer pin every momentum down. The authors sample the phase space with Monte Carlo simulation instead. Fifty thousand events per channel produced pion momentum peaks. The neutral pion channel peaked near one hundred three MeV per c, the negative near ninety-seven. Only a fraction of one percent of events escaped Pauli blocking in a channel. The peaks match experiments and theory. Kinematics, not interaction models, emerges as the dominant constraint.
arxiv-2606-15362:
Badás and coauthors derive the best beam shape for laser links between satellites in a 2026 optics paper. Such links carry far more data than radio, but vibrations make the beam jitter around the receiver, causing dropouts. Widening a standard Gaussian beam helps partly. Using a variational method, which optimizes a whole function at once, the authors find the ideal far-field light pattern for minimizing outage probability.

The optimum is a flat-top beam, flat across its width, needing only about a third of the power a Gaussian beam needs for the same reliability. A flat-top is physically impossible, so the paper studies super-Gaussian beams that approach it, plus practical shaping tricks. Combining simpler beam modes incoherently, or sculpting the beam with a phase mask, cuts the required power in half. Halving transmitter power matters on satellites, where every watt competes with payload and battery budgets.
arxiv-2606-15462:
Shvets proves a tower of supercongruences for a hypergeometric sequence in a 2026 number theory paper. The sequence comes from cubing a hypergeometric series. A supercongruence says its terms at prime-power indices agree with earlier terms modulo a high power of the prime. Earlier work proved the first level. This paper proves every level, for all primes from five upward.

The proof is modular: the generating function is realized on a modular curve through eta products, turning the sequence into coefficients of an Eisenstein series. The new device replaces a one-prime defect with a prime-power Hecke defect, whose lowest layer is a Cartier defect controlling the difference to be bounded. A Fricke involution argument on a two-dimensional space of modular forms kills the low-order part, and induction handles the rest. Such towers feed the broader program linking hypergeometric series to modular forms.
arxiv-2606-15562:
Xiao studies quantum corrections to the Page curve of charged near-AdS2 black holes in 2026, a controlled corner of the black hole information problem. The Page curve tracks radiation entropy during evaporation: it should rise, then fall after the Page time if evaporation is unitary. For near-extremal charged holes, the low-energy dynamics reduce to two soft modes, a Schwarzian reparametrization mode and a phase mode.

Xiao averages the energy and flux over both soft modes to get corrected balance equations for temperature and chemical potential. Feeding the corrected background into island and no-island entropy calculations then gives the shift of the Page time. The two sectors pull in opposite directions: the phase mode correction delays the Page transition, while the Schwarzian correction moves it earlier. The net shift is set by their competition, so even the timing of information release depends on the softest quantum modes.
arxiv-2606-15762:
Tal and colleagues ask whether large language models find the same security bugs twice in 2026, with Snyk VulnBench JS. Agentic reviewers now scan code before humans do, but unlike deterministic static tools they can improvise, over-report, or stop early. The benchmark reruns identical scans to measure how repeatable the findings are.

Across hundreds of runs, repeatability splits sharply by finding type. When a model matched a reference vulnerability from Snyk Code, the finding was stable: most appeared in all five repetitions. Extra findings were noisy: nearly half of the unique extras appeared in only one of five identical scans, few in all five. Models reliably catch familiar exploit shapes, and once surfaced a likely gap in the static tool itself. Static analysis, meanwhile, systematically enumerates repeated data-flow sinks that models sample unevenly. The verdict is to combine both, since they fail in different ways.
arxiv-2606-16062:
Rajan audits in 2026 how easily the test suites behind code reinforcement learning can be fooled. Such training rewards agents when their patches pass tests, so weak tests let wrong code earn rewards, a failure called reward hacking. Rajan generates incorrect patches and checks, inside Docker containers, whether the official tests wrongly accept them.

On a 49-task sample of SWE-bench Verified, 28.5 percent of tasks have suites weak enough to pass a verified wrong patch in the audit. A parallel check on R2E-Gym tasks gives a similar rate of 25.0 percent overall. A meta-analysis of 134 model submissions finds scores run higher on flagged tasks than on robust tasks of matched difficulty. Rajan then hardens tasks with a language-model judge guarded by a gold-solution sanity gate. That gate catches many flawed generated tests the judge alone misses, and the repair loop fixes most broken tasks tried.
arxiv-2606-16162:
Liu and colleagues present AutoDecompiler in 2026, a language model trained to decompile binaries through repeated, feedback-guided revision. Decompilation recovers readable code from executables, supporting flaw hunting and malware checks. Earlier model-based decompilers generate one output and stop. Their code may read well and even compile, yet still behave differently from the original binary.

AutoDecompiler treats the task as stepwise revision instead of one-shot generation. The model revises its output using compilation, execution, and input-output testing feedback across turns. Reinforcement learning trains this loop with rewards for valid code that builds again, reruns faithfully, and matches in meaning. Stage-aware feedback and turn-aware reward weighting support the training. Across settings, scales, and benchmarks, the system improves recompilability and re-executability over vanilla and single-turn versions in the reported tests.
arxiv-2606-16362:
Sengupta and Anastasio propose in 2026 a model-intrinsic way to see what a medical image classifier responds to, replacing heuristic heatmaps. Post-hoc explanation methods paint plausible pictures, but their link to the classifier's actual output distribution is indirect. The new framework uses the input-dependent Fisher information matrix, which measures how the predicted class distribution shifts under tiny changes to the input image. That matrix is far too large to build directly.

A Gram-matrix formulation recovers its nonzero spectrum without forming the full matrix. Projecting an image onto the leading eigenspace splits it into a high-sensitivity part and the rest. The method needs no extra labels and no second model. It works from the trained model alone. Tests cover controlled and clinical tasks. The authors position the tool as a Fisher-geometric complement to standard explanation methods, grounded in one defined quantity from the model itself.
arxiv-2606-16462:
Lopes and co-authors test in 2026 whether giving every brain a private encoder solves the oldest headache in EEG decoding: no two subjects' signals line up. Cross-subject training promises more data, but strong distribution shifts between people sabotage shared models. The usual fix, Euclidean Alignment, recenters each subject's covariance before a shared encoder runs. The hybrid alternative replaces that shared encoder with one encoder per subject, all feeding a common classifier.

Across four motor-imagery datasets, alignment clearly helps the standard shared baselines, EEGNet, AttentionBaseNet, and CTNet. The hybrid model, by contrast, barely changes when alignment is removed: it has internalized the alignment's role into the subject-specific encoders. Those encoders raise class distinctiveness and park each subject near its own latent manifold, improving results for most subjects. A method-sensitive subset remains, and choosing an encoder head for an unseen subject is the open bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-16562:
Mohammad and Sheikh audit anti-Muslim bias in frontier language models in 2026 under the conditions models actually face now, not the single-turn completions of older studies. Their benchmark, MIRAGE, holds 1,200 prompts across three deployment-realistic regimes: direct completion, chain-of-thought reasoning, and agentic decision-making in content moderation, lending triage, refugee claim summarization, and hiring screens. Six frontier models are tested.

Reasoning makes things worse: chain-of-thought amplifies Muslim-violence associations by 12 to 34 percent relative to direct completion. Agentic decisions show a 9 to 22 percentage-point asymmetry between Muslim and matched non-Muslim cases on identical evidence. Bias is also time-coupled, rising 18 to 27 percent when retrieval pulls recent-conflict news. Existing prompt-based mitigations transfer poorly: they suppress direct-completion bias while leaving the agentic asymmetry largely intact. The decision settings where models can do the most real-world harm are exactly where defenses work least.
arxiv-2606-16662:
Zhao proves a convergence criterion in a 2026 paper on random operators and singular stochastic equations. Paracontrolled expansions break hard nonlinear problems into blocks, and the mixed second-level blocks can be singular where plain product rules fail. Each block must be shown to settle down as the cutoff that regularizes it is removed.

At a finite cutoff, Zhao splits each operator into two parts. One part is a diagonal covariance term supported on matching Fourier modes. The other is a centered random tensor, a Gaussian chaos term with shifted mode relations. The random part is controlled with tensor estimates, time lifts and dyadic summation over frequency shells. The diagonal part needs only scalar bounds once finite cancellations are formed. The criterion works in any dimension, with colored noise, random starting data and frequency-dependent sizes. It isolates a reusable mechanism, leaving model-specific diagonal work as explicit input.
arxiv-2606-16862:
Jamneshan connects two families of uniformity norms in a 2026 mathematics paper. Uniformity norms measure how random a function looks, and Gowers introduced them to count patterns in sets of numbers. A quantum version, built by Bu, Gu and Jaffe for higher-order Fourier analysis on quantum systems, seemed to need its own theory.

Jamneshan shows the quantum norms are exactly pullbacks of the matrix-valued norms of Gowers and Hatami, transported along the Weyl orbit embedding. That single identification hands the quantum norms two basic tools for free: a Gowers-Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and a triangle inequality. Those were open questions posed by the quantum norms' creators. In the extreme regime, the same bridge describes the Clifford hierarchy levels of Gottesman and Chuang, central to fault-tolerant quantum computing, through unitary-valued polynomial maps on finite vector spaces. A short observation thus ties quantum Fourier analysis back to additive combinatorics.
arxiv-2606-17262:
Rodríguez and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on young stars still buried in dust, using JWST imaging of four nearby galaxies. Massive young stellar objects in the Magellanic Clouds are well characterised from earlier Spitzer surveys, and this work bridges those studies to more distant spirals. Colour and brightness selection rules, guided by the Magellanic catalogue, were tested with experiments that degrade image resolution step by step.

Hundreds of dusty young objects were picked out across the four galaxies, from single massive young stars to compact clusters hosting several. The colour selection stayed stable across the distance range, and the mid-infrared brightness distribution kept its shape. Blending and dilution still removed fainter sources, causing incompleteness of up to about half at the far end. The practical limit for studying single such stars with JWST is about three megaparsecs.
arxiv-2606-17362:
Sun and colleagues, including a team at NVIDIA, present a 2026 arXiv paper on judging self-driving behaviour with an agent that mixes rules and vision-language reasoning. Rule-based metrics are interpretable but blind to context, while pure vision-language judges see context yet give vague answers with weak physical grounding. DriveJudge aims for both virtues at once, reading the scene first and only then calling the deterministic rule checks that the context calls for on that clip.

Training and testing use a large curated set of challenging driving samples, each labelled by humans as reasonable or not for its scenario. Two benchmark tasks are introduced, classifying driving quality and choosing the better of two trajectories. DriveJudge beat a leading rule metric on quality classification by a wide margin in the reported area-under-curve score. It also beat a recent vision-language critic on trajectory preference.
arxiv-2606-17662:
Sujith and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper testing whether synthetic speech can usefully train speech recognition for Hindi, Kannada, and Telugu, three Indic languages short on recorded training data. Collecting and annotating real speech is slow and costly, and India's dialect diversity makes the shortage worse. The study mixes generated speech with real recordings and measures what the synthetic share actually buys, rather than assuming more data of any kind must help the recogniser in these low-resource settings.

Three design choices are varied in turn: which scripts seed the generated speech, which synthesis model speaks it, and whether cloned voices supply the speakers. Voice cloning receives special attention, including how the count of distinct cloned voices changes the payoff. The results map where synthetic data earns its place in fine-tuning for these languages. Such maps matter for teams choosing how to spend scarce recording budgets.
arxiv-2606-17762:
Huang and colleagues tackle a reliability problem in optimal control math in a 2026 paper. Solvers for finite-horizon control repeatedly face Pontryagin boundary value problems, and their accuracy can decay as the time horizon grows. The authors give a checkable certificate, stated at the level of the problem data, under which that decay does not happen.

The certificate rests on hyperbolicity of a reduced transition matrix plus a scaled split of stable and unstable boundary parts. From it they build a corrected Green inverse whose bounds do not depend on the horizon, then carry it over to the nonlinear problem. The result is a feedback map whose sensitivity stays uniform as horizons lengthen. Tests with symplectic and Riccati criteria show broad classes of standard control systems qualify, and worked computations illustrate both routes.
arxiv-2606-17862:
Biswas and colleagues build a faster numerical method for simulating two stacked liquid films, in a 2026 applied math paper. Their two-layer thin film model extends an earlier one by dropping a restrictive choice that fixed the Marangoni numbers of both layers at one. With that freedom restored, they prove the system still carries a full set of Riemann invariants, the special variables that simplify wave-like equations.

Those invariants drive a new scheme, RI-WENO, which reshapes the variables so the governing equations partly diagonalize and the eigenvector matrices turn sparse. The payoff is a method that keeps the oscillation-suppressing strength of standard characteristic WENO schemes at much lower cost. New benchmark tests in one and two dimensions show the balance holds up, making the scheme a practical pick for thin film flows.
arxiv-2606-18062:
Kim and colleagues dig through millions of real chatbot conversations to see what people actually ask about digital security and privacy, in a 2026 study. Earlier work judged model answers against expert-written misconceptions, never against genuine user questions. Drawing on the WildChat collection of over three million conversations, the team fished out nearly fifteen thousand security and privacy prompts and sorted them into nine topic categories.

A close reading of a sampled set revealed habits unique to chatbots, like using the model as a defensive agent or probing its internals. The team then posed hundreds of advice-seeking prompts to five models repeatedly and graded the answers. Commercial models clearly beat open-weight ones on quality and consistency. Yet even the strongest could still produce flawed security guidance. That is a caution for the many users now treating chatbots as their first security consultant.
arxiv-2606-18162:
Crismale and colleagues identify the algebraic type of a quantum probability space built from interacting particles, in a 2026 paper. Interacting Fock spaces deform the standard stage on which creation and annihilation operators act. The algebras they generate can show striking probabilistic behavior. The team studies the two-periodic case, where the interaction pattern repeats every two steps.

They prove the algebra generated by the position operators is a type II1 factor. That is the same class as the famous free group factors. On the probability side, the squared position operators follow a Marchenko-Pastur distribution under the vacuum state. That gives a natural home for free Poisson laws inside this framework. An abstract classification thus ties to a concrete, named law from free probability.
arxiv-2606-18462:
Ferudun attacks a stubborn special case of a graph coloring question posed by Dirac in 1970, in a 2026 combinatorics paper. The question asks for graphs that need four colors, lose that need when any single vertex is removed, yet keep it when any single edge is removed. Earlier work settled all larger cases, leaving this one open.

Focusing on the hypothetical case where every vertex has exactly six neighbors, he proves three results. A computational search rules out such graphs on up to fifteen vertices, apart from one exceptional thirteen-vertex graph whose critical edges form a ring. A structural theorem shows every smallest edge cut in such a graph is either one vertex's star of edges or separates two large shores, making small examples super-edge-connected. A third result bars any shore of such a cut from being bipartite. Several lemmas are machine-checked in Lean.
arxiv-2606-18662:
Bennett and Fridberg study the complexity of deciding whether two self-dual lattices are rotations of one another, in a 2026 paper spanning cryptography and the geometry of numbers. The lattice isomorphism problem has attracted attention because recent cryptosystems rest on its presumed hardness. Self-dual lattices, those equal to their own dual, arise naturally in many applications but had not been singled out for algorithmic study.

Exploiting two structural facts, the authors give a randomized algorithm running in roughly two-to-the-half-dimension time and a coNP protocol certifying non-isomorphism for a broad class of self-dual lattices. The facts are that every self-dual lattice splits off a standard integer part, leaving a core with no short vectors, and that such lattices possess characteristic vectors. Parallel structure also yields a polynomial-time algorithm for permutation code equivalence on certain self-dual codes with large hull.
arxiv-2606-18862:
Budi and the team measure oxygen in the oldest stars in the Galaxy using infrared lines, and check the method against the optical yardstick, in a 2026 stellar astronomy paper. Oxygen abundances in very and extremely metal-poor stars constrain how the first stars manufactured the elements. But the forbidden optical oxygen line is single and weak, while the near-infrared OH lines are numerous.

Using spectra from the Subaru Telescope for thirty-five stars spanning a metallicity range, the team derived oxygen from OH lines. They compared it with the forbidden line in optical spectra. The OH abundances proved sensitive to temperature. They showed an offset, running low in red giants and high in warm ones, as atmosphere effects predict. A calibration against temperature, gravity, and composition aligned the OH results onto the optical scale. That shrank the scatter, and flattened the abundance trend into agreement with chemical evolution models.
arxiv-2606-18962:
de Wet and colleagues report rich data in 2026 on supernova 2025kzr, a Type Ibn blast whose spectra show narrow helium lines. The star sits in a nearby galaxy and was found within about a day of its blast. Rare extra data catch a bright outburst from the same star, close to two months before the final explosion.

Early spectra show flash features for about ten days, lit by the shock as it hits gas near the star. Line tests show that gas has no hydrogen at all. The fade time of the flash, plus the speed of the gas, points to a big loss of mass just before the blast. That timing matches the outburst well, which hints at a direct link. The case gives rare proof that a dying star's last outburst can shape the gas its shock lights up.
arxiv-2606-19162:
Beltran-Velez and colleagues propose discriminator-guided reinforcement learning in 2026 to correct flow matching models. Score and flow models often use preference-based reinforcement learning for two ends, aligning with human taste and, oddly, recovering basic realism the matching training should have taught. The authors argue this reflects a structural mismatch. Matching losses gauge regression error under training-time conditions, a proxy poorly tied to sample quality at generation time.

Their method trains a discriminator to separate real data from base-model samples inside a pretrained representation space. Its logit serves as the reward in regularized reinforcement learning. The pretrained space keeps the discriminator focused on perceptually meaningful directions. The logit also estimates the log-likelihood ratio between data and model, the optimal reward for targeting the data distribution. Human preference labels are not needed, so the reward stays tied to data realism.
arxiv-2606-19262:
Rahman and colleagues test in 2026 whether hidden machine learning training can be detected with zero-overhead telemetry. Compute governance proposals rely on monitoring GPU workloads, but such schemes fail if developers can evade the monitor. The team uses only NVML telemetry that adds no overhead and preserves privacy. These signals watch physical effects of computation without reading model weights, training data, or settings.

Across five rounds of monitor-evader iteration, twenty evasion strategy families are tested on nine GPU models from four generations. A classifier reaches very high binary accuracy at spotting training workloads across the whole corpus. Against the hardest disguised workloads, accuracy stays well above chance, though it drops as expected. The results suggest hardware telemetry is hard to fool completely. Governance based on physical signals, rather than self-reported data, has a firmer footing than critics assumed, even against adaptive evaders.
arxiv-2606-19362:
Arshid Shabir claims to construct four-dimensional SU(N) Yang-Mills theory with a mass gap and confinement. His 2026 paper starts from a reflection-positive lattice formulation of the pure gauge theory. The claimed route runs through Euclidean methods: positivity, locality, and a transfer operator with a uniform gap.

Large Wilson loops are claimed to obey an area law via convergent character expansions, signaling confinement. A finite-range, gauge-covariant multiscale analysis then carries the gap and clustering to the continuum limit, with a strictly positive string tension. Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction would finally yield the relativistic theory. If the argument holds, it settles a Millennium Prize problem; as with all such claims, it awaits outside verification.
arxiv-2606-19562:
Gabriel Barros, Rômulo Silva, and Alvaro Coutinho survey scientific machine learning for coupled fluid flow and transport in 2026. Coupled systems pair incompressible Navier-Stokes flow with a carried scalar, as in turbidity currents and thermal convection. Strong nonlinear coupling and many scales make full simulations costly.

The chapter reviews surrogate models that stand in for full solvers. Linear reduced-order methods rest on singular value decomposition, including dynamic mode decomposition. Neural routes include physics-informed neural networks and beta-variational autoencoders. High-performance computing aids such as adaptive mesh refinement and data compression join the survey. Two fresh contributions apply physics-informed networks to turbidity currents and autoencoders to thermal flows. Lock-exchange flows and Rayleigh-Bénard convection serve as benchmark cases. Fast, accurate surrogates emerge within stated data regimes, at far lower cost than full-order runs.
arxiv-2606-19862:
Dipanjan Mitra and Kanak Saha profile two hundred five faint galaxies across three wavelength bands in 2026. Low surface brightness galaxies spread their light so thinly that surveys often miss them. Candidates came from the KiDS survey, imaged deeply by Hyper Suprime-Cam.

Single-component Sérsic models, fitted with GALFIT, yield the structural parameters. Diffuse systems dominate, with profile indices peaking near zero point seven in every band. Median central surface brightness sits firmly in the low surface brightness regime. Red systems dominate the catalogue at about eighty-seven percent. Blue systems make up the rest, yet both colours share near-identical structures. No measure differs significantly between the colour groups. Colour shows no link to axis ratio, arguing against dust as the reddening cause. The sample stands as a clean structural reference for faint galaxy work.
arxiv-2606-19962:
V. V. Bavula gives formulas for special subfields inside simple field extensions in prime characteristic in 2026. Any such extension mixes a separable part, where roots behave tamely, with a purely inseparable part driven by p-th powers. The paper pins down the largest purely inseparable subfield, the largest separable subfield, and their compositum, first for the extension itself and then after a purely inseparable base change.

Everything is expressed through the coefficients of the defining polynomial and two numerical invariants, with degrees computed as well. From these formulas come new tests for when the whole field splits cleanly into its inseparable and separable parts. Algebraists gain ready-to-use criteria instead of case-by-case arguments.
arxiv-2606-20362:
Heikki Mäntysaari, Björn Schenke, Chun Shen, Hendrik Roch, and Wenbin Zhao revisit whether gluon saturation is really visible in diffractive J/psi events. Their 2026 paper runs a global Bayesian analysis of coherent and incoherent production on protons and lead nuclei, inside a Color Glass Condensate framework. The underlying idea is that gluon growth at small momentum fractions tames itself through recombination. Ultraperipheral LHC data are used, corrected for electromagnetic dissociation, alongside older HERA data, with Gaussian-process emulators standing in for the heavy calculations.

Earlier fits showed tension between the proton and nuclear datasets. With that correction applied, that tension shrinks substantially. Proton and lead data can now be described consistently at once, with the inference pinning down the model parameters. A subtle experimental correction, it turns out, can masquerade as a physics disagreement.
arxiv-2606-20462:
Avraham Moriel and Howard A. Stone study how two polymer species interdiffuse, with and without a source feeding one of them. Their 2026 paper is motivated by biological subcellular processes where a source drives the mixing. Both unentangled and entangled chains are treated.

A two-fluid formalism yields scaling relations, self-similar reductions, and analytical solutions, all confirmed by one- and two-dimensional numerical simulations. Adding a source term breaks the self-similar structure, changing the boundary conditions and the domain of integration. Even so, the front of the diffusing droplet keeps spatial structures similar to the source-free case. The results give a baseline for reading source-driven mixing in cells and industrial blends.
arxiv-2606-20662:
Kaiwen Shi and four colleagues name a failure mode in agent systems in 2026 that they call confidence laundering. An upstream agent may make a fragile choice under uncertainty, then pass it onward as a clean, valid-looking artifact. Downstream agents inherit the commitment without the doubt behind it, so small local ambiguity can grow into system-wide error. The problem, they argue, sits at the handoff between components, not only inside single steps.

Shi and colleagues define uncertain decision handoff as that transfer, and propose latent uncertainty as a carrier attached to each handoff. Rather than replacing text with hidden states, the carrier keeps fragility in a usable form. Designing handoffs that preserve doubt could make long agent chains less prone to compounding mistakes.
arxiv-2606-21062:
Zhiyao Xiong, Xiaokui Yang, and Shing-Tung Yau introduce a broad class of flows in 2026 in the first part of a study of the prescribed Hermitian-Yang-Mills flow. A flow deforms a metric on a holomorphic bundle over time. Their flow adds a prescribed tensor term to the classic equation. The goal is a limiting metric that solves a prescribed tensor equation exactly.

Long-time convergence of the flow to that limiting metric is established. A class of prescribed tensors is covered. The crucial uniform bound along the flow comes from a parabolic comparison principle. Part one builds the flow machinery and its key estimate. The companion part applies it to a stability theorem. Together they show how a prescribed target, not only the standard one, can be reached by deforming a metric until curvature matches the demand.
arxiv-2606-21162:
Sang-Hun Han and five colleagues present PIAvatar in 2026, a framework that gives 3D human avatars physical interaction ability, not only good looks. Pose-driven avatars show high visual fidelity. They still cannot push, collide, or deform in believable ways. Earlier attempts add only limited deformation, so interaction behavior stays constrained. Their key insight separates two quantities that are usually tangled.

Kinematic velocity is decoupled from the deformation gradient. When outside forces act, stress no longer blocks the avatar from reaching a desired pose in the same way. A skeletal framework inside the avatar estimates pose in closed form during interaction. Real-time tracking continues even under non-rigid deformation.
