The method runs inside a standard material point simulation framework. Physically aware avatars could support games, telepresence, and training where bodies must contact each other and the world.
arxiv-2606-21262:
Zihang Tian and five colleagues propose ARCO in 2026, a training framework for multi-step language model agents that replaces opaque scalar rewards with rubrics. A rubric scores work against plain-language criteria, but earlier rubric methods grade whole trajectories and rely on a frozen closed-source judge. ARCO uses one model with two heads: one writes criteria for each step, the other scores steps against those criteria.

A decomposition rule ties the sum of step scores to the final outcome, giving credit assignment without step-level labels. The rubric model and the agent policy train together on fresh data, so criteria and scoring co-evolve. Across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with two open backbones, ARCO tops outcome, rubric, and process-reward baselines, and its rubrics stay step-specific enough to diagnose agent behavior.
arxiv-2606-21662:
Eric L. Graef, Jeff Murugan, Horatiu Nastase, and Hendrik J. R. Van Zyl test a claimed universality of complexity growth in 2026, inside N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. Gravity-side arguments suggest infalling probes in anti-de Sitter space grow complex in a universal way. The authors compute Krylov complexity for operators dual to open strings ending on giant gravitons, a tractable corner of the theory.

In protected and few-body sectors, the dynamics is governed by orthogonal polynomials tied to the seed spectrum: Lanczos coefficients stay bounded, set by spectral support alone. The motion is integrable and band-limited, far too tame to test the gravity claim. They therefore propose a finite-density program, with magnons scaling with system size. Its sharp test: does leading Krylov growth depend only on coarse data like density and energy, not on the probe's microscopic makeup?
arxiv-2606-21762:
Amit Devra, Emanuel Malvetti, and eight colleagues redesign dynamical decoupling, the pulse trick that keeps idle qubits coherent, in 2026. Standard decoupling repeats one short pulse block forever; small imperfections in the block pile up until state recovery fails over long idle times. Their universal optimal tracking designs sequences by watching the qubit's evolution at preset waypoints during optimization, compensating residual errors on the fly while keeping the regular refocusing rhythm.

Crucially, the design is state-independent, one sequence protects any state. Tests on a superconducting-qubit platform confirm that error growth is suppressed under static control imperfections, matching the numbers. Simulations add robustness under time-dependent noise. Short, robust, hardware-agnostic sequences matter because most qubits in a real processor spend most of their time idling, leaking coherence while they wait.
arxiv-2606-22062:
Rizvi and Tomar ask, in 2026, how a limited budget of real-robot measurement time should be split when training robot policies in simulation. Two strategies compete: system identification, measuring the real system's parameters directly, and domain randomization, training across a wide spread of simulated dynamics for robustness. The authors built a controlled sim-to-sim pendulum testbed where a hidden-parameter model plays the role of the physical robot.

Sweeping identification effort against randomization width delivered a clear verdict. A few identification rollouts largely closed the transfer gap across the tested reality gaps and noise levels. Once any real data existed, policies trained at the estimated parameters beat policies trained over a widened randomization band, even when that band contained the true system. The authors scope the claim: with only two unknown parameters, measurement wins; structural model mismatch is where randomization breadth may still pay.
arxiv-2606-22562:
A. Álvarez Cruz and E. A. Álvarez Gutiérrez present a claimed criterion for the Riemann hypothesis in this 2026 paper. The hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics, concerns the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. The authors work in the Colombeau algebra, a framework that handles singular objects by tracking nets of smooth approximations.

Their claim is an equivalence: the hypothesis holds exactly when a certain moderate net in that algebra, built from damped Báez-Duarte sums, is associated to a specific target. Two damping strategies are presented, one exponential and one polynomial. Under the hypothesis, the nets are shown to be moderate and correctly associated. Conversely, the authors argue, any moderate net of this form with the stated association forces the hypothesis to hold. As with all such claimed criteria, the equivalence itself is the result on offer, not a resolution of the hypothesis.
arxiv-2606-22662:
Ruslan Gokhman compares neural forecasters on a chaotic system in this 2026 paper, written for the AI-DEEDS 2026 Chaotic Systems Challenge. The target is the Lorenz attractor, the classic butterfly-shaped system where tiny errors grow exponentially over long rollouts. Seven recurrent and convolutional architectures compete under identical preprocessing and rollout rules.

The entrants include a vanilla LSTM, an attention-augmented LSTM, bidirectional LSTMs with and without a robust Huber loss, a temporal convolutional network, and CNN front-ends feeding recurrent cores. Scores landed in the middle range of the challenge scale. The bidirectional LSTM trained with Huber loss was strongest overall. Two findings stand out. Adding attention to the plain LSTM degraded its score by over ten points, and CNN front-ends did not help either recurrent core, slightly hurting both. On the hardest sequence pairs, the bidirectional family generalized best while the attention model collapsed.
arxiv-2606-22862:
Zhichao Fan, Yanhang Li, and Zexin Zhuang test whether forced chain-of-thought helps video question answering in this 2026 workshop paper. Forcing a vision-language model to reason step by step is widely assumed to make it more reliable. The authors propose a three-probe recipe to check that assumption.

The probes compare accuracy across direct, chain-of-thought, answer-first, and no-video conditions; swap the input video to see whether chains depend on it; and degrade the video through a four-rung ladder. Applied to Qwen2.5-VL on Video-MME subsets, the recipe gave a two-part finding. The chains were strongly video-conditioned: swapping the video collapsed chain overlap and flipped most final answers. Yet forced chain-of-thought did not improve multiple-choice accuracy, and on the smaller model it caused a small, statistically supported drop. The authors limit the claim to this model and benchmark.
arxiv-2606-23062:
Giulia Martinelli and colleagues release VolHuMe, a large dataset of moving three-dimensional human scans, in a 2026 paper. The scans come from a volumetric studio with sixty-four color cameras and thirty-two depth cameras. One hundred four people were captured individually at close range. That setup preserves fine detail in hands, faces, and body parts that full-body datasets often blur. Each capture ships with rich ground truth, including fitted body models, high-resolution meshes, multi-view images, point clouds, rigged meshes, and garment labels.

Martinelli and colleagues benchmark leading reconstruction methods on VolHuMe for three-dimensional and four-dimensional tasks. Four-dimensional here means shape changing over time. The dataset's quality lets the benchmarks expose weaknesses in current methods and in the testbeds used to judge them. The team presents VolHuMe as a sharper yardstick for human reconstruction research.
arxiv-2606-23162:
Nader Bshouty speeds up property testing for abelian groups in a 2026 theoretical computer science paper. Property testing asks whether a structure has a given property, or is far from having it, while inspecting only a small part of it. Here the structure is a finite set with a binary operation, and the property is being an abelian group, where the operation commutes and follows group rules. Two access models are studied. The weaker one hides the group size and shows random elements with their operation table.

Bshouty presents a tester whose running time grows with the square root of the group size plus a term in the allowed error. That beats the earlier testers of Goldreich and Tauber on both time and query counts. The result extends to subclasses of abelian groups closed under relabeling.
arxiv-2606-23362:
Vu Tuan Truong and Long Bao Le attack diffusion models with a nearly invisible backdoor in a 2026 security paper. A backdoor makes a generative model behave normally until a secret trigger appears, then produce attacker-chosen output. Earlier attacks traded off strength, stealth, speed, and poison rate. Strong attacks needed much poisoned data and long training, which made them easy to spot. Their framework, TooBad, optimizes the trigger itself. The tuning runs on sampled noise with the big model frozen, so it stays cheap.

Truong and Le report striking efficiency on the CIFAR-10 benchmark. At a poison rate of half a percent, attack success passed eighty-five percent. Earlier work typically needed ten percent for such results. At five percent poisoning, success reached nearly one hundred percent within a handful of epochs.
arxiv-2606-23462:
Sovesh Mohapatra, David Lydon-Staley, and Dani Bassett track militarized language in scientific writing in a 2026 paper. Scientists do not wage war, yet war vocabulary pervades their abstracts: fighting diseases, battling resistance, arsenals of methods. The team analyzes over twenty-one million papers from 2010 to 2025 across two large databases. They also run a within-subject experiment on war framing, with about eight hundred participants and over thirty-two thousand trials, to test causal effects on persuasion. Between 2010 and 2025, militaristic terms in abstracts rose by roughly half in one database and a third in the other.

Mohapatra and colleagues find the rise accelerated sharply after 2019, moving in near lockstep across both databases. The experiment arm probes how war framing changes whether readers find claims persuasive. The paper frames the trend as a shift in how science talks about itself, with measurable consequences for communication.
arxiv-2606-23662:
Rossa, Phillips, and Rainforth reformulate how experiments should be designed when the data serve a specific downstream decision, in a 2026 paper on statistical methods. Bayesian experimental design picks measurements that most reduce uncertainty about unknown quantities. The classic objectives are doubly intractable, meaning they involve nested averages that resist direct computation. They also value all information equally, even though only some of it matters for the decision at hand.

Following decision theory, the authors define design quality by expected future loss on the downstream action itself. They show every such objective can be rearranged into a singly intractable form. That form lets stochastic gradients optimize the design policy and the action policy together, with no explicit posterior or likelihood estimates. The method needs only samples from the joint model and a way to score the downstream loss. Designs can therefore be learned more simply and tailored to each task.
arxiv-2606-23962:
Liang proves a comparison principle linking how much delay costs to how early an optimal observer should act, in sequential testing and change detection, in a 2026 paper on statistics. Both problems watch a diffusion, a noisy continuous process, whose drift follows one of two hypotheses or changes at an unknown time. When the signal strength depends on the current observation, the posterior probability alone no longer summarizes the state; the observer must track it jointly with the process itself.

Fix the cost of a wrong terminal decision. Then a larger running penalty on delay raises the value of continuing, shrinks the continuation region, and forces earlier stopping. Where the stopping rule is a posterior threshold, the alarm boundaries inherit the order. A worked Shiryaev example computes the threshold numerically and confirms the monotonicity.
arxiv-2606-24362:
Zhou measures how sensitively tectonic tremors in northeastern Japan answer the tides. Tremors are faint, slow seismic rumblings along subduction zones, and the tiny periodic stress of Earth tides modulates them, offering a gauge of how close a fault sits to failure. Whether that response varies inside a system mixing fast earthquakes with slow slip was unknown before this 2026 study, the first systematic investigation of its kind.

Drawing on a tremor catalogue spanning 2016 to 2024, Zhou finds the strongest tidal sensitivity at the southern end of the Kuril Trench, a region of migrating tremor and relatively weak seismicity. The northern Japan Trench responds weakest. Spatial analysis adds a pattern: areas of weaker tidal sensitivity tend to host more moderate earthquakes and denser tremor activity. Zhou, who led the investigation and software, argues tidal response maps a fault's stress state in ways earthquake counts alone cannot reveal.
arxiv-2606-24962:
Thibaut Kulak asks whether one transformer policy can be pretrained across thousands of different reinforcement learning environments. Sequence models have shown one network can learn from very diverse data. Kulak builds LDM-v0, a Large Decision Model, on that bet. It is a multi task, multi modal transformer conditioned on histories of observations, actions, rewards, and end signals. Training is supervised next action prediction over offline trajectories from many domains.

The evaluation covers roughly one thousand of them. They include inventory management, robotics, autonomous driving, cybersecurity, trading, and video games. One pretrained model matches task specific reference policies trained alone across this spread. Kulak describes the setup, data pipeline, model design, and training method in full. The results show large scale offline pretraining across very different tasks works with one transformer policy. Specialists are no longer the default for each new task.
arxiv-2606-25062:
Rank aggregation merges ordered preference lists into one ranking. Dongqing Li and three colleagues note that classic models assume the lists cluster around complete consensus rankings. Newer ones let the consensus be a partial order, where some pairs simply cannot be compared. Their hierarchical partial order models go further, handling grouped data through a hierarchy of latent partial orders.

Information is shared across groups in a principled way while the partial order structure survives. The Plackett Luce model and its hierarchical variants fall out as special cases. A clustering extension handles settings where group labels are unknown. Inference over the latent hierarchy runs by Markov chain Monte Carlo. On synthetic and real data, including pairwise acoustic preferences and language model agent traces, the models beat existing approaches on prediction and on how interpretable the recovered structure is.
arxiv-2606-25362:
Online shops must assign each arriving order to a warehouse and carrier within a fraction of a second, under delivery times nobody can know exactly. Tinghan Ye and colleagues replace the repeated heavy optimisation behind that choice with a learned stand in, described in 2026. A neural network is trained offline on answers from a full stochastic solver, and a decoder then repairs its raw output so every assignment stays feasible. One forward pass replaces a solve that took seconds to minutes.

In a simulator calibrated on transaction records from a major retailer, decisions came roughly twenty eight hundred times faster than the reference method. Realised fulfilment cost also fell by a few percent against that reference, and by over ten percent against standard fulfilment policies. Late deliveries dropped to about half, at a speed that holds up during peak order surges.
arxiv-2606-25462:
Abstractive summarisation asks a model to write a fresh short version of a text rather than lift its sentences. Sadiul Arefin Rafi and colleagues fine tune the PEGASUS transformer for that job in 2026, training on the English portion of the XL-Sum corpus of news summaries. A general model called mT5 serves as the baseline to beat. Quality is scored with ROUGE, which counts overlap between machine summaries and human written ones at several phrase lengths.

The fine tuned model improved on the baseline across all three reported scores. Gains were about four percent on single word overlap, over fifteen percent on two word phrases, and about three percent on longest matching sequences. The authors report the result as the best known performance on this corpus and credit the task specific tuning of a model already pretrained for summarisation style gaps.
arxiv-2606-25562:
Medical image segmentation networks are heavy arithmetic, and edge hardware must run them on a tight energy budget. Muhammad Usman, Yousef Sadegheih, and Dorit Merhof accelerate the U-Net architecture on a programmable chip in 2026. They use digit serial arithmetic, which processes numbers one digit at a time starting from the most significant. That style is compact but each operation stalls before its first digit emerges, and chained operations stack the stalls.

Their merged multiply add unit fuses the two operations into one pipeline with a single, shorter startup delay per pass. Running many input depths in parallel lifts throughput further. Against a processor baseline the design delivered up to ten times the energy efficiency. It also used about nine times less energy than earlier digit serial chip designs. That suits it to latency sensitive imaging at the edge.
arxiv-2606-25762:
Cancer researchers cannot freely share patient records. Synthetic stand ins are tempting. But ordinary generators scramble the causal links between traits, treatment choice, and survival. Any effect estimate then comes out biased. Octavia-Andreea Ciora and colleagues built OncoSynth in 2026 to keep those links intact. Its diffusion generator works sequentially. First it models how traits steer treatment assignment. Then it models how treatment shapes survival. The result is a fake cohort that behaves causally like the real one.

Validation used large lung and breast cancer cohorts. They held roughly thirty seven thousand and seventeen thousand patients. The synthetic cohorts matched real distributions of traits, treatments, and outcomes closely. Treatment effect estimates improved sharply over existing generators. Population level error fell by up to two thirds. Patient level error fell by well over half. That supports evidence generation where data sharing is blocked.
arxiv-2606-26062:
Bo Chen, a computational social scientist, asks whether a striking published-style finding can be pure measurement error. Interviews with four public intellectuals supply the test data. The corpus spans a decade and holds 85 interviews. Keyword scoring finds a strong pattern there. Negative language and emphatic-certainty words appear together, with strong correlations across all four speakers.

Swapping the instrument breaks the pattern. A language model classifies stance semantically across all 32,625 sentences instead. The headline correlation collapses for the best-known speaker. Two speakers flip to negative values, and one shows none. A different coupling emerges instead: negative talk pairs with hedging, as common sense expects. Sentence-level checks trace the keyword failure to three blind spots. Syntax, word-sense ambiguity, and missing categories each distort counts. One scored phrase even inverts its plain meaning. Chen argues keyword counts track a quirk of vocabulary, not a speaker's certainty.
arxiv-2606-26162:
Agung Trisetyarso, Lenny Putri Yulianti, and Kridanto Surendro design an online learning method that runs on engineered quantum dynamics. Multiplicative weights is a workhorse rule for learning from repeated feedback. Their variant, DQMW-Sample, prepares a Gibbs state with a tailored open-system process each round. Measuring that state supplies the feedback. The twist is computational hardness: simulating the feedback classically is provably hard at constant temperature.

Separation results follow. On a crafted problem, their learner's regret shrinks toward zero per round over time. Every efficient classical learner keeps constant average regret there. Noise works in their favour as well: the dissipator's spectral gap contracts hardware noise, keeping noise-driven regret sublinear. A stronger result covers the whole adaptive interaction at once. An efficient classical simulator for all rounds would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Early tests run on an IBM Heron processor.
arxiv-2606-26262:
Gina Chen, Katelyn Breivik, and Lieke van Son trace how stable mass transfer sculpts the black hole pairs that gravitational wave detectors hear merging. One formation channel has a star steadily feeding its companion before both collapse. How much of the transferred mass is kept, and when transfer stays stable, decides the final masses. Analytic reasoning and population synthesis together map those choices onto observable distributions.

Role reversal splits the population in two. Under conservative transfer, pairs whose donor and accretor swap mass ranking form one subpopulation: heavy primary black holes at near-equal mass ratios. Pairs without reversal form the other: lighter primaries at uneven ratios. Stability rules at different life stages carve the two groups into separate peaks. Each assumption about transfer physics moves the peaks around. Detectors now flying, and near-future ones, may resolve the twin peaks and read the transfer physics back out.
arxiv-2606-26462:
Chia-Lung Lin and twelve colleagues make the case for Nautilus, a proposed space observatory that would watch stellar flares unfold second by second. A flare is a sudden explosion of radiation from a star's surface. Low-mass G, K, and M dwarf stars are prime targets in the search for Earth-sized planets in habitable zones. Yet their flares flood planets with ultraviolet and X-ray light that can strip atmospheres and drive harmful chemistry.

Current habitability models often use simplified flare recipes, such as fixed-temperature glows, which can badly understate ultraviolet energy. Nautilus would instead record fast, carefully calibrated spectra, meaning light split by wavelength, from the near-ultraviolet through the near-infrared, across many flaring stars. The team aims to build a library of real flare templates sorted by flare energy, flare phase, and star type. Planet researchers would gain measured inputs instead of guesses.
arxiv-2606-26762:
Le Tu Ngoc Minh, Jinyeong Lim, and Dongsu Han present ProtoKV, a memory system for understanding streaming video. Questions about a live stream can arrive late. A key cue may flash by long before anyone asks about it. Memory limits force the system to drop or dilute old content. Their design keeps the recent past exactly and summarises the distant past.

Older content is folded into a bank of prototypes with summary statistics. Each prototype acts like a compact stand-in token at query time. The total memory stays fixed no matter how long the stream runs. The approach fits standard attention machinery without changes. On streaming benchmarks, ProtoKV beat token-keeping rivals by up to twelve and a half points in the long-delay regime. Gains grew as the delay grew.
arxiv-2606-26962:
Ilya Bogaevskii and Michel Rouleux settle on a normal form for the simplest Lagrangian fold in semi-classic analysis. Such methods approach quantum problems with classic geometry as a small parameter shrinks. These folds arise where classic paths fold, as in glancing light rays. The Hamilton-Jacobi equation organises those trajectories. Its solutions project down to space and energy with singular behaviour at critical values.

The authors' normal form captures that fold in a standard shape. With it, they approach solutions of a driven equation. The driving term sits on a Lagrangian manifold, a surface of classic states. At the critical energy, Bessel functions describe the local form, making cylinder-like patterns. The result sharpens final formulas near grazing trajectories.
arxiv-2606-27062:
Catozi, Dal Lago, and Vanoni generalise a classic evaluation machine for the lambda calculus, the formal system behind functional programming. The Jumping Abstract Machine evaluates programs by jumping between linked parts of code. Their Parametric Jumping Abstract Machine adds one knob: a chosen backtracking depth, how far evaluation may rewind. Type theory then measures what the machine does, using non-idempotent intersection types that count resource use precisely.

For any normalising term, the machine's step count can be read off its type derivation exactly. Setting depth to zero recovers the original jumping machine and its pointer twin. Leaving depth unbounded recovers the older interaction machine instead. Cost analysis shows steps grow only polynomially with the count of main reduction steps, for each fixed depth bound. The family therefore forms a reasonable cost model, letting type derivations predict running costs faithfully.
arxiv-2606-27262:
Panda and colleagues describe SPOTLIGHT, a real-time system hunting fast radio bursts with India's upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope. These millisecond cosmic flashes demands detection, pinpointing, and capture at high resolution while they happen. The backend runs in parallel, piggybacking on routine observations without disturbing them. A dedicated computing facility with ninety top graphics processors handles up to two thousand beams at once. In 2026, brute-force dedispersion and single-pulse searching are accelerated on those chips.

A triggering system saves high-resolution raw data around promising events on its own. Synthetic bursts are injected live into the data stream to check performance. Across two observing cycles, the pipeline caught thousands of bursts from forty-two known sources. Reach matches the predicted survey threshold. Wide-field transient discovery gains a scalable base for next-generation surveys.
arxiv-2606-27762:
Unconstrained optimisation with variable bounds needs its own balance. Global exploration, late refinement, and evaluation efficiency all compete. Dikshit Chauhan presents DE-2LS in 2026 for this setting. The method is a differential evolution framework built on RDEx. The original evolutionary engine is preserved. Two conservative refinements are added, both aimed at the late stage of the search.

One refinement smooths an exploitation-biased branch-rate update. The other adds a guarded coordinate-pattern local search with a small budget. All choices rest on objective values alone. An ablation study fixed the final configuration. Settings for smoothing, sampling scale, selection pressure, and local search were each tested. Head-to-head, DE-2LS improved the RDEx U-score by about eleven and a half percent. Against several competitive algorithms, including IEEE CEC winners, it took the best overall U-score. The margin over the others was about thirty-four percent.
arxiv-2606-28262:
Stefano Mossa, Giancarlo Ruocco, and Walter Schirmacher compare Anderson localization, the trapping of waves by disorder, in classical and quantum systems. Textbooks often map waves in a disordered solid straight onto the standard electronic model, in which electrons hop between sites with random energies.

Mossa and colleagues show that this common mapping is not mathematically justified. A correct treatment reveals that wave systems in solids form their own disorder class, because a rule called the acoustic sum rule ties the random diagonal and off-diagonal entries together. Mapping all four disorder classes in one framework, they find localized states only near band edges for such waves, with free states surviving mid-spectrum even under strong disorder. Mass disorder produced a phase diagram different in kind from earlier claims.
arxiv-2606-28762:
Ruggiero and seven colleagues report experiments on a tiny superconducting device built from a germanium quantum dot, a small island that traps charge in a silicon-germanium layered material. They study a pi-junction, a link where the superconducting current flows with an unusual phase shift. In their device several energy levels of the dot take part at once, which changes what sets the junction's ground state.

Combining direct current measurements with microwave signals sent through a resonator built on the same chip, the team tracked how the junction behaves as voltages change. They saw phase transitions, meaning sudden switches in behaviour, that were sometimes sharp and sometimes smooth. Each kind left a distinct microwave signature, either storing energy or wasting it. Seeing this behaviour in germanium, not only in very clean carbon tubes, widens the platform for hybrid quantum devices.
arxiv-2606-28862:
Ma presents HKVLM, a system that answers visual requests needing reasoning, such as finding the object that could open a bottle. Ordinary detectors need an explicit category phrase. Vision-language models can reason, yet often point at the right region and name the wrong thing. Ma calls this a binding failure. In many designs, location passes through the language generator, coupling where something is to how the answer is worded.

HKVLM removes localisation from the language path. A frozen detector proposes regions without categories. A frozen language model turns the instruction into query embeddings. A small trained hook matches queries to regions by contrastive retrieval and assignment. A faithfulness veto blocks naming anything no region supports. Training only the hook lifted grounding accuracy fifty to ninety times over untrained matching on standard datasets. The veto raised accuracy on a hallucination test from near chance to a clearly better range.
arxiv-2606-29162:
Durbha, Tmar, Wu, Katsavounidis and Bovik expose a blind spot in image quality assessment: models miss damage that affects only part of a picture. No-reference quality assessment predicts how good an image looks without a clean original, and self-supervised learning drives its best results. Standard pipelines, though, apply synthetic distortions uniformly across the whole image, which can dull sensitivity to localised, overlapping degradations found in real content.

The team first demonstrate this reduced sensitivity across leading encoders. Their system, SLIDE-IQA, uses a two-branch vision transformer that injects degradations, bounded in space, into a contrastive pretraining objective, teaching it to notice local damage. A threshold-bounded exclusion mechanism resolves conflicts these distortions create, so the learned space respects damage type and spatial scale. Pretrained on synthetic data only, SLIDE-IQA grew much more sensitive to local damage while staying competitive on standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-29362:
Melin surveys the atmospheres of the four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. These four are dynamic worlds dominated by hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface. Jupiter shows its famous belt-and-zone pattern and the Great Red Spot; Saturn pairs a quieter atmosphere with its ring system; the two ice giants remain little known.

He explains the layered structure. In the troposphere, where weather happens, temperature falls with height as convection carries internal heat upward. Above it, the stratosphere warms as hydrocarbons absorb ultraviolet sunlight, driving rich photochemistry. Higher still lies an ill-defined mesosphere and then the upper atmosphere, heated by solar extreme ultraviolet light and auroral processes. Internal heat and sunlight, with fast rotation, drive circulation, waves and chemistry. Much knowledge comes from Voyager, Galileo, Juno and Cassini, with two Jupiter missions arriving in the 2030s.
arxiv-2606-29562:
Marwaha studies the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm, or QAOA, on the ring of disagrees, a cycle graph where good cuts separate neighbouring vertices. A cut splits the graph's vertices into two groups, and the goal is to cross as many edges as possible. Local algorithms that cannot see the whole graph have a known ceiling on the fraction of edges they can cut in expectation.

Marwaha proves the QAOA reaches exactly that ceiling, settling a long-standing conjecture. Curiously, the proof never finds the optimal algorithm parameters. Instead, the problem becomes equivalent to finding an optimal pair of Laurent polynomials of bounded degree. That recasting is possible because the QAOA on one qubit can be expressed in the language of quantum signal processing. The result gives an exact performance guarantee for a flagship quantum algorithm on a clean test case, using classical polynomial machinery rather than direct parameter search.
arxiv-2606-30062:
Dari Baturova, Elena Bruches, Ivan Chernov, Roman Derunets, Arsenii Fomin, and Andrey Kostin ask how far small language models can go. Big models dominate research, but small ones suit phones and laptops. The team studies the generation stage of retrieval-augmented generation systems. In such systems, a retriever fetches facts and a model writes the answer. Usually that writing stage demands a large, costly model.

The authors benchmark small models on open and proprietary datasets. The datasets cover diverse subjects and question types. Their findings show a full retrieval system can run on-device. No graphics processor is needed, and response times stay reasonable. That matters for privacy, cost, and offline use in the field. The team also shares its code and supplementary material openly. Small models, they conclude, deserve more attention than they get.
arxiv-2606-30162:
Zhile Jiang and Stratis Skoulakis study what a simple pricing scheme guarantees a seller facing mixed bidder types. Online advertisers increasingly bid as value maximizers, chasing return on spend. Classic bidders instead maximize ordinary utility from each purchase. Anonymous pricing posts one price to everyone, with no personalization. The question is how much optimal revenue that simplicity keeps.

The authors prove a structural equivalence between the two bidder behaviors. With that bridge, anonymous pricing at the right price achieves a fixed share. It secures at least a one-over-e fraction of optimal revenue. That beats the earlier guarantee known for pure value maximizers. It also extends the result to mixed populations of both types. An upper bound shows the guarantee cannot rise too far. Strangely, more competition can reduce revenue with value maximizers present. A first-price auction can earn less than anonymous pricing itself.
arxiv-2606-30262:
Soyoun Won, Aryan Yazdan Parast, Basim Azam, Jean Honorio, and Naveed Akhtar stop image generators from ignoring unusual instructions for famous objects. Some entities exist in one canonical form: the Earth, landmarks, artworks. Generators render those from strong visual priors, overriding the prompt. The authors call this concept association bias. Prompting alone often cannot break the ingrained identity.

An information-theoretic analysis locates the information loss. The final text embedding discards concept detail present in intermediate layers. Less mutual information then reaches the image denoising process. Their fix injects intermediate text representations during early denoising steps. No extra training, optimization, or external models are required. A new benchmark, OAO-AttackBench, uses counterfactual prompts against such objects. Across four benchmarks, prompt alignment improves by up to nineteen points. Generation fidelity and human preference stay intact meanwhile.
arxiv-2606-30662:
Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti and Emanuele Frontoni propose ELEVATE, a framework for AI tutors that runs locally in schools. Most AI tutoring today is a cloud chatbot: text-only, centrally controlled, weak on transparency, and risky for privacy. It also assumes constant connectivity and paid API access, which shuts out many institutions and widens digital divides.

ELEVATE pairs language-model dialogue with embodied 3D avatar tutors, so interaction is multimodal rather than plain text. Its design has three layers: a student-facing avatar layer, a local AI core that runs the model and synthesises speech and motion, and a teacher-facing governance layer. The system runs on consumer hardware, standard PCs and smartphones. The team built a working prototype and deployed it inside a real school curriculum. Performance measurements showed responsive interaction under realistic hardware limits, supporting a privacy-preserving path to inclusive AI tutoring.
arxiv-2606-30862:
The CMS Collaboration searches for physics beyond the Standard Model in the rarest top quark events at the Large Hadron Collider. The data are proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV recorded by the CMS detector from 2016 to 2018, totalling 138 inverse femtobarns. The analysis selects events with three or four leptons, or two of the same sign. That is the signature of four top quarks produced together, or three tops with a W boson or light quark. Such rare production grows in many theories with new heavy particles.

No discovery is claimed; instead the data constrain six Wilson coefficients, parameters that encode possible new interactions among top quarks and the Higgs boson. Narrow resonances that couple preferentially to top quarks are excluded across mass ranges from 400 GeV to 1.6 TeV, depending on their spin and colour. The top quark Yukawa coupling is also extracted, allowing both CP-even and CP-odd parts.
arxiv-2606-31262:
Ding constructs several classes of permutation pentanomials, polynomials with at most five terms that shuffle every element of a finite field. Such permutation polynomials matter in coding and cryptography, and sparse ones with simple coefficients are prized. Ding works over fields with a squared number of elements and a standard factored form.

For each prime and each prime power, two large classes are presented. Their coefficients all equal plus or minus one, with at most one exception. The constructions cover pentanomials with coefficients of that simple form and quadrinomials beside them. Roots of unity drive the proof that each class truly permutes the field, giving builders a ready supply of sparse permutation polynomials with tightly controlled coefficients.
arxiv-2606-31662:
Kormann, Nazarov and Wen add a correction step to dynamical low-rank methods for the Vlasov equation. It describes how a plasma's particle distribution evolves under its own electric field. Low-rank approximations tame the high-dimensional phase space, but they can break a basic physical requirement: the distribution must stay non-negative, since it counts particles.

Structural properties such as positivity are imposed as constraints, and a quadratic programming problem finds the smallest correction that makes the low-rank solution obey them while staying close to the original. Two schemes are given, and one also preserves total mass and momentum. Tests on Vlasov-Poisson and Vlasov-Poisson-BGK models, using spectral space discretization and explicit Runge-Kutta time stepping, show the corrected solutions keep the required properties.
arxiv-2606-31762:
Lee and four others test whether a language model can protect minority voices in group decisions where power is unequal. Social pressure often pushes minority members to echo the majority in public. The team built a support system with two designs and ran a mixed-method experiment with 96 people in 24 groups.

One design posts AI-generated counterarguments against the majority view. The other privately takes minority messages, paraphrases them, and posts them without naming the author. Counterarguments loosened the atmosphere and raised satisfaction in the groups. Mediated messages increased minority participation, yet, to the team's surprise, they lowered psychological safety. That tension between speaking up and feeling safe shapes the design advice offered.
arxiv-2606-31862:
Bezhanishvili, de Groot and Moss develop modal measurable logics, a formalism for reasoning about measurable spaces with a modal operator. Their base language allows countable meets and joins, aimed at dynamical systems and point-free ergodic theory. A Kripke-like semantics is defined over measurable spaces, with a designated modal sigma-ideal handling the exceptional sets.

Completeness comes through representation theorems. A restricted Jónsson-Tarski duality handles the algebraic side first. The modal analogue of the Loomis-Sikorski theorem then represents every measurable sigma-modal algebra as a quotient of a concrete set-based algebra. One infinitary rule, the Infinite Descending Chain rule, is needed for the modal version. Together these results secure completeness of the logics for the new semantics.
arxiv-2608-00262: A Structural Matrix Autoregression Framework for International Spillovers, arXiv 2608-00262. The spillover framework. The paper endures in the archive. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
arxiv-2608-00362: An essay on d0 in neutron-based strain measurement techniques, arXiv 2608-00362. The strain essay. The work is kept for study. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
cia-0000009862:
Three American pilots died in Xieng Khouang province, an April 1968 CIA report records. Xieng Khouang holds the Plain of Jars, the most bombed ground of the Laos war. Airmen lost there often vanished into a landscape of craters and caves.

A report naming three deaths at once suggests a shared event or a single source for several losses. Officials would split the report into three men's files after checking. Each name then carried the province as his place of death. The entry preserves the joint report as it arrived, before that splitting into separate griefs.
cia-0000012262:
Letter number three, dated October 20, 1960, moves through the files under a document transfer and cross-reference slip. The subject line names Chalk, one of the code words attached to the operation that ran the Soviet colonel Oleg Penkovsky. Penkovsky was then beginning to pass military secrets to the West, the most valuable haul of the Cold War.

The slip records the letter's routing rather than its contents. It shows how the case's paper was logged, numbered, and sent on under strict control. Small as it is, the form is one procedural trace of the great spy case's filing system.
cia-0000012762:
How would the communists react if the United States took certain steps in South Vietnam? Special estimate SNIE 10-4-61, from October 1961, games out the answers. Washington was then deepening its commitment to Saigon, and each new step risked a wider war with Hanoi, Beijing, or Moscow. The estimate lays the possible reactions out in order, from protest to escalation.

Gaming the other side's responses was the Cold War's highest staff art. The community's coordinated judgment carried weight at the summit. For readers, the paper shows the war's widening being rehearsed on paper before it was lived.
cia-0000013862: Moving hurt enemy troops and American prisoners northward is the subject of a CIA note dated July 6, 1967. North Vietnamese and Viet Cong wounded, plus U.S. prisoners, were taken from South Vietnam to the north. The trip was long and hard for men who were hurt or bound. The note shows the road system that fed the northern camps.
cia-0000014762: A weekly meeting of the executive board of the PSP, Cuba's Communist Party, fills a CIA file dated January 6, 1953. The file reports on the party's top table at work. Watching foreign Communist boards was routine Cold War collection. The Cuba file predates Castro's rise, when the old party still ran its own course.
cia-0000015262: One late summer night in 1973, a source saw an unidentified object, in a CIA file dated November 2, 1977. The witness name is cut out as deleted. The report came four years after the sighting itself. Old sightings still got filed, since a late report could match a pattern no one had seen at the time.
cia-0000015462: Reading lists on parapsychology, also called psychoenergetics, and kindred subjects fill a CIA record dated in 1972. The title adds a Soviet angle in its clipped ending, suggesting the lists tracked work behind the Iron Curtain. Mind reading, mind over matter, and like claims drew agency curiosity then. A bibliography alone shows the range of topics staff were told to watch.
cia-0000022362: Finns refuted Powers' testimony at his trial, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. The heading adds that Sodankylae airfield was to be used by the United States, in clipped form. Finland sat between East and West, and its airfields drew keen interest. Finnish voices correcting the pilot's account show how far the trial's ripples spread across the north.
cia-0000024962: Results of the Defense Intelligence Agency's request for CIA assistance fill a CIA record dated in 1975. The DIA was the Pentagon's intelligence arm, and the two agencies often worked the same questions. A results entry closes the loop on a formal ask between them. It shows the machinery of cooperation that sat behind the better known rivalry of the spy world.
cia-0000037162:
An American soldier was allegedly killed and buried in Da Nang City in 1968, according to a CIA record dated May 1, 1983. The claim reached the files fifteen years after the event it describes. A former resident's account appears to stand behind the report, judging by the title.

Inside, the allegation is set down so it can be checked against other records. Late claims of this kind were hard to prove, yet none could simply be ignored. The file shows the accounting still reaching back, in 1983, to single deaths from the war's hardest years in the south.
cia-0000049162: Major Mauricio Beltran gave a 1990 statement about senior Salvadoran military officers, and a CIA item preserves its text. Statements by serving majors about their own generals were rare and dangerous paper, and both sides knew it. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, where such testimony carried special weight.
cia-0000049262: A social evening in Guatemala City is noted in a partly blacked-out CIA item from 1990, kept with the Truth Commission records. Social notes were intelligence too: who dined with whom mapped the region's real alliances. Why this evening earned a file sits behind the redactions, among the guests' hidden names.
cia-0000049362: Dated July 1, 1983, declassified CIA document 0000049362 is Central American Monthly Report number one, noted for the Truth Commission. It opens the monthly series that continued through that summer. Readers find the first dated installment in the run. It is a routine reporting item. Its significance lies in its place at the start of the monthly Central America sequence.
cia-0000096662: Chinese Communist Foreign Ministry order on conduct of talks, in shortened heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000096662, dated August 3, 1968. The title names the ministry that issued it and its topic, how such talks should be run. The brief file is a rules record, companion to the nearby order on embassy mistakes. Its catalog entry preserves the original heading word for word.
cia-0000098762: Dominican Government Moves Against Rebellious Cult is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098762, dated January 5, 1963. The title describes a government acting against a group it calls a rebellious cult. Readers find a short declassified action record from the Dominican Republic, its loaded label preserved exactly as the heading gives it.
cia-0000100162: Worldwide Issues, with new thinking on Krasnoyarsk welcomed, in the heading's quoted phrase, is declassified CIA document 0000100162, dated October 2, 1989. The title pairs a broad series label with one place name. Readers get a short declassified worldwide-issues item, its specific subject a welcomed change in thinking about Krasnoyarsk. The record survives in the CIA Reading Room mirror collection.
cia-0000105162:
Study on the Japanese Red Army is a CIA memorandum released as declassified document 0000105162, dated November 1, 1974 in the catalog. The sample memorandum is dated December 23, 1974, and went to members of a working group on terrorism. It sent along a copy of the emergence study as an attachment.

The memo says the attached study traces the group's origins, stressing its past terrorist operations with the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. The discovery of a large network in Paris is also discussed in detail, it adds. Copies of a revised edition were being sent abroad to selected liaison services.
cia-0000109062: Continued Soviet Economic Aid to Cuba and Public Soviet Attacks on Castro's Int is the heading, cut off mid-word, on CIA document 0000109062, dated February 5, 1968. The title pairs aid and attacks: Moscow funding Cuba while publicly attacking something of Castro's. The attacked thing breaks off at Int in the heading. The brief record preserves the pairing and the break as released.
cia-0000112362: Remaining Sections, Draft Report is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112362, dated May 1, 1986. The title describes a fragment: the remaining sections of a draft report. The main body is not named or included in the heading itself. The brief record is a draft fragment item, filed in the spring of 1986 as released in the files.
cia-0000126862: An April 1994 CIA contracting officer's report covers proposals sent in answer to request RFP-54-94N, the heading breaking off. Procurement papers like this one show the agency at work as a buyer of goods and services. The report preserves that contracting record in full. Contracting records rarely draw readers, yet they show the scale of the agency as an institution that bought, hired, and built like any large department.
cia-0000126962: A July 1967 CIA document reports preparations by Haitians in Cuba to slip back into Haiti. Exiles training under Castro's protection were plotting to overthrow Duvalier. The paper tracks those invasion plans as the agency learned of them that summer. Exile invasion plots against Duvalier surfaced again and again in the file, most failing before launch, each one tracked because a landing might have forced Washington's hand.
cia-0000132662:
The Castro regime answering a rise in resistance fills a CIA paper dated November 2, 1960. The regime met its foes with arrests and firing squads that fall. Armed bands were forming against it in the Escambray hills and in the cities at the same time.

The paper tracks the regime's response move by move. Each new act of repression fed the revolt it was meant to crush. For readers, the entry shows the island sliding toward open internal war. That war would burn for years in the hills while the world watched the quarrel with Washington instead.
cia-0000132762: Dated May 4, 1960, this CIA paper on Cuba was written as a same-day companion to another briefing. Together the pair capture the spring mood: an American government losing patience as tensions with Castro climbed steadily. The declassified companion survives through the CIA Reading Room mirror held by the Internet Archive, under document number 0000132762.
cia-0000134262: Peru's ties with Cuba fill item 5 of the CIA's Latin America series, dated April 5, 1960. Within months Lima would be weighing a full break with Havana. At this point the stance of Peru was still taking shape in public. The short item reports the state of the ties as analysts found them that spring.
cia-0000135962: A declassified CIA cable dated 1 January 1954 turns to the propaganda effort, the loud front of leaflets, radio, and planted stories against Arbenz. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136262: A CIA cable from 6 May 1954, now declassified, deals with Instruction 12 for broadcasts, the script book growing deeper into the teens by May. Lincoln was the station cryptonym for PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation against President Arbenz in Guatemala that ended in June 1954. Taken with the rest of the station traffic, it helps map who handled what, and when, inside the mission.
cia-0000136562: This Spanish-language record, dated 6 November 1960, comes from the papers of Brigade 2506, the Cuban exile force built by the CIA. The date falls in the brigade's first autumn of training. No subject appears in the catalog record for this item. It is kept in Spanish as a dated primary source, part of the heavy November run of brigade documents that the agency later declassified and released.
cia-0000136762: This Spanish item comes from the 2506 Brigade papers and is dated only to 1961 in the catalog, with the date marked as estimated. The brigade landed in Cuba in April of that year and was broken within days. The record does not say whether this document predates or follows the landing, and no subject is stated. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the CIA's declassified release.
cia-0000136962: Correct the distortions, this June 1954 cable urges about coverage of the uprising against the Guatemalan regime. Reports received through agency channels, it claims, reveal no bombing nor large-scale invasion, though a small number of anti-communist patriots may have returned. Headquarters urgently desires correction through the best available means.
cia-0000139162: Cooperation with the National Resource Evaluation Center is arranged in this 1968 memo. The copy is badly garbled, though. Officials visited the center. A letter requested cooperation from it. A director told staff to keep talking but make no promises. No personnel or material resources were promised. A package of training materials was prepared with the emergency office. Its director and deputy were expected for a tour. The file records routine agency work of the imagery era.
