Flexion-type fractures tripled the odds of open reduction. Low fractures below the isthmus and the pucker sign each roughly doubled those odds. Older age independently predicted failure of the closed route. Small cartilaginous distal fragments explain why low fractures resist stable pinning.
pmc-13242462:
Jessica Nikolovski and co-authors interviewed physiotherapists and nurses about using patient-reported outcome measures during routine chronic care. Their study appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. Twenty-two clinicians from New South Wales clinics joined video interviews between October 2024 and May 2025. All worked with conditions such as lung, heart, kidney, and joint disease inside a state digital program that collects these questionnaires.

Clinicians accepted the questionnaires most when the choice of form, its content, and its timing matched the purpose of the visit and their own workflow. A single ideal moment for handing them out proved elusive, since clinics and patients run on different rhythms. Flexibility made the forms feel more relevant, but the clinicians warned it can also make combined results harder to compare. Good timing, they suggest, is negotiated rather than fixed.
pmc-13242662:
Paola Marchisio and co-authors surveyed Italian pediatricians about treating ear infections that drain fluid through a burst eardrum. Their national survey appeared in the Italian Journal of Pediatrics in 2026. Five hundred family and hospital pediatricians answered twenty questions on how they define, diagnose, and treat acute otitis media with otorrhea. The condition peaks in winter, and most respondents see a steady stream of cases each month in season.

A large majority said they start antibiotics at the first visit when discharge is present, usually a systemic drug rather than ear drops. Practice varied on how long to treat and whether watchful waiting is ever appropriate. Respondents also differed in what they call the condition, though one term won a clear majority. The authors see broad agreement on early antibiotics but real uncertainty elsewhere. They call for clearer, practice-ready guidance and more research on topical treatment.
pmc-13242762:
Olga Golubovic and co-authors present a 2026 single-center study of irritable bowel type symptoms in inflammatory bowel disease patients judged to be in deep remission. Gut symptoms can persist even when inflammation is fully controlled, which confuses care. Earlier estimates used looser remission definitions and may have inflated the numbers.

All patients were on biologic drugs and met clinical, blood marker, and camera-based remission criteria at once. About one in five still reported symptoms matching irritable bowel syndrome under standard criteria. The overlap was roughly twice as common in Crohn disease as in ulcerative colitis. Women and smokers with Crohn disease reported symptoms more often. The authors stress that remission definitions shape the measured overlap.
pmc-13243362:
Victoria Sánchez-Gómez and colleagues study hidden rules that limit freedom in disability support services in 2026. Blanket rules on time, money, and daily choices apply to everyone and can quietly shrink autonomy. Because such rules blend into routine, staff often stop noticing them.

The team surveyed 45 support organizations in Spain with a scale built to spot restrictive practices. Teams included 194 professionals, some family members, and 25 people with disabilities. Structural rules proved far more common than other restrictive practices, even though overall rates looked low. Naming these routines is a first step toward services that respect rights and personal choice.
pmc-13243762:
Asma Baniasad and colleagues traced how people living with HIV in Iran experience treatment, using their own accounts. Their qualitative study appeared in AIDS Research and Treatment in 2026. At a counseling center and positive club in Kerman, the team interviewed seventeen patients, five caregivers, and five professionals between late 2023 and mid 2024. The transcripts yielded more than twelve hundred initial codes, sorted into themes.

Seven families of challenge emerged. Emotional and psychological tension ran alongside practical strains, social deprivation, and hostile labeling by others. Unfavorable policies, disrupted life plans, and patchy, low-quality medical services rounded out the picture. Treatment, in other words, is the smallest part of the journey patients described. The authors call for comprehensive backing from families, caregivers, and society, steadier access to good services, and public education that lowers stigma. Support, they argue, must be social as much as medical.
pmc-13244262:
Mandana Nikpour and colleagues report the SPHInX trial, the first randomized test of blood thinners as add-on therapy in scleroderma lung hypertension. Their report appeared in Pulmonary Circulation in 2026. Whether anticoagulation helps in systemic sclerosis-related pulmonary arterial hypertension has been equipoise, argued from registries. The Australian trial assigned patients to low-dose apixaban or placebo for three years, watching for clinical worsening or death.

Recruitment fell short: only twenty-five patients joined against a planned eighty-five per arm, leaving the trial unable to settle the question. Within that limit, apixaban showed no benefit on worsening or survival, and function and quality of life matched placebo. A side signal did appear: iron-deficiency anemia struck most apixaban patients, far more than controls. The authors present the results as inconclusive on benefit but instructive on harm. The anemia rate alone, they suggest, should temper enthusiasm for anticoagulation here.
pmc-13244662:
K. Alexandra Sanchez and colleagues followed newly diagnosed myeloma patients given apixaban to prevent blood clots. Their prospective study appeared in EJHaem in 2026. Myeloma and its treatments carry one of the highest clot risks in cancer care, and plain aspirin often underprotects. Eighty-seven consecutive patients at one center took the oral factor Xa blocker as their main preventive and were watched for clots and bleeding over a median of eleven months.

The record was strikingly clean. No major bleeding occurred, and no deep vein thrombosis or lung embolism appeared during follow-up. Two patients developed symptomatic clots in surface veins, the only thrombotic events recorded. The authors judge the drug safe in this role and its event rates very low. They stop short of declaring victory, calling for controlled comparison before guidelines change. For a population used to injectable prevention, an effective pill would simplify life considerably.
pmc-13244862:
Yan Wang and co-authors tested whether sugar-linked compounds from a traditional calming herb rescue memory by fixing the gut. Their study appeared in Chinese Medicine in 2026. Yuanzhi root has long been used for insomnia and forgetfulness, and its oligosaccharide esters showed brain-protective hints. The team induced memory damage in mice with two chemical stressors, then dosed the esters while probing behavior, brain tissue, gut bacteria, and blood lipids.

Treated mice learned and remembered better. Inside the brain, inflammation and oxidative stress eased. In the colon, the barrier tightened, the microbe mix shifted toward balance, and fat pathways normalized in step. The test was transfer: giving the gut contents of treated mice to untreated ones reproduced the tissue repair, pinning the benefit on the microbiota. The authors frame the esters as working along the gut-brain axis. The work strengthens a remedy's case while naming its route.
pmc-13245062:
Ayla Pauwels and colleagues revisited the gut microbes of multiple sclerosis with stricter methods, suspecting earlier contradictions were artifacts. Their study appeared in Gut Microbes in 2026. They counted actual bacterial loads rather than mere proportions. The study covered 228 MS patients against nearly three thousand controls, and corrected for stool moisture, a hidden confounder.

Total bacterial load ran lower in the relapsing form of MS. After cleanup, twenty-one genera differed, with Blautia enriched and Bacteroides depleted among them. Pooling ten past studies overturned some famous markers. Akkermansia and Roseburia did not hold up, while low Bacteroides and high Blautia and Methanobrevibacter stood firm. Two butyrate-producing genera also ran low. The larger point is humility: without load counts and moisture correction, microbiome studies manufacture mirages. Future marker hunts should start cleaned up.
pmc-13245462:
Jun Zheng and co-authors build a fast gene test to guide psychiatric drug choice in 2026 work. Genes shape how people respond to antidepressants and antipsychotics, yet testing each gene one by one is slow. Their method reads seven key gene variants in a single tube.

The test uses melting curves from fluorescent probes to call each variant. It worked on very small DNA amounts and gave no false calls in checks. A first set of 98 patient samples set the calling rules. A blinded second set of 124 samples then matched gold-standard sequencing on every call. A one-tube test like this could bring gene-guided prescribing to more clinics.
pmc-13246462:
Mahmoudabadi and co-authors report a poisoning scare in this 2026 Clinical Case Reports article. A fourteen-month-old girl was brought to emergency care with altered consciousness after accidentally swallowing brimonidine ointment left within her reach during play. Brimonidine, a drug used for skin redness and eye pressure, acts on the nervous system and can be dangerous in toddlers.

Within two hours the child grew drowsy and unsteady, with pinpoint pupils and floppy muscle tone, though her vital signs held steady. The authors stress that unexplained drowsiness in a toddler after possible exposure should trigger suspicion of this drug, prompt airway support. Close monitoring, noting that the overdose antidote naloxone may help in such cases.
pmc-13246562:
Spencer, Kyloh, and Travis mapped the sensory nerves of the mouse bladder in this 2026 Cell and Tissue Research study. The bladder receives feeling nerves from two spinal regions, and the team had already charted the lower, lumbosacral set. Here they traced the upper, thoracolumbar set by injecting a marker into the nerve clusters and following the fibers into the bladder wall.

They found four shapes of nerve ending, the same family as the lower set. Arranged in mirror image: most upper-region endings sat in the bladder's surface lining, while most lower-region endings sat in the muscle wall. Nearly all upper endings carried a pain-related peptide. The split suggests one system guards against irritation while the other senses stretch.
pmc-13246862:
Dastmaltschi and co-authors built software to count blood vessels and their helper cells in microscope images, in this 2026 Scientific Reports paper. Capillaries are wrapped by pericytes, and measuring both in stained tissue slices is normally done by eye, which makes results vary between examiners and laboratories. Their tool, called CAPPER, automates the counting with adaptive thresholds and shape analysis.

The software quantified capillary density and pericyte coverage reliably across brain, heart, muscle, and kidney tissue, in mice and pigs, and in several disease states. The team also proposes a panel of markers to pin down pericytes, a cell type whose identity markers are notoriously unreliable. Standardized counting, they argue, will make vascular studies comparable across research groups.
pmc-13247262:
Zhou, Yun, Chen, and co-authors published this correction in Cell Death and Disease in 2026, fixing a figure in their much older paper on kidney cancer. The original article, published in 2017, studied compounds derived from oridonin, a plant molecule, aimed at a protein called PDK1 in drug-resistant renal cell carcinoma. During a recent internal review, the authors found a mistake in one panel of a key figure.

A western blot image showing the actin loading control for a cell line had been assembled from the wrong raw file, so the published panel showed the wrong band image. The correction supplies the proper figure panel with the correct actin control. The authors present it as a figure-assembly error caught on re-examination; the correction notice itself reports no change to the paper's experiments or conclusions.
pmc-13248362:
Gideon Onyedikachi Iheme and a large team survey feeding and growth of Nigerian toddlers in a 2026 multi-site study. Poor feeding in the first two years stunts growth and raises illness risk. The team gathered mothers at four large hospitals across Nigeria.

Digital surveys covered 1,295 mother and child pairs with children aged 6 to 23 months. Most children ate often enough and started solid food on time. Early breastfeeding starts, exclusive breastfeeding, and diet variety all fell short of guidance. Growth measures split two ways, with stunting and overweight both common in the group. Breastfeeding patterns tied to several growth scores. Tailored local programs are needed, the authors conclude.
pmc-13248462:
Yehia and co-authors sequenced duck hepatitis viruses from Egyptian farms, reported in BMC Veterinary Research in 2026. Outbreaks during 2022 and 2023 hit ducklings across five northern governorates, killing half or more of some flocks despite vaccination. The team tested liver and spleen samples and read the full genomes of the viruses found.

Seventeen of thirty samples carried the virus, and most were type 3 rather than type 1. The type 3 strains clustered with Chinese strains and differed sharply from the vaccine strain in use. The authors urge continuous genome monitoring and updated, better-matched vaccines to protect Egypt's duck industry.
pmc-13248962:
Mu, Qin, and Wang reviewed how sound surroundings affect sensitive groups, in a 2026 systematic review. They gathered one hundred eighty studies published between 2000 and 2025 on people whose senses make them vulnerable, including older adults, children, people with hearing loss, and patients. Outcomes covered health, thinking, and emotion.

Hostile soundscapes were generally tied to worse health, weaker thinking performance, and poorer mood, though the pattern shifted by group. Older adults' studies stressed disease risk, children's stressed learning, and patients' stressed sleep and recovery. Ratings of evidence quality were mostly low. The authors still see lessons for designing schools, hospitals, and nursing homes, and they ask for stronger studies.
pmc-13249062:
Park and a large international team studied what kills patients after bone surgery, in a 2026 VISION substudy. The parent project followed forty thousand surgical patients across fourteen countries, and this analysis covered the eight thousand three hundred eighty-five who had orthopedic operations. Deaths within thirty days and the complications preceding them were examined closely.

About one death occurred for every sixty patients, with risk highest after above-knee amputation and lowest after knee replacement. Six complications tied independently to death, led by silent heart injury, major bleeding, and sepsis. The authors argue that screening for heart injury after surgery deserves special attention, since it accounted for the largest share of deaths.
pmc-13249262:
Omar Abdullah Omar Alshehri and co-authors test structured AI help for English writing among Saudi students in a 2026 study. Chatbots can draft text fast, yet unguided use may dull student thinking. The team asked whether guided teamwork with AI lifts both writing and digital judgment.

Fifty-three undergraduates split into an AI-guided class and a standard class for about ten weeks. Guided students framed tasks, drafted with AI, revised, and checked claims and sources. At the end they scored far higher on writing quality and on a digital critical thinking scale. Student reflections showed AI used mainly as a planning and revision scaffold. Careful guidance, not the tool alone, drove the gains.
pmc-13249462:
Anyimadu and colleagues applied a contrastive learning method to predict radiation injury of the jaw, in a 2026 computing paper. Head and neck cancer radiotherapy can kill jawbone tissue, a complication called osteoradionecrosis. Standard risk models read dose distribution charts, but those charts are bulky and overlap heavily between patients who do and do not suffer injury.

Their framework, SC-NTCP, first compresses each chart into a compact code trained to pull similar patients together and push unlike patients apart. That representation predicted injury more accurately and with better calibration than four standard classifiers, and adding clinical details helped further. The authors argue the approach could personalize radiation planning for other organs too.
pmc-13250062:
Taha and colleagues compared two routes of allergy immunotherapy for dust mite allergy, in a 2026 pilot study. Forty-three adults received either injections under the skin or drops under the tongue for nine months. Blood tests tracked the protective antibody IgG4, total allergy antibody IgE, and regulatory T cells, while questionnaires scored asthma and nose symptoms.

Both routes raised IgG4 sharply and nearly doubled regulatory T cells, with IgE drifting down. Patients who responded clinically carried the strongest immune shifts, and IgG4 levels tracked symptom scores closely. Injections produced higher IgG4 than drops, though symptom relief was similar. The authors suggest the two blood markers for early monitoring of who is benefiting.
pmc-13250862:
Lorio and co-authors compare long-term results for dialysis catheters placed through the skin versus placed by surgery. Their 2026 Renal Failure study reviews one hundred seventeen peritoneal dialysis catheters in ninety patients treated at a home dialysis unit between 2014 and 2020. Needle-placed catheters had matched surgical ones in the short term but were underused over durability doubts.

Median catheter life ran slightly longer for skin-placed catheters, at about twenty months versus seventeen months. Infections caused most removals in both groups, and mechanical complication rates were similar between them. Follow-up stretched beyond five years, making this one of the largest modern series of its kind. The authors argue that skin placement deserves wider use so patients can start home dialysis sooner.
pmc-13251662:
Zhang and co-authors link low vitamin D with muscle loss in older adults, especially those with diabetes. Their 2026 Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging study combines two national aging cohorts totaling more than seventy-five hundred people with experiments in aged diabetic rats. Sarcopenia here means low grip strength plus low muscle mass.

Across the cohorts, low vitamin D raised the odds of sarcopenia, and the link ran stronger alongside diabetes. Joint exposure to both factors showed an added effect beyond each one alone in one cohort. In rats, vitamin D shortage worsened blood sugar, muscle fat, and cell aging signs, while supplements restored strength and fiber size. The authors support vitamin D as protection against diabetes-related muscle decline.
pmc-13251762:
Doostparast and co-authors measure stress in the bodies of eye surgery trainees during cataract operations. Their 2026 Clinical Ophthalmology study enrolls fifty-nine ophthalmology residents and fellows performing phacoemulsification, a technique demanding microscopic precision. Heart and blood pressure readings were taken before surgery and at key steps.

Blood pressure and heart rate climbed significantly as surgery advanced, peaking during lens removal and implant placement. Less experienced trainees ran higher pressure trends, and women and junior trainees reported more perceived stress on questionnaires. A common blood pressure drug taken beforehand lowered felt stress but not the body readings. The authors urge targeted support for trainees most prone to stress during surgical training.
pmc-13251862:
Yuhan Guo and colleagues laser-print soft robot parts in this 2026 engineering paper. Shape-shifting soft machines promise octopus-like flexibility, but making complex three-dimensional motion has usually meant trading away manufacturing simplicity.

Their method writes patterns with a laser into a carbon-based film, tuning heat flow and stiffness place by place. Four basic motion units result: straight bending, directed curling, rigid support, and soft joining.
