Jinqin Zhang and co-authors measured brain responses to familiar voices in patients with disorders of consciousness in a 2026 study. Hearing one's own name spoken by a loved one is used in therapy, but protocols vary and brain effects were unmapped. A portable light based scanner offered a bedside way to watch the cortex respond.

They recruited 64 patients and recorded blood oxygen signals while names were spoken by familiar and unfamiliar voices. An unfamiliar voice switched off part of the left frontal cortex, while a familiar voice did not. Response peaks differed between the two conditions in frontal and temporal areas, and several signal measures tracked with standard consciousness scores. The authors offer the findings as guidance for auditory therapy and assessment.
pmc-13275762:
Wenzhen Li and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on sorghum, a grain crop used for food and for brewing Baijiu liquor in China. Grain shape matters for brewing quality, above all the ratio of length to width. The genetic basis of that shape was still poorly understood.

The team scanned the genes of two hundred fifty-five Chinese sorghum lines and found one gene, called SbTPP1, that strongly shapes grain form. The gene helps process trehalose, a plant sugar. Round-grain and long-grain types carry different small changes in it. Adding extra copies in test plants widened grains but lowered grain weight. Tracing over seven hundred world lines showed the round form came from Africa, while the long form arose as sorghum spread into China.
pmc-13276462:
Paul Telengech and co-authors describe a 2026 method for growing a fungal virus inside a model plant. Persistent viruses live quietly in plants and fungi, often without symptoms, which makes cause-and-effect studies hard. No reliable way existed to introduce a fungal virus into plant tissue for study.

The team inserted a fungal partitivirus, RnPV18, into cells of Nicotiana benthamiana, a standard laboratory plant. Callus tissue and liquid cell cultures grown from those cells kept the infection over long periods. Two lines carried the virus at different levels, and small RNA patterns shifted across growth stages. Mutations also appeared at particular sites, giving researchers a workable system for future experiments.
pmc-13276762:
Jorun Rugkåsa and co-authors present a 2026 journal article mapping compulsory community mental health treatment across Europe. Community treatment orders force care outside hospital for people with severe mental illness. Their spread continues despite weak consensus on benefits and ethical unease about coercion.

Through a researcher network, the team gathered laws and regime details from thirty-three European countries. Only thirteen regimes existed; two thirds of countries manage without such orders. Most laws spell out criteria, enforcement, and safeguards restricting the person. Many details, though, sit in individual care plans rather than the law itself. Most regimes also allow endless renewals, so total restriction length is visible only afterward. The authors argue overall restrictiveness cannot be judged from law texts alone and urge proof of benefit before new regimes appear.
pmc-13277262:
Alexander Elser and colleagues present a 2026 interview study on using virtual reality to treat long-term pain in outpatient physiotherapy in Germany. Virtual reality can help pain and function, yet few clinics use it. Nine physiotherapists taking part in a rollout study described what helps and what blocks adoption before the work began.

Barriers included lack of time, no insurance payment, gaps in pain and technology knowledge, and a sense that virtual reality sits outside their role. Choosing suitable patients also worried them. On the plus side, a dedicated space and a distinctive offer for the practice helped. Training, payment reform, and fitting the tool into daily flow are needed, the authors say.
pmc-13277362:
Laura Carucci and colleagues present baseline results from the ARHINASD study of children's noses, published in 2026. Allergic rhinitis is among the most common childhood allergies, and a bent nasal septum appears in about a third of children. Whether the two conditions feed each other was largely unexplored.

One hundred thirty-eight children aged six to fourteen took part across several centres, half with septum deviation. Allergy was far more common in the deviation group than in the comparison group. Affected children reported worse blockage, breathed more weakly through the nose, and carried more allergy-linked inflammation in nasal fluid. Family allergy history added further risk. The authors call for long-term studies on cause and effect.
pmc-13277662:
Antonis Valachis and colleagues chart HER2-positive breast cancer outcomes across Sweden in a 2026 nationwide study. Adding pertuzumab after surgery improves survival for patients whose cancer reached the lymph nodes. The team asked how many patients still qualify for it as pre-surgery treatment spreads.

Registry data covered more than 135,000 breast cancer patients treated between 2007 and 2023. About three and a half thousand patients formed the after-surgery cohort, and their share shrank over time. Ten-year survival in that group sat near seventy-two percent, with tumour size and nodal stage driving risk. Patients who cleared all visible cancer before surgery fared excellently, prompting questions about added drug benefit.
pmc-13277762:
ELsiddig ELzubair Ali Mohamed leads a 2026 study of toe amputations in diabetic patients at a specialist center in Khartoum, Sudan. Diabetes drives most non-traumatic amputations worldwide, yet Sudanese data are limited. The team reviewed 100 patients with type 2 diabetes and foot ulcers who had a toe removed during 2021.

Most patients were men, with an average age near sixty-one. Wet gangrene, dead tissue with infection, was the main reason for surgery, and most cases removed a toe with part of the foot bone. Two-thirds healed fully, while small shares had new ulcers, further amputation, or death. Artery disease, longer diabetes, and smoking tracked with worse outcomes.
pmc-13278462:
Ana Paula Gomes Ferreira leads a 2026 design and implementation study of a machine-readable standard for public health case definitions. Case definitions tell officials what counts as a case during an outbreak, but they are usually written as prose, which blocks data sharing and computer analysis. The team built the Open Syndrome Definition format and open-source conversion tools.

Official definitions from several institutions were converted into the structured format with high fidelity, checked by experts. A public platform lets users browse, analyze, and add definitions, and a prototype lets users test their own datasets against them. Unified, computer-ready definitions could make research more reproducible and collaboration easier across regions, the authors argue.
pmc-13279762:
Hongliang Ma and colleagues published a 2026 paper presenting LiteMS-YOLO, a featherweight detection model for counting wheat spikes in field photographs. Spike counts feed yield estimates, yet the targets are small, densely packed, and photographed against messy backgrounds. Built on a nano-scale detection architecture, the model adds a module that lets spatial and semantic features complement each other. A multi-kernel unit reads features at several scales, while deliberate redundancy cuts shrink its size.

Training used a combined set of 6,378 high-resolution images holding over 44,000 annotated spikes, drawn from a public global dataset plus 100 local field images. The model scored 92.28 percent on the standard detection metric while using only 0.627 million parameters. That is roughly three quarters fewer than the two nano models it was compared with, at competitive accuracy. The authors aim the design at real-time use on modest hardware in the field, where heavier models cannot run.
pmc-13279962:
Josile Maria da Conceicao Albuquerque and colleagues report a 2026 study of vitamin D and nutrition risk in advanced chronic liver disease. Vitamin D turns active in two steps, first in the liver and then in the kidneys. Since the liver starts the chain, low blood vitamin D is common when liver disease is advanced. Low levels link to malnutrition and muscle loss in many age groups. The team test links in outpatients with advanced disease.

The title states the core link: low 25(OH) vitamin D, the main blood form, went with nutrition risk and with disease severity. Background pages note that the active form may curb collagen build in liver star cells, which drive scarring. Immune, cell growth and swelling roles add weight to the link. Clinic checks of vitamin D could flag patients who need food and muscle support early.
pmc-13280062:
Sonia Grigorascu and colleagues report a 2026 study of scan based entry rules for a targeted radiation therapy in prostate cancer. The therapy uses a radioactive drug that homes to PSMA, a protein on prostate cancer cells. It serves metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer, an advanced form that no longer answers hormone blocks. Two rule sets face off: a company phase one set and the VISION trial set, both read from PSMA PET scans.

One hundred ninety one patients from one centre database were split in four groups by which rule sets they met. One hundred thirty eight had the newer scan agent and fifty three the older one. One hundred sixty one patients, about eighty four percent, met both rule sets. Thirteen met neither. Prostate marker response, time to marker rise and overall survival were compared. Rule choice decides who gets the drug, so gaps in access matter.
pmc-13280462:
Qunru Jiao and colleagues report a 2026 study that builds an exosome related gene signature for gastric cancer prognosis. Exosomes are tiny parcels shed by cells that play a crucial role in tumour progression. Reliable exosome biomarkers for prognosis in gastric cancer remain scarce. RNA data from exoRbase and TCGA datasets were mined for exosome genes linked to survival. A multivariate Cox model built the risk signature and a prognostic nomogram, a scoring chart.

Four exosome related genes emerged as independent prognostic factors: TRAF2, ASCL2, NOX4 and MMRN1. Patients with low risk scores showed significantly better survival outcomes. Kaplan Meier and ROC curve analyses tested the signature in training and validation datasets. Links with clinical features, copy number variation and immunotherapy sensitivity were explored as well. Protein blots validated key gene levels in gastric cancer tissues. The four gene score could stratify care.
pmc-13280662:
Dan Liu and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on how a common virus may help cause multiple sclerosis. The illness harms the brain and spinal cord and affects close to three million people worldwide. Nearly all patients carry the Epstein-Barr virus, which hides in immune cells for life. The review draws on three recent studies in a top science journal.

One path is mistaken identity, where virus-fighting cells attack the body by error. A second path is harm to B cells, a type of immune cell, which then show body proteins in a risky way. A third path helps those cells live too long in the brain. The authors say these paths point to new drug ideas.
pmc-13281162:
Alishba Javaid and colleagues surveyed sleep paralysis in Pakistan for a 2026 study. In sleep paralysis, a person wakes but cannot move for a short time. Four hundred twelve people filled in an online survey. They told how often episodes came, how long they lasted, and what they felt. The team also asked about stress, trauma signs, sleep habits, coffee, and smoking.

Close to half of those surveyed had felt sleep paralysis at least once. Not being able to move was the most common feeling in episodes. Episodes often came while falling asleep and while lying on the back. More episodes went with more stress and trauma signs. Coffee use and smoking also tracked with more episodes. The authors say daily habits and mental strain may shape how often this odd state strikes.
pmc-13281762:
Qiqian Zheng and colleagues compared two pain drugs after weight loss surgery in a 2026 trial. The surgery trims the stomach to a sleeve through small cuts. Pain and vomiting are common after it. Seventy-two patients with obesity were split by chance into two groups. One got a new kind of opioid that aims at pain paths with fewer side effects. The other got a standard strong opioid. Recovery was scored a day later with a fifteen-part form.

The new drug group scored higher on recovery quality. Their pain at rest and in motion was lower in the first hours. They also waited far longer before asking for extra pain relief. Nausea and vomiting were less common in that group, the authors report. Rescue drug use and swelling markers in blood did not differ. The authors call the gain modest but real, and ask for larger trials.
pmc-13281862:
Putu Ayu Pradnya Swastiantari and colleagues mapped gentle dental care for children with brain development disorders in a 2026 review. Such children may face bright lights, odd sounds, and touch as threats. Fear and sensory overload can stall dental care. The review hunted studies from 2020 onward in four databases. It kept only drug-free methods used at the dental chair. Six studies from six countries made the cut, most on autism.

Five method families emerged. One walks the child through each step before doing it. One eases fear step by step, often with video views from the child's seat. Others use picture guides, calm sensory rooms, or gentle holding for safety. Reported gains ranged from cooperation scores to distress and body signs. The authors say proof is thin and mixed in form. They call for wider disorder coverage and shared outcome measures.
pmc-13282062:
Michael H Li and co-authors wrote a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, a pooling of many studies, on a tissue flap best known for breast rebuilding. The flap, called DIEP for short, takes skin and fat from the lower belly while sparing the muscle beneath. Surgeons wondered how well it works for rebuilding other body areas, where reports were scattered.

Eighty-nine studies covering four hundred sixty-seven patients met the review rules. Uses included head and neck, legs, arms, the vaginal area, hip and thigh, and trunk. About ninety-six percent of flaps survived overall, with similar high rates in each area. Harm at the belly donor site was low, and nearly all patients had that site closed without problems. The authors call the flap a versatile, reliable choice for hard rebuilding jobs beyond the breast.
pmc-13282162:
Areeb Tiwana and co-authors describe a 2026 case of sarcoidosis first showing as inflammation across a long stretch of the spinal cord. Sarcoidosis is a disorder where clusters of immune cells form in tissues, and spinal involvement is rare. The inflammation pattern, called longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, can mimic other nerve diseases, infections, or tumours. Their patient was a thirty-five-year-old man with a month of back pain, leg weakness, numbness, and falls.

Scans showed a long enhancing lesion running through most of his thoracic spinal cord, the middle section of the back. Spinal fluid tests pointed to inflammation but not infection. Chest scans found enlarged lymph nodes, and a later node biopsy showed the cell clusters typical of sarcoidosis. Steroid treatment first helped, then weakness returned, and plasma exchange was added. The authors stress early tissue proof and prompt immune-calming treatment.
pmc-13282262:
Mesfin Wubishet Gurmu and co-authors report a 2026 study on survival of critically ill children in an intensive care unit in southeastern Ethiopia. Child deaths in such units stay high in poorer countries, yet local prospective data, gathered as events unfold, were scarce. The team followed three hundred five children admitted between June 2023 and November 2024, until death or discharge from follow-up.

One hundred twenty-nine children died, a rate the authors call alarmingly high. Most deaths came within the first seven days, and median survival was ten days. Five factors independently raised death risk. They were lacking health insurance, failure of several organs, kidney injury, anaemia on arrival, and a high severity score. The authors urge early risk checks, fast targeted treatment in the first week, and policies that widen insurance cover for families.
pmc-13282362:
Rizki Radhitya Menaldi and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on how a diabetes drug protects heart muscle cells from a form of cell death called ferroptosis. Ferroptosis is driven by iron and fat damage in cell membranes. The drug, dapagliflozin, belongs to a class known for heart benefits beyond blood sugar control. The team stressed mouse heart cells with low oxygen for five hours to mimic a blocked artery.

Low oxygen raised reactive oxygen chemicals, iron, and fat damage markers, all signs of ferroptosis. Adding the drug reduced each of those signs. A gene pathway centred on interferon-gamma, an immune signal, switched on under low oxygen and off with the drug. Silencing that signal cut fat damage, while adding it back restored the damage. The authors identify this pathway as a new target behind the drug's protection.
pmc-13282462:
Ying Yang and co-authors report a 2026 modelling study on where to plant grass species for restoring vegetation on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau. The high plateau faces warming threats, and picking the right restoration species matters. The team modelled six typical grasses with a species distribution tool, adding centre-of-range movement and niche analysis. They tested current and future climate scenarios.

Altitude and yearly rainfall dominated the maps, jointly explaining about half to over four fifths of each species' pattern. Most species' best zones clustered in the northeast plateau. One grass, Elymus nutans, had the largest suitable area and the broadest niche, making it most adaptable. Under warming, most species expanded and shifted westward. High overlap between some species warns of competition if sown together in poor soils. The authors offer the framework as a guide for climate-resilient restoration planting, pending field validation of the mixes.
pmc-13282862:
In Sweden, formal choice between public and private care gets a hard look in a 2026 register analysis headed by Anna Axmon. The work compares children and adults with disability against the wider public. It asks whether formal choice between public and private providers leads to similar use in practice.

Records came from the Skane register for large disability and general cohorts. Children with disability used private care at rates close to their peers. Adults with disability were less likely to add private care after public care. They also used public mental health specialist care more often. The authors argue that choice systems need stronger support for access and navigation.
pmc-13282962:
Planners bracing for disasters get a 2026 survey of machine learning tools from Sampson Akwafuo and fellow authors. Disasters and health crises are growing more frequent and strain supply systems. A core task is choosing depot sites and matching them to regions in need before a crisis hits.

Older planning used fixed math models and map-based sorting methods. Newer work uses machine learning to handle fast change and complex local needs. The review gathers these attempts from varied sources and compares their aims. It seeks an updated model for grouping at-risk regions and guiding urgent response. Better depot placement can speed delivery of medicine and supplies in a crisis.
pmc-13283162:
Blood sugar after a tongue-nerve implant for sleep apnea is the thread Ahsan Ahmed and partners follow in a 2026 chart study. The implant stimulates a tongue nerve to keep airways open at night. All patients also had type 2 diabetes, so sugar control was tracked.

Charts covered 17 patients treated from January 2020 to October 2024 at one center. Average age was about 65 years, and baseline apnea was in the severe range. The main sugar marker fell slightly after implant, but the change was not statistically clear. Half of the six insulin users stopped insulin during follow-up. Better apnea scores tracked with better sugar scores in the analysis.
pmc-13283662:
Shane Miller and colleagues compared running form in 2026 between teenage girls and boys across a five-mile run. Girls suffer running injuries more often, yet past mechanics studies disagree, and teen data are scarce. Twenty healthy high school cross-country runners wore motion markers and force-sensing insoles, running an indoor-outdoor course at their own pace while form was captured each mile.

Pace differed only in mile one, where boys ran faster. Boys showed more inward knee angle at every mile, plus stronger hip and ankle moments. Peak forces under all foot regions and the speed of force build-up also ran higher in boys. The study tracked how form changed from the first mile to the fifth, giving a fatigue-aware picture of sex gaps in young runners.
pmc-13283862:
Whole-person assessment for older adults gets a full model in a 2026 review by Yinrun Wu and colleagues. Population aging brings many diseases at once, fading organ function, and complex social needs. Single-disease care models strain under that combined load for many elders.

The model pairs broad geriatric assessment with a standing interdisciplinary team. Literature from three databases through December 2025 fed the synthesis work. Core ideas, key steps, and practical rollout paths are laid out in sequence. Outcome proof is weighed next to current limits of the model. Future directions close the review, aimed at lasting integrated care systems. China-focused sources inform much of the discussion.
pmc-13284062:
Smart carriers that release gene silencers through skin on cue are reviewed by Yanmin Jian and colleagues in 2026. Small interfering RNA can treat skin disease, but the outer skin layer blocks it. Bare RNA also breaks down fast outside protective carriers.

Carrier size, charge, breakdown, and shape all shape skin passage and cell entry. Responsive carriers react to acidity, enzymes, light, or heat to release cargo. Physical aids like microneedles and ultrasound boost passage through skin further. Lipid-polymer hybrids balance stability, safety, and dual cargo loading well. Disease-tailored designs cover psoriasis, melanoma, and chronic wounds.
pmc-13284462:
Sheng Gong and co-authors analyze the global burden of birth defects of the urinary and genital systems in a 2026 study. Using Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, the team tracked new cases, total cases, deaths, and disability in children under nine years from 1990 to 2021. They also split results by sex, age, region, and social development level, and projected future trends.

Rates of new and total cases stayed broadly stable, while death and disability rates fell over the study period. Girls had higher case rates, but boys had higher death and disability rates. Burden grew more centered in low-development regions. The authors stress early-life harm and unmet need where resources are low.
pmc-13284562:
Xiaoli Huan and colleagues surveyed depressed teenagers in 2026 across fourteen psychiatric hospitals in nine Chinese provinces, asking how support from family and friends eases loneliness. Perceived support is known to buffer loneliness, yet the two sources may work differently. A total of 2,343 adolescents aged twelve to eighteen with depressive disorder completed scales for support, coping strategies, and loneliness, and path analysis traced the routes between them.

Support overall predicted less loneliness. Friend support carried a stronger direct effect than family support. Problem-focused coping, meaning tackling the problem itself, carried the support effect for both sources. Emotion-focused coping played only a weak role for family support and none for friend support. The authors suggest building both perceived support and practical coping skills in care for depressed youth.
pmc-13285362:
Stiffness after knee replacement sometimes needs a forceful bend under anesthesia, and Julius Sala with co-authors hunt risk factors for that step in Finnish registry data from 2026. National records held 154,883 first knee replacements from 1999 to 2020. Within a year, 3,861 patients needed the bending procedure.

Women faced higher odds, as did patients with diabetes, heart artery disease, or high cholesterol, while each added year of age lowered the odds a bit. Needing the bend also more than doubled later odds of a full revision, with one in seven such patients revised by ten years. The authors say early stiffness marks a group worth close watch.
pmc-13285662:
Community pharmacists trimmed drug lists for older outpatients in a 2026 Japanese intervention study by Takahiro Furuta and co-authors. Taking six or more daily drugs raises clash, side effect, and adherence risks. Surveys first asked older patients and their caregivers, from home helpers to visiting nurses, how the load felt.

A third of older patients wished for fewer pills, and caregivers often flagged strain from many scripts. Pharmacists then flagged poor-fit drugs and, with patient consent, proposed cuts to each prescriber. Follow-up at least four weeks on found fewer drugs, mostly gut and pain pills, with most patients no worse and some finding dosing easier. The authors back an active pharmacist role.
pmc-13285962:
HaiQuan Huang and co-authors hunt blood proteins that causally link kidney disease to heart artery disease in a 2026 gene-based study. People with failing kidneys die of heart disease at high rates, yet the protein messengers between the two organs stay murky. Gene tools that mimic lifelong protein levels can sort true drivers from fellow travelers in the blood.

The scan flagged six proteins sitting on the path from kidney disease to artery disease, three pushing risk up and three pulling it down. A test panel built on the six sorted patients with strong accuracy in the team's models. The proteins gather around fat and inflammation paths and shape immune responses in vessel walls. Computer docking even pointed to an old drug, imatinib, as a snug match for one protective protein, a lead for reuse studies.
pmc-13286762:
Fengling Liu, Hanyu Liu, and Sihan Peng chart twenty-one years of research joining diabetic kidney disease with sarcopenia, the loss of muscle with aging. Their 2026 analysis combines a map of the literature with a search for shared genes. The two conditions increasingly appear together in diabetes care, yet their overlap had not been mapped in full.

Publication grew steadily, led by Japan, China, and the United States, with hot topics shifting from kidney damage alone toward function, dialysis, and wider metabolic problems. Gene databases yielded 761 shared candidate genes. Those genes clustered around oxygen response, energy use, insulin signaling, and cell aging. Inflammation and insulin resistance look like common threads worth testing in the laboratory.
pmc-13286862:
Zohreh Azarkar and co-authors report a fulminant case of Weil's disease, the first documented in Iran's South Khorasan province, in a case report from 2026. The 20-year-old soldier arrived in July with seven days of high fever, muscle pain, headache, and light sensitivity, plus bleeding signs: coughed blood, dark urine, and black stools. Weeks earlier he had worked barefoot in rice paddies back home in Golestan, a northern province where leptospirosis is endemic.

Scans showed hazy lung patches and an enlarged spleen, while many rival infections tested negative. Liver enzymes and inflammation markers stayed elevated deep into the hospital stay. The team sent blood and urine to a reference lab for molecular confirmation of the water-borne bacterium. Their warning: deployment moves soldiers from endemic to dry regions, and only a careful exposure history cracks such cases where suspicion runs low.
pmc-13286962:
R. S. Soundariya and P. Thangaraj present a network that reads emotions from brain-wave recordings, tackling noise, signal drift, differences between people, and lopsided emotion classes. Their 2026 study combines wavelet signal cleaning with transformer attention layers. Two datasets served for testing: a custom collection from twenty-eight people and the public DEAP collection from thirty-two.

Reported accuracy exceeded ninety-nine percent when the model was tested within the same people it trained on. Stricter tests that hide whole trials or whole people still scored in the high nineties, well above simpler recurrent and convolutional baselines. A loss function that focuses on hard cases helped with class imbalance. The authors see uses in healthcare monitoring and responsive computing.
pmc-13287062:
Jessica Hemberg, Renae Schmidt, and Viviana Horigian introduce a 2026 journal collection on loneliness among teenagers and young adults. Loneliness is climbing in this age group and travels with depression, anxiety, and even higher mortality. The editors argue that loneliness works as a central mechanism through which social, psychological, and behavioral pressures shape young lives.

Studies in the collection trace online focus groups where young women described stigma and unmet emotional needs, alongside the double edge of digital spaces that can isolate or connect. Other work links heavy social network use to anxiety through loneliness and a fuzzier sense of self. Weight misperception, sports participation, and academic success also connect through loneliness, which the editors cast as the organizing thread.
pmc-13287262:
Mike Tombu tested depth perception through two-eye night vision goggles in 2026 under messy, task-like viewing rather than clean laboratory setups. Earlier work with such goggles gave mixed answers on whether wearers can judge depth from the slight difference between the two eye images.

Depth judgement survived poor viewing and gave wearers a real advantage on tasks where judging distance matters. Crucially, limits on depth sharpness did not follow limits on ordinary sharpness of vision, so the two abilities appear separable under goggles. Tombu argues that buying and training decisions should measure depth performance directly instead of inferring it from standard eye chart style results.
pmc-13287362:
Josephine Zachodnik and colleagues translated a questionnaire into Danish in 2026. The questions ask what patients expect from treatment. The team gave the Danish version an early quality check among people awaiting spine surgery. Translation followed forward and back steps with clinician review.

Patients rated the wording as clear, scoring items near the top of a six-point scale. Consistency and repeat stability were good for most sections, though some sections varied. A few sections showed many top scores, limiting spread. Total scores showed no link to disability and only a small link to quality of life. The authors advise care with single-section scores until larger studies confirm the structure.
pmc-13287762:
Omniya E Azmi and colleagues fed rats in 2026 two protective compounds, l-carnitine and quercetin. Each came in plain form and packed into tiny fat bubbles called niosomes. The test asked which form better shields male fertility against the weedkiller atrazine. Thirty rats were split across six groups and dosed by mouth for 56 days.

Atrazine alone cut sperm count, movement, and shape quality, lowered sex hormones, and damaged reproductive tissues under the microscope. Both protectors eased the harm, restoring sperm traits, antioxidant balance, and hormone-making gene activity. The bubble-packed versions worked best. The authors propose niosome delivery as a stronger shield against farm chemical harm to male reproduction.
pmc-13287962:
Mohamed Belmouhand, Jens Folke Kiilgaard, and Carsten Faber describe in 2026 a man aged twenty with three benign blood vessel tumours in his left retina. At a five-week check, stitched ultra-wide eye images seemed to show a fourth tumour, hinting at worsening disease.

Direct examination still found only three. Review of the stitching showed the software had misread the optic nerve head in one source photo, warping alignment and inventing the extra spot. Body checks found brain tumours and a kidney cyst, and gene testing confirmed von Hippel-Lindau disease. The authors warn teams to verify apparent new eye lesions by hand before calling progression.
pmc-13288762:
Sameer Sharma and colleagues test a chymase-blocking drug in a mouse model of a bile duct disease in 2026. Primary sclerosing cholangitis scars the bile ducts and slowly destroys the liver. Mast cells gather in the diseased liver and release chymase, an enzyme that fuels inflammation and scarring. The team first checked human liver samples, then treated Mdr2 knockout mice, which mimic the disease.

Human samples from late-stage patients held more chymase-positive cells than healthy liver samples. Mice received the drug INVA8001 daily for two weeks by injection. Treatment lowered chymase activity and cut mast cell buildup in the liver. Inflammation, tissue damage, scarring, and duct overgrowth all eased under the drug. Signs of bile flow problems also improved. The authors propose chymase blockers as candidates for this disease and other mast cell disorders.
pmc-13288962:
Margot B A Aalders heads a 2026 protocol on a pain marker study in Australia. The study sits in a large hospital and a lab. It deals with knee arthritis pain. Surgery choices now rest on self-reports. Some patients stay unhappy after good surgery.

The team will enroll 20 adults set for knee replacement. Each bad knee will pair with the good knee. Twenty healthy peers will also join. Staff will test blood and joint fluid cells. Cells will be provoked in the lab. One immune signal will be tracked closely. Light scans will sort cell types too. Results will be tied to pain and mood scores.
pmc-13289162:
Ingrid Charlotte Kongerud and colleagues draft a 2026 trial plan in Norway. The DEAK study deals with new kidney transplant patients. A drug called dapagliflozin slows kidney decline in others. Transplant patients were left out of past trials. This trial will test the drug in them.

The trial will enroll 330 adults in all. Ages will run from 18 to 75. Joining starts six to eight weeks post-transplant. Half will get the drug each day for three years. Half will get a dummy drug. Kidney function slope is the main check. Biopsy scores and safety will also be tracked. Registry checks will run for ten years.
pmc-13289362:
Abdukadir Nigus Mohammed, Edris Abdu Debesay, and Ashagire Zenebe Woldearegawi studied a 2026 cohort on high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes moving together in post-conflict Tigray, Ethiopia. The two conditions often coexist and jointly raise heart, kidney, and early death risk. War damage to clinics and drug supply in Tigray may have sped worsening for many patients.

Records came from Ayder Comprehensive Specialized Hospital in Mekelle and covered 1024 adults with at least three visits from December 2022 to April 2024. Mean age was 49 years, most patients were women, and most lived in urban areas in this sample. A joint model tracked blood pressure and fasting glucose over time together. Rising age and weight stood out among drivers of joint worsening.
pmc-13289662:
Shuang-Li Zhu and coauthors report a 2026 case of community pneumonia caused by two germs at once: Chlamydia psittaci and drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. He arrived after two days of fever, fatigue, muscle pain, and poor appetite, and he also had diabetes and high blood pressure. He had watched a chicken being slaughtered two days before symptoms began, a key exposure clue.

Chest imaging showed dense lung consolidation, raising suspicion for the bird-linked germ. Standard cultures are slow and often miss it, so targeted gene sequencing was used and found both infections together. Treatment with omadacycline and linezolid led to recovery for the patient. Diabetes likely raised risk for the resistant staph infection alongside. Care was prompt once both germs were known.
pmc-13289762:
Wenbin Yang, Shan Yu, and Jingdong Li wrote a 2026 letter commenting on a study of remimazolam versus propofol for kidney transplant anesthesia by Han and coauthors. The original work found better blood pressure stability and less injection pain with remimazolam. The letter praises the question, then raises methods points about how repeated blood pressure data were handled and reported.

A stated correction threshold conflicts with figure notes, and averaged change scores were treated as many comparisons, which the writers call overcorrection. A mixed model would better respect repeated measures over time, they argue. A unit error in a results table also needs clearing up. Sharper statistics would strengthen trust in the stability claim.
pmc-13289862:
Jaehoon Yeom, Minji Kim, and Sang Don Kim built a 2026 literature framework to estimate the dry weight of freshwater invertebrates living in Korean rivers. Weight per species underpins biomass modeling, vulnerability checks, and toxicity forecasts, yet validated values are scarce. Length-weight relationships from field guides and global literature offer a way to fill gaps without new field sampling.

Coefficients were fitted at genus, family, and order levels under controlled cleaning rules. Genus-level averaging matched field-measured dry weights best, beating broader levels in the validation. More source relationships improved accuracy, especially at genus level in the analysis. Final weights were estimated for 563 taxa, giving modelers a ready quantitative base for river ecology.
pmc-13290862:
Keeping attention steady falters in Lewy body dementia, and its brain signature shows on scans, Davide Braghittoni and colleagues report in an imaging study from 2026. Sustained attention underpins higher cognition, so the team compared patients and healthy controls on a vigilance task inside the scanner.

Thirty patients with dementia with Lewy bodies and 25 controls took brain tests plus a listening vigilance task during 3T fMRI. Patients scored worse, chiefly on spatial tests, and on the vigilance task they lapsed more and responded more slowly. During the task their brains also fired less in the precuneus and cuneus, and in the angular gyrus and intracalcarine cortex, regions tied to sustained attention. Braghittoni and colleagues say the pattern could guide tailored cognitive training for this dementia.
pmc-13291262:
A greener test for a new antifungal drug is built by Omkulthom Al kamaly and Mustafa Sayedahmed in 2026. The drug treats vaginal yeast infections that resist older drugs. Labs need a fast, cheap way to check tablet strength. Their method uses light given off by a tagged drug.

A dye-like reagent binds the drug and glows under light. Glow strength was read at a set color band. The test stayed straight across a wide dose range. Checks for accuracy and steadiness passed world rules. Tablet fillers did not disturb the reading. Green scoring tools rated the method eco-friendly. It suits routine quality checks in drug plants.
pmc-13291362:
A new alkali-loving bacterium can heal mortar cracks. Sahar M Ibrahim leads a 2026 study from Egypt’s Wadi El-Natrun soils. Fifty strains were pulled from those harsh soils. Each was screened for chalk making skill.

One strain beat all others at chalk output. Gene tests named it Bacillus albus. Best chalk making came under mild alkaline settings. Lab tools proved the chalk was pure, nano-sized calcite. Living cells were then mixed into cement mortar. Three cell doses were cured for ninety days. Strength rose clearly with bacterial mortar. Best dose hinged on calcium supply nearby. Self-healing, greener mortar is the long-term aim.
pmc-13291562:
A barium swallowing test led to gut ischemia in a rare case. Peng Xu, Shili Zhong, and Xiaoyu Peng report the 2026 survival case. Barium contrast helps image the upper gut. Gut blood loss after such tests is very rare.

Their patient was a 62-year-old man. Eight hours after his test, pain and shock signs hit. Scans showed gas in liver and gut veins. That gas marks serious belly trouble. Strong anti-infection care started at once. Gas cleared within twelve more hours. He recovered fully by one month. Fast intensive care saved him, the authors stress.
pmc-13292462:
Maria Tzoraki and co-authors chart a 2026 nationwide picture of deaths before age five in Greece from 2016 to 2020. Using Hellenic Statistical Authority records coded by ICD-10, they computed neonatal, infant, and under-five mortality rates and split deaths by cause, age, sex, and region. International datasets from WHO, UN IGME, and Eurostat supplied context.

Greece recorded 1,877 under-five deaths in the period, and 58.3 percent of them fell in the first month of life. The under-five rate dropped 22.9 percent across the five years, from 4.97 to 3.82 deaths per 1,000 live births. Perinatal conditions and congenital anomalies together caused over 70 percent of deaths, boys accounted for 56 percent, and deaths clustered near big tertiary hospitals. The authors call for stronger perinatal care to close the gap with leading European countries.
pmc-13292562:
Emmanuel Malematja and colleagues swap an antibiotic for termite meal in young broiler diets, in a 2026 feeding trial. Zinc bacitracin is a common growth-promoting antibiotic under pressure for replacement. One hundred fifty day-old chicks ate one of three matched diets for two weeks. One diet was plain, one carried the antibiotic, and one carried termite meal at one hundred grams per kilogram. Gut bacteria, blood measures, digestibility, and growth were compared.

Termite-fed chicks carried a distinct caecal community led by Firmicutes. Their crude protein digestibility beat both other groups, while fiber digestibility ran lower. A liver enzyme fell, uric acid rose slightly, and weight gain plus feed conversion improved. The antibiotic group also performed well on several measures. The authors conclude the insect meal matched the antibiotic on gut composition, protein use, and growth without obvious metabolic harm. They still call for confirmation trials before farm adoption.
pmc-13292662:
Arlet Guusje Reinhard, with co-authors, reviews a 2026 acceptance question in children's dentistry: how do children, parents, and dentists feel about effective cavity treatments that look ugly? Silver diamine fluoride stains decay black, and steel crowns or the Hall technique skip drilling but show metal. The systematic review searched four databases and sorted studies by who was judging.

One hundred twenty-six studies qualified, though most carried high bias risk. Children accepted silver fluoride on back molars at a median 93.2 percent across studies; parents followed at a median 69.9 percent and dentists at 61.6 percent in the pooled picture. Steel crowns and Hall crowns flipped the order, with parents most accepting. Everyone preferred the plain-looking options on back teeth over front teeth. The authors say acceptance is real but uneven.
pmc-13292962:
Hayoung Song and colleagues describe, in 2026, a smart contact lens that tracks uric acid in tears to mirror levels in blood. High uric acid drives gout and links to other illness, yet repeat blood draws make close tracking hard.

The wireless lens was tested in rabbits and people, including some with high uric acid or gout. Daily wear showed how tear levels rose and fell with food and activity, with a personal lag time for each user. Tear and blood values moved in a straight-line pattern, allowing blood estimates from tears. Models built from those patterns could then forecast daily levels without wearing the lens.
pmc-13293262:
Daniel Schwarzkopf and colleagues recount a difficult heart emergency treated in 2026, involving a fifty-four-year-old man in cardiogenic shock after a major heart attack. Doctors reopened his blocked coronary arteries with stents, yet shock persisted because the mitral valve leaked severely. Pumps and a heart-lung machine kept him alive while the team considered how to fix the leak without open surgery.

The chosen fix was a catheter procedure that clips the mitral valve leaflets together, here performed with a flexible nitinol device for the first time in this setting. The leak was eliminated while mechanical support held his circulation steady. The authors present the case as evidence that clip repair can work even during shock, and they call for studies comparing devices for this high-risk situation.
pmc-13293462:
Gonzalo F. Del Rio Montesinos and co-authors review a rare and deadly turn that Paget's disease of bone can take in the spine, in a 2026 narrative review. Paget's disease makes bone break down and rebuild in a disordered way, and the spine is a common site. In a small share of cases the diseased bone transforms into osteosarcoma, a malignant tumor, and the authors gathered what little evidence exists on that event.

The review finds that spinal transformation most often strikes the lumbar region in older men, usually announcing itself through back pain or nerve problems. Diagnosis calls for imaging plus a bone biopsy, and care combines drug therapy, possible surgery, and rehabilitation. Five-year survival has been reported as low as ten percent. The authors press for multicenter studies to improve surveillance and treatment guidance.
pmc-13293562:
In a 2026 pilot study, Rohit Jhawar and colleagues check whether self-reports in an online health cohort can find people with mitral valve prolapse for a registry. The valve fault is common and, in a minority, links to heart failure or dangerous rhythms.

A survey went to 5746 members of the Health eHeart Study in Northern California, and 520 replied, with 85 saying they had the condition, a share the authors give. Heart scans were obtained for about half of those, and prolapse was confirmed in 28 people, who all joined the registry. People with worse valve leakage answered more accurately about their condition.
pmc-13293662:
Zhiheng Xia and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how steering the bone healing environment can help large bone defects repair themselves by coupling bone and blood vessel growth. Big defects fail to heal alone, and the local setting decides whether repair stalls or proceeds.

Early healing is dominated by bone removal, with inflammation, low oxygen, and acid clearing dead tissue. Later, immune cells shift to a repair mode, acidity fades, and signals boost vessel growth and new bone laying. Stress factors such as oxygen lack and oxidation shape both phases. Targeting those shared stresses may break harmful loops and switch on self-repair.
pmc-13293762:
Dagmawi Mengesha reviews how well health facilities in Ethiopia deliver tuberculosis care, in a 2026 analysis of 112 sites. The country faces infectious disease, chronic illness, and injury at the same time, with a thin workforce. Mengesha mixed older facility data from 2010 and 2011 with mapping, record review, and talks with staff and policy makers.

Tuberculosis in children was found far too rarely, at about two percent of cases against a world target of twelve percent. Success in curing patients was high in hospitals and much weaker in small primary care units. Short staff and broken supply chains tracked with failed treatment. Mengesha sets out a five-part reform plan that spans testing, community work, supply, digital tools, and oversight.
pmc-13293862:
Jungang Wang and a large team untangle the genetics of sugarcane, a crop whose genome carries ten to twelve chromosome sets, in a 2026 genomics study. That tangled inheritance, built by crossing species and repeated backcrossing, long blocked efforts to explain how cane stores so much sugar. The group assembled a fully separated genome of POJ2878, a foundational breeding variety, resolving 118 chromosomes.

The assembly exposed extensive mixing between subgenomes and pinpointed breeder-favored segments, including one that raises sucrose content. Resequencing nearly a thousand cane varieties traced how widely this ancestor contributed to modern cultivars and flagged genes under selection for cold tolerance, cell size, and shoot branching. A genome-wide scan, adapted for many chromosome copies, found loci tied to sugar storage, with one transporter gene confirmed by experiment. The work gives breeders a firmer map for improving yield.
pmc-13294362:
Luis Kersten and colleagues dissect which parts of the synapse protein RIM1 form droplets in a 2026 cell study. Liquid-like condensates may organize vesicle release zones, and droplet tendency depends on disorder, charge patterns, and sticky contacts. Full protein and cut-down fragments were overproduced in human kidney cells, and droplet richness was scored against fragment length.

Full RIM1 condensed most strongly, yet pieces near 250 amino acids still clumped. For most fragments, droplet pull rose with length. A minimal core stitched from five regions copied full protein droplet counts and sizes. A partner protein, RIM-BP2, helped only at low RIM1 levels in cells, unlike test tube hints.
pmc-13294562:
Juan Ismael Almonte and colleagues published a comprehensive review in 2026 on how clinicians confirm success during ablation for common atrial flutter. The procedure burns a line across the cavotricuspid isthmus, linking the tricuspid annulus to the inferior vena cava. Success means electrical conduction is blocked in both directions along that line.

Each assessment method is covered in turn, with how measurements are taken, how reliable the method is, and where errors can arise in daily practice. Most methods rest on small patient studies rather than large comparisons, and long-term recurrence data remain scarce. Combining several methods raises confidence that the line truly blocks conduction, so the authors advise learning and using multiple approaches.
pmc-13294762:
Xiongwei Xiang and colleagues examine social drivers of depression among Chinese youth in a 2026 analysis. They cover ages 10 to 24 and ask how wider social conditions shaped the burden between 2003 and 2021. Results are broken down by age band and by sex to reveal differing patterns.

Data came from global disease burden records, World Bank figures, and a national social survey. Higher income per person, city living, and health spending were linked with lower burden, while rising higher education enrolment tracked with higher burden, notably for females aged 15 to 24. Education pressure showed effects within a year, underlining the need for age-specific support.
pmc-13294862:
Jesús Endara-Mina and a large team review clotting events after COVID illness in a 2026 combined analysis. Some people develop post-COVID syndrome, with symptoms lingering long past the first infection. Whether they also face higher risk of blood clots, and by how much, remained unsettled.

Following standard review methods, the team searched many databases and screened well over a thousand records. Twenty studies qualified, five feeding the pooled numbers and fifteen summed up in words. The authors report a meaningful clotting risk in this group and argue for early spotting, active monitoring, and preventive treatment tailored to each patient, with vascular specialists in mind.
pmc-13295262:
Eun Young Seo and colleagues squeeze Korean winter spinach for its most useful chemistry, in a 2026 study of the Allseason cultivar. Spinach leaves carry phenolic compounds with antioxidant and other protective effects, but earlier work profiled summer or greenhouse leaves with fewer tests. Using high-end mass spectrometry plus nuclear magnetic resonance to confirm structures, the team compared extraction solvents and conditions, then ran five different bioactivity assays on the extracts.

A half-methanol extract won, and patience paid off: seventy-two hours at mild warmth pulled out the richest levels of the three main flavone compounds. Twelve phenolics were identified in all. One isolated compound stood out as the strongest antioxidant in two radical tests, beating its siblings clearly. Statistical grouping separated the extracts cleanly by solvent strength. The authors pitch winter spinach as a nutraceutical source worth harvesting under tuned conditions.
pmc-13295362:
Paula Cortés and colleagues measure how long ampicillin lingers in broiler chickens in a 2026 study. The antibiotic treats poultry infections, but traces left in meat can trigger allergies and feed resistance in people. Data on tissue clearance after muscle injection were still limited.

Chickens received the drug by injection, and muscle and skin were sampled at set times afterwards. Muscle showed the drug only during the first day, while skin held traces longer before they faded. The team estimated nine days as a safe wait before slaughter, stretching to 19 days under a stricter reading, giving regulators firmer ground for limits.
pmc-13295762:
Mohamed H Derbala and colleagues use artificial intelligence on tumour samples to predict immunotherapy benefit in rare cancers in a 2026 study. Immune cell crowding inside tumours may forecast who answers pembrolizumab, but rare tumours are seldom studied. Biopsies before and during treatment came from 84 patients across ten rare tumour groups.

A learning tool counted tumour-infiltrating immune cells and tumour content on stained slides. High starting immune density tied to longer control in one subgroup and to friendlier immune mixes. Rising immune density plus falling tumour content during treatment tied to longer survival, suggesting paired biopsy measures could guide care in rare cancers.
pmc-13295962:
Claire Brown and colleagues outline a 2026 protocol to agree a core set of outcomes for families of people who survive critical illness. Relatives often face months of strain on their health and daily life, yet trials measure that burden in scattered ways.

The FOCUS study will use interviews, repeated Delphi surveys and a consensus meeting with researchers, clinicians, survivors and caregivers. The goal is a short agreed list of outcomes every trial in this area should record. The authors say a shared set would make future studies easier to compare and more useful to families.
pmc-13296162:
Stella Schellhorn and colleagues track how a strong cystic fibrosis drug trio affects activity, sleep, and nose symptoms in preschool children, in a 2026 pilot study. The drug mix, elexacaftor, tezacaftor, and ivacaftor, greatly lifts outcomes in older patients, but data in the young are thin. Ten children aged two to six wore motion sensors while parents rated symptoms and performance over a year.

Step counts and active play rose at three and six months, then drifted back near the start line by twelve months. Parents, though, kept rating their children's performance as better. Sleep measures and nose symptom scores held steady, which backs the trio's safety in this age group. The authors warn that season and other outside pulls may explain the activity bump, and they call for bigger controlled studies.
pmc-13297062:
Ja Young Cho and co-authors optimise, in 2026, freezing methods for sperm stem cells of olive flounder, a fish bred through surrogate parents. Such cells must be enriched and stored without losing their seeding power, so two sorting methods and several antifreeze mixes were compared.

Density sorting enriched the stem cells best, and adding a plating step gave no further gain. A mix pairing propylene glycol with raffinose sugar kept the most cells alive after thawing, at just over half. Thawed cells transplanted into zebrafish larvae reached the future gonad area and persisted briefly. The protocol supports flounder breeding programmes.
pmc-13297162:
Khrystyna Ryabenko and colleagues review whether diabetes drugs called SGLT2 inhibitors could modify hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in a 2026 article. This inherited heart-muscle thickening is driven at first by gene faults, yet oxidative stress and faulty energy handling push it forward. No current therapy targets those secondary drivers well.

The drugs protect failing hearts even without diabetes, through several routes the review details. They ease oxidative stress, improve mitochondrial function, restore sodium and calcium balance, and quiet inflammation. Early laboratory and translational findings fit the heart condition's known weak points. The authors build a mechanistic case for trials, while the evidence remains short of patient proof.
pmc-13297262:
Hunter Cohn and colleagues describe an endurance athlete whose watch-estimated aerobic capacity fell after starting a prostate drug in a 2026 case report. The runner began tamsulosin for urinary symptoms, then noticed training felt harder. Smartwatch records from 113 outdoor runs were compared across periods before, during, and after the drug.

Estimated maximal oxygen uptake dropped clearly during daily tamsulosin use. The decline also appeared when runs at similar paces were compared, reducing the chance that easier training explained it. After switching to tadalafil, the estimate recovered only partly. One case cannot prove cause, and the authors ask for larger controlled studies of alpha-blocker effects on exercise capacity.
pmc-13297562:
Making CAR-T cells inside the patient's body, instead of in a factory, could widen access to a powerful cancer therapy. Junya Yamaguchi and co-authors review that prospect in 2026, with a focus on the especially hard case of malignant glioma.

Current CAR-T production removes a patient's T cells, engineers them outside the body, and returns them, a slow and costly process. In vivo engineering delivers the receptor blueprint directly, using viral carriers or nanoparticles, and early clinical work in blood cancers looks promising. Glioma adds its own barriers, from drug delivery to the tumor's protected setting. The review weighs those obstacles and the strategies researchers are testing to overcome them.
pmc-13298262:
Charlotte Aßmann and co-authors examine short-term effects of red blood cell transfusion in very low birth weight infants, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Transfusion thresholds for preterm babies remain debated, with little evidence on immediate physiology. Records covered 68 infants and 99 transfusions, comparing the day before and the day after each transfusion.

Slow heart rate episodes became less frequent after transfusion, and oxygen dips became shallower. Transfusion did not significantly change oxygen needs, baseline heart rate, or how often dips occurred. The authors describe modest, selective gains in stability for clinically stable infants, and they call for work identifying which subgroups benefit most.
pmc-13299062:
Romina Georgiana Bita and colleagues compare how three dental treatments affect bad breath and oral quality of life, in a 2026 prospective study. Adults starting gum treatment, fixed prosthetic work, or fixed braces were assessed at baseline and eight weeks. Measures covered sulphur compound emissions, smell ratings, tongue coating, and a standard oral health questionnaire.

Breath measures and quality of life improved after gum treatment and prosthetic work, yet worsened after brace fitting. Change in sulphur compounds tracked quality-of-life change and carried part of the contrast between gum treatment and braces. The authors flag orthodontic patients as vulnerable and urge hygiene reinforcement during appliance therapy.
pmc-13299562:
Soil bacteria near Chilean volcanoes brew soap-like molecules that fight germs, report Claudio Lamilla and colleagues in a 2026 study. Screening eighteen strains from rhizosphere soil in the La Araucanía region, they picked two Bacillus producers of the biosurfactant surfactin.

One strain peaked early at 90 mg per litre within a day; the other kept producing to 224.4 mg per litre by seventy-two hours. Both extracts emulsified strongly and stayed stable across wide heat, acidity, and salt ranges. Their fluids blocked Staphylococcus aureus growth and biofilms, with the stronger strain reaching 81% biofilm inhibition, and also suppressed a plant bacterium and a crop fungus. The authors flag agricultural and sanitation uses.
pmc-13299862:
An immune signal better known for fighting viruses may also help build bone, suggest Camilla Albertina Dantas de Lima and colleagues in a 2026 genetic and cell study of postmenopausal osteoporosis. They genotyped 251 patients and 115 healthy controls for a variant in the interferon-gamma gene.

The variant's G allele raised osteoporosis odds, with an odds ratio of 1.45, though blood interferon levels did not differ by genotype. In bone-forming cells grown in dishes, a low dose of interferon-gamma improved survival and increased mineral deposition in a dose-dependent way. The authors describe the cytokine as a possible anabolic influence worth testing in primary human bone cells.
pmc-13300162:
Xuan Zhou and colleagues sequence the full mitochondrial genome of a wood-boring beetle attacking the Potala Palace in China, in a 2026 study. The species damages wooden structural parts of the famous heritage site. Genetic comparison with relatives showed typical beetle genome features, a stable gene order, and a close relationship to another furniture beetle species.

Some genes in this beetle change relatively slowly over evolutionary time. Field notes add that it produces one generation each year, with peak activity from May into July. The authors offer the genome and life-cycle baseline for future work on beetles threatening wooden cultural heritage, including monitoring and control planning.
pmc-13300862:
Sangho Lee and co-authors hunt for simple predictors of the blood pressure crash that can follow tourniquet release in knee replacement, in a 2026 prospective study. Ninety elderly patients had blood pressure and a finger sensor index of fluid responsiveness recorded around their operations. Hypotension after deflation was defined as mean pressure falling below a set threshold tied to organ injury risk.

The crash occurred in about twenty-nine percent of patients and struck more often when pressure was already low before release. Adjusted analysis kept two independent predictors: lower pre-release mean pressure and a higher variability index measured right after intubation. Together they discriminated moderately well. Similar patterns held for stricter systolic definitions, and the episodes did not clearly track with early complications or longer stays. The authors suggest the pair can flag patients who deserve extra preparation before the tourniquet comes down.
pmc-13301062:
R Chantrakul and W Boonyapisit run a double blind randomized trial of local tranexamic acid during cardiac device implantation, published in 2026. Half of device patients take blood thinners, and pocket bleeding is their signature complication. So gauze soaked in the clot protecting drug or placebo was laid into the pocket before the generator went in. The trial enrolled 132 patients on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, split evenly between drug and placebo.

Pocket hematoma appeared in about nine percent of the drug group and eight percent of controls, a statistical tie. The broader tally of device related bleeding complications also matched, near seventeen against twenty percent. Checks the next morning and at two weeks caught no hidden divergence. The authors state plainly that local tranexamic acid did not significantly reduce bleeding in this setting, a negative result they offer to counter enthusiasm for an inexpensive ritual without proven payoff.
pmc-13301462:
Xu Cao and co-authors review piezoelectric materials as active surfaces for dental implants in a 2026 survey. Unlike passive coatings, these materials turn chewing forces, cell traction, or ultrasound into local electrical signals, and with defect engineering and layered structures they can generate reactive oxygen species on demand. The review lays out the bioelectric logic of bone, then walks through uses against biofilm, for bone bonding, for steering immune responses, and for soft tissue sealing.

The field's center of gravity is shifting, the authors argue, from a goal of growing bone toward one platform coordinating infection control, immune remodeling, and integration by stages. The caveats take space: composite polymer systems are immature, realistic activation windows are unmapped, evaluation standards and device integration lag, and long term safety data are thin. Their verdict is that piezoelectric surface engineering is platform science whose clinical value still awaits mechanism work and preclinical testing.
pmc-13301862:
P Rodriguez Fraga and colleagues test in a 2026 study whether CT scan features of heart scar can locate zones where electrical signals slow down. Such deceleration zones help drive dangerous ventricular rhythms and are targets during ablation. Detailed mapping inside the heart finds them, but a scan-based shortcut could improve planning.

Scans from 38 patients having their first ablation for these rhythms were compared against electrical maps made during the procedure. Channels of thicker wall within scar predicted slow zones with reasonable sensitivity, and longer channels predicted them more strongly. Fatty change inside the scar, measured by scan density, also tracked with slow-zone presence. Combining channel length with fatty change sharpened the predictions, which may help when MRI is unavailable.
pmc-13301962:
Weaving social and emotional learning into science lessons lifted both skills and marks, Ahmad Basheer and Ibrahim A. Asadi report in a 2026 experiment. One hundred one Arabic-speaking sixth graders in two northern Israel schools were randomized to SEL-enriched science classes over thirty sessions or to traditional teaching. Struggling readers were included and tracked separately.

The enriched group gained more in emotional skills, science motivation, and science achievement than controls, while mathematics scores stayed level in both arms. Children with reading difficulties benefited just as much as typical readers. The authors argue that collaborative, reflective science teaching can serve inclusion, especially for linguistically marginalized pupils, without costing academic ground.
pmc-13303062:
The fading echoes of an ultrasound pulse carry a three-dimensional map of weld flaws, Guiwu Chen and colleagues prove in simulation in a 2026 numerical study. Their method re-indexes scans from two opposing lines into a virtual array, then feeds first-arrival shifts plus coda-wave stretching, decorrelation, and energy ratios into one inversion. A parameterized welded-steel model hosted four defect types, from voids to porosity clusters.

The tomography recovered tighter, more accurate defect volumes than total focusing and migration benchmarks under the same conditions. In the hardest interference case it placed the defect center within 0.48 millimeters with zero false-positive volume. The authors stress that real welded specimens must come next.
pmc-13305862:
Ngo Ha-Son used silica pulled from rice husk ash to build a porous framework in a 2026 materials study. The ash-derived silica was about 98.4 wt% pure and served as the only starting source in a fluoride-assisted gel route.

By varying acidity, mix ratios, heat and ageing, the team found best results at pH 2 with a set ratio held at 60 °C for 96 hours. The product showed wormhole-like pores, a surface area of 816 m2 g−1 and mean pore width near 3.6 nm in the reported measures. Heat tolerance reached 700 °C, and a test use supported crystal growth for pollutant capture.
pmc-13306362:
Maria Rashidi fused radar and heat camera data to find hidden separation inside concrete bridge decks in a 2026 study. Radar senses deeper flaws while heat imaging catches near-surface ones, yet their unlike signals resist easy combination.

A physics-guided fusion design joins the streams with transfer learning, cross-modal attention and gated mixing to learn robust shared patterns. Feature selection keeps only indicators that stay meaningful across different bridges in the training plan. Tested on a public dataset, the framework aims for steadier detection of delamination and rust-weakened decks before surface failure appears.
pmc-13306462:
Semonti Mukherjee proposed a leaf-based index for city air stress in ginkgo trees in a 2026 study from Budapest, Hungary. Leaf pigment health was combined with dust load into a single Pigment Integrity-to-Dust Ratio for comparing sites and seasons.

Early summer leaves at a moderate-traffic site held more chlorophyll and carotenoids, while high-traffic leaves lost pigment and formed more breakdown product in reported measures. A low-traffic site gave a clean baseline for contrast. Links between pollutants and the new index ran negative, though the authors treat those patterns as exploratory rather than settled proof.
pmc-13306562:
Huanhuan Zhu reported a rare lung abscess in a three-month-old boy in a 2026 case account from China. A lasting cough and a mass in the right upper lung first suggested a birth defect or tumour rather than infection.

Routine tests gave no answer, so gene sequencing of lung wash fluid found a single read of Mycobacterium abscessus as an early clue. Targeted sequencing then found 13,272 reads in wash fluid and 31,474 reads in removed lung tissue, naming the subspecies massiliense. Tissue study showed granuloma patterns matching this infection family, and targeted drug care followed.
pmc-13306862:
Jiazhi Dai split wind turbine fault hunting into two stages to handle skewed operating data in a 2026 study. Normal running records swamp fault records in SCADA logs, so single supervised models miss many real faults.

Stage one uses a one-class support vector method with two anomaly scores to pull odd records aside. Stage two runs a convolutional classifier only on those flagged records to name true faults among them. Trials on real turbine data beat plain supervised methods on accuracy and missed-fault rate in reported results, supporting the staged design.
pmc-13306962:
Wenjuan Su mapped the WOX gene family in Masson pine and singled out one root-linked member in a 2026 study. Root regrowth from cuttings limits clonal copying of elite trees, and WOX factors steer root start and growth in many plants.

Twenty-one family members, named PmWOX1 to PmWOX21, spread unevenly over nine chromosomes with a cluster on chromosome seven in reported mapping. Duplication under purifying selection shaped the family, and promoter scans tied members to hormones, stress and growth. Expression checks pointed to PmWOX4 as a key partner in new root formation.
pmc-13307062:
Haijie Zhao compared grazing and rest rotations in an alpine shrub meadow of the Qilian Mountains in a 2026 field study. Five regimes ran from ten days grazing with twenty rest to nonstop grazing and full exclusion, judged in the third treatment year.

Plant richness and diversity rose under the two shorter grazing spells against nonstop grazing and exclusion in reported measures. Four dominant species supplied leaf trait data, and community pattern tests confirmed clear separation between regimes. A fifteen-day graze with fifteen-day rest stood among the strongest options for diversity on this fragile plateau pasture.
pmc-13307362:
Jie Yin and co-authors study in 2026 how a green tea compound changes the oxidation behaviour of turkey haemoglobin, a driver of off-flavours in stored meat. The compound, EGCG, attached permanently to a cysteine site on both alpha chains of the protein. Crystal images placed each attached molecule inside the protein, near its iron centres.

Binding slowed hemin loss and cut formation of the damaging ferryl form under peroxide attack. At the same time, the protein oxidised itself faster, a trade-off the authors note plainly. Protection against fat oxidation worked better for the met form of haemoglobin than for the oxygen-carrying form. Electron transfer from the bound compound is one proposed mechanism. Food scientists may use such binding to keep turkey products tasting fresher.
pmc-13307662:
Inka Romero-Ortells and co-authors run in 2026 an eye tracking study of how Hindi and English bilingual students watch subtitled lesson videos. Students schooled in English viewed clips in three pairings: English sound with English text, Hindi sound with Hindi text, and English sound with Hindi text.

When both channels were English, gaze split fairly evenly between faces and the text line at the bottom. With Hindi text in either pairing, viewers spent more time on faces and less on the text below. Quiz scores did not differ in a firm way between pairings. Text pull thus depends on the worth viewers grant the written channel, not on its mere presence.
pmc-13307762:
Ahmad Almajali and co-authors investigate peste des petits ruminants in Bahrain in 2026, testing sheep, goats, camels, and wild ruminants for antibodies to the virus. More than twenty-six hundred animals were screened with a competitive antibody test. The disease threatens small livestock production and trade across borders.

About a quarter of sheep and goats carried antibodies, while camels and wild ruminants showed none. pmc-13308962:

pmc-13309562:

pmc-13309662:

pmc-13310362:

pmc-13310562:

pmc-13310762:

pmc-13310962:

pmc-13311162:

pmc-13311362:

pmc-13311762:

pmc-13311862:

pmc-13311962:

pmc-13312162:

pmc-13312462:

pmc-13312962:

pmc-13313262:

pmc-13314162:

pmc-13314862:

pmc-13315662:

pmc-13315962:

pmc-13316562:

pmc-13316662:

pmc-13316762:

pmc-13317362:

pmc-13317662:

pmc-13318162:

pmc-13318862:

pmc-13319162:

pmc-13320262:

pmc-13320462:

pmc-13320562:

pmc-13320662:

pmc-13321262:

pmc-13322462:

pmc-13322862:

pmc-13322962:

pmc-13323962:

pmc-13324662:

pmc-13325362:

pmc-13325862:

pmc-13326962:

pmc-13327862:

pmc-13328362:

pmc-13329562:

pmc-13329662:

pmc-13335562:

Chia-Yih Wang and colleagues explain how the tumour suppressor CHEK2 maintains primary cilia, the cell antenna, in a 2026 study. CHEK2 is known for guarding genome integrity in the nucleus, and it also sits at the mother centriole, yet its role there was unclear. When nutrients were scarce, CHEK2 switched on to preserve cilia by breaking down Aurora kinase A, which would otherwise degrade the cilium shaft, and by activating AMPK to promote autophagy. Both routes were needed for placental cell ciliation, movement, and invasion. In pancreatic cancer cells, glutamine shortage triggered the same CHEK2 programme. pmc-13372362:
Edun and colleagues validated in 2026 the math used to make HIV viral suppression figures comparable across countries that count with different cutoffs. Global targets define suppression as a viral load at or below one thousand copies, but many programs report at lower thresholds, so an international model adjusts their figures upward. The formula had been fitted on clinic cohort data and checked in only a few settings, so the team tested it against nationally representative household surveys in sub-Saharan Africa.
