Against those references the team could judge whether the adjustment formula recovers the standard figure from lower-cutoff reports without bias. The study supplies the real-world check that global monitoring rests on, since skewed adjustments would distort country rankings and the tracking of the shared 95-95-95 treatment goals.
pmc-13373262:
Catharina F van der Boor and co-authors set out a clash in aid work in a 2026 paper. Crises grow in size, yet most people in poor lands still lack mind care. Smart computer tools are sold as a way to stretch care, but rules and guards for their use lag far behind.

The authors call this gap the aid AI clash. They map where such tools may help at each tier of mind support in a crisis. Help for front-line aid staff looks the most ripe and safe first step. The paper gives aid leads a clear frame to judge tools before they are rolled out to weak groups.
pmc-13374062:
Yohan Benchimol and colleagues test whether removing one fallopian tube harms ovarian response in IVF in a 2026 study. Cutting the mesosalpinx during salpingectomy can injure ovarian blood supply, raising concern about follicle recruitment. The team compared 114 patients with a prior unilateral salpingectomy for hydrosalpinx or ectopic pregnancy against 228 matched controls treated in the same month.

Matching covered age, AMH level, and body mass index. The main outcome was the difference between ovaries in follicles at least 13 millimetres on trigger day, with mature follicles, cancellation rates, and eggs retrieved as secondary outcomes. The design isolates the operated ovary within each patient, giving a direct test of whether tube removal costs eggs in later IVF cycles.
pmc-13375662:
Vivian Reckers-Droog and colleagues examine two severity measures used in Dutch drug reimbursement in a 2026 study. Proportional shortfall is the primary metric for setting cost-effectiveness thresholds, while absolute shortfall is also reported. Though related, the two can disagree, and debate continues over which should capture disease severity in health technology assessment.

The team analysed 56 of 57 reimbursement dossiers published by the National Health Care Institute between May 2018 and April 2026. Twenty-eight dossiers formed a distinct group. Their proportional shortfall averaged 0.88, high, while their absolute shortfall averaged only 14.28 quality-adjusted life years. Twenty-seven of those concerned cancer drugs for older patients. The pattern shows that metric choice can systematically favour or penalise older cancer patients.
pmc-13376362:
Xiaohu Li and colleagues show that USAG-1 worsens kidney ischaemia-reperfusion injury by driving ferroptosis in a 2026 study. Ischaemia-reperfusion injury is unavoidable in kidney transplantation and a leading cause of delayed graft function. Ferroptosis, iron-dependent lipid peroxidation cell death, contributes to that injury, yet USAG-1's role in it was unknown. Mouse models and human transplant biopsies from circulatory-death donors were studied.

USAG-1 rose under ischaemic stress, and higher donor expression tracked with worse graft function after transplant. Removing USAG-1 markedly eased ferroptosis and acute injury severity. Mechanistically, USAG-1 promoted breakdown of GPX4, a key ferroptosis guard, while the chaperone HSPA5 normally stabilises GPX4. The work presents USAG-1 as both a biomarker for graft risk and a target to protect transplanted kidneys.
pmc-13377162:
Jane Liao and co-authors checked allergy tests after surgery scares in a 2026 study. A bad act to sleep drugs or care drugs can look like an allergy, but true culprits are hard to name. Skin tests for this use are not yet proved in full.

The set held 74 adults seen at one large US center over ten years. Tests were found in three in ten cases. Germ drugs led the culprit list, then numbing drugs and muscle soft drugs. Of 29 who had surgery next, 28 had no ill act. Full allergy work, the team says, can free most folk for safe next care.
pmc-13377762:
S Donya Razavi and colleagues examine barriers to a menstrual hygiene programme in South Sudan in a 2026 study. Menstrual hygiene is hard in conflict-affected, low-income settings where products, soap, water, and private toilets are scarce. The Canadian Red Cross, with the South Sudan Red Crescent and government, ran Healthy Bodies Healthy Minds from 2020 to 2023. Fourteen people involved in design and delivery were interviewed.

Barriers were interrelated and compounding: resource limits, logistics, competing stakeholder priorities, ongoing conflict, and climate change, plus COVID-19 disruption. Solutions identified in interviews point to flexible supply, local partnerships, and adaptive planning. The study gives implementers a grounded account of why menstrual health programmes stall in fragile settings and how they can be made to work.
pmc-13378362:
Jin Wook Hwang and co-authors report a 2026 study building a lab model of a rare form of lung cancer. Some non-small cell lung cancers carry changes in a gene called RET, which drives their growth. The team used stem cells carrying two such cancer-linked RET changes.

From those stem cells they grew lung cells, then cultured them so they formed structures resembling air sacs in the lung. When the cells were placed into mice, they formed tumours with features of human lung cancer, including airway-like structures. Gene tests on single cells pointed to genes linked to response or resistance to a RET-blocking drug. The model may help find treatments for cancers that stop responding.
pmc-13380962:
Marcus H A Morais and colleagues report a 2026 case series on using a dense hyaluronic acid filler to build up a recessed chin. Chin projection strongly affects facial balance and appearance. The filler used is a stabilised gel not derived from animals, given as deep injections against the bone.

Each patient received one millilitre in the chin as part of wider filler treatment of the middle and lower face. Patients reported high satisfaction and a natural look, and independent doctor ratings showed overall improvement. Side effects were mild and short-lived. The series offers short-term, real-world observations rather than trial evidence, and the authors present it as a practical guide to technique.
pmc-13385962:
Chien Truong-Quoc's team designed DNA origami from scratch with a generative diffusion model, in a 2026 study. Generative models pushed protein design forward, but DNA origami design lagged for lack of large standard shape data. The team trained a diffusion design system on simulated steady shapes from a multi-scale math model.

Given target shapes, the system produced sound origami designs through guided diffusion sampling and strand routing, with built-in structure scoring. Among over 100 generated designs, chosen builds were lab-tested, folding well and showing auxetic change and modular joining. The approach widens the open design space for DNA nano work.
pmc-13386462:
Miracle O. Olatunde and Jetze J. Tepe attack the cancer driver MYC by forcing its destruction in 2026 work. MYC lacks steady pockets for drugs, which long made it seem untouchable despite driving many tumors. Their plan pairs a molecule that breaks MYC's partnership with MAX with a drug that switches on the 20S proteasome shredder.

Combined treatment drained MYC fast from MYC-dependent colon cancer cells and shut down its gene programs. Cell death rose markedly, and the loss did not rely on the usual turnover route. The authors frame disorder itself as a weakness that proteasome activation can exploit in other hard targets.
pmc-13386562:
Ran Wang and colleagues map immune and metabolic rewiring tied to Candida colonization in COPD in 2026 work. Candida often sits in the airways of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, but its body-wide effects were unclear. The team modeled gene and chemical data with an interaction term to isolate effects unique to the COPD setting.

A distinct gene set shifted only when Candida met COPD, clustering in immune and inflammatory pathways. Blood chemicals also split by that pairing, with sugar-linked compounds rising and protein-building pathways falling. A zinc-finger regulator family may steer the gene changes, the authors propose from motif evidence.
pmc-13386862:
Miriam Cherkaoui and colleagues weigh pandemic strain against early development in preterm toddlers in a 2026 study. Sixty-nine children were assessed in 2022 and 2023, most born prematurely, with a parent-rated Corona-Index gauging family burden. A matched subgroup was compared with a pre-pandemic group on standard infant development scales.

Thinking and motor scores did not differ between eras, but language scores ran significantly lower in the pandemic group. Within that group, burden interacted with sex on motor scores in exploratory models. The authors urge caution, since headline models for thinking and language missed significance overall.
pmc-13387062:
Hanke Zheng, Jonathan D. Campbell, and Julie A. Patterson track Medicare Part D coverage shifts after a major law change in a 2026 study. The Inflation Reduction Act capped patient out-of-pocket costs and raised plan liability from January 2025. That shift may push plans to exclude more brand drugs in crowded classes, the authors reason.

Using a commercial formulary database, they compared Medicare plans with commercial plans from 2024 through 2026. Classes counted as competitive when at least three eligible brand-only drugs were on the market. Beneficiary impact was projected from 2024 enrollment, framing a watch on access in contested drug classes.
pmc-13389062:
Shannon and colleagues test cannabidiol, the cannabis compound CBD, in mice modeling Angelman syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by intellectual disability, seizures, and broken sleep, in 2026 preclinical research. The mice lack the Ube3a gene whose loss causes the condition. Families use CBD off-label for children, ahead of evidence. Treated mice gained REM sleep during the dark cycle, the active phase. CBD restored the siesta, a midday rest bout that mice show and the model mice lose. Sleep homeostasis, the rebound regulation of sleep after loss, improved. After kindling, spontaneous seizures were reduced in the CBD-treated model mice compared with controls. Shannon argues the results justify controlled study of CBD for sleep and seizures in Angelman syndrome, where options are thin.
pmc-13389762:

Median differences were tiny: minus 0.061 gray for bladder dose and minus 0.066 gray for rectum dose against the hand calculations. About half of cases agreed within a tenth of a gray on each measure. Pavičar concludes automation removes transcription risk while matching manual accuracy, and standardizes reports.
pmc-13390362:
Zhi-Jing Xu, Tao Li, and Ning-Yi Zhou identify, in 2026, the bacterial transporter that pulls the diabetes drug metformin into cells. Metformin is a first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes and also a widespread pollutant in water, and bacteria that break it down must first take it up.

Loss of the gene blocked growth on metformin, showing the transporter is essential for entry. The protein belongs to the NCS1 family and binds metformin with high affinity. pmc-13391762:

pmc-13392262:

pmc-13393262:
Luiz G Bonato and seven colleagues show how stirring time and heat can programme the crystal form and glow of a layered hybrid perovskite. A broad glow appeared as excited states trapped themselves in the distorted lattice. Heating reversed the journey, restoring the original symmetry and a sharp emission line. pmc-13393762:
Gillian Kolla leads an eleven-author qualitative study of prescribed safer supply in Canada, where people dependent on street opioids receive pharmaceutical opioids to cut overdose risk. Those experiences bred deep mistrust and pushed people toward the unregulated supply. pmc-13393862:

pmc-13393962:

It held high efficiency for eighty hours while current climbed, thanks to the tough amorphous layer and ongoing interface renewal. The authors offer laser shock as a general catalyst factory.
pmc-13394862:

pmc-13395462:

pmc-13395962:
Mohamed J Saadh and others review acute myeloid blood cancer in HIV-positive people in a 2026 paper. Blood cancer in this group may speed up through long defense flare, oxygen stress, and marrow upset, while blood cancer-linked defense loss can worsen HIV illness.

pmc-13396062:
Ankit Raj and co-authors measured what eight hours in a scleral lens does to the cornea in eyes that have already had a transplant, in a 2026 study. Scleral lenses vault over the cornea and can give clear sight after graft surgery, but they rest on the eye all day and may swell the tissue.

pmc-13396462:

pmc-13396862:

pmc-13398762:

pmc-13398862:
Maren Jinks and co-authors watch liver cells' chemistry unravel dose by dose under hydrogen peroxide attack. Pretreating cells with rifampicin to wake their cytochrome P450 enzymes, normally sleepy in this cell line, changed how the high dose played out. The work shows dose and metabolic readiness together shape what a toxin appears to do.
pmc-13399062:
Makéla Jeffrey-Watson and colleagues describe the first year of CHIRO-Force, a peer-assisted learning program in a university chiropractic course, in a 2026 report. The program grew out of force-sensing table technology, which measures the forces students apply during manual therapy practice. Two senior students were trained as mentors so classmates could book extra supervised practice outside class hours.

During the pilot year, which ran from September 2023 to April 2024, the mentors built five session protocols and gave more than 100 sessions to over 100 students. Group mentoring was also folded into clinical internships. Students rated 97 percent of sessions as highly appreciated. The authors present the scheme as a promising support for hands-on skills, while noting that its effect on clinical competence and confidence still needs measuring.
pmc-13399662:
Mohammad Ayati Firoozabadi and colleagues present a low-cost, all-inside repair for meniscal ramp lesions of the inner knee meniscus. Their 2026 technical paper addresses tears at the meniscus-capsule junction, often seen with anterior cruciate ligament injury, which worsen instability if left untreated. Standard repairs often need a back-inside portal or costly devices.

The method works entirely through front portals, passing FiberWire sutures across the tear with an 18-gauge angiocatheter, a thin hollow needle, and tying them with a sliding Duncan knot. It avoids back-inside dissection, shortens operating time, and removes dependence on expensive implants. The authors call it safe, reproducible, and cost-effective, a practical option where standard repair systems are unavailable, while healing outcomes need follow-up.
pmc-13399862:
Xintong Xu and colleagues reinterpret aplastic anemia through an old teaching metaphor, seed, worm, and soil, in a 2026 review. In the metaphor the seed is the blood-forming stem cell. The worm is the immune attack or toxic insult gnawing at it, and the soil is the bone marrow environment that should nourish growth. The authors argue its modern picture, an immune-driven stem cell failure shaped by genetics, needs the full three-part framework rather than any single cause.

Each element of the metaphor maps to a treatment logic: protect or replace the seed, suppress the worm, repair the soil. The authors close by anticipating that this comprehensive framing, joined with precision medicine, will sharpen both classification and therapy.
pmc-13400162:
Mohammad Arif Rahman and colleagues, with senior author Genoveffa Franchini, combined a drug-releasing vaginal ring with a vaccine to protect female macaques against vaginal SIV challenge, in a 2026 study. Here it was delivered continuously by a ring, layered on the ΔV1-SIV vaccine, a DNA/ALVAC prime-boost regimen with a V1-deleted envelope protein in alum.

Across fourteen weekly low-dose vaginal challenges, the combination cut infection risk by 82.8 percent, and 58 percent of the animals stayed uninfected. About half of those protected animals also survived a second challenge phase still uninfected. Protection tracked with a distinct local immune profile. CD73-positive dendritic cells, interleukin-10-producing macrophages, and innate lymphoid cells all featured, plus antibody-driven natural killer cell killing aimed at the envelope's V2 region. The authors present sustained ring delivery plus the V1-deleted vaccine as a promising HIV prevention strategy.
pmc-13400462:
A N Saidi and co-authors revisit, in 2026, data from the FRANCIS trial to link fatty liver with heart risk in rheumatoid arthritis. Arthritis of this type raises the chance of fatty liver, which may add to cardiovascular danger. The trial had tested intensive risk management in patients without heart disease or diabetes.

Liver fat was estimated from a blood and waist measure called the lipid accumulation product in 236 patients. Those flagged with fatty liver had higher blood pressure, higher blood sugar and worse blood fats. Their neck artery walls also tended to be thicker, though the adjusted link fell short of clear proof. Three-year changes were tracked by liver status and treatment arm.
pmc-13400862:
Rui Cao and a large team introduce, in 2026, a statistical framework that finds disease genes along the path of cell development rather than in fixed cell types. Standard transcriptome-wide association studies link gene activity to disease using genome data. Single-cell data add resolution, but most methods assign genes to discrete cell stages.

Their method models gene expression as a smooth curve over developmental pseudotime, pooling genetic effects across neighboring stages. Simulations showed higher power than existing single-cell approaches, and the method draws confidence bands that pinpoint where along development a gene matters. Applied to childhood B cell leukemia, it recovered known risk genes and identified their relevant cell stages.
pmc-13401162:
Yingkun Xu and colleagues published a 2026 study of MYDGF, an immune-related protein, as a possible biomarker in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, the most common kidney cancer type. They combined single-cell profiling, bulk gene data, and machine learning to judge its role in the tumor microenvironment.

Single-cell data showed MYDGF concentrated in malignant epithelial cells and tied to the mix of myeloid and lymphoid cells nearby. In the TCGA kidney cancer dataset, high MYDGF tracked with immune checkpoint activity, immune dysfunction signals, and PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathway activity. Tumors rich in MYDGF looked immune-infiltrated yet impaired, and were predicted to respond poorly to checkpoint blockade therapy.
pmc-13402262:
Raju Vaishya and colleagues gathered eleven systematic reviews to judge whether robot help beats standard technique in total hip replacement. Ke Han and six colleagues report a rescue manoeuvre after a guidewire was lost during an ultrasound-guided drainage procedure in a 60-year-old man with a blocked bile duct at the liver hilum. Earlier scope attempts had failed against a complete obstruction, and the patient had refused surgery and skin drainage, leaving the endoscopic route as the only option.

The target duct was punctured and a wire passed, but during device exchange the wire slipped out and leaking bile collapsed the ducts. Working under direct vision through the new tract into the abdominal space, the team recovered access and completed the internal drainage to the jejunum. The case shows a salvage path when standard wire control fails mid-procedure.
pmc-13423962:
Burke and a large team test home-based digital monitoring in this 2026 longitudinal study of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, a disease where trial endpoints struggle to detect slow progression. Participants completed weekly smartphone tasks covering speech and hand and body movement, a computer mouse-clicking task, and three remote phone visits over 24 weeks.

Forty-two people, 19 with ALS and 23 controls, logged 10,237 smartphone assessments and 459 mouse sessions in total. Baseline models separated patients from controls with accuracy scores between 0.75 and 0.92 on the AUC scale, and digital measures correlated strongly with the standard self-reported function scale. Both groups improved slightly on practice-sensitive tasks, patients less so, though only one feature separated the groups significantly over time. The authors call remote monitoring feasible and worth scaling into larger, longer cohorts.
pmc-13424062:
Sharifi and colleagues review in 2026 bacterial-based cancer therapy, the use of living bacteria as anticancer agents. Bacteria naturally home to tumors, can be reprogrammed genetically, and stir the immune system, which makes them candidates for reaching tumor regions that drugs penetrate poorly.

The review organizes the field into four themes. First come the basic mechanisms: selective tumor colonization, direct killing of cancer cells, immune activation, and reshaping of the tumor's surroundings. Second are engineering strategies that load bacteria with cytokines, antibodies, enzymes that activate prodrugs, toxins, or gene therapies, alongside safety switches. Third are combinations with chemotherapy, radiation, light therapy, and immunotherapy, aimed at oxygen-starved and treatment-resistant niches. Finally the authors weigh early clinical experience, manufacturing hurdles, and long-term safety, including unpredictable spread inside tumors and clearance by the host.
pmc-13424562:
Van Der Veken and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether planned treatment of unruptured brain aneurysms on the anterior communicating artery harms thinking and memory. This artery sits deep in the brain, and harm after treatment of burst aneurysms there has been known for decades. The team searched six databases for studies that tested cognition before and after planned treatment and reported this site apart from others.

Van Der Veken found only eight studies covering 95 patients, most treated with surgical clipping and a few with a catheter method. In five of the eight studies, patients treated at this site had worse cognitive results than patients treated at other sites. Careful testing can thus reveal real deficits in a large share of patients. The authors stress that the evidence base is small, tests varied widely, and surgical cases dominate, so firm numbers need bigger studies.
pmc-13425462:
Hong Li and colleagues made a five-metal powder that breaks down the antibiotic tetracycline in water with the help of peroxide. The powder mixes iron, cobalt, nickel, copper, and aluminium in near-equal shares, a blend classed as a high-entropy alloy.

The team first cast thin alloy ribbons, then ground them by ball milling, a method that smashes material with hard balls. Powder milled at 280 revolutions per minute cleared about 95 percent of the drug within 60 minutes. Milling opened a spongy surface and fresh active sites, which sped the reaction and helped move chemicals to the surface. The milled powder beat gas-made powder, offering a workable route to clean drug-laden water.
pmc-13425862:
Géraldine Layani and colleagues map help for people living with obesity that crosses sectors, from health care to community and social services. Obesity is a long-term condition shaped by genes, habits, social life, and surroundings, so single-sector care often misses the point.

The team ran a scoping review under the Arksey and O'Malley method, searching MEDLINE, Web of Science, CINAHL, and grey sources for work from 2006 to 2025 in high-income countries. Community and primary-care programs for adults were the focus. Readers get a chart of what joined-up help looks like and where its delivery still lacks study.
pmc-13426362:
Murugan and Rangasamy describe in 2026 a small-molecule drug conjugate aimed at prostate cancer cells that display the PSMA marker on their surface. The construct joins a PSMA-binding guide molecule to exatecan, a potent cancer drug. They are linked by a bond that breaks open inside cells where a common antioxidant is abundant, releasing the payload on site.

Computer modeling predicted strong binding to PSMA. In lab tests the conjugate killed PSMA-positive prostate cancer cells at low doses, with a half-maximal effect near one hundred seventeen nanomolar. It barely harmed PSMA-negative cancer cells or normal kidney cells, showing sharp selectivity. The conjugate stayed stable in acid, buffer, and serum. In mice, it proved far safer than free exatecan, which caused severe weight loss and deaths, supporting targeted delivery as the safer route.
pmc-13426462:
Akhtar and co-authors frame climate change as a direct health security threat, in this 2026 policy analysis of Pakistan. The country now ranks as the world's most climate-vulnerable on the Germanwatch index. Recurrent floods from 2022 to 2025 affected more than 26 million people. The floods damaged health facilities and interrupted basic services across the country.

The authors trace how each shock multiplies existing weaknesses: surges in malaria and waterborne disease, worsening child malnutrition, rising antimicrobial resistance, and displacement into crowded informal settlements where drug-resistant typhoid spreads. Roughly a thousand people died in the 2025 floods alone, and total damage exceeded 30 billion US dollars by the estimates cited. Their prescription has four parts. One is climate-resilient health infrastructure. The others are digital and geospatial disease surveillance, prevention-first primary care, and a One Health framework. That framework joins human, animal, and environmental health planning.
pmc-13426962:
Dupraz and colleagues published a 2026 study on how well a new knee implant fits real bones. Knee replacement parts must match the cut top of the shin bone closely. Poor fit can leave edges hanging over bone or patches left bare. The team used shape models built from scans of 232 patients.

Models covered both Caucasian and Asian patients with worn knee joints. The new oneKNEE design covered more bone than three older rival designs. Its coverage topped the field for both average and unusual bone shapes. Stronger contact with the hard outer bone shell also favored the new design. Better fit on the screen suggests fewer fit problems in surgery. Virtual fitting let the team compare designs without new surgeries.
pmc-13427062:
Wu and colleagues studied in 2026 how HIV clinicians actually work with an AI decision support prototype, aiming to design the tool around people rather than predictions alone. At a South Carolina health system, sixteen clinicians, including doctors, nurse practitioners, pharmacists, social workers, and case managers, tested the system between March and September 2025. They completed surveys, thought aloud during hands-on sessions, and sat for in-depth interviews.

Clinicians judged the AI's risk predictions against familiar clinical indicators they already trust. They stressed that social factors, such as housing and income, sit at the centre of their own risk judgements, yet the model largely ignored them. Trust in the tool was conditional and grew only with time and use. Two features decided whether predictions became actions: clear explanations and advice specific enough to act on. The authors argue decision support must fit clinical thinking and social reality, not just be accurate.
pmc-13427662:
Qirong Mao and colleagues map, in a 2026 study, where different forms of the dystrophin gene are active in the mouse brain. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is known for wasting muscle, yet about a third of patients also face learning difficulties. Dystrophin is made in the brain too, in several lengths. The team used spatial transcriptomics, a method that reads gene activity while keeping each spot's place in the tissue.

Long forms clustered in deeper cortex layers and one memory region, while short forms favored the cortex surface and another memory area. In mutant mice, a therapy that skips a faulty gene section restored the full-length form at gene and protein level. Treated brains also showed immune activation worth watching. Drug developers gain a brain map for judging therapies aimed beyond muscle.
pmc-13427762:
Sultan Ahmed Nazir uses mathematical modelling to explain why temperate viruses of bacteria, which can hide inside the bacterial genome as prophages, so often carry extra accessory genes such as virulence factors. Mobile genes face two obstacles: chromosomal locations are stable, and rival mobile elements without the cargo compete against them. His 2026 paper models the viral lifecycle together with the geography of bacterial populations.

Two mechanisms overcame the obstacles. First, movement between bacterial populations favours gene-phage linkage when the gene helps in environments that also trigger prophages to wake and spread. Second, within a population, virus particles drifting into patches of bacteria that lack the gene give phage-carried genes an edge over immobile chromosomal copies. Nazir argues these mechanisms apply weakly to plasmids and other mobile elements, giving phages a distinctive role in bacterial adaptation and in the emergence of new pathogenic strains.
pmc-13427962:
Wong and colleagues built and beam-tested in 2026 a trigger detector for a Swiss experiment hunting the muon electric dipole moment. That tiny property could reveal new physics beyond current theory. The setup must spot incoming muons that can be stored and fire a magnetic kick fast enough to trap them in a magnet's center. Missing or mistiming that trigger wastes the rarest events.

The detector pairs a hair-thin plastic scintillator gate with a thicker aperture plate, each read by light sensors. It triggers only when a muon passes the gate but misses the aperture plate, the signature of a storable path. Beam tests with real muons matched computer simulations of the light signals at about 97 percent agreement. The authors judge the design ready for the experiment's first full phase.
pmc-13428062:
Ryan M Sullivan and co-authors test a virtual reality method for measuring attentional bias, the tendency for alcohol cues to capture attention. Their 2026 study checks whether the Alcohol Cue VR paradigm provokes craving and biased gaze as theory predicts.

One hundred and five adults with varied drinking histories experienced three virtual scenes containing alcohol and three neutral scenes while their eye movements were tracked. They also completed a standard visual probe task and craving measures. Drinking history, age when regular drinking began, recent use, and binge episodes all predicted how long participants fixated on alcohol cues. Feeling present in the virtual scenes did not change these effects. Alcohol-related factors explained more variance in the VR measures than in the standard task, supporting VR as a realistic way to assess cue attention.
pmc-13428762:
Nikola Sladojevic and co-authors examine RGS5, a protein that tunes signals from G-protein coupled receptors, in the growth of new blood vessels after birth. Their 2026 study asks how RGS5 inside endothelial cells, the cells lining vessels, affects signalling by VEGF, a key vessel-growth factor.

In mice with blocked leg arteries, deleting Rgs5 everywhere or only in endothelial cells impaired new vessel growth, slowed blood flow recovery, and raised rates of limb self-amputation. Without RGS5, the VEGF receptor was activated less because a phosphatase called SHP-1, which switches the receptor off, became more active. In cell culture, RGS5-deficient cells migrated less, died more, and survived poorly when VEGF was added. The authors propose targeting the RGS5 and SHP-1 link to improve vessel growth after ischemia.
pmc-13430162:
Yanning Bao and colleagues engineer, in a 2026 study, an antibody that smuggles immune therapy across the blood-brain barrier into gliomas. These tumors are the deadliest common brain tumors, and checkpoint immunotherapy that works elsewhere in the body cannot reach them. The team fused a checkpoint-blocking antibody to a peptide that ferries cargo across vessel walls. A linker between them is cut by an enzyme common in tumors, freeing the antibody where it is needed.

In dishes, the fusion freed T cells from suppression and sharpened their killing of glioma cells. In mice it gathered at tumor sites more than a plain antibody, extended survival, and stirred stronger immune responses. It also teamed well with the standard glioma chemotherapy drug. Barrier-crossing delivery, the authors argue, may be the missing step for brain tumor immunotherapy.
pmc-13430262:
Jing Zhou and co-authors build, in a 2026 study, a heart-seeking nanoparticle to treat a lethal side effect of cancer immunotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitors can inflame the heart muscle, a complication called myocarditis that often kills. Current care blunts the whole immune system and ignores oxidative damage inside heart cells. Their particle joins Prussian blue, a pigment that acts as a multi-purpose antioxidant enzyme mimic, with a plant compound called astragaloside IV and a peptide that homes to heart tissue.

In heart cells stressed by peroxide, the particle reduced injury and nudged immune cells toward a calmer state. In mice with the modeled myocarditis, it gathered in the injured heart, cut immune cell invasion and scarring, and improved pumping measures. Gene and protein analysis pointed to a growth signaling pathway as part of the action. Targeted delivery could spare patients body-wide immune suppression.
pmc-13430662:
Gerald Bright Businge and colleagues reviewed measles records for Ugandan children aged eighteen months or younger in a 2026 study of national watch data from 2018 into early 2024. Uganda gives a first measles shot at nine months and a second at eighteen months. Outbreaks still recur despite a safe and strong vaccine.

Of more than two thousand suspect cases, well over half proved to be measles. Most sick children fell in the nine to eighteen month band, while a fair share were still too young for the first shot. Among sick children old enough for shots whose records were known, three in five had never had a dose. Some districts also fell short of the global watch standard. The authors urge a fresh look at shot timing and stronger watch systems.
pmc-13430762:
Ellen Benestad Moi and colleagues explore talk between Norwegian-first-language nurses and Norwegian-second-language nurses in home care, where language gaps can threaten safety and follow-up. Fourteen nurses, seven from each group, gave in-depth interviews, read through reflexive thematic analysis.

Two themes stood out. One was the need for shared understanding at work, with double-checks of written notes and clarifications of spoken exchanges. The other was the value of social contact among colleagues, strained by cultural differences. Home-care leaders get a grounded case for paired checks, plain wording, and social time that builds trust across language lines.
pmc-13430862:
John K. Yue and colleagues test blood inflammation markers for judging traumatic brain injury in the TRACK-TBI study. Proteins in blood mirror injury patterns after head trauma, and markers of later nerve and body injury might flag who will decline or face lasting disability.

Patients arriving at eighteen United States trauma centres with a day-one head scan were enrolled prospectively. The analysis used day-one and two-week blood samples plus six-month function scores, covering 369 brain-injury patients, 100 orthopaedic-trauma controls, and 69 healthy controls. Acute and subacute markers were tested for separating diagnosis and severity and for predicting half-year outcomes.
pmc-13431562:
Tomohiro Yoshida and co-authors reported a rare dog case in 2026 in which milky lymph fluid pooled around the heart and in the chest at once. The dog also bore clots in two large veins near the heart and a cancer of tissue linings. Each fault fed the others, which made both diagnosis and care a hard puzzle.

Care joined three prongs: surgery to ease pressure in the lymph system, drugs to guard against fresh clots, and cancer drugs placed right into the chest. Over a long span, the stray fluid around the heart and lungs came under control despite the stacked threats. The authors argue that hunting for root causes and layering treatments can still win good outcomes in such tangled cases. The case may guide vets who meet the same rare mix.
pmc-13432362:
Hille and colleagues searched for blood markers that predict who fares poorly on ramucirumab. Ramucirumab is a vessel-blocking antibody used as second-line therapy for advanced stomach and junction cancers. The search ran within the phase II RAMIRIS trial. Plasma from 99 patients was sampled at baseline and during treatment. The team measured placental growth factor, carbonic anhydrase IX, and tryptase levels.

Placental growth factor rose substantially during therapy. Carbonic anhydrase spiked briefly then eased, and tryptase stayed flat across the sampled timepoints. High growth factor levels at baseline carried a hazard ratio of 1.75 for death in unadjusted analysis. That signaled shorter survival for those patients. After adjustment, only the early on-treatment level kept statistical support. Its hazard ratio was 1.85 at the start of cycle two. Neither of the other two markers tracked survival consistently. The authors label all findings hypothesis-generating, pending validation.
pmc-13432762:
Joseph F Carr and co-authors probed one bacterial protein in 2026 with two jobs in gut kin germs. The protein sets the length of a shared surface sugar. It also enables a round form of that sugar. The sugar helps the germ wall shrug off antibiotics. In the round form, it also tunes wall flow and the stock of a sister form.

The team built changed copies of the length-setting protein in a lab strain and read both outputs. Changes that broke length control in two zones of the protein killed round sugar output in full. Two changes at one spot parted the jobs: one cut round output in half, while its twin left output at full strength, though length control read the same for both. The split proves length control is needed yet not enough on its own.
pmc-13434462:
Cho and colleagues built and piloted in 2026 an artificial intelligence virtual simulation program that trains nursing students in safe drug giving for children. Dosing for children is error-prone, and practice with real patients is limited. The program was built on a four-stage learning cycle of experience, reflection, concept building, and active trial. In South Korea, 48 third-year students were split into program and control groups of 24 each.

Cho found the program group improved clearly in medication safety skill compared with controls, based on pre- and post-program scores. Two other measures, confidence in dose calculation and learning immersion, did not differ between groups. The mental load reported by program students fell over the course, which suggests the task grew easier to handle. The authors back wider use in children's nursing courses, with more tailoring to each learner.
pmc-13434762:
Yifan Zheng's team studied why people keep using mobile fitness apps in 2026, using 704 valid survey replies and three linked methods. They framed staying power as value made, satisfaction judged, and lock-in built. Links were tested with structural modeling, truly needed factors were checked, and mixes of conditions that lead to staying were mapped. Fun features and service quality lifted satisfaction, which lifted the wish to stay, while switching costs also helped directly.

Social features alone did not lift satisfaction, yet they mattered inside some winning mixes, and three broad paths to staying emerged. App makers get a less simple story than one killer feature: keep users through good service, fun, and built-up value together. Product teams can use the three paths to sort users and shape retention plans.
pmc-13435162:
Gabriela Acevedo's team tested VisionMD in 2026, an open video tool that measures bradykinesia, the slowed movement that marks Parkinson disease. Clinical rating scales grade movement in coarse steps and can miss slow change, so the team studied finger-tapping videos from 36 patients at two visits about 1.6 years apart. Speed and timing were read from video and set against the standard finger-tapping score.

Video measures tracked the clinical score, yet only the video measures caught the slow decline in speed over time, while the coarse score stayed flat. Patterns also differed by how severe patients were at the start, showing varied paths of decline. Clinicians get evidence that short phone-style videos can sharpen follow-up between visits.
pmc-13435462:
Le Chang's team reviewed iron-based magnetic nanoparticles in 2026 as active shapers of the tumor immune setting, not just drug carriers. Immunotherapy has changed cancer care by waking the immune system, yet tumors often shield themselves with a suppressive local environment that blunts lasting response. The review frames these iron particles as tools that, under magnetic control, can heat tissue, jolt cells, and spark oxidative stress.

Those triggers can push tumor cells toward immunogenic death, ease low oxygen, reprogram macrophages, wake dendritic cells, and strengthen killer T cells. The authors still flag safety, iron handling over time, delivery, and factory scale-up as open problems. Cancer teams get a unified cascade model and a frank list of barriers before clinic use.
pmc-13435662:
Tian and co-authors chart which symptoms travel together after lung cancer surgery. Their 2026 longitudinal study follows 205 patients who had lung cancer resected, measuring symptoms with a standard inventory at twenty-four hours and three months. Statistical clustering extracted symptom groups, regression hunted each cluster's risk factors, and network analysis identified the core symptoms holding the web together.

At one day after surgery, pain, fatigue, disturbed sleep, breathlessness, and lost appetite were most prevalent; fatigue, breathlessness, and sleep problems persisted at three months. Five clusters emerged, spanning digestive, emotional, cancer-related, respiratory, and autonomic groupings. Fatigue stood out as the network's core symptom by strength centrality, the node whose relief might cascade widest. The authors argue postoperative care should target core and bridging symptoms rather than chasing each complaint separately.
pmc-13436062:
Madison Blake and coauthors test whether retuned illness weights predict death better for autistic older adults in 2026. Hospital claims for 2,829 Medicare patients aged sixty five and up span 2021 to 2023. A learning search reweighted the twelve Charlson illness items to fit this group.

Standard weights predicted thirty day death poorly, and retuned weights did no better. Both scores landed near the same modest accuracy for one year death as well. Weight tweaks alone thus miss what drives risk in this group. Missing illness items may matter more than weights do. The authors call for a purpose built risk index.
pmc-13436662:
Christian Angelo I Ventura, Ava D Cabanilla, and Edward E Denton comment on racial gaps in wait for a clinician with cardiac chest pain in 2026. The study under discussion found door to clinician times of 18.2 versus 14.9 minutes across groups, with an adjusted ratio of 1.22. Triage level, age, sex, and vitals were counted in that math.

The letter urges capture of language preference and interpreter use in future work. Interpreter waits at triage may drive part of the gap through system design. Triage level itself may carry the gap rather than merely confound it. Asian and Hispanic patients cluster at mid level triage in the data. Fixes differ by mechanism, the authors stress.
pmc-13437962:
Zelin Hao and colleagues sequenced the full genomes of tuberculosis bacteria from Kashi, Xinjiang patients, to map drug resistance and teach a computer to predict it. Resistance slows TB control because lab tests take weeks. Their 2026 study gathered 160 isolates from confirmed lung TB cases over five years, read their genomes against a reference strain, and matched results with standard drug tests.

About thirty-nine percent of isolates were fully sensitive, forty-two percent resisted one drug, and eighteen percent resisted several, a few at the extreme end. Resistance centered on the classic first-line drugs. Family trees showed resistant strains clustering, with multi-drug cases enriched in the Beijing lineage. A random forest model predicted resistance to three key drugs with strong accuracy, leaning on those mutations. The authors argue genome reading plus readable machine learning could speed resistance checks in high-burden clinics.
pmc-13438562: A 2026 correction in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences repairs errors in a study of how paramyxoviruses enter cells by gripping sugar chains. The notice is a correction only. One error sat in a figure mislabeling the genes deleted in one engineered cell line, swapping two names for the correct pair. The author contributions footnote was also wrong, and it is reprinted in full. The corrected figure and legend appear with the notice, and the paper is updated. The study's data and conclusions are not revisited.
pmc-13441962:
Wen-Zhuan Huang and colleagues build a trait-based frame for how mosses and their kin handle heavy metal pollution, reviewing the field in 2026. Metals do not degrade, so contamination lingers and builds up through the wild. Bryophytes are champion metal sponges with a long record as living sensors, yet research on them is scattered. The review links plant traits, from surface chemistry to growth habit, with metal capture, body responses, and ecological roles.

Defence layers include trapping metals outside cells, detoxifying them inside, redox buffering, and metabolic rewiring, with partner microbes weighed carefully for proven versus plausible help. Applied chapters grade bryophytes as readable biomonitors and as living stabilisers or engineered absorbers at spoiled sites. Named weaknesses include taxonomic bias toward a few species and thin field validation. The authors offer directional, testable expectations rather than universal prediction formulas.
pmc-13442662:
Kang Liu and colleagues review fast-track recovery plans for children with broken bones or sports harm in a 2026 paper. Such plans, called ERAS, are proven in adult surgery but still new in child trauma care. The review pulls what is known on child fractures, with a close look at hand breaks and sports wounds.

Core parts span pain care with mixed drugs, low-cut surgery, early movement, and strong family roles. Proof so far hints at faster rehab, better life quality, and lower costs for young patients. Yet child-fit standard plans still lack firm shape, and proof stays thin next to adult work. The authors call for child-specific trials and joint work across care teams. They frame family engagement as a core drug-free tool that child plans can lean on now.
pmc-13442862:
Mustafa Kurban and colleagues present a 2026 computational screening of how single-atom dopants change gas binding on tiny anatase particles, a material of interest for hydrogen storage and catalysis. The team swapped one surface titanium atom at a time for ten different metals, then modeled adsorption with quantum calculations, thermodynamic models, and interpretable machine learning.

Most dopants kept binding in molecular form, while iron showed early signs of splitting the molecule, and binding strengths spanned a useful tuning range. Niobium and zirconium gave the most balanced uptake and release, tin sat near the edge of viability, and hafnium and molybdenum bound more strongly but less evenly. The workflow offers a lean, explainable route to picking dopant chemistry before any lab synthesis begins.
pmc-13444262:
Nicole Rose Lukesh and colleagues load B cells with antigen grains to teach immune tolerance in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis in a 2026 study. Near a million people in the United States live with the disease, and stock drugs mute all immunity without cure. Their grains, built from a sugar polymer, carry a myelin bit, MOG35-55.

Grains cling to B cell surfaces and coax them to show the bit in a calming way, with more IL-10 and display marks. Sick mice dosed late with grain-loaded B cells recovered to a striking degree in the report. Brain and cord swelling fell, while fired-up dendritic cells and macrophages eased. The authors pitch B-cell tolerance as a scalpel beside today's blunt drugs.
pmc-13445362:
Marcela Koudelková and colleagues report the first results of a nationwide organized prostate cancer screening pilot in the Czech Republic, published in 2026. The country moved away from scattered, unplanned testing toward a set program run through primary care. Men aged fifty to sixty-nine form the target group, offered testing by their own doctors during routine visits.

Early results show wider use of the blood test for prostate markers and closer fit with guideline steps, among them more MRI scans before biopsy. The authors call the shift workable at national scale, a first such population check in Central Europe. They caution that effects on cancer found, health outcomes, and use in lands with letter-based invites still need study.
pmc-13445662:
Christopher Dugan and coauthors present a 2026 simulation study warning that unreported frailty imbalance can distort intensive care trial results. Using records from 6,968 intensive care patients, the team simulated hundreds of two-arm trials at sizes from 100 to 1,000 patients per arm under simple and block randomization.

Frailty imbalance alone produced mortality gaps of at least 2 percent in 36 percent of small trials. The share fell to 9 percent at 400 patients per arm, while 5 percent gaps nearly vanished at larger sizes. Even balancing frail versus non-frail splits left ordinal imbalance that could still shift mortality. Trials should report full frailty distributions and account for frailty in design and analysis.
pmc-13445862:
Richard Kimera and colleagues present a 2026 multilingual question-answer data set for maternal health in East African languages, where language gaps block mothers from health information. Built at two Western Uganda facilities from 150 mothers and providers, the corpus holds 3,694 pairs in English, Luganda, Runyankore, and Swahili.

Certified linguists ran forward-backward translation, and independent clinicians validated content, covering core maternal health domains. The resource lets developers fine-tune language models and conversational tools for low-resource settings. Culturally grounded AI for maternal care gains a foundation, though field deployment must test real-world use.
pmc-13446262:
Muhammad H. A. Saleh and colleagues test three ways to fix a collagen sheet over a bone graft in jaw ridge defects, in a 2026 study on cadaver heads. Eighteen sites in six heads received grafts of cow bone mineral under a membrane, held by nothing, by stitches to the lining, or by titanium pins. Scans before and after flap closing measured how much graft slipped.

Pins near froze the graft in place and kept about eight in ten parts of its volume, the best hold of the three. Stitches kept about seven in ten, while no fixing kept under half and let the ridge slump most. The authors say unfixed membranes should be skipped in open defects, since even a loose, tension-free close shifts the graft.
pmc-13446562:
Namrata Pramod Kulkarni and colleagues build a fruit fly model of a rare ALS form, ALS8, and pin its brain inflammation on a gene switch in glial cells, in a 2026 study. The model carries the same fault, in the VAPB gene, that causes the human disease. Flies aged with worsening movement and shorter lives, much like the human course.

Gene reads across the brain showed low-grade firing of several immune paths that grew with age, centered in glia, the brain's support cells. The fly form of the Fos switch, called Kayak, held that firing in check. Boosting Kayak in glia cooled inflammation and eased movement, while muting it sped decline. The team casts glial inflammation as a driver worth targeting in this ALS form.
pmc-13447062:
Tong Liu and colleagues hunt gene data for membrane proteins that could serve as blood marks for type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 computing and bench study. Membrane proteins relay insulin signals, so their faults sit close to the disease. The team screened unlike gene activity between patients and controls, then let three learning methods pick the hubs.

Two genes survived every filter: ICAM1 and EZR, the second coding ezrin, a protein that links membrane to cell skeleton. A model built on the pair sorted patients with strong accuracy. Fat-fed cell models and diabetic mice both raised the pair's output, and ezrin was caught holding the insulin receptor in cell tests. Silencing work followed, which the authors offer as a base for a clinic test.
pmc-13447362:
Wai Yee Choon and fellow editors open a third 2026 volume on patient-generated real-world data for medicine policy. Trials alone leave gaps on long-term outcomes, mixed illnesses and lived experience that routine data can fill.

Seventeen articles in the collection span study design with routine data, patient subgroup work, outcome measures rooted in patient experience, registry links and stakeholder teamwork. Patient-reported outcomes and preference data now appear regularly inside regulatory and assessment submissions, the editors note. Earlier volumes started this discussion on turning abundant routine data into decisions that improve care. Patient-centred methods across the full medicine life cycle form the shared thread here.
pmc-13447462:
Sarama Shehmir and Rasha Kashef introduce a 2026 automated red-teaming framework for testing large language model recommenders, whose usual defenses face only a few hand-written attacks. Their adaptive loop creates varied hostile prompts spanning sixteen attack classes, scores them by ranking distortion, and feeds successes back into defense hardening.

Against RoLLMRec, attack success reached 42 to 52 percent across the three benchmarks, far above static and paraphrase baselines. Hardening cut vulnerability by 56 to 74 percent while holding false positives at or below 1 percent, with the prompt shield contributing most. The public attack corpus supports reproducible benchmarking.
pmc-13448662:
Younes Aminpour and coauthors test a 2026 plan for adding freedom to pumped watering networks in Iran without costly pipes rebuilds. Using water-flow mock and a supply freedom index, the team tested limited on-demand running in two rotating drip networks, the gravity-fed Ziviyeh and pump-supplied Lali systems.

Under limited on-demand running, shortfalls fell below 2 percent of hydrants within freedom limits while steadiness held. The approach offers a workable stepping-stone upgrade for water-scarce, cash-strapped systems.
pmc-13449062:
Run Xu and colleagues review in 2026 how magnetic resonance imaging can reveal the molecular subtype of a breast cancer without a tissue sample. pmc-13455262:

pmc-13463762:

pmc-13464762:

pmc-13465162:

pmc-13465962:

pmc-13466862:

pmc-13468562:

pmc-13469062:

pmc-13469262:

pmc-13469862:

pmc-13470062:

pmc-13470362:

pmc-13471462:

pmc-13471562:

pmc-13472562:

pmc-13473062:

pmc-13473462:

pmc-13474162:

pmc-13474762:

pmc-13474862:

pmc-13475062:

pmc-13476262:

pmc-13476962:

pmc-13478862:

pmc-13479462:

pmc-13479562:

pmc-13479862:

pmc-13479962:

pmc-13480062:

pmc-13480262:

pmc-13482362:

pmc-13483462:

pmc-13483562:

pmc-13483662:

pmc-13483862:

pmc-13487962:

pmc-13489762:

pmc-13489962:

pmc-13490462:

pmc-13491062:

pmc-13491862:

pmc-13492362:

pmc-13492862:

pmc-13495162:

In interviews, people tied shifting rains and heat to failing crops and to more insect-borne and water-borne illness. Most respondents had lived in their settlement for over a decade, so the strain is chronic rather than passing. The authors urge community disaster readiness, climate-tough farming, and better water and sanitation systems to build resilience in the camps.
pmc-13495262:
Jinfu Xu, Jing Cai, and Liying Yao examine, in a 2026 study, how home- and community-based services shape life satisfaction among older adults in China. As families shrink, such services have become a core part of elder care, yet how they mix with family and social ties was little explored. The team used a 2023 national aging survey and applied several methods to strip out selection bias.

Across all elders, service use showed no clear main effect on satisfaction. Among rural elders alone, it did lift satisfaction. Emotional ties amplified the service gain, while hands-on help networks weakened it, as if family help and formal help substitute for each other. Hands-on networks were the strongest shield for frail and low-income elders on their own. Emotional ties helped city elders yet hurt rural ones, a split the authors say policy must respect rather than assume family care always rules.
pmc-13499362:
Ka Yee Chaw, Jamie Zhi Guo Ong, and Murtaza Karimjee Salem examine in 2026 whether anaemia measured after vascular surgery predicts early problems better than anaemia measured before surgery. Low blood counts are common in these patients, who are often older and frail. Their review of records covered inpatients at a large teaching hospital trust in Nottingham, United Kingdom, operated on between July and October 2024, with blood counts before and after surgery.

After exclusions, 196 patients remained, and four in five met the combined bad-outcome measure of long stay, unplanned readmission, or death within 30 days. Blood counts fell on average after surgery, and moderate anaemia became far more common. Models built on post-surgery anaemia severity performed best among the approaches compared, which the authors present as a practical risk signal for ward teams planning follow-up.
pmc-13500862:
Lusha Li and others report a rare Rosai-Dorfman disease case presenting as blood sugar illness insipidus with master gland stalk involvement. In 2026, the Chinese-language case concerns a thirty-eight-year-old man whose excessive thirst and urination began fifteen years earlier. His illness progressed to complete master gland failure, with thickened stalk, dural nodules, bone destruction, lung changes, and urinary involvement. Biopsy of the stalk showed the finding.

Testing revealed a BRAF V600E mutation, prompting aimed therapy with dabrafenib plus hormone replacement. After eight months, stalk thickening improved, dural nodules disappeared, and quality of life rose clearly. The look-back analysis helps doctors work through the hard differential finding of a thickened master gland stalk.
pmc-13501562:
Kexin Yuan leads a fourteen-author team reporting a 2026 cohort study of brain arteriovenous malformations in older patients, tangled vessel clusters that can bleed inside the brain. The study drew 94 patients aged 60 or older from the multicentre MATCH registry, covering care between August 2011 and December 2021. Management fell into six groups, from watchful conservative care to surgical removal, embolization, focused radiosurgery, and combinations. Outcomes tracked the yearly bleeding rate and functional status on the modified Rankin Scale.

Median age was about 65 years, and most patients began with mild disability. No clear group differences emerged in complications around treatment or in discharge function scores, though small event numbers limit certainty. During follow-up, 9.57 percent of patients bled, with higher rates after embolization and radiosurgery. Resection-based treatment achieved the highest rates of complete malformation closure. The authors advise individualized choices and close follow-up for this age group.
pmc-13501662:
Irmak Gezginer leads an eleven-author team with a 2026 brain stimulation study in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Triple-transgenic mice underwent resting-state functional MRI after single and repeated sessions of transcranial pulse stimulation, a low-intensity technique delivering brief mechanical pulses to the brain. The team measured network connectivity and how signal power spread across bands. Separate animals took a novel object test to gauge exploring and short-term memory after repeated pulses or a sham procedure.

Diseased mice showed widespread connection loss and a shift of activity from the slowest band, slow-5, toward slow-4 bands. The pulses raised low-band power, rebalanced that slow-5 to slow-4 split, and strengthened network coherence, especially in cingulate, insular, piriform, and striatal regions. Effects built up with repeated trains and lasted up to five days. Treated mice also kept exploring objects instead of declining like the sham group.
pmc-13501762:
Arthur Shiyovich leads a twenty-two-author team reporting a 2026 registry study of coronary CT angiography in patients with and without diabetes. The Mass General Brigham registry covered 22,377 people scanned at two centres between 2006 and 2024, excluding anyone with prior coronary disease, advanced kidney disease, or cancer. Diabetes, defined by diagnosis codes or raised haemoglobin A1c, affected 3,245 patients, or 14.5 percent. Scans were graded as no disease, nonobstructive narrowing, or obstructive narrowing of at least half the vessel.

Over a median six years, the combined outcome of cardiovascular death or heart attack struck 7.8 percent of patients with diabetes against 3.1 percent of the others. Obstructive disease appeared in 33 percent of the diabetes group versus 19 percent without it, and clean scans were far rarer there. After adjustment, obstructive disease roughly tripled risk in both groups, with hazard ratios near three in each. Event rates climbed with severity at every step.
pmc-13503462:
Havabulut and colleagues test whether dexpanthenol, a vitamin B5 relative used in skin repair, can shield kidneys from imaging dye. Contrast dye injected for scans occasionally triggers kidney failure, especially in vulnerable patients, and no reliable preventive drug exists. In their 2026 rat study, thirty-two animals were split into four groups: untreated, dye alone, dye plus dexpanthenol for three days, and dexpanthenol alone. Kidneys were then scored for damage, oxidation, inflammation, and cell-death gene activity.

The dye alone did clear harm, raising oxidation measures, damaging kidney tissue visibly, and switching on inflammatory and death-promoting genes while silencing protective ones in the reported assays. Dexpanthenol treatment partly reversed each of those shifts, preserved the kidney's architecture, and pulled blood markers back toward control values. The benefit ran through a pathway involving SIRT1, a longevity-linked regulator, and the p53 death switch.
pmc-13505162:
Muhammad Hamza and co-authors compared depression screening results between adults with type 2 diabetes and adults without it. Their study ran from August 2025 to April 2026 and enrolled 114 people, split evenly between the two groups. Everyone completed the nine-item PHQ-9 questionnaire, and a score of ten or more counted as significant depression.

About sixty-one percent of the diabetes group screened positive, against about thirty-three percent of the comparison group. Depression clustered most in the late forties age band and was linked with gender and with how long diabetes had lasted. The spread of severity levels, though, did not differ clearly between groups. The authors conclude that depressive symptoms are far more common among their diabetic patients, a finding that supports routine mood screening inside diabetes care.
pmc-13507262:
Lei Zhou leads a 2026 team that links the protein RanBP3 to protection against tracheobronchial tuberculosis, a form of TB infecting the windpipe and airways. In this disease, infected macrophages often die by pyroptosis, a fiery death that spreads inflammation and helps bacteria escape. RanBP3 levels fell in diseased airway tissue.

Raising RanBP3 in mouse macrophages boosted mitophagy, the disposal of worn mitochondria, and calmed pyroptosis while cutting bacterial survival. RanBP3 frees the enzyme SIRT1 from its holder CCAR2, and freed SIRT1 switches on the cleanup. Blocking SIRT1 erased the benefit in animals. The axis offers a fresh drug target for airway TB.
pmc-13508262:
Haixiang Zhang and four co-authors build an AI system that reads both lung CT images and written scan reports to aid lung cancer diagnosis, in 2026 work. Single-source tools miss details that the other source carries, and simply joining the two data streams aligns poorly. Their data covered 5,847 people seen from 2020 to 2025, including cancer cases, healthy controls, and people with lung nodules. Separate deep learning models first turned images and text into feature sets. Each source then made its own diagnosis call.

A weighting method based on information entropy blended the two calls, trusting the more certain source more in each case. On the clinical test set, the blended system reached accuracy above nine in ten cases. The authors report the blend beat single-source models and common joining methods. They present it as decision support that could even out diagnosis quality where expert readers are scarce.
pmc-13508462:
Sinead Prince and five co-authors ask whether artificial intelligence may ethically help decide when medical treatment has become futile, in a 2026 analysis. Futility judgments are disputed in concept, evidence, and ethics, yet wards must still settle them case by case. The team used a critical narrative review in three steps. They mapped the main positions in the futility debate, surveyed real and possible medical AI tools, and then weighed the ethics with standard principles like autonomy, benefit, harm avoidance, and fairness.

One risk stood out: AI can bake in self-fulfilling prophecies, learning from outcomes that past pessimism itself caused. Bias in training data could also tilt life-and-death calls unfairly. Under the right guardrails, though, the authors find AI could help prevent or settle futility disputes. Careful integration and regulation are the conditions they attach. The piece gives hospitals and lawmakers a map of a sensitive frontier.
pmc-13508562:
Sven Jonsson and William Beckworth report a 60-year-old woman with chronic lung disease whose breathing eased on an inhaled fatty compound, in a 2026 case report. Her COPD included emphysema of the central lobes, which destroys air sacs and traps air. Standard inhalers had left her breathless and limited in exercise. She received the compound, a potassium form of conjugated linoleic acid, through a nebulizer for two months. Symptom scores, breathlessness grades, and a six-minute walk test were tracked, along with lung function tests.

Her symptom score fell from 23 to 7, a large improvement on that scale. Her breathlessness grade dropped from two to zero, and effort scores after exertion improved strongly. Lung flow measures inched up without a response to a reliever drug. The authors urge controlled trials, and note that one lung volume figure needs checking with fuller methods.
pmc-13509362:
Zafeiris Tsinaris leads an eleven-author team reporting drug resistance in bacteria from urine samples of children treated at a large hospital in northern Greece, in 2026 work. The group reviewed lab records from 2015 to September 2025, covering 776 isolates in total. Most were Escherichia coli, with smaller shares of Klebsiella pneumoniae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Escherichia coli stayed sensitive to a few drugs, notably nitrofurantoin and amikacin, yet resisted ampicillin in over half of cases. Klebsiella carried the heaviest burden, with high resistance to a common class of strong antibiotics and frequent signs of broader drug resistance. Pseudomonas kept low resistance to key drugs used against it. The authors say local records like these should guide which drugs doctors pick first for children with urine infections.
pmc-13509562:
Lucas J. Rooney and Laura J. Claxton examine whether fine motor skills go together with early thinking skills in two-year-old children, in a 2026 study. Thirty-three children aged twenty-five to thirty-five months completed standard tasks covering grasping and joining what the eyes see with what the hands do. Each child also took a standard test of executive function, the mental skills used to guide behavior toward a goal.

Better fine motor scores went with stronger executive function scores across the group. When age was taken into account, the eye-hand joining skill kept its link while grasping alone did not. A combined analysis then found both skills helped predict executive function beyond age alone. The authors suggest that supporting hand skills in toddlers may bring wider gains for early thinking, though the study only shows a link, not a cause.
pmc-13511062:
Umm E. Habiba and six co-authors map which brain regions near-infrared light studies target in children with developmental and nerve disorders, in a 2026 review. The portable method shines light through the scalp to track blood changes that reflect brain activity, and its use in young patients is growing. The team searched five databases for studies from 2015 to 2025 and kept 72 that met standard review rules.

The front decision-making region of the brain appeared in work on all five conditions covered: autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, cerebral palsy, oxygen-starved brain injury at birth, and epilepsy. Side and top regions appeared in four of the five. Each condition also leaned toward regions matching its own features, such as social brain networks in autism and movement areas in cerebral palsy. Across conditions, studies reported altered front activity, broken connections, and backup responses in the brain.
pmc-13512662:
Sus Sola Corazon, Maria Stoltze Fray, Gitte Saldern Schroeder, Carina Wedell Andersen, and Stine Bekke-Hansen evaluate a nature-based program for young adults living with advanced cancer, in 2026 work. Young patients face heavy psychological and existential strain yet are poorly served by standard rehabilitation and palliative offers built for older groups. Four groups in a row joined a six-week program with an overnight camp in nature plus three outdoor sessions, with quality of life scored before and after each cycle.

Mixed methods paired the scores with interviews on lived experience. Gains appeared most clearly in the moment: time outdoors brought relief from distress, room to breathe, and peer contact with others in the same rare situation. The authors call the approach nature-based rehabilitative palliation and argue it can sit beside existing services. Researchers, they add, must learn to catch situational benefits that broad quality scores can miss.
pmc-13514262:
Enas N. Morgan and co-authors test whether vitamin C can shield the rat hippocampus from harm caused by monosodium glutamate, the flavor enhancer coded E621, in 2026 work. Forty adult male rats split into four groups: plain control, vitamin alone, glutamate alone, and both together, with daily injections for thirty days. Brain tissue was stained for cell structure and for three markers covering scar-like support cell growth, synaptic protein, and a cell death enzyme, plus chemical measures of oxidative stress.

Glutamate alone produced shrunken, damaged granular cells and hollow spaces in the memory region, with all three markers strongly raised and oxidative balance tipped toward damage. Giving vitamin C alongside preserved much of the normal cell shape and eased the marker surge. The authors read vitamin C as a partial neuroprotective partner against additive-driven brain injury in this rat model.
pmc-13515962:
Dhaffouli and colleagues built an electrochemical sensor in 2026 to measure dopamine, a brain chemical whose levels shift in disorders such as Parkinson's disease and depression. Their sensing layer mixes reduced graphene oxide, magnetic nanoparticles coated with polypyrrole, and a Nafion film on one electrode. Each part adds current flow, surface area, or shielding against other substances.

Using differential pulse voltammetry, a sensitive current reading method, the sensor reached a detection limit of 5.4 nanomoles per liter, a trace level, and common interferents barely disturbed it, among them ascorbic acid, uric acid, and acetaminophen. Repeat runs varied by only about eight percent, showing the device gives steady, consistent results. Tested on real urine and blood samples, it found between seventy-five and one hundred sixteen percent of the dopamine present. The authors present it as a useful tool for clinical dopamine testing.
pmc-13517062:
Yinjian Ji leads a ten-author team building an eye-drop gel that keeps an anti-vessel drug on the cornea in a 2026 formulation study. Unwanted blood vessels growing into the cornea cause major vision loss, yet drops wash away in tears within minutes. The team loaded luteolin, a plant compound that blocks vessel growth, into fatty nanocarriers. They then set those carriers in a gel that thickens on contact with tear fluid's ions and acidity.

The finished particles measured about twenty-five nanometres, and the gel's thickness jumped forty-five fold in simulated tears. In rabbits, drug levels in the cornea ran more than two and a half times higher than with carriers alone. In mice with alkali-burned corneas, the gel curbed vessel growth as well as a steroid drop and lowered two growth signals. Ji's team offers it as a gentle, drop-based option.
pmc-13519462:
Sabiha Islam and colleagues reviewed 55 ectopic pregnancy cases treated during 2022 at a university obstetrics unit in Dhaka. Published in 2026, the retrospective study used urine pregnancy tests and a hormone blood assay for early diagnosis, with ultrasound confirming each case. In an ectopic pregnancy the embryo implants outside the womb, most often in a fallopian tube, where rupture can threaten life.

The authors stress full risk-factor checks and fast diagnosis to protect fertility and cut death and illness. Catching unruptured cases early, especially at smaller outlying centers, allows timely referral and treatment before rupture. Readers get a compact case for awareness drives and referral pathways that move patients to equipped care without delay.
pmc-13520262:
Hao Li leads a seven-author pan-cancer analysis in 2026 of MEN1, the gene behind an inherited tumor syndrome, asking how its activity tracks with patient outcomes and immune surroundings across cancers. Public multi-omics databases and protein atlas staining profiles supplied the data.

MEN1 appeared in all normal tissues yet ran higher in many tumors, where elevation tracked with worse survival and carried strong diagnostic value. High levels also accompanied greater tumor mutation burden. Activity correlated with immune checkpoint genes and shifting immune cell infiltration. Pathway analysis tied MEN1 to cell cycle progression, DNA damage response, and growth signaling. Li and colleagues propose it as a prognostic marker and possible treatment target.
pmc-13520362:
Takuya Minamishima and colleagues explore in 2026 why some kidney patients respond poorly to a newer anaemia drug class that mimics low-oxygen signalling. Poor nutrition was suspected, since malnutrition and anaemia often travel together in chronic kidney disease.

Records from one centre covered patients with and without dialysis who received these drugs. A nutrition score called CONUT tracked closely with a resistance index, with moderate to severe malnutrition marking high resistance. In the subgroup taking daprodustat, the link held after adjustment. The authors suggest checking nutrition before raising doses, since high resistance raises cost and safety worries.
pmc-13520562:
B. Roshan Arbaaz and colleagues weigh in 2026 whether disease around dental implants starts mainly from bacterial film or from prosthetic design flaws such as poor crown angles and leftover cement. Framing matters, since prevention differs under each view.

Evidence synthesis across microbiology, mechanics and prosthetics finds film-driven inflammation central to disease onset, with a foreign-body reaction possibly adding bone loss. Load overload, trapped cement and wide crown angles did not start disease alone, yet sped progression once inflammation existed. Past gum disease, smoking and systemic illness complete a multi-factor picture. Planning should treat crown design as a health choice, not only a cosmetic one.
pmc-13522362:
Gabriel Henrique Simoni and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing two treatments for small visible leg veins. One approach combines laser treatment with cooling and an injected solution, while the other uses injection alone. The review searched major medical databases through February 2025 for studies in adults with thread veins or slightly larger reticular veins.

Six studies covering 833 patients were pooled, with three giving direct comparisons. The combined laser approach was linked to less matting, fewer tiny clots, and less bruising than injection alone, while differences for darkened skin and skin death were unclear. Clearance of the treated vessels was high, near ninety-one percent in single-group data, and satisfaction was also high.
pmc-13522862:
Brownlee and colleagues reported in 2026 for Nutrition North, a coalition of nutrition experts across the North of England, on the region's deep health and diet gaps. The North, home to nearly sixteen million people, sees shorter lives and more disease than the rest of England, with deprivation a major driver. National survey data show diet quality and nutrient status are worst in the poorest households.

Poor diet is named the world's leading avoidable driver of illness and early death. The coalition sets three tasks: advocacy for better food and health, support for clinical nutrition services, and tighter links between universities and the food sector. The authors argue that coordinated regional action gives the North its best route to closing the gap.
pmc-13523262:
Romesa Qazi and co-authors report early prenatal detection of a severe brain malformation in Pakistan in a 2026 case report. A thirty-four-year-old woman with no known risk exposures attended her twelve-week scan. Ultrasound showed a single fetus with a missing dividing membrane in the brain, fused deep brain structures, one large rear fluid space, and facial anomalies. The picture pointed to alobar holoprosencephaly, the most severe form of failed brain separation.

Follow-up ultrasound confirmed the fused brain portions and showed excess amniotic fluid. The fetus died in the womb at seven months of gestation. The authors stress that prompt imaging at the first scan enabled early diagnosis, better antenatal counseling, and informed family planning, given the poor prognosis. They add the rare case to the documented record for future comparison.
pmc-13523362:
Xingyu Duan and co-authors develop a radiation-free scoliosis screen from photographs of the bare back in a 2026 study. Six hundred adolescents, half with scoliosis and half without spinal disease, were drawn from two hospitals over four years. Their back images were enlarged by augmentation, and a new deep learning network was compared with four established image models and with three clinicians of differing seniority.
