All five models performed well, with the proposed network best on accuracy, precision, recall, and combined score. Its discrimination fell between the senior and mid-level physicians, beating the junior physician, while working far faster than any clinician. The authors present image-based screening as an efficient option for large-scale adolescent scoliosis checks where X-ray capacity or radiation concerns limit current practice.
pmc-13523462:
Ahmet Ozturk, writing alone in 2026, compares two ways of counting childhood disability in Türkiye and shows that the method chosen changes the answer sharply. One approach relies on medically documented impairments. The other uses parent reports of functional limits from the Washington Group and UNICEF Child Functioning Module, which reflects a social model of disability.

Data came from Türkiye's 2022 child survey, covering 14,705 children aged 0 to 17 in 9,010 households. Medical records gave a prevalence of 2 percent, while the functional module gave 14.1 percent. Functional answers grouped into physical, sensory, and cognitive domains, social domains, and emotional domains, each with distinct social patterns. Children with medical reports were three times more likely to show depression or anxiety symptoms. Ozturk argues that using both measures gives fairer policy and resource decisions.
pmc-13525062:
Walaa Yehia Abdelzaher and others test, in a 2026 rat study, whether the diabetes drug imeglimin protects the gut when blood flow returns after a blockage. This ischemia-reperfusion injury brings oxidative stress, inflammation, and cell death. Imeglimin had shown it protects cells through mitochondria, so the team probed its action in gut tissue.

Thirty-two male Wistar rats were split into sham, drug only, injury, and drug plus injury groups. Injury raised damage markers, an inflammasome protein, a cell death enzyme, inflammatory gene action, and a key inflammatory switch, while antioxidant stores and a helpful energy sensor fell. Every metric got better with imeglimin treatment. The authors credit the effect to antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-apoptotic actions routed through the AMPK energy pathway, which restrained inflammasome signaling.
pmc-13526862:
Meng and colleagues report a 2026 optical computing chip built to give artificial intelligence hardware far more speed without the energy costs of standard electronics. Their optical processing unit packs four analog light-based cores onto one chip and runs 124 channels of tasks at the same time.

The chip reached about 65 trillion operations per second, a pace the authors describe with the measure TOPS. Built into a hybrid light-and-electronics neural network, it classified handwritten digits from the MNIST test set with about 95 percent accuracy. That score beat the single-core version by roughly nine percent, a gain the team credits to fusing features from four kernels at once. The design points toward larger many-core optical systems.
pmc-13527062:
Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 study on acceptor molecules for organic solar cells. Organic solar cells turn light into power with carbon-based films. Cutting energy waste while keeping charge flow strong has been hard to do both ways. The team built four acceptor variants, tuning bulk and chlorine placement stepwise.

A nitrogen-rich core kept wasted energy unusually low across the series. Added chlorine and looser backbones reshaped how molecules packed together. Better packing sped the splitting of light-born charges in the films. The best variant, Z4, reached a power conversion of about 20 percent. Its voltage stayed high at the same time, a rare pairing. Low loss plus high power is the pairing makers chase hardest.
pmc-13527962:
Deborah A. Dadson and six colleagues review in 2026 what research says about aging in Ghana. Following standard review guidelines, they gathered peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025. The review covers population trends, health problems of older adults, support systems, and unmet needs, with an eye toward age-friendly policy.

Four themes emerged: health care use, health status, social support, and policy. Older adults with strong family and community support felt better and used health services more. They also reported less loneliness. Unmet needs included food insecurity, money strain, and help with daily tasks. Many lived with several chronic conditions and physical limits. The authors call for coordinated action on health access, social inclusion, and community engagement.
pmc-13528062:
Jinchun Ye and six colleagues report a fatal adult case of a rare urea cycle disorder in a 2026 paper. The missing enzyme, called CPS1, normally clears ammonia from the blood. A 34-year-old man arrived after two days of fatigue that slid into coma. He had vomited and had convulsions, plus a past history of epilepsy. His coma score was five of fifteen.

Blood ammonia was extremely high at about 598 micromoles per liter. Brain scans showed diffuse swelling. Gene testing found three variants in the CPS1 gene, two of them new. Liver and kidney tests looked normal, which can mislead doctors. Despite ammonia-lowering care, he died on day nine. The authors urge checking ammonia in adults with unexplained coma. Early treatment and transplant review may save others, they say.
pmc-13528162:
Manyang Zhang, Fuhan Li, and Fanli Meng probe how a plant fungus builds pressure to break into leaves in a 2026 study. The fungus causes poplar anthracnose. It forms a dome cell called an appressorium. Pressure inside the dome drives a peg through the leaf skin. The team profiled chemicals in the dome at several growth stages.

Thirty-nine chemicals shifted with pressure building. They spanned amino acids, fats, sugars, and organic acids. Four chemical routes stood out. Fat-like phospholipid handling looked central to pressure gain. Three blocker drugs against that route were tested. Neomycin hit the fungus hardest and controlled the leaf disease well. The authors name phospholipid handling as a weak point. Blocking it could become a greener spray strategy, they suggest.
pmc-13529662:
Pouya Bohlol and three colleagues pair an electronic nose with camera vision to name plant leaves in a 2026 study. Twenty-six species were gathered over two years in varied conditions. The nose, with eight gas sensors, logged 15,600 readings. Photos were boosted to 156,000 samples by augmentation. Several learning methods were tuned on each stream.

A neighbor-based method read scent best, at ninety-seven percent accuracy in five milliseconds. A deep vision network named InceptionV3 read images best, at ninety-nine percent. Its answers took eight milliseconds. Fusing both streams pushed accuracy to 99.8 percent in ten milliseconds. The authors say two senses beat one for tough field calls. Such fusion could serve smart farming and plant protection. Rare species tracking is one use they name.
pmc-13530262:
Ravi Renuka Devi and co-authors grow zinc oxide nano thin films in 2026 with help from rice extract, aiming at a greener antibacterial coating. Rice extract acted as a capping agent that steers crystal growth. Films with and without the extract went through diffraction, microscopy, chemical, and light testing.

Extract-treated films favored a different crystal face and formed even needle-like shapes at the highest extract level. The light energy gap narrowed slightly with treatment. Bacteria tests against two common species showed widening clear zones as rice content rose, with the strongest film performing best against both germs.
pmc-13530762:
Bui and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 10, a study of non-tobacco nicotine dependence and surgical outcomes after Achilles tendon repair. The dependence covered e-cigarettes, vaping devices, and nicotine pouches. The Achilles heals on a fragile blood supply, and nicotine's harm from smoking was known; the newer products were not.

Searching a national research network, the team found 25,874 repair patients, then matched the three exposure groups one-to-one at 1,592 patients each. Within ninety days, the non-tobacco nicotine group suffered roughly double the odds of wound splitting and surgical site infection compared with non-users, plus more emergency visits and hospitalizations. Against traditional tobacco users they still fared worse on wounds and infection. At two years their tendons re-ruptured more often than either comparison group's.
pmc-13532762:
Hui-Mei Tsai and colleagues present in 2026 shinyDeepGxP, a web app that predicts surface protein levels from single-cell RNA data. Protein levels shape what immune cells do, yet many datasets record RNA only because paired protein tests cost a lot and are hard to run. The app runs a deep learning model trained on blood cells.

Users upload RNA count tables and get predictions for 224 surface proteins, plus charts that help split cell groups. An explore mode shows which RNA signals drive each protein call and which pathways they touch. Readers without coding skills gain protein-level detail from RNA-only files.
pmc-13533062:
Berfin Vural and Mustafa Kemal Sezginturk describe in 2026 a sensor for TRAP-1, a mitochondrial protein tied to cancer growth and cell survival. Early cancer detection needs cheap tests that can spot tiny amounts of such marks in blood. Their sensor uses a flexible electrode coated to catch the target protein.

Electric measures tracked binding, tuned the settings, and confirmed the build step by step. The sensor worked across a wide range from very low levels and gave steady, repeatable results in real human serum. Readers gain a low-cost design that could support early screening once clinical testing follows.
pmc-13534462:
Gharam A Alharshan and colleagues make in 2026 phosphate glasses doped with erbium oxide and test their structure, electrical traits, and radiation shielding. Such glasses suit many uses, and rare-earth doping can tune their behaviour. Samples were made by melting and rapid cooling at several doping levels.

Checks confirmed a glassy state, and density rose as erbium replaced phosphorus oxide. Low doping tightened the network and lowered electrical response, while higher doping raised it again. One mix gave the best gamma shielding, supporting use in medical and industrial radiation protection.
pmc-13534662:
Xiaoqi Duan and colleagues propose in 2026 a method to predict a transit passenger next station using knowledge graphs with reinforcement learning. Older models use fixed graph shapes and miss shifting links between riders and stations. Their method enriches the learning setting and updates rider-station links together from travel knowledge.

Removal tests and comparisons with classic methods showed clear gains for next-station calls, route calls, and travel distance estimates. The richer shared representation captured complex travel habits more faithfully. Transit planners gain a tool for demand forecasts, service timing, and long-term network planning.
pmc-13535662:
Bing Zhao and colleagues evaluate in 2026 RPL5, a ribosomal protein, in triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive subtype with few treatment options. Tissue from 37 patients and nearby normal tissue was stained for the protein, and public gene datasets added a second check. The team also mapped genes that move together with RPL5.

Staining showed lower RPL5 protein in tumours than in nearby normal tissue, while gene data showed higher levels in this subtype than in other breast cancers. Levels did not track with stage, spread, or survival in this group. Linked genes centred on ribosome building and p53 pathways.
pmc-13536562:
Mary Balogun and Anne Clayson survey in 2026 anxiety, depression, and distress among small and medium business owners in Lagos State, Nigeria. Owners face money uncertainty, long hours, and job insecurity, yet local mental health data were scarce. A structured questionnaire reached 156 registered entrepreneurs with standard mental health scales.

About one in eight reported anxiety or depression, and close to one in five reported distress. Having dependents and high work stress raised distress odds, while good job control protected against all three outcomes. Male owners were less likely to report depression in adjusted models.
pmc-13536762:
Robert Fekete reports a difficult case of IgG4-related disease in a 2026 single-patient account. The condition causes inflammation and scarring across organs and rarely presents as tightening of the sac around the heart with fluid buildup. A previously healthy 45-year-old man developed breathlessness, belly fluid, and leg swelling months after a viral illness affecting hands, feet, and mouth. Large fluid collections around the heart and lungs required drainage.

Steroid treatment helped only while doses stayed high, and dose cuts brought back breathlessness while also causing severe high blood sugar. Surgery to remove the stiffened heart sac finally provided tissue that confirmed the diagnosis, showing dense scarring and characteristic immune cells. A targeted infusion drug then kept the disease in remission. The author stresses tissue proof when blood tests mislead.
pmc-13537462:
Carla Martignoni and colleagues compare two fracture risk tools in the Swiss Osteoporosis Registry in a 2026 analysis of records from 2015 to 2023. The newer tool adds spine density, bone texture, recent falls, steroid dose, and fracture site and timing to the standard tool. Data held 28,708 people, mostly women with an average age near sixty-six years. Ten-year risks for major and hip fractures were calculated both ways.

Most people received higher risk estimates with added factors, with a modest average rise, while about one quarter received lower estimates. Texture and spine measures touched nearly every estimate, yet single falls and recent spine or hip fractures caused the largest personal jumps. Using Swiss treatment cutoffs, many estimates moved up a category. The authors note real shifts in treatment advice.
pmc-13538662:
Jiyin Lai and colleagues built a graph-learning tool that spots which cancer drug pairs work better together. Published in 2026, the tool, DSimSynergy, maps drug likeness from biology and clinic use, then learns drug profiles through graph math. It pairs those profiles with chemical prints and cell-line gene readings to score drug pairs.

Tests on several other sets showed the tool beating current best methods, and checks of its inner workings flagged key genes and pathways behind drug teamwork. Trials on patient and group data showed real clinic promise and traced teamwork to matching pathway networks. By flagging winners early, the tool cuts lab screening costs and guides tailored treatment. Readers get a clear route to better drug pairs for stubborn tumors.
pmc-13540062:
Chongyang Wang and six colleagues review, in a 2026 article, water-rich gel materials designed to help wounds inside the nose heal after surgery or injury. The nasal cavity is acidic, swept by moving mucus, and lined with delicate tissue, so old packing materials often hurt on removal.

The review sorts hydrogels by their building blocks and by how their internal bonds form, including bonds that respond to acidity, heat, or harmful oxygen compounds. Highlighted examples include a self-assembling peptide gel that cut post-surgery sticking in trials, and gels that stay in place for a full day while mopping up irritants. Practical hurdles around matching tissue softness and breakdown speed get close attention.
pmc-13540262:
Yindan Yao and eight colleagues review, in a 2026 hospital study, short-term results of placing a Neuroform EZ stent inside narrowed brain arteries when poor blood flow keeps causing symptoms. Such stenting can help selected patients, yet lesion shape may decide who is harmed.

Sixty-four patients treated between January 2020 and October 2023 were followed for stroke, death, and re-narrowing inside the stent. Technical success was nearly universal, and the thirty-day stroke or death rate was low overall. Every early complication, and nearly half the re-narrowing, clustered in the most complex Mori type C lesions. The authors advise strict selection and caution for that group.
pmc-13540862:
Zhao Zhang and six colleagues catalogue, in a 2026 study, tiny circles of DNA that break free from chromosomes in bermudagrass facing salty conditions. Such extrachromosomal circles help genomes flex under stress, and bermudagrass is planted to reclaim salty land.

Using a circle-focused sequencing method, the team found 1,068 circles spread across all chromosomes, mostly short and poor in one DNA base pairing type. They favoured regions between genes and inside coding stretches. Statistical modelling traced their birth to fragile attachment zones that shatter and get patched into rings. Salt stress enriched circles born from jumping DNA elements, hinting at an adaptive shuffle.
pmc-13542762:
Anina Zuercher and colleagues published a 2026 randomised trial with five-year follow-up on rebuilding bone where an implant leaves the outer jaw wall thin or missing. Patients needing a single-tooth implant with a defect of at least 3 millimetres received guided bone regeneration. The filler was deproteinised bovine bone mineral, given either as loose particles or as a shaped block, each covered by a collagen membrane. Scans measured the outer bone thickness after surgery, at six months, and at five years.

Twenty-two of twenty-four patients completed the five years. Bone thinned over time in both groups, yet the block held its shape far better: at five years its average outer thickness was about 1.36 millimetres against nearly zero for particles. Gum health, bone levels at the implant neck, and survival were similar, with no implant lost. Shaped blocks therefore preserve the jaw's outer contour far longer.
pmc-13543362:
Joanna Nevison de Klerk and colleagues published a 2026 modelling study mapping Culex mosquitoes across England and Wales to prepare for possible West Nile and Usutu virus arrival. Culex pipiens, widespread in Britain, can transmit both viruses, which are spreading northward in Europe. The team built distribution models from the first nationwide structured mosquito surveillance programme, run in 2023 with extra sampling in 2024, separating the pipiens and molestus forms plus Culex torrentium.

One form, pipiens, was predicted far more abundant than the others, concentrated across most of England except the northwest, peaking in eastern and estuary areas. High ground, including most of Wales, held far fewer. Rainfall drove pipiens numbers, while temperature mattered more for molestus, so the forms must be modelled separately. The maps tell surveillance teams where to look first and give planners a base for targeted mosquito control.
pmc-13544862:
Gajewski and colleagues ask how fast the benefit of clot retrieval fades for the severest strokes, those with large cores of already-damaged brain. Six randomised trials proved thrombectomy, threading a device to pull the clot out, beats medicine alone even in these cases, but they enrolled at different speeds. Their 2026 analysis pools the six trials, 1,881 patients, and models how the treatment's advantage on a quality-weighted disability scale shrinks as each trial's typical onset-to-randomisation time grows.

Time eroded benefit with near-certain statistical confidence in the Bayesian model. The absolute advantage slipped below a tenth of the scale's useful range at around ten hours after onset. It fell below a thirtieth at roughly eighteen hours, though the uncertainty bands around both landmarks are wide. The estimates serve to design the next trials.
pmc-13545062:
Hirano, Iwano, and Ohara author a 2026 focused update to Japanese echocardiography guidance, devoted to stress echo performed with the Valsalva maneuver, the strain-against-closed-airway push patients can do on the examination table. The parent 2023 guidance broadened stress echo beyond blocked arteries into valve disease and heart failure. This update argues the Valsalva strain deserves its own chapter, because it is essential for judging diastolic function and for detecting a patent foramen ovale, the flap between the heart's upper chambers.

Timing drives the update: new myosin inhibitor drugs for hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy gained insurance coverage in Japan. Prescribing them properly requires provoking the obstruction they treat, exactly what the Valsalva strain does at the bedside. The guidance standardises how to perform and interpret the strain during stress studies so results are comparable between labs.
pmc-13545362:
Ziv Harel and co-authors wrote in 2026 about whether a woman's kidney function before pregnancy predicts severe illness or death around childbirth. Their letter describes a population study in Ontario, Canada, built from linked health databases covering hospital births from 2009 to 2023. The exposure was serum creatinine, a blood marker of kidney function, measured in the year before conception.

Roughly a quarter of the nearly 1.87 million births in the period had such a measurement, giving a final cohort of 471,242 women. The analysis compared outcomes across creatinine levels, including unusually low as well as high values, using models that adjust for other health factors. The question matters because creatinine thresholds are already used during pregnancy, yet their meaning before conception was unknown.
pmc-13546562:
Jin Wang and co-authors linked in 2026 a copper-related gene, LOXL2, with the stomach bacterium Helicobacter pylori in driving stomach cancer growth. The bacterium is a known cause of the disease, while LOXL2 helps remodel tissue around cells. Gene data analysis first flagged LOXL2 as the standout candidate among copper-linked genes, and tissue tests confirmed it ran high in infected cancers.

In laboratory experiments, extra LOXL2 made cancer cells multiply, move, and invade more, while silencing it slowed them, and exposure to the bacterium amplified the effect. The pair switched on a signaling route that loosens cells from their neighbors, a step toward spread. The authors propose LOXL2 as more than a marker: a working partner in infection-driven cancer.
pmc-13547362:
Li Meng and a large team traced in 2026 where toxic elements in Chongqing's paddy soils come from and how far they travel into rice plants. They sampled 225 soils and 90 rice plants across a rice-growing region of southwestern China and measured eleven elements, from cadmium and arsenic to zinc and selenium. A source-splitting statistical model separated natural background from human inputs.

Natural geology supplied about forty percent of the soil load and farming about thirty-five percent, with industry and irrigation making up most of the rest. Inside the plants, roots trapped cadmium, arsenic, and selenium strongly, while movement into the grain stayed limited for most elements, a natural barrier protecting the food supply. Cadmium moved upward most readily, which the authors flag for monitoring.
pmc-13547662:
Lee, Cho, and Lee test whether back muscle scans can stand in for whole-body muscle checks. Their 2026 paper studies sarcopenia in older Korean women. Sarcopenia means age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Standard assessment uses appendicular lean mass from DXA scans. CT scans of the lower back offer another possible window.

Fifty-eight women aged sixty-five and older joined the study. Twenty-five of them met criteria for sarcopenia. Software called TotalSegmentator measured lumbar muscle volumes in 3D. Volumes were normalized by height cubed for fair comparison. Paraspinal muscle volumes showed no real link to overall muscle mass. The iliopsoas muscle told a different story. Its volume index correlated positively with the standard measure. The correlation reached 0.424 with strong statistical support. Yet sarcopenic and healthy groups showed no volume differences overall. CT back-muscle measures cannot replace DXA, they conclude.
pmc-13548562:
Malik El-Boudali and colleagues check how often ambulance physicians' first diagnosis for breathlessness matches the hospital's, in a 2026 retrospective study from Orléans, France. Shortness of breath is common, dangerous, and hard to pin down outside hospital. The team reviewed adults treated by a physician-staffed mobile intensive care unit during 2023 and 2024, comparing working diagnoses with the first coded hospital diagnosis.

Of 313 patients with paired diagnoses, the two agreed in about five cases out of six, a level the authors call substantial. Heart failure, flare-ups of chronic lung disease, pneumonia, and asthma led the list. Death within twenty-eight days was more frequent when diagnoses disagreed, though the link weakened after adjustment for other factors. Most mismatched cases still received care judged consistent with good practice, which softens concern that a wrong first label usually means wrong treatment.
pmc-13548662:
Katherine R. LeBlanc and colleagues review the case that tau, the protein tangled in Alzheimer's disease and related disorders, is also an RNA-handling protein, in a 2026 article. Tau is famous for steadying the cell's internal rails, yet it was spotted binding RNA early on and may grip some RNAs more tightly than its usual partners. The review gathers what is known about this second life, in health and disease.

When tau goes wrong, RNA processing stumbles: splicing of messages goes awry, protein production falters, normally silenced jumping genes wake up, and RNA export and breakdown shift. Tau clumps also trap RNAs and the proteins that manage them. Because tau's shape differs between health and each disease, untangling which effects matter will take work. The authors frame RNA regulation as a neglected half of tau biology.
pmc-13550462:
Tomoka Hasegawa and colleagues peer at artery walls under the electron microscope to catch vascular calcification at its birth, in a 2026 mouse study. Mice lacking the klotho gene harden their arteries early, modeling the vessel disease of kidney failure and aging. The team examined aortas for the first deposits and tested a calcium-sensing drug, upacicalcet, already used for parathyroid problems.

The earliest mineral sat on the shredded surfaces of elastic fibers as tiny nodules holding calcium phosphate, unlike the vesicles or bone nodules of later disease. Deeper in badly calcified zones sat true bone-like tissue with bone-forming and bone-eating cells. The drug preserved the elastic layers, cut calcification, and lowered blood calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone while quieting the genes that chew elastin and build bone. The authors describe a two-track disease: passive crusting plus active bone making.
pmc-13551762:
Taofik Oluwaseun Ogunkunle, leading nine colleagues, published a 2026 retrospective analysis of stillbirth at a Nigerian tertiary hospital. Stillbirth rates signal the quality of pregnancy care, yet local burden and drivers vary. The team extracted records for women who delivered at Dalhatu Araf Specialist Hospital in Lafia between 2016 and 2020, then modeled predictors by regression.

The overall stillbirth rate was high in the reported count, though yearly rates eased downward across the five years. Unbooked pregnancy, meaning no prior antenatal registration, and prematurity carried the largest raised odds, while first pregnancies and multiple gestations also raised risk in the authors' reading. Maternal age and employment showed no significant link, so the authors urge stronger antenatal care for the high-risk groups named.
pmc-13554062:
Xiaojun Li, Rui Sun, and Ning Wang test simpler ways to model earthquake loads on bridges that cross a fault in a 2026 study. A fault break shakes the ground and also shifts it for good, hitting both ends of such a bridge differently. True records of that mixed motion are scarce. The team split the load into shaking alone plus the lasting shift, added either slowly or as a moving signal.

A three-dimensional model of a simple bridge over a sideways-slipping fault tested each method. Feeding the same motion everywhere badly underplayed peak and lasting damage, above all near the fault. Both split methods matched the full uneven-motion answer within sound engineering limits. The authors offer the split approach for lab tests and design work alike.
pmc-13554162:
Giandomenico Roviello leads a large Italian team hunting signs that bladder cancer will return fast after chemotherapy and surgery in a 2026 study. Patients had cancer deep in the bladder wall, treated first with two chemo drugs, then bladder removal. Return within a year counted as early. The team weighed clinic, lab, and tissue features against that outcome.

Early return tracked with deeper tumour stage after chemo, spread to lymph nodes, and invasion into small vessels. Few such patients had seen their tumour vanish fully under chemo. Unusual tumour cell types and vessel invasion after treatment each raised risk on their own. Early return mostly meant body-wide spread and shorter survival. The authors urge sharper risk sorting after surgery.
pmc-13555862:
Liselore De Rop leads a fourteen-author team studying breakthrough COVID infections in Belgian nursing homes during 2021 and 2022 in a 2026 study. More than sixteen hundred residents and twelve hundred staff were followed after full vaccination. Infection rates, risk factors, and antibody levels before illness were all tracked. Cases were matched against peers who stayed well.

Staff faced higher breakthrough rates than residents in 2021, while resident rates climbed the next year. Past infection protected both groups strongly. New variant waves drove risk sharply upward, and younger staff faced slightly higher risk. Cases carried lower antibody levels before infection than controls. Protective thresholds differed by variant, and the authors back tailored vaccine timing for this vulnerable setting.
pmc-13556062:
Nath Adulkasem and three colleagues checked in 2026 what happens when a revised Asian definition of sarcopenia replaces the older one. Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of muscle and strength, gained updated criteria from the Asian Working Group in 2025. The team reanalysed a nationwide Thai study of 2,456 community-dwelling adults aged 60 and over, reclassifying everyone under both rule sets.

Prevalence rose from about eighteen percent under the old rules to about twenty-eight percent under the new ones. The wider net caught more people with higher body mass and more people under 65, while their measured function looked much like that of people caught by the old rules. Possible sarcopenia, by contrast, became far less common. Clinicians and researchers comparing studies across the changeover need to know that the yardstick itself moved.
pmc-13558562:
Xiaoyu Pan and four colleagues used a national Chinese ageing cohort in 2026 to relate a blood marker of insulin resistance to grip strength. The triglyceride-glucose index is a cheap stand-in for insulin resistance, and muscle strength forecasts disability in later life. Their longitudinal sample held 2,086 middle-aged and older adults who were free of chronic disease, an unusually clean group for isolating the link. Strength was measured both as raw grip and as grip adjusted for body size.

People with a high index showed weaker size-adjusted grip than people with a low index, while raw grip did not differ between the groups. Adjusted models confirmed the negative link for relative strength only, and curve analysis found no bend in the relationship. The authors suggest that metabolic health tracks muscle quality even before disease appears, once body size is accounted for.
pmc-13559562:
Jianlin Yue and four colleagues use the US SEER cancer registry to study distant lymph node metastasis in head and neck cancer. It is a rare pattern where cancer reaches nodes far from the original tumor. Their 2026 population-based cohort covers 42,908 patients diagnosed between 2016 and 2022. The team measured how often this spread appears, what predicts it, and how it shapes survival.

Only 325 patients, 0.76 percent of the cohort, had distant nodal spread at diagnosis. Older age, hypopharyngeal primary tumors, advanced stage, and certain rare cancer types raised the odds. Median survival for affected patients was eight months, against seventy-eight months without distant spread. Patients whose distant disease stayed within nodes lived longer than those with organ spread as well. Combined chemoradiotherapy beat no active treatment in a landmark analysis. The authors argue for splitting metastatic disease into subtypes when judging risk.
pmc-13560162:
Anouk Putker and four colleagues explore how advance care planning conversations land with Dutch patients who have an Islamic migration background and are receiving palliative cancer treatment. Their 2026 qualitative study pairs two focus groups of cultural experts and health professionals with interviews of six patients. Planning frameworks built on individual autonomy and blunt talk may clash with these patients' values.

Three themes emerged. Decisions are mostly family-driven, with patients exercising autonomy through their family network, though younger generations vary. Religious meanings of illness and suffering shape how the end of life is understood, and palliative care was sometimes mistaken for hastening death. Hope proved decisive: communication that stripped hope away distressed patients and damaged trust. The authors recommend exploring each patient's preferred family role, explaining symptom care clearly, and framing talks in language of meaning rather than quality of life.
pmc-13560362:
Veronika Rysinova and three colleagues rate the Eating Disorder Support App, a co-produced mobile resource from a Bristol health partnership. Their 2026 mixed-methods evaluation surveys sixteen users spanning people with lived experience, supporters, and health professionals, then interviews four of them in depth. The app aims to give trusted, easy-to-reach guidance that backs up care at clinics.

Satisfaction ran high: 93.8 percent of respondents rated overall quality good or excellent. Users praised how easy it was to use, its clarity, and its non-judging tone, and spoke of gains in knowledge, confidence, and a greater urge to seek or support help. Interviews cast the app as a calming add-on that supports insight and a sense of safety. Requests included more personalization, richer media, and clearer navigation through dense opening content. The authors recommend larger, more diverse samples with follow-up before impact claims harden.
pmc-13562662:
Zihan Fang and six colleagues follow belly fat over time to see how it pushes a heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome toward its advanced stages. Visceral fat, packed around the organs, is a driver, yet long-run data is thin. The 2026 analysis uses a national Chinese ageing cohort: 3,322 middle-aged and older adults measured in 2012 and again in 2015. A metabolic score stood in for visceral fat, counted at baseline and cumulated across the two waves. Roughly four years of follow-up tracked who reached stages 3 or 4 of the syndrome.

One participant in five progressed. Higher scores at baseline and higher cumulated scores each raised the risk, with odds ratios of 1.13 and 1.06 per unit after adjustment. Risk bent upward past score thresholds near 6.71 and 20.11, checks confirmed by repeated resampling. The score discriminated modestly, near 0.60, similar to older fat indices. Sustained visceral load, the authors argue, is what deserves attention.
pmc-13568762:
Alamgir and colleagues analyzed in 2026 nearly twenty thousand United States hospital cases of TIPS. The procedure threads a shunt through the liver to relieve pressure from liver disease. The team asked how muscle wasting changes the hospital course. Muscle loss, called sarcopenia, is common in chronic liver disease. Its effect on risks right after the procedure was unmeasured at national scale.

About eighteen in a hundred patients carried a sarcopenia diagnosis. Their death rate in hospital ran about twelve percent against about eight percent without the diagnosis, and their overall complication rate was far higher, roughly fifty-six versus thirty-nine in a hundred cases. Gut, heart, lung, and infection problems all rose, and stays stretched to about twice as long. The authors urge screening for muscle loss before the procedure.
pmc-13569062:
Chanwoo Kim and colleagues trace, in a 2026 study, how the conductive plastic PEDOT:PSS changes state under laser light and then relaxes when water touches it. A mechanically locked form of the material stayed stable through repeated laser and water cycles, letting the team map color, shape, molecular, and electrical changes step by step.

Laser exposure produced a distinct blue state that differed from burnt, carbonized damage. Water then shifted that state partly back, along paths set by how the laser had written it, rather than restoring the untouched material. Water acts as an active editor of the material's history, a finding useful for rewritable electronics and sensors that respond to moisture.
pmc-13569962:
Johanna S Sturm's team presents an ionic liquid that safely stores and delivers sulfur dioxide for synthesis, in a 2026 study. Sulfur dioxide is a valuable building block for medicines and materials, but as a toxic gas it is awkward and hazardous to handle. The team reports a triethylmethylammonium chloride-based liquid that reversibly holds up to 3.66 equivalents of the gas at room temperature.

The liquid released its cargo on heating or pressure release, stayed stable for over six months, and proved cheaper and more atom-efficient than common surrogates. Its synthetic value was shown by making sulfolenes and related sulfur products in good to excellent yields, with scale-up demonstrated. The reagent offers labs a safer, user-friendly route to sulfur-containing products.
pmc-13570762:
Man Teng Iong examines the ethical and legal puzzles of increasingly autonomous AI in health care, in a 2026 article. As systems move step by step from decision support toward fully self-run care, old ideas of medical duty and the doctor-patient bond strains. The author explores opacity and consent, bias, privacy, automation bias, deskilling, and a less discussed harm: the thinning of relational trust when machines mediate clinical judgement.

Legally, the article rejects making AI itself liable and instead defends keeping humans in charge, pairing clinician duty for assistive tools with enterprise liability and post-market oversight as autonomy grows. Insurance and governance measures should back that split. The piece closes with regulatory and hospital recommendations for safe, fair, and trustworthy integration of medical AI.
pmc-13571062:
Rikki Mangrum and colleagues build, in a 2026 analysis for the Migraine Clinical Outcome Assessment System, a patient-centered model of what living with migraine involves. The model draws on two qualitative studies of seventy-one United States adults conducted in 2020 and 2021. Concepts patients raised were arranged into a diagram with definitions and links, then turned into a measurement framework for clinical trials.

The goal is a core set of outcomes that reflects what patients themselves say matters, for both attack treatments and prevention. Input also came from advocates, trial researchers, and subject experts. Drug developers get a patient-built map for choosing or designing outcome measures that regulators can accept.
pmc-13572462:
Yasin Khalili, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 model that forecasts failure and remaining life for electric pumps deep in oil wells. These pumps lift oil where natural pressure falls short, and they wear fast under heat, grit, and gas. A surprise failure means lost output and a costly repair trip down the well.

The model, HF-ESPNet, reads many data streams at once: electric signals, pressure, heat, vibration, well facts, and repair history. Physics rules on fluid flow, heat, and vibration wear are built into its training aim. It learned from a real data set of more than 58,000 time-series samples from working wells. The model beat standard machine learning and transformer rivals on both tasks. Tests that dropped parts showed vibration features and the physics rules mattered most.
pmc-13572562:
Ariel Cherro, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 account of a national campaign week against cancer pain in Argentina. Pain is the most feared symptom in cancer, yet in Latin America system gaps, thin training, and family myths delay good care. The week, first held in 2022, ran again in 2025 under the Argentine Society of Medicine.

The program joined online advocacy, local teaching events, and a volunteer network that gave free consultations through a web platform. Famous voices boosted the message on social media. The push reached near 50,000 direct digital views, with far more through shares. More than 100 free consultations took place across 13 provinces, in person and online. National and regional outlets covered the week over 50 times. The authors offer the model as one other middle-income countries can copy.
pmc-13574762:
Shan Jiang, with two colleagues, presents a 2026 lightweight network that cleans up underwater photos for robots and divers. Water warps colour, flattens contrast, and blurs detail, yet heavy models cannot run on small underwater gear. The network aims for sharp results at a cost low enough for live use.

The design joins two views of each image: its frequency pattern, which holds broad colour casts, and its spatial layout, which holds edges and detail. Attention blocks in both views, plus varied kernel shapes, balance quality against compute. On public test sets, the method beat mainstream rivals on two standard quality scores while using less compute. Code is posted in public for others to verify. The authors target marine exploration and robot vision on tight hardware.
pmc-13575162:
Wosen Gultie and Abyot Dibaba survey the plants of Mehal Wonz-Zego forest in northern Ethiopia in a 2026 study. The forest lies in the North Shewa Zone of the Amhara region. Knowing what grows there, and in which groupings, helps guide protection of the site.

The pair laid out 67 plots along five transects, recording plants and site conditions such as altitude, slope, grazing, and disturbance. They logged 106 species in 96 genera and 59 families, with herbs the most common growth form and the daisy family the richest. Grouping analysis found five plant communities. Altitude, grazing, and disturbance shaped the patterns most strongly. The authors urge local and regional bodies to draw up a conservation plan for the forest.
pmc-13576362:
Xinyu Tang and four colleagues report a 2026 case of sudden vision loss after neck spine surgery, treated late with oxygen therapy. Blockage of the central retinal artery is a rare but devastating complication of surgery done face down, where pressure on the eye can cut its blood supply. A 53-year-old man had upper spine fixation in that position.

After surgery he reported blurred sight in the right eye, with a pressure mark over the orbit. Eye checks showed hand-motion vision, a swollen retina, and the classic cherry-red spot of artery blockage. Clot-busting drugs were judged too risky so soon after surgery, and vessel intervention unlikely to help. Oxygen treatment in a pressure chamber began about 52 hours after the complaint, daily for 14 sessions. Vision later recovered to 20/25, though a severe field defect barely improved.
pmc-13578262:
Zhong Wu, Lili He, Juan Li, and Wenhuan Wu present a 2026 vision network for depth from paired cameras. Matching pixels between left and right views gives depth. The most exact methods lean on heavy math. Small devices cannot afford that cost, so light models often lose accuracy.

Their design swaps the heavy step for cheaper layered volumes. Flat filters process those volumes instead of bulky ones. A learned map then reweights the depth guesses by place in the scene. A fusion step borrows context from low detail views. That step makes up for the thin stack of layers. The authors report depth scores and speed that close much of the gap. Gains like these suit robots, cars, and medical scans.
pmc-13583562:
Adam I Kramer and a large Canadian team lay out the design of a national registry for lipoprotein(a) in this 2026 paper. Lipoprotein(a) is a fatty particle in the blood that is passed down in families and raises the risk of heart disease and stroke. Guidelines advise testing it once in a lifetime, yet doctors have little shared data on how high readings are handled in daily care.

The registry follows patients whose level sits at or above a set cutoff, recording risk factors, lab values, and outcomes each year. In its first year, from April 2024 to April 2025, it enrolled 127 patients with a middle age near 58 years. Most already took cholesterol-lowering drugs, though nearly one in five took none, a gap the registry aims to track and close.
pmc-13591662:
Kang and co-authors reported a 2026 materials study on organic photodetectors, which are light sensors made from carbon based films. One type boosts its signal by trapping electrons, yet that gain usually brings a surge in unwanted dark current when voltage rises. The group tested whether a very thin charged polymer layer could block electrons without killing the boost.

Kang built detectors with ionic conjugated layers that differ in their side chains and measured how charge moved through them. The layers stayed stable under reverse bias up to ten volts while efficiency stayed above two thousand percent of the incoming light. A layer only nanometres thick blocked electrons about as well as a much thicker aluminium oxide film. Charged side groups also shifted energy levels and changed how holes were selected.
pmc-13598562:
Xu and colleagues test a traditional Chinese herb on immune ageing in mice. Their 2026 paper asks whether Angelica sinensis, known as danggui, can help the thymus regrow after damage from rapamycin, a drug that shrinks this T-cell training organ. Seventy-eight female mice received rapamycin to trigger acute thymic decline, then varying doses of the herb during recovery.

Rapamycin shrank the thymus, weakened grip strength, and disrupted the cortex, the region where T cells mature. Medium and high herb doses enlarged the cortical area in a dose-dependent way and repaired the support-cell network inside it. Treated mice also matured their T cells more evenly and restored normal cell positioning. The herb raised activity in the Wnt signalling route and its downstream partner Foxn1, which the authors credit for the regrowth.
pmc-13599962:
Tuğba Erdem and four colleagues set out a protocol for tracking skin health in intensive care patients, to catch pressure injuries before they appear. Pressure injuries are wounds from sustained pressure, common and costly in critical care. Nurses now rely on visual checks and risk scores, which can miss early changes beneath the surface. The SKIN-BAR project will instead measure the skin barrier directly.

The plan recruits 165 critically ill adults at one intensive care unit in Turkey and follows them until discharge. Staff will use non-invasive devices to measure water loss through the skin, surface hydration, acidity, and temperature, starting within four hours of admission on a set schedule. Clinical and nursing details will be recorded alongside. Models will then trace how barrier readings change and which factors predict a new pressure injury. Ethics approval and consent procedures are in place.
pmc-13613162:
Murat Kılıç and colleagues report a study of enzyme proteins in lung tissue from 50 people with non-small cell lung cancer, the most common form of lung cancer. They measured six enzymes from two families, CYP and GST, which help the body process foreign chemicals and are often tied to how tumours behave. Tissue came in pairs: tumour samples and nearby normal lung from the same patient.

Staining scores ran from 0 to 3, and the team compared the two cancer subtypes, 27 gland-like tumours and 23 scale-like tumours. One enzyme, CYP2E1, showed clearly higher levels in tumour tissue than in normal tissue. Readers get a side-by-side map of these enzymes in sick and healthy lung, which may help explain why tumours differ in how they handle drugs and toxins.
pmc-13616862:
The RES-NOVA Collaboration reports a first test of a tiny cryogenic detector built to hunt for dark matter particles. Its target is a thirteen-gram crystal of lead tungstate grown from ancient lead, which carries very little natural radioactivity. The crystal was cooled underground and read out through a germanium thermistor, a sensor that registers minute heat pulses.

With this prototype the team set the first dark matter exclusion limits using lead tungstate as the target, for two kinds of interaction with atomic nuclei. The run also showed that mechanical vibration and low-energy noise can be controlled in such a cold system, a key need for rare-event searches. Though far smaller than the planned detector, the prototype validates the concept and lays groundwork for larger versions with better thermal sensors.
pmc-13617362:
Chuan-Yuan Lin and Jui-Yu Lin write a letter to the editor about how longevity should be judged for polycaprolactone-based collagen-stimulating fillers. These injectable treatments first fill tissue and later prompt the body to build its own collagen. They argue that longevity is not one outcome: early visible correction, lasting clinical improvement, measured volume change, and tissue remodeling are related but not interchangeable.

Their proposed framework splits assessment into three phases. In the early carrier-dominant phase, the gel carrier and swelling drive appearance, so safety matters more than durability. In the transitional phase, as the carrier fades, reassessment becomes reliable. In the late remodeling phase, claims should match the endpoint actually measured, whether rating scales, three-dimensional imaging, or tissue evidence such as ultrasound thickening and new collagen on biopsy. The authors stress the framework is a practical lens, not yet a validated instrument.
pmc-13617662:
Rebecca G. Simmons and six colleagues document how repeated federal rule changes battered Title X, the only United States program that directly funds family planning care. Rules swung back and forth between 2018 and 2024, forcing clinics in and out of the network. In 2024 the team interviewed twenty-five grantees and national partners and ran listening sessions with thirty-seven more grantees and subrecipients.

Five themes emerged. Grantees see the program as both administratively burdensome and essential to the reproductive health safety net. Responses to the 2019 rule change depended heavily on organizational and state context, and outside pressures added strain. Returning after the 2021 reversal was taxing, and pre-existing differences between grantees still shape who can keep participating. The authors warn policymakers that recovery from a policy disruption is slow and uneven, and even clinics that never left paid a price.
pmc-13618062:
Hua Xuan Dat and two colleagues develop theory for how size and shape change the thermodynamics of silver, aluminum, and copper nanostructures. Shrinking metal to the nanoscale swells the surface-to-volume ratio, shifting bonding and vibration behavior away from bulk metal. Their approach couples the statistical moment method with a bonding-energy model that counts how many atoms sit at the surface for a given size and shape.

They derive formulas for atomic vibration amplitude, thermal expansion, heat capacity, and Debye temperature. As particles shrink, the first three quantities rise while Debye temperature falls, and values glide back to bulk behavior as size grows. Below five nanometers, temperatures bring pronounced nonlinear effects from anharmonic, non-ideal vibrations. Shape matters strongly through the surface-atom fraction: regular tetrahedra vary most with size, thin films least. The authors offer the results as design guidance for catalysis, electronics, and biomedicine.
pmc-13618562:
Mohamed A. F. Ghoneim and five colleagues run a trial of two drugs that reverse muscle paralysis after gallbladder surgery, using ultrasound to watch breathing muscles recover. Sixty patients having laparoscopic gallbladder removal between August 2023 and September 2024 received either sugammadex or the older neostigmine. Ultrasound tracked the thickening of an abdominal expiratory muscle and the travel of the diaphragm, the main inspiratory muscle, at set recovery milestones.

The expiratory muscle's power dropped far less from baseline with sugammadex, a change of about nine points against about nineteen points with neostigmine, and the diaphragm held up better. Thirty minutes after arrival in recovery, sixty-seven percent of the sugammadex group had regained baseline expiratory strength, against forty-seven percent with neostigmine. The authors present ultrasound as a practical bedside way to verify that breathing muscles, not just a thumb twitch monitor, have truly recovered.
pmc-13618862:
Chul-Hyun Cho and three colleagues describe a technique for repairing large to massive rotator cuff tears, which often fail because the tendon quality is poor. Their technical note combines arthroscopic inspection and subacromial decompression with a small open incision on the front-side of the shoulder. Through it they perform a triple-row tendon repair reinforced by an onlay patch of acellular human dermal matrix, a processed donor skin scaffold.

Fully arthroscopic patch augmentation is technically demanding and slow, and the authors designed this hybrid to simplify patch handling while keeping fixation strong. The miniopen route gives visualization, reliable tendon mobilization, and suture management while limiting deltoid damage through the incision. A step-by-step description and accompanying video let surgeons reproduce the approach. The note presents the method as a practical alternative. The patch is meant to share load and scaffold healing during the vulnerable early months.
pmc-13618962:
Santosh Varughese and three colleagues ask how common disease-causing variants in the polycystic liver disease genes are. Seven genes are implicated in autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease. The same genes appear on kidney panels because their variants can produce kidney cysts. Pulling variants from gnomAD, they counted loss-of-function and rare damaging changes under two strategies: their own rules and existing clinical classifications.

The answer surprised: predicted pathogenic variants appeared in one in ninety-one people by their criteria, and one in one hundred thirty by clinical database calls. The mildest genes, LRP5 and ALG8, contributed most. Frequencies varied by ancestry, reaching one in forty-three among African and African American participants versus one in one hundred eighty-seven among Europeans. The authors caution that, with incomplete penetrance, many carriers never develop cysts. These counts describe potential, not disease burden, and will sharpen as more genes emerge.
pmc-13619062:
Ling Shan and five colleagues report brain findings after death from a woman whose narcolepsy never fit standard categories, in a 2026 case study. Sleepy since age fifteen without the sudden muscle weakness called cataplexy, she twice had sleep latency testing years apart. Her spinal fluid hypocretin, the wakefulness signal lost in classic narcolepsy, sat borderline low rather than absent. She later died by suicide after severe depression. Her hypothalamus became available for study.

Only the front of the hypothalamus survived for analysis, so hypocretin cells could not be counted, though staining confirmed the nucleus was fully present. There, neurons making corticotropin-releasing hormone were almost completely gone, matching the loss documented in classic narcolepsy with cataplexy. The authors argue this cell population can collapse even when hypocretin is borderline reduced, possibly driving the sleepiness while sparing the cataplexy trigger, and blurring the boundary between narcolepsy types.
pmc-13619762:
Takeshi Matsumura and colleagues compared two software tools that score bone spread in prostate cancer from bone scans. Bone scan index programs from Japan and from Europe and the US were built on different training data, and their compatibility was untested. Their look-back study processed 339 bone scans from 34 prostate-cancer patients through both aBSI and BONENAVI.

Scores tracked closely, with a correlation near 0.95, though aBSI ran slightly higher on average, by about a third of a percent, and by about 1.6 percent when disease burden topped 7 percent. Longitudinal change calls agreed substantially. Matsumura and colleagues warn clinicians to mind the gap when comparing scores across programs.
pmc-13623662:
Md Joynal Abedin leads a prospective study testing a bedside score for predicting failure of non-invasive ventilation in patients with severe flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The patients had acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, meaning carbon dioxide builds up in the blood. Spotting failure early matters because late switching to a ventilator tube worsens outcomes.

Ninety-two patients were treated at a chest hospital in Dhaka between May 2022 and September 2023 and scored before treatment and one hour in. The score, called HACOR, bundles heart rate, acidity, consciousness, oxygen, and breathing rate. About thirteen percent of patients failed the mask treatment. In those who succeeded, scores fell within the hour, while in failures they stayed high. A score of six or more at one hour caught most failures, and eight or more flagged early failure missing none. The authors call it simple and reliable, pending larger tests.
pmc-13625662:
Eduardo Tavares Gomes, Larissa Braga Celes, and Geovana Aparecida dos Reis Cirino review the final forty-eight hours of patients who died in a Brazilian cardiac intensive care unit. Good end-of-life care should be planned with patients and families and written down, yet intensive care often keeps fighting the disease to the end. The team read the records of eighty-three deaths from 2022 through 2024 at a large university hospital in the country's southeast.

Few charts recorded what patients or families wanted. Only twelve files held limits on life-sustaining treatment, and eleven held do-not-resuscitate orders for the team. Treatments meant to change the disease's course outweighed comfort-focused care in the last two days. The authors propose trigger-based palliative reviews and training in talking with families.
pmc-13626362:
Jingru Sun and colleagues build a desktop virtual reality game that teaches color composition to beginning design students. Headset systems are dear and scarce in classrooms. So the team made BD-VRG to run on ordinary computers. It follows a standard instructional design cycle and wraps practice in game play with instant feedback. Forty-two first-year art and design students then put the finished game through a full evaluation battery.

Test scores jumped clearly after play, a large short-term gain, and students rated every acceptance measure above neutral. A standard usability scale returned a good verdict, the software ran stably, and few students felt discomfort afterward. Players praised the live support and engaging drills, while asking for clearer first steps and navigation, which marks a workable path for cheap classroom VR.
pmc-13626862:
Kurtis H Dekker and Jennifer A Everaars automate one of radiation therapy's fiddliest planning jobs. Treating several brain tumors in one session from a single center point saves time and hardware, yet building those plans by hand means repeated rounds of structure drawing and objective tweaking. Their tool, written into the Varian Eclipse planning system through its scripting interface, generates target ring structures on its own and drives the optimization loop.

Twenty past cases were replanned automatically and matched against the plans patients actually received, using measures of how tightly dose hugged each target and how complex the delivery was. Portal checks confirmed the automatic plans could be delivered as designed. Comparable quality with far less planner effort is the promise such in-house automation holds for busy clinics.
pmc-13627462:
Elaine Gardiner and co-authors explore what happens to obstetric sonographers after a diagnostic error. The mothers and babies harmed are the first victims. Yet the scanner who missed a finding can suffer as a second victim. Obstetric work carries high stakes, with little study of that fallout. Eight sonographers with error experience answered a survey and sat for long remote interviews, analyzed for shared themes.

Five themes emerged, painting distress, shaken confidence, burnout, and trauma-like symptoms beside strong professional pride. Two burdens stood apart: errors often surface long after the scan, denying closure, and the sonographer grieves for mother and baby at once. Peer support helped most, while managers often felt procedural, and participants asked for learning cultures that treat error as a system lesson rather than a personal shame.
pmc-13627762:
Taeseok Choi, Sangbin Lee, Wansuk Choi, and Seoyoon Heo systematically review shoe orthotics for flexible flatfoot, and end up warning how thin the ice is. Searching three databases to October 2025, they kept eight controlled studies with 382 participants and recomputed every effect themselves. No outcome, pain, balance, or foot pressure, had two studies clean enough to pool, and one included paper was dropped as arithmetically impossible to reproduce.

Each verdict therefore rests on a single small study. The sturdiest finding is mechanical: arch supports shift load from heel and outer forefoot to the inner midfoot, as designed. The headline pain result flipped size with the questionnaire chosen inside its own trial. Certainty was graded very low across the board, a call for honest, bigger trials.
pmc-13629262:
Bethany Griffin and three colleagues interviewed twenty staff in English mental health wards. They asked what helps or hinders safe-feeling care when restrictive practices are in play. Their 2026 study used a behaviour framework to sort the forces staff described.

Staff valued safe settings and proper resources, for patients and for themselves. Yet clashing demands from above undercut both. Gaps in knowledge shaped what staff did. So did trust in judging risk, and teamwork. Those forces decided whether gentler, mind-aware options got used. Empathy and compassion pushed staff toward those options. Burnout pulled the other way. The authors say two supports matter most. Backing staff trust and ward safety together is the practical route. It leads to less restrictive care that feels safer.
pmc-13629562:
Teri Lee Turner and nine colleagues name a paradox in health professions training. They write with their global collaborative team. Competency-based education has reshaped how students learn. Yet the staff growth meant to prepare their teachers has barely changed. Teachers must coach, watch, and judge in new ways. They are rarely developed by those same principles.

The authors propose competency-based staff growth. It translates the model's five core parts into structures for teacher growth. Their scheme defines teacher skills and builds growth paths. It embeds coaching in the workplace. It models the teaching it preaches. It also tracks progress over time. A capstone ideal caps the scheme: the master adaptive teacher. That figure captures the reflective, flexible expertise they want programmes to grow.
pmc-13629762:
Xinning Wang and seventeen colleagues built machine learning models for kidney cancer care. The models predict which patients will lose kidney function after the tumour-bearing kidney is removed. Their study gathered 649 patients from eight hospitals. Five algorithms were trained at one centre. Results were tested at home and on patients from seven other centres.

About a third of patients advanced a chronic kidney disease stage within three years. A gradient boosting model performed best in both test sets. Ranking of the drivers put prior kidney function first. Tumour size came next. The creatinine change after surgery also ranked high, and age mattered too. The authors offer the model as a screening aid. High-risk patients can then get stricter preventive follow-up from the first treatment visit.
pmc-13631462:
Min Sung Seo and four colleagues report a brain imaging study on telling similar memories apart. Their work asks what happens when many other experiences come between two similar events. That gap, called temporal interference, should make the two memories harder to separate. The team used detailed brain scans while volunteers did a continuous recognition task.

Volunteers saw items again after ten, sixty, or one hundred forty other trials had passed. Longer gaps made both discrimination and plain recognition worse. The hippocampus itself showed no clear gap effect in its small subfields. Instead, nearby medial temporal areas and frontoparietal control regions changed their activity as the gap grew. The patterns also differed between telling lures apart and recognizing exact repeats. The results point to a wide brain network, not the hippocampus alone, handling this kind of memory confusion.
pmc-13634562:
Zhen Wang led a 2027 study building a gene signature for colorectal cancer from the adenoma-to-carcinoma pathway and a newly described form of cell death called disulfidptosis. As benign adenomas turn cancerous, cells rewire metabolism and remodel their internal skeleton, which may leave them vulnerable to death from disulfide buildup and skeletal collapse. The team combined single-cell and bulk gene data to find genes tied to both that pathway and disulfidptosis.

From thousands of candidates, thirty-six shared genes emerged, and statistical selection kept six with prognostic value: CXCL2, LGALS2, SELENOP, S100P, ETS2, and TIMP1. Patients scored as high risk fared significantly worse, and the model held up across the main dataset and three independent cohorts, beating four published models on discrimination. Oncologists get a candidate risk tool for tailored follow-up, with modest accuracy that still needs prospective testing before clinical use.
pmc-13634762:
Arvinder, Ravindran, and Gumathannavar present in 2026 a dataset pairing soil particle photographs with standard sieve measurements. It was built to train image-based methods that could one day size soil grains without sieving. Their material is black cotton soil, a clay-rich soil common in India.

A 1,500 gram sample from a university geotechnical laboratory stock was shaken through standard sieves from coarse to fine in three batches. From the separated fractions the team captured 1,350 smartphone photographs at three heights, disturbing the piles between shots for variety, and another 1,350 microscope images at three magnifications. Matching spreadsheets record the imaging settings for both sets. Because everything comes from one soil source, the authors present the collection as a benchmark for developing characterization methods, with other soils needing fresh validation.
pmc-13637362:
Elaheh Shoushtari-Moghaddam and four colleagues published this 2026 randomized trial of a health program for Iranian retirees. Retirement rearranges identity, routine, and social ties, and some land badly. The program was built on an ecological framework working at several levels at once: the person, the family, and the organization. One hundred seventy-eight retirees from education and oil industry centers in Fars province split into program and control groups.

The program blended face-to-face sessions with mobile lessons over a messaging app, plus family and workplace support. Scores for retirement adjustment, well-being, and coping were measured at baseline and at three and six months. The program group improved clearly on adjustment, well-being, and problem-focused coping, with strong group-by-time patterns. Emotion-focused coping did not budge. The authors conclude multi-level support helps retirees settle, and recommend the model for healthy aging programs.
pmc-13641962:
Nielsen S. Pereira and Luis G. F. Santos report a ten-year experience building a fully interoperable dental imaging network on open-source software alone, a 2026 letter from a private multi-site practice in Rio de Janeiro. Dental radiology often stays trapped in vendor systems and isolated workstations, even though medicine long ago standardized image exchange through DICOM. The practice built a central archive on DCM4CHEE over a standard Linux, Apache, MySQL, and PHP stack, with mini-archives at six branches sending images nightly and a VPN-secured setup for remote reading.

Over 2010 to 2020, the network served about 27,400 referring dentists and 190,356 patients, handling over 3.1 million image files totaling about 9.34 terabytes with no downtime or data loss. Avoiding proprietary licenses saved over two hundred thousand dollars, redirected to storage redundancy and backups. The one break in the chain was third-party cephalometric software that forced nearly 39,000 images into JPEG.
pmc-13642462:
Jessica L Ward led a 2026 behavioral study of how noise shape affects female mate choice in Cope's gray treefrogs, where choruses force females to pick attractive calls amid competing sound. Male calls are costly to produce, and females should prefer high-effort callers, yet noise can erode that preference. The team ran two-choice phonotaxis tests, varying whether noise sat with or apart from signals and whether its loudness pattern was flat, correlated across frequencies, or uncorrelated.

Females responded in nearly all trials but chose lower-effort males and took longer under noise. Performance was worst when steady noise sat alongside signals, while spatial separation improved every measure. Amplitude modulations generally raised response rates and cut delays, though their effect on which male was chosen varied, with limited support for a special benefit of correlated modulation.
pmc-13642862:
Pain that persists because spinal cord circuits stay overexcited is reviewed by Krotov and Kopach. Chronic pain counts today as a disease in its own right. It often resists drugs that merely dampen incoming pain signals from the periphery, since lasting changes in the spinal dorsal horn amplify signals on their way to the brain. The pair summarise how disrupted excitation and inhibition, strengthened synapses, and rewired networks in the dorsal horn sustain that hyperexcitability across diverse pain conditions.

Rather than globally suppressing nerve activity, the review highlights strategies that target specific cell types and maladaptive plasticity to restore circuit balance. Such precision approaches, the authors argue, could improve specificity, effectiveness, and safety over broad suppression, which helps only a minority of patients fully. Krotov and Kopach call for mechanism-based therapies that correct the dorsal horn's altered wiring instead of merely muting pain signals at their source.
pmc-13643662:
Daddis, Metzger, and Said published a 2026 study on how Muslim mothers learn what teens do. Parental knowledge guards teens, yet how mothers gain it varies by topic. The sample held 99 Muslim mothers of middle and high schoolers in America. Mothers rated six activity areas, from moral choices to religious practice.

Asking teens directly tracked with knowledge across most activity areas overall. For religious activities, knowledge rested solely on teens choosing to share. Moral topics drew on both asking and clear family rules. For sons, asking led on everyday topics; daughters shared more freely there. Strong religious belief also tracked with higher knowledge across the board. Domain and gender patterns held even after accounting for religiosity levels.
pmc-13643862:
Wenyan Ma and twelve colleagues present a 2026 study of how lifetime social mobility relates to difficulties in daily living among Hispanic and Latino adults in the United States. Data came from a large community health study with visits in 2014 to 2017 and again in 2020 to 2024.

Childhood and adult social position were combined into four paths, from lifelong adversity to lifelong advantage. People with lifelong adversity had notably higher odds of difficulties across senses, thinking, mobility, and independent living than the advantaged group. Downward mobility also raised odds and predicted new difficulties over six years. The authors tie daily function to whole-life social trajectories.
pmc-13645562:
Changlin Xie and four colleagues examine simple blood-based scores as markers of heart disease in adults who already have type 2 diabetes. Their cross-sectional study covers 3,964 adults treated in one cohort. The team compared six scores built from blood counts and three built from blood fats. They asked whether adding these scores improves on a standard clinical model.

Heart disease was present in about a third of the group, and several scores ran higher in those patients. One score, built from platelets, neutrophils, and lymphocytes, showed the clearest link in the main analysis. Adding it lifted the model's accuracy only slightly, and two rival scores performed about the same. The authors conclude that these cheap scores track with heart disease, though none stands out as clearly best for clinic use.
pmc-13646062:
Hana Taha and eight colleagues interview social workers in Amman, Jordan, about violence against women during the COVID-19 pandemic. Twenty social workers from family and juvenile protection centers spoke in depth between February and July 2022. Their accounts were sorted into themes about barriers to help and about stress. The study's title phrase, nowhere to go, captures the trap many victims described.

Lockdowns and fear of infection raised the barriers to reaching services, and cultural pressure to stay silent weighed heaviest on poorer women. Workers reported more abuse during the crisis, driven by hardship, crowding with abusers, and rising alcohol and drug use. Social workers themselves felt the strain and worried about how victims could even call for help during quarantine. The authors call for stronger support for victims and for prevention work that also reaches perpetrators.
pmc-13646862:
Chunghwan Ro and three colleagues compare heart event rates in psoriasis patients treated with biologic drugs against matched patients who never used them, in a 2026 study. Psoriasis raises the risk of major cardiovascular events, and calming body-wide inflammation might lower it. The matched comparison held more than thirty-six thousand patients per side, followed for ten years. Four biologic classes were also examined separately, and results were split by race.

Biologic-treated patients had a thirty-seven percent lower rate of major heart events over the decade. Every class showed a reduction, from older TNF blockers to the newest IL-23 drugs. Event risk looked broadly similar across racial groups, with one isolated subgroup finding the authors urge readers to treat cautiously. The study supports the idea that controlling psoriasis inflammation with biologics carries a heart benefit beyond the skin.
pmc-13647162:
Aarka Undar and seven colleagues review a signaling protein called GNA15 that is normally confined to blood cells yet turns up switched on in six unrelated cancers. High levels track with worse patient outcomes in each. The protein answers to more receptors than its close cousins, and its cancer effects converge on four programs covering growth signals, blood-cell signaling, energy reprogramming, and shape-shifting that helps tumors spread. Silencing the gene weakened malignant behavior in four tumor models.

High GNA15 also goes with tumors crowded by calming M2 macrophages and with gene patterns of immune suppression. The authors are careful here: that immune link is still only correlation, never yet proven in a living immune system. They weigh what the protein might mean for checkpoint drugs, engineered cell therapies, and antibody treatments. Their verdict is a plausible, druggable target whose immune role remains a hypothesis to test.
pmc-13647462:
Sadegh Ghaderi and five colleagues critically review brain imaging of the thalamus, the brain's relay hub, using a magnetic method that can hide as much as it reveals. The standard map measures only net magnetism, so iron-like and myelin-like contributions can cancel out. Newer separation methods split the signal into its two opposing parts. The review weighs human evidence in aging and disease, keeping animal and methods work in a separate ledger.

Reduced thalamic magnetism appears again and again in multiple sclerosis, while findings in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases stay inconsistent. Method differences explain some clashes, though not all. The separated components may expose biology the net map conceals, yet they rest on modeling assumptions and lack tissue proof. The authors conclude these measures remain research tools, awaiting standard methods, validation, and thresholds that would make them clinically useful.
pmc-13647962:
Alexander Muacevic and eleven colleagues describe a year spent building an immersive virtual reality program that trains dementia caregivers by letting them live care situations from the inside. Caregivers face hard communication and behavior moments with few chances to practice safely. The program, VR SIM Carers, delivers teaching through first-person scenarios set in realistic homes. Development ran in cycles with user feedback from several cohorts shaping each version.

The report details design and technical choices, from scenario structure to refinements driven by testers. Pilot testing with twenty-four caregivers then gauged whether the program was feasible, acceptable, usable, and tolerable to wear and watch. Early feedback is presented as preliminary, meant to guide deployment rather than prove learning gains. The authors frame the work as groundwork for scalable, skills-based caregiver training that clinics and community groups could actually run.
pmc-13648062:
Thaina Calaça Futamata and four colleagues found a one-step heat route that turns tube-shaped layered crystals into zinc oxide balls at the nano scale. The starting crystals act as a throwaway mould for the final shape. Heat breaks them down and the oxide takes their place.

Fine scans and X-ray checks showed pure, well-formed zinc oxide balls. The metal europium, added at the start, did not spread evenly. It clumped into rich zones next to the balls, and stayed in its plus-three state. The balls broke down about nine in ten parts of a test dye under ultraviolet light in five hours. The team credits the ball shape and the europium zones, which help split charges, and they pitch the stuff for clean-up of dirty water.
pmc-13649162:
Sarah E. Rashdan and three colleagues report a seven-year-old boy who developed an epidermal nevus, a benign wart-like skin growth, exactly within a healed burn scar on his trunk. The pattern fits Wolf's isotopic response, where a new and unrelated skin condition appears inside the borders of an earlier, fully healed injury.
